Please do not park boats in the windsurfing rigging area.

You know that elderly chap that potters around the river in
that odd little boat with the high coachroof, and the bloke
with the frizzy hair, bit unsteady when he gets in the
tender? And what about him who always wears bright
stripy jumpers over his rather large belly? Well, those guys,
and I bet most of us didn't know this because they're too
modest to tell, have been some of the most competitive
sailors on the East coast.

June 27
th
July 11th and 25
Aug 8th

Now, you can never lose that competitive nature, its just
that over time the physical effort required to stay out on the
race course, gets a bit much. The desire to compete still
remains however and it took a casual chat with one of
these chaps to remind me of the fact.

So if you fancy getting your old crew back together,
building a new team or badgering some of the younger
members into service, to do all the grinding for you while
you get that competitive buzz again, next season could be
the time.

So I asked around, took the opinions of others and at the
request of some, agreed to offer to organise a competitive
event that would be of interest to these past masters as
well as some of our younger, less experienced club
members.

There is one caveat however. We need a minimum of 6
boats to agree to sail the series.

The event will go something like this:

1. A series of 4 cruiser races, open only to Marconi boats.
2. Races will be no longer than 2 hours max.
3. Boats will race with a PY handicap number.
4. Start and finish will be Marconi line.
5. Races will be around HW off Marconi.
6. Courses will be set around local navigation and race
marks.
7. Results will be available in the bar, immediately after

CAMPING RULES – 2010
• No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday
• Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.
• Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.
• No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on
site at all times.
• The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS
ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.
• All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for
that guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present.
• Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.
• Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play
in the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also
ensure that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball
games etc.
• Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed
to roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.
• Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the
site. If you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from
other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require
access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers
etc.
• Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so
are probably not paying much attention to traffic.
• Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap.
DO NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.
• The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises
vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.
• All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This
is for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is
left unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access.
• All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.

Membership Renewal Guide 2011
1 Classes of Membership
A FULL MEMBER - Shall be a single person over the age of twenty-two. Shall have the full use of all the Club
facilities and shall have one vote

A FAMILY MEMBER - Shall include a married couple, or couple living together as a family, one of whom is
over the age of eighteen, one or two parents, one of whom is over the age of eighteen, and all children under
eighteen years of age. The family unit shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall have one vote
exercisable by one person over the age of eighteen.

A RETIRED MEMBER - Any member over the state retirement age shall pay one half of the full fees paid for
Full or Family Membership as appropriate

A YOUNG ADULT MEMBER - Shall be a single person who at the commencement of the subscription year is
aged eighteen and is under the age of twenty two. Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities and shall
have one vote

A JUNIOR MEMBER - Shall be a single person who at the date of election or at the commencement of the
subscription year is under the age of eighteen and joins the club other than as a Family member. They must be
supported by a sponsor who is a full or family member and who will be accountable for his or her conduct.
Shall have the full use of all the Club facilities but may not purchase alcoholic drink or cigarettes from the bar
and shall have no vote

A SENIOR LIFE MEMBER shall be a single person who is over the State Retirement age (currently 65 years),
has been a FULL or FAMILY member for the a minimum of the preceding fifteen years, has paid the senior life
member fee, does not keep a boat at the Club and shall have one vote.

2 Annual Boat Permit Fee
All craft incur a Boat Permit Fee. The first boat of a member is always deemed to be the craft incurring the highest fee.
Subsequent craft under 10ft used solely as tenders are free of charge.
3 Winter Storage
Storage Fees are payable in advance at these rates on boats, trailers and cradles to be kept at Stansgate during all or
part of the period 30th November to 1st March following the date of renewal.

6 Resignations

7 Late Renewal

The official date for the start of the Marconi Sailing Club's Summer Cruise to The Walton Backwaters & Beyond, was Saturday
the 24th of July. However, for Evenstar & her crew, it started the week before. We went down to her to take down some of the
stuff that we would need the following week.

This coincided with the departure of the single-handers, who were leaving that Sunday for their preliminary weeklong cruise to
the Rivers Alde & Ore. They would then join the MSC Summer Cruise at Titchmarsh Marina, on the Walton Backwaters the
following Saturday.

Sunday morning dawned & I eventually surfaced at 09:30, the allotted
departure time, to find that they had gone. Was this an omen for what was to
come? However they had gone, as far as Brightlingsea & we had a lazy day
before returning home after getting Evenstar ready for our return the following
week. Leaving work that Friday morning, I wasn't too sure if we would be
going, but thankfully Angela drove me down. For what was to follow, I am very
grateful.

the 'briefing', we retired to our respective vessels, with an agreement to slip at 11:30hrs.

off, time to sit down. All became clear as we approached

estimate their fleet to be over 100. Fortunately the wind was to

2010 COMMODORE'S REPORT
Marconi SC
Remarks to 2010 AGM (held 23rd Jan 2011 following a postponement due to bad weather)
Simon Elwell - Commodore

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN
As usual, I start my report by reminding you that our club is a company, limited by guarantee and that our principle activity
during the past year has been the provision of sailing facilities to our members.

Responsibility for the company and thus the club rests with the board -- elected here by you each year. The board during the
last financial year comprised six directors:

Myself (Simon Elwell) -- I acted as managing director and chair
Peter Clayton -- whose responsibilities cover moorings and equipment
Murray Bates -- Murray looks after premises and the site
Bryan Spencer, our rear commodore for sailing who has responsibility for sailing activities at the club and cadet training
Michaela Glynn, who as our second rear commodore is on point for the events programme
and Maurice Balfe-- our treasurer

Once again Ray Ball has acted as honorary secretary for the company and club and, as ever, shoulders a significant part of the
administration burden that the club generates. I'd like to offer a personal thank you to Ray for his support during my tenure as
Commodore. Without his unfailing eye for detail and tireless management of our administration, we would have achieved only a
fraction of what we have in recent years.

The board has met regularly throughout the year -- as has the management committee. Additionally a number of
sub-committees meet to manage and organise the day-to-day activities and events of the club. On your behalf I'd like to express
our thanks to all those whose service in this way makes the continued running of the club possible.

Following the postponement of the AGM, and to facilitate the smooth transition of the chairmanship of the board, I resigned as
Commodore so that the board could co-opt Neil - the only candidate for the role. I'm grateful to Neil for stepping in and picking
up the reins.

I'll return to the subject of the club generally in a minute or two. Before I do that, I wanted to explain why I stepped aside as
Commodore and to reflect for a moment on the last four years.

It's not about wanting to spend more time with the family or anything like that. I think that the club deserves an injection of fresh
ideas, new motivation and for someone to bring a new perspective to the board from time to time. That's the Commodore's job,
and whilst others may serve longer in other roles at the club, I think it's right that there's a different hand on the helm to stop us
becoming staid and unimaginative.

Some time before I took on the role of Commodore, we had witnessed the Marconi company facing financial difficulty, and we
had taken the bold step of buying the site and assuring the secure future of the club at Stansgate. Clive Shenton and Neil
Pembleton led us through those troubled waters superbly, followed by Chris Davies. Chris was the first managing director of
Marconi Sailing Club ltd - the limited company that sits behind our club. Suddenly we no longer had the support and resources
of either Marconi or MASC and we had to stand on our own two feet.

When I was elected Commodore, four years ago, Chris had already put wheels in motion by defining our strategy and setting
priorities. Stretching out in front of me, however, was the challenge of making it happen... of realising the ambition. Four years
later, I think I can say we've taken some important steps, but the journey is by no means over.

We've updated our clubhouse - or part of it. In so doing we've thrown the other parts of our clubhouse and site into sharp relief -
and there are already calls for further modernisation. We achieved this during a difficult financial climate and still maintained a

February 2011 Navigans 10

healthy financial position which must be a factor in any future plans. In addition, the club has updated, replaced and repaired
key pieces of equipment - tractors, winches, hoists as well as carrying out continuing maintenance on the jewel in our crown -
the hard.

Our web site, too, has proved an invaluable asset - many of our new members first find us on the internet, and email
communication has proved a useful and cost- effective alternative to post. As time goes on the work that Andy Dowley does to
improve and maintain the site will be crucial in keeping us up to date in more ways than one.

In recent years, we have expanded the training we provide for youngsters beyond cadet week itself, with the introduction of our
popular training days. Bryan Spencer has, as you know, driven this forward and needs your collective support to continue the
good work. Reflecting on some of the things I hear, I am sometimes dismayed by the way in which criticism ignores the laws of
physics and travels faster than others of support and help.

I am also pleased to see that a new generation of younger members is taking up its rightful place within the leadership of our
club. You know who you are; and you are the future of Marconi Sailing Club - I urge you to stay involved and to stay vocal.

Now, at this point I'd like to present a couple of awards; The Seamanship trophy is awarded to someone who shows outstanding
seamanship, sometimes in the face of adversity or in an emergency, but this year honouring a crew that has made a passage I
suspect many of us envy. Just to compound things, the skipper also wins the Mamgu trophy for the best log - for the #rst time
an online entry. So, this year's Seamanship trophy and Mamgu trophy goes to... Dave Onyons and the crew of Happy Morning
for their Atlantic crossing.

The other trophy I'd like to present is the Commodore's plate. I broke with tradition last year and awarded it to Murray Bates. I'd
like to revert this year to the practise of awarding it to a non-committee member who has made an outstanding contribution to
the club. This year's Commodore's plate, therefore, goes to the member who single-handedly designed, built and installed our
new card entry system: Andy Redman.

Going forward, it's no longer for me to set the agenda, but I know that there is much to do. A number of you are concerned that
support for racing at the club is not as strong as it once was - and a number of initiatives are already in train to address this.
Please support those who are sincerely trying to improve matters in this respect. We need even more participation from the
dinghy and cat fleets as all too often they are under-represented among the club's leadership. This will only be remedied,
however if people from the dinghy and catamaran fleets step up and get involved.

Whilst our clubhouse modernisation has been successful, there is still much work to do around the site. Our buildings and
infrastructure require constant maintenance and improvement and we'll need to prioritise investment carefully. Finally we will
need to continue our efforts to attract and retain members. We've been successful in this in recent years but a slight fall in
membership this year shows we mustn't be complacent.

I've enjoyed working on your behalf and working closely with many of you - it's been a pleasure and a privilege to have been

CAMPING RULES – 2011
THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES
ENDORSE AND ARE DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE
RULES.

• All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.
• No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday
• Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.

• Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.
• No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.
• No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.

• No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site
at all times.
• The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY.
No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.
• All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that
guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present.
• Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.

• Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in
the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure
that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc.

• Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to
roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.

• Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If
you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other
people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require access to the
site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc.
• Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are
probably not paying much attention to traffic.

• Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO
NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.

• The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises
vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.
• All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is
for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left
unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access.

On Another Tack
or “Such Larks”
Coming on over the last couple of years, like a growing itch was this feeling when sitting on the boat on the mooring,
considering the latest forecast for the upcoming weekend cruise there didn’t seem to be quite the same tingle of excitement that
I used to get.

Don’t get me wrong I love these “Muddy Waters” of ours. As an example - a glorious day sail then the experience to be had of
nosing into Pyefleet Creek on a mid summers late afternoon past all the other boats, dropping the hook and gaining the peace
and solitude that the top of the creek provides. Taking an evening meal in the cockpit washed down with a couple of glasses of
a good red whilst watching one of Pyefleet’s spectacular sunsets. All the while knowing you will get a good nights sleep because
your anchor is safe at the end of its chain nicely dug in to gloriously sticky Essex mud. Cruising experience hard to surpass!

But – and here’s the rub - for me in cruising the thing I get the biggest kick out of is planning a new passage, starting off, ticking
off the waypoints, watching the pierheads or entrance to some new destination appear over the horizon. The excitement of
entering a new harbour, tieing up then finding out what this new destination has to offer and shall we stay or go – it wasn’t there
anymore.

We’d become familiar with pretty much all of our cruising ground from North Foreland, the Thames to St Kat’s, Medway and all
the rivers to Wells Next the Sea. The itch persisted though and with work dominating life, a weekend or even our two weeks
annual leave meant we couldn’t get much further and the itch grew.

The remedy though was at hand – retirement in late 2009 meant the 2010 season could be planned to venture into sailing
pastures new.

The boat, a bilge keel Sadler 26 called “Edal” was pretty much already equipped to go further afield as I’d spent like an idiot in
previous years replacing pretty much everything that could be replaced. So that winter was spent just making sure she was
ready and a plan hatched or in corporate speak “an overall strategy developed” to sail round the UK. Now, back in the day we
reckoned if you get 80% of a strategic plan to work you’ve done pretty well – I though didn’t want to tie myself to anything
rigorous – it would be take it as it comes – no strict plan to be anywhere at any time, yes it would be going round – but if I liked
somewhere I’d stay, if not, I’d move on, if I wanted to spend some time at home I would - if it took two/three years then so be it.

So on the 19th May “Edal” and me left Titchmarsh marina on a singlehanded odyssey, to crawl up the East coast with an outline
plan to get to the West Coast of Scotland through the Caledonian canal to lift out for the winter somewhere by mid September.
The night before we left when I did that check of the forecast, this time the itch had gone and the tingle was very definitely back.
As we left Titchmarsh I remembered the thoughts I’d had when I left work for the last time – and now - as Joe said to Pip in
Great Expectations, “what larks we shall have, such larks !

The table below shows the sequence of destinations to Loch Creran just North of Oban where Edal is now ashore for the winter.
It clearly doesn’t tell the whole story we had a wonderful summer. Don’t believe what people say about the East coast of
England and Scotland being grey and uninteresting with long distances between harbours – not so.

A small capable boat particularly one that can take the ground or lean against a harbour wall can cover the distances with
relative ease in daylight and there’s lots of interesting places to see.

The two longest passages came at the beginning of the trip and were both achieved OK.

The 54nm Lowestoft to Wells passage can be shortened in quiet weather and with bilge keels/shallow draft by anchoring
overnight inside the breakwater at Sea Palling - something over four hours out of Lowestoft. We (me and Edal) did the passage
in one go by timing for a neap and punching the tide either end of the passage, this meant the middle part where the fair tide
was fastest as it sweeps round the corner of East Anglia gave us pace over the passage speed to reach Wells by HW.

The 52nm from Wells to Grimsby had almost no tide against as the tide on leaving Wells sweeps East out of the Wash and
along the East Anglia coast so was more or less on the beam for the first part of the passage. I followed the advice of Wells HM
Bob Smith to go due North out of Wells and at the East Docking Buoy turn Nth West catching the fair tide. Closer to the Humber
as the tide turns South again – if you are close enough to the mouth of the river it sweeps you into the Humber. Bob says this
route does make the passage a bit longer but as well as not facing the tide quite so much early on you also stay in deep water
which in rougher weather is more comfortable than the shallow water of the more direct route.

All the other passages were much shorter and they pretty much matched the planning. The only one that came out a bit different
was from Peterhead to Whitehills where the HM said “Reeds is wrong you need to set out two hours earlier” we did – and he
was right. So if you get to Peterhead and intend going round into the Moray Firth – go have a chat with him !

Guess the point about both of the above is – it’s always someone’s local waters and they will tend to know the local wrinkles.

Places I didn’t particularly like? Only a couple Whitby and Arbroath, strange because they’ve both a strong reputation for
seafaring.

Whitby is an attractive town to visit walk round and see the sights. But its harbour is controlled by the local council who seem to
have a take it or leave it attitude to anyone visiting the marina by boat. The charges for a day’s visit are not frantically high just
shy of £20 per day for Edal (high enough though) But I couldn’t avoid going home for a few days to get something done – and
Whitby’s policy is to charge the day rate on a continuous basis. So nine days in total – just shy of £20 per day for a restrictive
harbour that’s only +/- HW 2hrs. It cost me more to stay in Whitby for nine days than it did to stay in Anstruther for nearly a
month and most harbours along the whole East Coast have a weekly or longer stay rate – so much for being a seafaring town,
what if you were storm bound!

Arbroath is well placed as a stop over on the way up Scotland’s East Coast, its charges too were close to £20 per night and you
pay extra for showers, electricity and – water. The toilets and showers on the fish quay were filthy. I walked in the town and felt
it had a sort of threatening atmosphere. A chap on the pontoons took his wife to a local hostelry for dinner and in the end walked
out as they felt intimidated – maybe we picked the wrong time and places. Guess my opinion would be - both Whitby and
Arbroath are well placed to use as stopovers on the way North but personally I would only stay one night if I had to.

Places that are good passage ports? Grimsby, easy entrance behind dock gate and for a singlehander a huge outer dock in
quiet water to drop sails and rig fenders before entering the HCA marina. The HCA remind me of Marconi they are self help and
funding and have made a terrific job building their pontoons clubhouse yard and security fencing. They have oil and diesel
available in the yard plus water and electricity on the pontoons. The town itself feels a bit down at heel though and it’s a fair walk
from the dock.

Sunderland, wide and easy entrance with the marina just inside off to starboard. A real Geordie welcome, good modern
facilities. Water, electricity and diesel available. Good walks along the river to enjoy the industrial heritage.

Blyth, again an easy entrance with the RNYC pontoons in a large dock off to port where you have room to stow sails and rig
fenders etc. RNYC write the pilot book so advice on going North from these chaps is worth having. There is water and electricity
on the pontoons, a bar and food in their clubhouse, provisions and diesel in the rather dismal town couple of miles away –
terrific sandy beach for walks.

Peterhead, enormous harbour, wide easily gained entrance with a modern marina in Southern corner. Good facilities, water,
electricity and diesel available. Make sure you have chat with the HM about the timing of the tide !

Inverness, modern marina with an easy entrance to port after Kessock bridge. It’s in an industrial area a couple of miles out of
town. I’ve got a folding bike on the boat so could get into Inverness which is pretty much like a lot of other provincial large towns
having I think lost its identity to “retailisation”. There are still some good buildings though and along the banks of the Ness are
some fine villa’s and the footways along the Ness are very pretty.

Places most liked on the way North were, Wells Next the Sea, very friendly place, bustling quayside atmosphere, terrific walks
and countryside with places to go inland and along the coast. Good clean facilities and a laundry.

Bridlington, earthy kind of place with a busy fishing harbour, friendly, a fisherman even moved his boat so I could get a more
comfortable berth. Basic but clean facilities. You have to lie along the wall or raft and take the ground – but it was only £15 for
three days!

Holy Island, an absolutely magical place, where else can you sit on a mooring with two castles in sight Bamburgh and
Lindisfarne, golden beaches to one side Holy Island to the other and the sea and Farne islands in the distance – bliss!

Eyemouth, a serious fishing harbour, bustling activity, welcoming HM although he did say “ye’ll no forget the code fer the
shoooowers It’s 1320 The Declaration of Arbroath when Scotland declared it’s Independence ye ken”. Great walks along the
cliffs either side of the harbour with fantastic views of the gannets diving into clear waters for the fish. Good clean facilities.

Anstruther, a drying harbour on the North bank of the Firth of Forth, a pretty little place which has everything one could need.
The other fishing villages along this stretch of coast are just as well kept as Anstruther and walking between them kept me
occupied for days.

The ancient university town of St Andrews is a short bus journey away and well worth visiting. The berthing costs were one of
lowest I’d encountered so I left the boat there for four weeks and travelled home by train. Good clean facilities – tell the
attendant you are a visiting yachtie with a boat in the harbour or he will charge you – even for a wee pee!

Stonehaven, grey and uncompromising to look at - it really is a Stone Haven. A fantastic natural setting, with the long arm of the
outer wall of the harbour protecting the two inner drying harbours. The grey stone is replicated in the buildings of the town and
gives the place a wonderful air of solidity and permanency. The romantic ruins of Dunnottar Castle on its headland a few miles
South of the town is well worth a visit just to marvel at its position and also to wonder how it held out for eight months as
Cromwells army “knocked it abart a bit”.

To stay afloat you lie against the tall outer harbour wall, maybe even rafting up. The facilities are a bit basic, water, toilets,
showers but don’t let it put you off – it’s a charming evocative sort of place – even got a first rate fish restaurant just along the
quay.

Whitehills, first port of call in the Moray Firth – you call up Bertie the HM when a couple of miles off and he gives you best advice
about entry and when you get there he and another chap are on the pontoon to take your lines. He then gives you a welcoming
speech describing the harbour, its facilities and impresses on you don’t fail to call him on his mobile if there’s any help you need.
He then provides the free WIFI key and hands over what he describes as the welcome pack, security gate code, harbour bits
and pieces and all about the town and its history and facilities - - - WOW ! Can’t speak highly enough about Whitehills, although
it’s a small harbour – the welcome is fantastic, the people go out of their way to be helpful and I’ve never seen toilets, showers
and laundry so spotless. And - joy of joy’s, the longest softest loo paper you could wish to apply to your person – no nasty short
and shiny hard bog roll here! They’ve even got a reading room with books and armchairs so you can go ashore to a quiet area
to read if you need to.

Findochty, (pronounced Finechty) very pretty little ex fishing harbour now populated by local sailing boats on a set of drying
pontoons. Visitors lie along the inside of the outer harbour wall and take the ground. Finechty village is unusual in that the
houses are painted, giving the place a colourful appearance. Most of the cottages in the fishing villages along the coast are left
in natural stone. There is a shop, public loo and a tap but no other facilities. There’s also no HM based here. Finechty is worth
visiting just to soak up the atmosphere.

In truth along this Moray Firth coastline you could choose several other small harbours to visit Portsoy, Banff, Portnockie, truth is
once you turn the corner into the Moray Firth at Rattray Head they come thick and fast so guess you’ve got to draw the line
somewhere. It’s a great coastline for exploring though.

Findhorn, of all the places visited on the cruise North this is my favourite. It’s actually a large bay behind a series of sand dunes
fronting the Moray Firth with a narrow entrance channel to one side. The entrance is tortuous with a shifting bar which the pilot
book likens to the entrances to the Deben and Ore, so I felt quite at home. After the narrow entrance though the bay opens out
and is quite glorious with views on every hand. South and inland are gently rolling hills, to the West pine plantations, to the
North dunes, the Moray Firth and beyond the Firth the towering mountains of Northern Scotland in the far distance. The village
backs itself into the Eastern shore of the bay, old stone buildings fronting the water and a series of rows of small single storey
cottages arranged face to face down narrow grass or shingle tracks leaves an impression of what it must have been like as a
fishing village. There is water for fin keelers to stay afloat on a mooring or two piers to tie up to but on the piers you take the
ground. I chose the pier so I could walk ashore and I had only been there 20 minutes when a member of the RFYC came up,
welcomed me and pointing to a magnificent three storey stone edifice on the shoreside and said that’s the club house and you
can use facilities showers etc, there’s water on the pier and oh there’s no charge for visiting yachtsmen, here’s the code to get
in if the clubs locked up. Later when I visited the club they even gave me their internet key so I could sit in the sun lounge
fronting the bay, cup of coffee, answering my e-mails.

It’s an enchanting place, which has a gentle alternative air about it with a welcome that’s motivated out of the fellowship of
sailing rather than profit. I stayed several days and after speaking to a couple of RFYC committee members asked if I could
present a Marconi burgee to hang on one of the vacant flagstaffs which decorated their entrance hallway, they agreed and
presented one of theirs in return which I’ve passed to Murray with RFYC’s compliments.

Caledonian Canal, almost too much to say about the scenery from quiet and pastoral to the outright magnificent. Turning the
corner into Loch Ness for the first time and seeing this enormous body of water (and it’s not the sea) is breathtaking. Then
seeing the depth sounder register around 190 metres and go blank because it can’t find the bottom is eerie – maybe Nessie is
down there after all ! The peace and quiet of the wee Drumnadrochit harbour under the ruins of Urquhart Castle in Loch Ness
on our first night in the canal was sublime. It was here I got my best ever sighting of a Kingfisher, I was still and looking over the
Loch when this magnificent little bird perched within six feet of me and right in my eye line, I kept still and he stayed - it must
have been about a couple of minutes – wonderful experience.

If you’re worried about going through locks and lock gates on the Caledonian – don’t, because every bridge and lock is manned
– they know you are coming watch out for you and help you through. My only regret and I understand it’s quite common for this

April 2011 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

to happen is we had to motor virtually all the way through the canal. We did try to sail once as we found the wind for once
coming from astern – out came the genny – we zapped up to 6kts quite quickly for about five minutes, then over the next few
minutes the wind switched first from one side then the other, ahead, astern, port, starboard, we gave up and switched the
engine back on.

I’m told in mountainous lochs it’s something I’m going to have to get used to!

Final leg to the West coast, at the end of the Caledonian the descent down Neptune’s Staircase towards Corpach basin was a
real experience when you come out at the bottom and look back up the eight flights it’s remarkable to see how far down you’ve
come. One more flight just before Corpach and we were in the basin to overnight before leaving the sea lock in the morning for
the last leg of my summer’s lark.

One of the enduring memories of the summer is standing by the side of the sea lock that evening – it was a beautiful clear
sunlight early evening, looking round the bay that is formed by the head of Loch Linnhe, across to Fort William, then further
round seeing clear to the top of Ben Nevis and knowing that tomorrow we would be heading past the red of the channel marker
down the Loch and towards the West coast. The coast I’d explored with my Mother and Father when we lived in Scotland close
to 50 years ago – it was quite frankly an emotional moment.

The summer’s final destination was Barcaldine in Loch Creran roughly 28nm from the head of Loch Linnhe a passage which in
a small sailing boat is very definitely controlled by the tides. Part way down the loch at Corran Narrows the tide runs at 6kts and
when we got there our SOG peaked at just over 10kts. It was a spring and it was interesting to say the least to see as we went
through the Narrows small whirlpools in the surface of the water that appeared left and right then disappeared just to reappear
somewhere else!

The entrance to Loch Creran is made on the flood, it’s a fairly narrow entrance and there’s a lot of water behind it in the loch –
once inside things go a bit quieter and we soon made up to the moorings at Barcaldine Marine. A call ashore and the manager
Martin came out took me ashore and showed me round – the decision made this was where Edal would overwinter.

Four days later she was lifted ashore and I got the train home.

Early May 2011 she will be lifted back in and the “larks” continue North of Ardnamurchan.

There is more to this tale about preparation, musings on each leg of the trip, passage planning, people I met plus photo’s and a
few (badly made - I’m no Dylan Winter) video’s on a Blue which is accessed by invitation. If any member of the club wants to
access the Blue just send me your e-mail address to and I’ll issue an invite.

David Lakin

MSC Ambition – a reference document to guide development
The following paragraphs express the Board’s view of our key ambitions for
the status, style and operation of the Club for the foreseeable future. This
document will provide a reference point for the consideration of any plans
that affect the future structure and direction of the Club.

Status
• We will be member-owned and independent
• We will be recognised as the premier club in Essex for our style of
• mixed fleet family sailing.
• We will be recognised nationally (and in Europe) as a club that hosts well – run open events
(national and international) and sends competitors to open events across a wide area.
• As a consequence of all of the above and our own self-promotion we will be known as one of the
premier sailing clubs in the UK

Activity
• There should be good training provision for all ages
• The Club will promote a strong racing calendar for its major fleets, will encourage members to
compete nationally and internationally and will seek to attract Open event activity.
• The club will promote non-racing on–water activity for all members.
• The club will actively promote formal and informal social activity for the benefit of active members
and their non-sailing family members.
• The Club will actively and exclusively promote wind-powered sailing activity in all it forms but will
avoid the creation of harmful conflicts of interest (eg kite boarding). It will not provide a base for
powerboat activity or Personal Water Craft (eg Jet skis etc).

Presentation
• Comfortable and high quality facilities for non-sailing social activity to include a dry lounge with
capacity for 100+ and an adequate outside seating area.
• Sufficient space on site to meet all our needs in terms of movement, storage, social activity,
parking and camping commensurate with the size of the membership.
• Consistent high standards of presentation and décor across the site that match the best
commercial amenities
• Full accessibility.
• Sufficient undercover storage and maintenance space for club equipment in secure buildings that
blend with the rural setting. (Commenced in 2009 and ongoing)
• Good access to the water and easy access to the hard.
• A high standard of handling equipment and full H&S compliance.
• Changing facilities on a scale that matches the needs of the active sailing membership.
(Achieved in 2010)

Financial
• Income from membership fees will underpin all our spending activity.
• Additional income to aid and support development may come from the following:
1. Grant aid
2. Donations
3. Non-conflicting rent-producing commercial activity on
4. site (subject to planning and other considerations)
5. Members loans
6. Commercial Loans
• It should be noted again that the latter two are dependent on sustainable levels of membership
income.

Membership
• Membership should not fall below 400 members or rise above 550 members (as presently
defined).

• Membership increases must be sustainable if project funding is largely or wholly reliant on such
increases.
• Overall membership numbers must be managed within the constraints of available common
facilities (changing, toilet, parking, storage).
• Individual fleet membership may also need to be managed in line with available fleet-related
facilities.

Style
• Family-friendly. No restrictions to membership by boat class. Fee structure to encourage family
involvement. Strong training and development support. Support for both racing and non-racing
activity.
• Self-help to the extent that members will be involved in routine housekeeping and maintenance
(particularly in respect of their own storage areas, mooring facilities, boat recovery and
movement).
• Non-exclusive. Straightforward membership criteria, no fleet restrictions and a fee structure that
can be described as affordable.
• A management style that is positive, open and direct – built upon excellent communication with
members, utilising appropriate modern techniques.

Staff
• A level and style of staffing commensurate with our needs, within our means and allowing the
fundamental character of the club (as expressed here) to remain unchanged.

“Protecting the waters of Essex”

To All Members,

Thank you, for taking your time to read this article. Let me introduce ourselves to you. We are the General Aviation and
Maritime Unit for Essex Police force area. We are a small team of dedicated Counter Terrorism officers and cover all the
maritime sites apart from the port of Tilbury and Harwich.

We want to impress on you the importance of contacting us if there is something that you feel suspicious about whilst out on the
waters around our coastline. You, ‘The Public’ are our eyes and ears and no piece of information that is sent to us will be
overlooked or seen as trivial. We would rather have lots of information than none at all and will never be wasting our time.

Project KRAKEN is a national initiative which has been launched UK wide. So, whether you travel to Cornwall or Edinburgh and
wish to report something suspicious or that you are not happy with it is called Project KRAKEN. This is the neighbourhood
watch of the marine world and this system is here for the long term. There have been local initiatives in the past but this is the
first national project of this nature.

So if nothing else, please remember Project KRAKEN if you see anything of a suspicious nature. This could be counter
terrorism or criminal activity but if you don’t tell us we will never know!! Our leaflets have been left at your club; please take one
and all our contact details are on it.

We presently cover 78 general aviation sites and 66 maritime sites that we know of!! We would love to visit you more but there
are only two of us unfortunately. We do what we can and if you need any further information we would be more than happy to
pay you a visit.

Regards,

DC Jacque Howe
DC Sean Adams

Wayfarer Rally on the Orwell and Stour rivers, July 2011
THURSDAY 7TH JULY
Dawn on Friday in Brightlingsea at the end of the Blackwater River brought a dilemma; one faced by seafarers the world over.
Richard Higgs, Myrtle (my 40 year old Wayfarer) and I needed to be in Ipswich that evening for the UK Wayfarer Association
rally, the weather however had other ideas. The wind whilst not feeling too strong in the shelter of Brightlingsea harbour was
forecast to be a force 6 south westerly, 25 knots gusting 30 in the North Sea. We had two choices (if we were to make the
rally), the first was to turn back up the Blackwater for a 3 to 4 hour beat against tide (and tow Myrtle), the second being to
continue our journey, running downwind with tide. Neither prospect much appealed at 0700.

The previous evening Richard and I had met at Marconi sailing club around 1600, loaded up Myrtle with clothes and provisions
for at least the weekend and set off down the Blackwater for the short passage to Brightlingsea. We had planned for a full week
of sailing, visiting some of the East Coast Rivers as well as meeting up in the Orwell at the Royal Harwich Yacht Club for the
rally organised by Anne and Dennis Kell, and the lovely Emma. A force 4 on the starboard quarter and the last of the ebb
ensured a pleasant and uneventful late afternoon sail. The harbour master allowed us to moor up for the night on the inside of
his pontoon (negating the need to get a taxi to the shore from the mid-river visitor’s pontoon). Fish and chips from the not so
local shop and a pint at the ‘Famous Railway Tavern’ set us up for the night; Richard in a land tent at the local campsite, me on
Mrytle under the boom tent. The forecast was not looking too good for tomorrow but eh that would be another day.

* Warning for those attempting to use the inside of the pontoon at Brightlingsea. At low water springs the pontoon sits on the
mud whilst you continue to fall on the tide for another two feet. I awoke at midnight approaching low water to find Myrtle
hanging off the mooring warps, oops!

FRIDAY 8TH JULY
I awoke at 0600 to find Myrtle somewhat
embarrassingly floating 2m away from the pontoon, it
now being high water and having loosened her warps
somewhat excessively at low water the previous night,
oops again!

Neither Richard nor I fancied the beat back to Marconi
sailing club; we knew from experience that it would be
pretty horrible, cold, choppy and tiring. The wind did not
seem that bad (in harbour it never does) and running
down wind would reduce the apparent wind. Continuing
our passage to the Orwell some 20 miles down tide and
down wind seemed the best option, and so at 0730 we
pulled out of the shelter of Brightlingsea harbour; full dry
suits and sailing jackets, two reefs and the small jib
flying.

A short period of beating into wind got us out of the
harbour and around the point at Lee-over-sands
heading down wind on a near run. Past Clacton pier
and then Frinton sea front, the wind picking up as
forecast, waves 2m from trough to peak rolling along and over Myrtle’s starboard gunnels. By now travelling at some speed we
were being over powered by 30 knot gusts, Myrtle rounding up to wind alarmingly. ‘Time to take the main down I said’ as we
passed Walton pier, Richard nodded ‘just what I was thinking’. Turning to drop the main we felt the full force of the wind, a scary
time but once back on course things calmed down, on jib alone we reckoned we were still doing some 3 knots through the
water. Not fast enough unfortunately now to out run the waves and minutes later without warning a wave broke over the stern
leaving a cockpit half full of water. Easy this sailing lark isn’t it?

Rounding Walton Naze to port we headed across the Backwater entrance now with Harwich in sight. The wind and waves
persisted until we finally rounded the harbour breakwater and in calm conditions we made our way into the Orwell; Felixstowe
container terminal on our starboard and Harwich town to port. We moored up on the welcoming Halfpenny pier for a deserved
rest at 1200, some 4½ hours after leaving earlier that morning. Both were extremely cold and it would be some 2 hours before
we felt ready to continue our journey (most of it spent getting warm in the café on the pier).

The Royal Harwich Yacht Club occupies an enviable position overlooking the beautiful Orwell River just short of Ipswich and
some 8 miles up river from Harwich; Richard and I sat having a final beer on the grass outside the club house as darkness fell.
Earlier that afternoon we had left the comfort of the café on Halfpenny pier and sailed up the river on a force 4 beam reach,
passed the Yacht Club to port, under the bridge on the A14 and on towards Ipswich docks for a ‘look-see’. The return to the
yacht club entailed the use of the outboard as Myrtle struggled to cope with the short tacks needed to retrace our course into
both the wind tunnel effect caused by the bridge and a rising tide. The berthing master offered Richard the grass bank in front of
the club house as a pitch for his tent, very decent indeed, prime views. Throughout the evening friends both old and new
arrived, food and drink a plenty consumed, plans for the following day analysed in detail and salty tales swapped. A typical
Wayfarer rally was beginning and we were really chuffed to have arrived under sail.

SATURDAY 9TH JULY
The East Coast north of the Thames comprises a series of rivers each travelling considerable distances inland and all running
roughly parallel to the Thames itself; rivers such as the Crouch, Blackwater, Stour, Orwell, and Deben. Each is very tidal, varied
in nature but essentially muddy, ideal for Wayfaring about. The Stour made famous by Constable’s paintings of a working river
December 2011 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

whilst actually navigable for 40 miles in land, for all intents can be sailed only up to Manningtree some 10 miles from its mouth
at the North Sea, The Orwell likewise with its all be it more recent industrial heritage runs from its junction with the Stour and
North Sea to Ipswich. The weekend rally would see us sail both rivers; we were to sail down the Orwell on the ebb to Harwich,
cross into the Stour and up on the flood before camping overnight in a creek on the northern shore.

Leaving mid morning on ebb, 7 Wayfarers left the Royal Harwich Yacht Club, a brisk north westerly ensuring a fast passage
down-river. The hamlet of Pin Mill (featured in the children's novel by Arthur Ransome: We didn’t mean to go to sea) quickly
passed to our starboard and in the distance the looming cranes of Flexstowe’s container terminal soon announced our arrival at
Harwich. Turning to starboard past Harwich and up the River Stour we now headed upwind, the wind strength force 4, with
waves breaking over the top of the dinghies (in ‘The Green One’s’ case breaking into the forward bouyancy tank through a very
large crack in the deck seams). Crossing into Essex we pulled the boats up the beach for lunch and some collected oysters.

After lunch we sailed further up the Stour, beating energetically, eventually arriving at Mistley where a delicate bit of light wind
short tacking and the ocasional running aground was the order. Returning to the Suffolk side of the river we passed the Royal
Hospital School built by Greenwich Hospital to educate the children of Navy personnel. Our intention being to dry the boats out
overnight at Holbrook Creek, required that we arrive bang on high water which we duly did.

The evening meal was taken at the Baker’s Arms in Harkstead village following a nice half hour walk through the Suffolk
countryside. Most people slept in their Wayfarers with their boat tents that night with some pitching tents on land.

SUNDAY 10TH JULY
Sunday morning was a very early wake up as high water
was 0720 (remember we beached the boats at high water
the night before). Boats can only get in and more
importantly out of Holbrook Creek 30 minutes either side of
high water, otherwise it would be a 12-hour wait! A lack of
wind meant that the the boats paddled out into Holbrook
Bay, anchored as a group in lovely flat calm waters and
cooked breakfast.

Becalmed with no wind it was a slow drift downriver to
Harwich town. Myrtle got out her oars and showed the fleet
what a determined Wayfarer could do; about 2 knots.
Approaching Harwich the wind picked up nicely, just as well
as we needed to avoid the 1030 Harwich to Hook ferry. We
glided into the marina adjacent to to the Halfpenny pier and
moored for lunch (tea, scones and ice cream to be exact)
awaiting the turning tide. Some took the opportunity to walk
around the beach and the historic town in glorious sunshine.
Soon after lunch the tide turned and a sea breeze set in, the
wind obligingly turning 180 degrees ensured another quick
downwind sail on the flood this time up the Orwell. A north westerly on Saturday to a south easterly on Sunday helping us both
ways, not often you can say that happens?

Returning to Royal Harwich Yacht Club around mid afternoon, gave plenty of time to pack the boats away for the various road
journeys home, There were fond farewells from each to all and of course many a well deserved thank you to Dennis and Anne
for organising such a lovely weekend. Eventually though folk drifted away, ………. apart of course from one Wayfarer and her
intrepid crew who still had many adventures ahead.

MONDAY 11TH TO WEDNESDAY 13TH JULY
Over the next three days Richard, Myrtle and I would work our way up to Woodbridge at the end of the Deben and eventually
via a short stay in the Walton Backwaters sail back to Marconi sailing club. The south westerly wind that took us north turned
kindly into a north easterly force 5 taking us speeding back south (see it happens all the time). A wild run down wind and tide to
finish a journey which over 7 days and nights, covering some 135 miles would take in the full length of 4 rivers, a Backwater and
a rally. Just about perfect.

Many thanks to Richard for being my companion and for putting up with my rants and impatience, many thanks also to Anne
and Dennis Kell for the excellent hard work they put into organising such a terrific rally.

Retiring West
After 32 years of teaching, the end of April was my final month as a Primary school teacher, having been eventually persuaded
to retire by my Skipper…. the aim being to embark on some extended cruising. Time and length of day for such retirement
‘jollies’ weren’t the only things that were important; the weather was as well… but it wasn’t until later in June were we to realised
that ‘crucial’ would have been a better adjective!

Planning and research for a trip to the South and South West Coast of England was extensively worked upon. Christmas gifts
of The Solent Pilots and South-West Cruising Guides were welcomed and avidly read by the Skipper. Many friends gave us
the benefit of their local knowledge of the areas we hoped to travel. Naturally, E-bay was well used for purchasing Charts,
[certainly to be recommended].

21/5/11

Finally we are ready to leave, with house locked, cars sorted out and boat loaded…. a bit too much according to the Skipper!
Alas, the first problem to arise was that the weather was due to be pretty dire for 2/3 days! We adopted a strategy of “..must go
somewhere…”, so two intrepid sailors set forth for Brightlingsea to sit it out until we could cross the Thames estuary. After 4
days of winds force 5/8 we finally got away…. to the Orwell. This is, of course, the wrong direction for Dover/Ramsgate but the
weather was clearly not going to abate so a change of scene was decided upon ‘come what may’ in the short weather window
we were offered.

25 to 27/5/11

Wrabness, BBQ ashore with our ‘cruising in company’ companions Sue and Peter Arnold aboard ‘Last Dream’, relaxing and
enjoying a red sunset. This did not follow the correct pattern as a gale warning for later was given. The 26th proved wet, windy
and rough, we did get ashore briefly and discovered the new Community shop in the village – it’s great, well stocked with good
quality groceries. Also at the top of the path to the village is a farm stall selling delicious pasties, quiche, fruit, jam and eggs - all
in aid of charity. After a short walk curtailed by a thunderstorm we returned to the boat, gale warning immanent! So rough in the
evening that the dinghy threatened to capsize so we dragged it into the cockpit and got the engine safely stowed. Phew… I felt
seasick!

The rest of the week we spent in the Orwell…at Pinmilll Picturesque walk along to the Clamp House, returning via the House
Boats and The Butt and Oyster…lovely Aspall’s cider and Adnams! The new concrete walkway at Pinmill makes getting ashore
much easier and less muddy.

28/5/11

Sailed to Ipswich in 22kwind. Loads of washing to do and is one of the less enjoyable aspects of cruising. It can take ages and
needs some patience. You need to find an empty laundry room, have 2/3hrs. to spare and be ready for a fitness routine
[considering the number of times you have to keep returning to move laundry between washer and drier] and hope that no one
has done this for you by putting theirs in and jumping the queue. This is when ‘laundry rage’ can set in!

The MSC Bank Holiday cruise to Ipswich (that we’d not expected to do) was great fun! Joining in with everyone renewed our
spirits somewhat as did the promise of improving weather. The only disappointment was Manchester United losing to
Barcelona…. but it was fun watching it with fellow fans at Ipswich Yacht Club.

31/5/11

Left Orwell at 0300. Very dark but interesting in Felixstowe Harbour - lots of lights. Daylight by the time we reached Medusa.
Good sail across Thames Estuary making up 2hrs so pressed on for Dover 1300, wind 3/5 NW/W.

1/6/11

Dover to Eastbourne, set off 1200, pleasant 2/3 NW
calm but not so after Dungeness as the wind
increased to 5/6 SW, with wind over tide and really
lumpy - kept falling off waves. Locked in 2000 only
1/2hr later than planned but wet and weary - huge
marina…loos etc miles from berth!

2/6/11

Eastbourne to Brighton, sunny…Beachy Head
spectacular - light winds. Concrete surround at Marina
is rather ugly. Once in, can’t see the sea, which is
useful when the Skipper persuades you that even
though it sounds windy in the marina it’ll be fine when
you get outside!

3/6/11

Sailed rapidly to Cowes, one reef in, 26k at times -
great arriving in the Solent…marked by The Isle of

February 2012 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Wight, Spinnaker Tower, Napoleonic Forts, Cruise ships and hundreds of yachts. All sights I’ve seen each summer for eleven
years while taking 20/30 Primary school pupils on their school journey and now here was my chance to share my favourite
places with just companions!

Queen Mary 2 liner was immediately to starboard as we neared Cowes, getting abeam of her we double jibed! “Where are you
going?’’ the Skipper asked - but I hadn’t done anything! The wind shadow from such an enormous vessel had caused this.
Luckily he’d just re-entered the cockpit after taking photos. Immediately, the VHF sounded a ‘May Day’ – a very small gaffer in
Osborne Bay just behind us had capsized! Other closer boats went to her rescue and the RNLI attended. Once moored at
Shepherd’s Wharf, we chatted to the Lifeboat crew and they seemed to think an involuntary jibe had caused the capsize, so be
warned of Cruise ships.

4/6/11

Cowes the yachting Mecca of the UK! We’re here – and so is the sun at last! Had lovely day wandering around shops, museum,
yacht clubs and waterfront. Certainly to be recommended is to have lunch at the Island Sailing Club – most welcoming and a
great view from the terrace of the Medina River’s traffic. Our berth was rather choppy and noisy opposite the Red Funnel
terminal - amazing how many times 5 hoots had to used due to ignorant boat handling…not us!! We moved to an inner spot for
the second night but it wasn’t quiet as the wind increased during the night. We decided shelter was needed for the next night.

5 to 9/6/11

Travelled further up the Medina away from the main marinas, boat yards and ferries to a beautiful spot called The Folly. Mid-
river pontoons are close to shore and The Folly Inn! Also close by
are Osborne House and regular bus routes. Berthed here for the
next few days. We did a lot of walking and used the excellent bus
services [free for 3 members of our party!]

Ah! Osborne House. No matter how many times I visit it, Osborne
House is special – a full day is needed to do it justice. From The
Folly it’s a relatively short walk to the main entrance.

Buses took us to Newport, Alum Bay, the South side of the Island
and across the centre via Brighstone. The views from the top deck
were superb. We ventured forth in a 40k gale to the Needles
Battery, finding that keeping upright to be quite difficult! Never the
less, a very interesting place. Suffice as to say the weather was still
poor and quite wet at times. Thank goodness we’d invested in a
cockpit tent…this proved invaluable during the whole holiday even
though the Skipper thinks it makes C’est Moi look like a caravan!

9/6/11

Made a break for new surroundings, headed from The Folly to Newtown Creek. Pilot describes it as a pretty, quiet, anchorage.
The creek lived up to its description. The entrance was quite tricky needing a lot of care following the pilotage instructions.
Unfortunately we didn’t get ashore due to winds being force 5/6, picking up a mooring was difficult and anchoring out of the
question. Certainly, venturing ashore in a rubber dinghy would not have been a good idea.

Costs of marinas, moorings and anchorages on the South coast are higher than those on the East - we were ready for this but
didn’t expect to pay The National Trust £16 for a night’s stay on a mooring. However, it was with regret that we didn’t return to
go ashore as it was a very peaceful pretty spot.

10/6/11

Headed across to the Hamble for the weekend, as we were to provide our daughter Alice and her partner Damian with a base
while they competed in a Firefly dinghy event at The Hamble River Sailing Club. At last, light winds across the Solent and a
quiet drift…. but…looking across at Southampton, things were about to change. Black clouds like ‘ink’ loomed! An hour later
we had torrential hail and winds 5/6 as we navigated carefully up the busy ‘car park’, which is the Hamble River! A gale forecast
for the next 2 days somewhat spoiled the dinghy racing.

Saturday night we booked in at The Royal Southern Yacht Club, an imposing building with grey-suited permanent staff manning
reception. They made us feel most welcome, the only problem was that the pontoon berth we were given wasn’t normally used
for visitors and we created a certain amount of consternation by our presence. We think we were given it in error…. Still, we felt
quite special all weekend!

A jolly Saturday night was had with the Firefly sailors –sausage and mash+ice cream for supper - raising money for charity and
a big raffle in which we all won a prize. The Skipper won a 10yr old bottle of Malt….and it’s not finished yet (for those of you
who would like to take note)!!

12/6/11

February 2012 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Rain all day –the UK had this across the country – washing needed doing so went up to Swanwick Marina - I got as wet as the
two loads of washing I had to do with all the ’to-ing and fro-ing’ to the laundry – at least in a warm heated boat I dried out
quickly.

13/6/11

Left for Lymington – due to meet friends – quite lumpy wind over tide in a force 5/7 but we made it to the Town Quay – sheltered
here and near the old part of the town –a lot like being in the Netherlands.

Intended to meet up with friends during the next 2 days then go up the Beaulieu and meet family on the 15th but weather altered
that…. heavy rain and winds 5/7 kept us here ‘til 19th.

During our stay we made the most of the beautiful New Forest surroundings with bus trips to Beaulieu and Christchurch and
also walking along the coastline to Keyhaven. Nature reserves here are unique with a variety of birds. A fun diversion, part of
Lymington Arts and Music week, was a rock concert in the grounds of the Congregational church! We listened to an excellent
Police tribute band as well as a local Heavy Rock band! Never to young to rock…. even in retirement! Heavy rain brought our
enjoyment to an abrupt end.

However interesting the visits ashore may be, you can imagine that not continuing with our cruising was frustrating. Here in
Lymington both Skippers decided defeat at the hands of the weather had to be considered and may be we’d have to return to
home waters earlier than planned.

19 to 21/6/11

The plan to sail up Bucklers Hard and not just go on the bus was still on, so we left Lymington and moved in to the Beaulieu
River.

We split from our companions for a while, as they had to return home to attend to family business. They left their boat in
Lyminton for a few days [at a very reasonable weekly rate].

The Beaulieu river entrance is interesting – similar to that of the Deben - careful pilotage is essential – we rolled our way in but
once in the river it was idyllic – calm with wooded sides. Once berthed we enjoyed a lovely walk to Beaulieu…no rain for a
change.

I was hopeful we’d have a day at Buckler’s Hard Museum and a meal out at ‘The Master Builder’…also do the laundry…but
no…it was not to be! The Skipper checked the outlook…winds increasing again – so sadly we had to make an exit from the
Beaulieu – to Swanwick again

21to 23/6/11

Swanwick – enjoyed good value meal at the Spinnaker pub – relived Howard’s Way at The Jolly Sailor – got laundry done –
walked around the Hamble river path to Warsash. Squally conditions made us think the ‘Pink’ ferry wouldn’t be running but the
intrepid Ferryman came to fetch us, laughing at the thought that we’d gone out walking in such changeable weather! Back at
Bursledon we visited the ‘Chandlery Barge’, a real education. Especially if you are renovating any craft built around 1930’s!

23/6/11

Returning home – definite! Decided to complete our Solent cruising by going to Portsmouth. Pilotage entering the harbour is not
difficult but relies on lining up two high rise buildings – suffice as to say on our way we were caught in a squall that cut down
visibility and left us running out to the Forts to find deeper water in 35k of wind! More settled weather after an hour or so. The
rest of the weekend was fun visiting The Historic Dockyard – going across from the Gosport side on the Ferry.

Saturday was The Round Island Race – winds of 5/7 expected- we did this two years ago but as we listened to calls on the VHF
we were worried for the competitors. The coastguard had to stack up the ‘Pan Pan’s’ in preference to the ‘May Days’. Later
when reading the Internet reports, sailors had experienced waves of 20 feet and Ben Ainsley described the Race as ‘extreme’
sailing! We decided this year was a good year to have given the race a miss.

The Dockyard was fascinating. We split the visit into two days, ‘The Victory’ and a boat trip around the Naval Base followed by
a special inter-services day, allowing us to visit HMS Daring (brand new stealth- designed warship), HMS Warrior (Victorian
era), and the Mary Rose Museum - all thoroughly to be recommended.

26/6/11

Fog rolled in…. but hey… the sun came out and it was hot!!

27/6/11to2/7/11

Returned to the Orwell, via Brighton, Eastbourne and Dover. Taking a few days to explore surroundings. Ironically weather was
on many occasions lacking in wind and quite dry!

Eastbourne was a place I’d wanted to linger in on the outward journey but didn’t get a chance - now we had time and the
weather. Got out our bikes for gentle peddling and sightseeing. Skipper had other ideas - we cycled all the way up Beachy
Head! Completely …ackering! Worthwhile though - an amazing view from above the lighthouse. On arrival at the marina,
Gordon and Cynthia (from MSC) appeared along the pontoon…coincidence - we enjoyed their company on the evening of the
29th.

February 2012 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Dover was also somewhere I’d also missed visiting on route south. 1/7/11Climbed up to the Castle, it’s years since we’d been
here but many features have been revamped. D-Day Operation Dynamo exhibition in the tunnels used during World War 2 was
the highlight and inside the Medieval Keep locally made reproduction furnishings and artefacts now fill many rooms, giving an
amazing atmosphere to the building. A whole day is needed here to enjoy the surroundings. Sun and zero wind filled the day –
a treat…. may be summer is going to come!

2/7/11

Final day of Cruising West or now East …the best sail of the 7 week trip…. how ironic…left Dover 10:15 – Lavington 18:30 –
tide all the way – wind 3/4 – listened to Wimbledon Ladies final in peaceful sailing conditions!

Our Cruise has been an adventure – most enjoyable and opened up our travelling knowledge. Disappointing in many ways –
maybe we should have stuck it out and been more patient waiting for the weather to change, but sailing is all about doing what
you’re happy with and feel is within your capabilities. Returning South and West in future is something we’d like to do again.

By Hilary Gardner ‘C’est Moi’

Answer to the Cruiser Knowledge was:

False. Absolutely untrue, though it is a commonly held misconception. In fact, there are few cases when power must give way
to sail. Examples where the vessel proceeding under power has right of way are - vessel engaged in fishing, vessel towing,
vessel constrained by draught, i.e., it must stay in a narrow channel of deep water, vessel in a ship separation lane - such as the
English Channel, etc. Also, if the sailing vessel is the overtaking vessel it must keep clear of the motor vessel.

Cruiser Fleet News – Cruiser Knowledge Answer
Steer to port

You are seeing the port light of a vessel ahead, and is about to pass in front of you from your starboard side. She is the stand
on vessel and you must give way. Your best choice to avoid collision is to steer hard to port. In the same situation in a power
boat or a sailboat on a port tack you would steer hard to port so that the two vessels pass port to port, but on a starboard tack
you don't want to get caught in irons with another vessel head on.

On another Tack. An elongated odyssey around Britain.

TO HEAD SOUTH OR NOT TO HEAD SOUTH – THAT IS THE QUESTION.
I’m not usually this indecisive, maybe it’s post operative stress after being under the surgeon's knife. (we’ll examine that in a bit
more detail later) But give me a situation and usually I can weigh up the alternatives and come to a decision pretty quickly, this
decision though is giving me some difficulty and I need your help.

If you read my previous account of sailing up the east coast you’ll know end of summer 2010 we ended up (me and the boat)
being lifted out on Scotland’s West coast in Loch Creran, just north of Oban where “Edal” (the boat) would overwinter before we
turned south again in the spring 2011.

Thing is - I’m still there.

Sure, we got lifted back in but the siren call of Scotland’s West coast got to me and we spent the summer cruising in waters
which OK can sometimes be a bit boisterous – plus it don’t arf rain - but and here’s the big BUT – when the weather’s “clement”
it’s breathtakingly beautiful.

It’s not that we’ve done loads of sailing because “stuff” at home during the summer of 2011 got in the way. Retirement what
retirement – it just means for one’s children “one” is more accessible.

We did though cruise up to Skye (just missing Malcolm Robertson who’d gone to Stornoway for the Tall Ships) plus two other
short cruises and enjoyed them all enormously.

I’d also discovered two things about cruising Scotland. First is, the tides are in the main pretty benign – it’s just those places
where you get narrow gaps for all that water to squeeze through that it’s better to go with the flow, Kyle Rhea for example.
Second is you are never far away from another stunning anchorage and even if the wind’s in the wrong direction for the one
you’ve chosen there’s usually a sheltered one you can plan to get to. Oh - and a third – if it’s pontoons you prefer you can now
pretty much day sail between them from Oban all the way up to Kinlochbervie, they do get a bit busy in July though. Put those
“larnins” together and with all the places left to explore and you can start to see my dilemma - to stay another season or head
south ?

To stir the decision making pot for the jury and make the case for the defence (to stay in Scotland) here are a couple of cruising
experience’s cut out of the Blue from last summer.

AROUND ARDNAMURCHAN FROM TOBERMORY, WEDS 13TH JULY.
I'd heard tales from fellow sailors of passages attempted round the fearsome Point of Ardnamurchan and how they or fellow
rovers (they'd heard of) had battled for what (in the telling) seemed like days to get round the Point against the nastiest seas
imaginable. Some (the tales go) even tried several times - each time turning back to the safe arms of Tobermory harbour. The
tales said - what seemed like OK sailing conditions in the Sound became untenable when the Point itself was reached so it was
with some caution I anticipated the "Roundin o the Point". In the event it was a "pussy cat" nothin to it - why was I worried - big
brave sailor boy like me - easy peasy - nix - nuttin - doddle - why Well, best answer is the reason reputedly signalled by the

March 2012 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

heavy cruiser HMS Cumberland at the battle of the River Plate when she was asked how she managed to get there so quickly -
she signalled back - - - A N T I C I P A T I O N. Or to put it another way - planning.

The pilot says best is wind with tide and stay 2nm off if there's a strong onshore wind of even a short duration. With an opposing
tide very heavy seas build up 2mls offshore. There's also a strong inshore set on the ebb just south of the Point. For a first timer
then my planning said - do it in fair weather with wind
and tide in the same direction - so Wednesday the
13th it would be.

After a couple of nights in Tobermory I was glad to be
away - it was not that I didn't enjoy my stay, it was
great but "Tob" as I heard it called is very much on the
tourist trail and after a while the appeal palled
particularly when a giant cruise liner put in, disgorging
crowds of passengers along the front and pontoons. I
also (and with my history this is very strange) felt at
odds with the Scottish Piper who in dress jacket and
kilt was employed to play Scotland the Brave and
such tunes along the harbour for the entertainment of
visitors. Now I absolutely love the pipes and after a
couple of malts, Flowers of the Forest has been
known to move me to tears but this seemed contrived
and somehow unworthy - - but hey - what do I know, Edal on the Tobermory pontoon.
the tourists loved it - and am I not a tourist in my own
way ?

The weather for the 13th was to be good and the wind light and variable, predominately from the south and
west, HW Tobermory was approx 0526 and the tide off the Point was slack at roughly midday, turning north about an hour later.

The distance from Tobermory to the Point is approx 11nm so planning at the usual 5kts, if we left about 1000 we'd reach
Ardnamurchan at slack or with the tide just turning north. Our destination was to be Mallaig 36nm's away where despite its
reputation as strictly a fishing and ferry port they'd recently installed extra moorings and pontoons to become "yacht friendly"
and encourage rich yachties "tae spend in the toon “

Places to divert to were numerous, from Muck just 16nm from Tobermory, to the Isle of Eigg, Loch's Moidart and Ailort, Arisaig,
Armadale, Loch Nevis and further up the Sound of Sleat, Isle Ornsay all pretty tenable in the forecast settled weather for next
couple of days. So with plans laid and on a lovely summer morning we left Tobermory at 0940 bound for the north.

The morning was delightful with clear blue sky and few
white clouds, the wind was light and to maintain our
passage plan speed the engine stayed on with the main
up motorsailing to the Point.

As we reached the Point and gradually came round to a
more northerly course the wind increased slightly, moved
aft of the beam and then onto the port quarter. The log
entry for 1255 shows a course east of north having come
round Ardnamurchan in very quiet conditions, making for
the Sound of Sleat.With the direction and lightness of the
wind, relatively flat sea Edal sails best under cruising chute
- so up it went - engine off - the big red white and blue
chute pulling us up to Mallaig on a sparkling sea through
the most glorious scenery - bliss !
The lighthouse on the Mull shore just north of Tobermory, looking
towards Ardnamurchan,
By just after 1600 it was time to put Mallaig to the test to
see just how friendly they were - so called the harbour
by phone and a very nice lady answered but said "we're
full". She apologised and said their new pontoons were
now due to go in next week and all the moorings were
taken - I could though lie outside a fishing boat against
the wall if I liked. I pictured the scene of being wakened
by a burly fisherman at three in the morning wanting to
go to sea - me full of roast chicken, vegetables and red
wine from my evenings repast and thought plan B should
come into play. I thanked her for her time and looked at
the alternatives.

We had been making up the middle of the Sound
of Sleat and the next potential place to overnight was
either Loch Nevis or Armadale. I opted to
call Armadale on the shores of Skye as it was closest and for leaving the following morning was right in the Sound.
