Another nice lady said yes we've a mooring and as you're a "wee one" come close in and pick up one of our blue buoys closest
to the shore and you'll have a quieter night. She asked the name of the boat and when I said Edal she said "Och you're in good
waters here with a boat of that name, you're not far from Sandaig". I’d already plotted that Armadale was only
9nm from Sandaig where Gavin Maxwell wrote Ring of Bright Water and if the weather was fair I could land there and do a bit of
exploring.

By 1645 we'd arrived Armadale - sure enough a blue buoy close inshore was vacant we picked it up and it wasn't long before a
chap came out in a launch and welcomed us. We were told the moorings were laid in the bay by Skye Yachts a charter
business and they offered us diesel, water and advice about toilets, showers and the shops ashore. Water and diesel was not
something we needed but he showed how they carried diesel on their launch in a bulk tank which had a pump so they could
refill their yachts when they came back off charter without having to go ashore, The water was supplied by a long long floating
blue pipe which the launch towed out to the boats in the bay to fill their tanks - ingenious. The overnight mooring cost was
£12.50 which I guess for the west coast is pretty average.

The evening went by in glorious technicolour, watching the ferry to Mallaig come and go on the same route Carole and I took
when we were touring Scotland all those years ago in our old Rover 110. At least here I thought I'll have a quiet night and my
stomach will have the peace and time to digest my roast chicken dinner without that imagined fisherman banging on my hatch in
the early hours.

I didn't have to be up early as Sandaig and Kyle Rhea were not far away and the fair tide to take us through Kyle Rhea started
roughly 1320 - after a wonderful first day north of Ardnamurchan there was more to look forward too - - so to bed, and as Peter
Dawson the old time baritone used to sing - -

Rocked in the cradle of the deep,
I lay me down in peace to sleep,
Secure I rest upon the wave,
And calm and peaceful is my sleep,
Rocked in the cradle of the deep.

PART OF A CRUISE TO LOCH'S SUNART, DRUMBUIE, ALINE AND ON TO OBAN, 23RD AUGUST TO 3RD SEPTEMBER.
After a month at home -this time the outline plan was to go back to Tobermory and once there make a decision whether to go
round Ardnamurchan again or cross the Sound of Mull to explore Loch Sunart.

We left the mooring in Loch Creran at 0735 on Tuesday 23rd August roughly an hour after LW Oban it was a neap and there
would be enough water for us in the entrance of the loch and not too much tide against us till we could get into the fair tide up
the Sound of Mull.

The sail to Tobermory was now familiar and the day opened out as fine with a light breeze, so for the bit out of Loch Creran and
around the top of Lismore Island we motored, then as we shaped towards the entrance to the Sound of Mull we raised full sail.
The passage completed in an easy seven hours for the 32km.

When we first visited Tobermory the pontoons were packed and a call to the harbour master was necessary, this time there
would be no such problem. Later in talking to the HM he said as it was now getting late in the season there was always a fairly
dramatic fall off in the numbers of visiting boats after mid August - I thought "blimey" it would still be busy in popular harbours
"Dahn Sarf". Met a fellow yachtie in the showers - as you do and fell into conversation - told him I was just starting a cruise and
he said "oh it's a bit late in the season for that isn't it " Must say with the cautious nature of most sailors kicking in - I wondered if
he knew something I didn't.

I still hadn't finally decided where to go - so settling down in the cockpit after a good meal and with a glass of something I
opened the excellent book published by CCC called Cruising Scotland to see what Loch Sunart had to offer. The book said
most boats turn North round Ardnamurchan and miss the delights of Sunart - it described several lovely anchorages and the
delights of Salen and Strontian - all in the relative safety of a 17 mile long sea loch - so I decided - exploring Loch Sunart it
would be.

Was I influenced not to go round Ardnamurchan by the "Oh it's
late in the season” comments - well who's to say - all I know is
the thought of lying to my anchor in the anchorages described
in Cruising Scotland was very appealing and enjoying quiet
nights on mooring buoys in Salen and Strontian had a strong
attraction !
The distance between anchorages was also small making the
passages easy (although that's true of a lot of the west coast)
plus as I'd decided to stay in Scotland and overwinter, there
was always next year for beyond Ardnamurchan - - so
exploring Loch Sunart it would be.

For our first overnight I decided to make for Loch Drumbuie
which to describe to East Coast sailors is a bit like leaving
Brightlingsea and overnighting in Pyefleet Creek except it's
Into Loch Sunart with the entrance to Drumbuie about a mile about three times the distance at just over 5nm and a "tad"
away hidden in the mist. more dramatic ! An easy day was in prospect - this is the way
cruising should be - a good night's sleep, a decent breakfast at
a reasonable time in the morning - an easy walk along the harbour to the supermarket to get final stocks for the larder - then

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

another cup of coffee in the cockpit before eventually
setting off just after 1130.

There was a good breeze as we left the left harbour - as
soon as we had sea room the main went up and out came
the genoa and we were sailing across the sound of Mull
with a course to miss the rocks known as The Stirks just
off the mainland shore. Half way across the wind piped up
and it was obvious from the sudden drop in the light and
visibility that there was more wind on the way - I reefed the
genoa down to about a third and off Edal tramped for the
far shore. The conditions on this day were perfect for her
to fly, a stiff breeze, full main, third of the genoa and the
relatively flat water in the shelter of the Sound. We tacked
once in the Sound to come a bit further south to make
absolutely sure we could be far enough away from the
Stirks (and also because I was enjoying myself) then made
past Auliston Point and into Loch Sunart towards Loch Drumbuie before the wind died away.

Gradually the visibility improved as the sky lightened and the narrow entrance to Loch Drumbuie could be seen. The entrance at
its narrowest is only about 120yds across and with steep hillsides on each side as you approach - on a murky day it looks
forbidding. However it is deep and the sides fairly steep to with only one isolated rock on the starboard hand just inside the
entrance.

Once inside, Drumbuie is a delight almost completely surrounded apart from its narrow entrance it provides complete shelter.
You can tuck into the corners to get away from the prevailing wind and sink your hook into good holding. We made up to the
head of the loch and dropped the hook in about four
metres of water.

By the time we'd scouted the borders of the loch for
potential anchorage spots, picked one and anchored the
entry in the log says we were secured at 1320 only an
hour and fifty minutes out of Tobermory. Drumbuie though
is a world away from the hustle and bustle of busy
Tobermory, it’s remote, no roads and as the skies cleared
and the afternoon came on bright and sunny it showed
itself as very beautiful. After a coffee and making sure
Edal was secure - as soon as I could I took the dinghy
ashore and did some exploring.

Back onboard after a dinner of pork loins, steamed veg
and a good red – replete, watching the sun go down - it
was breathtaking - this picture gives an impression but
really doesn’t do the colours justice. The shallow head of the loch as the afternoon comes on
One of the great things about cruising Scotland is - on the
water (providing you are about 100yds offshore) the
midges don't get you. So with settled weather in a quiet
anchorage you can leave the hatches open, light a light
and read a good book till you feel sleepy enough to slip
into your pit and sleep the sleep of the just.

Plus, there are times and anchorages where, although you
wake every so often - you feel secure, feel the light breeze
on your face coming in through the open hatch above you,
move slightly to stretch and in the seconds you are awake
have checked out the sounds of the boat and know she's
fine, then soon you are back asleep once more - and wake
in the morning feeling good.. This anchorage is one of
those and it's a wrench to leave but I've promised myself
I'll come back sometime, for now though the rest of Loch
Sunart beckoned.

So there ladies and gentlemen of the jury you have the defence case for staying in Scotland one more year.

In summary, we’ve hardly scratched the surface, there’s lots more to see, get the planning right and the cruising is easy, the
scenery magnificent plus we’ve got a good yard to overwinter and for summer moorings and it’s not frantically expensive (as
long as you pay up front for a year)

The prosecution’s case for turning south is not so easily made and is made up of a few actual benefits and some emotional
reasons.
March 2012 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

OK the cruising is great in Scotland when it’s fair – but try sitting at home looking for a weather window to go sailing – there ain’t
many.

It’s a long way to go sailing (476 miles front door to boat)

Travel costs are getting more expensive.

The journey is tedious.

If something goes wrong with the boat over the winter it’s a long way to go.

I’m bustin to go South into the Firth of Clyde where I wus brung up !

I like the idea of progressing on my odyssey around the UK – do I want to leave that progress for another year?

I’m really looking forward to sailing into Cardigan Bay to see my elder brother (we ain’t getting any younger)

And believe it or not I’m starting to miss the muddy Blackwater and cruising home waters.

And finally, members of the jury - the last point for the prosecution comes in the form of a tale about a hernia – almost “a tale of
two hernia’s”.

There I was in an Addenbrookes Operating Theatre, lying on the operating table, the surgeon who had examined me and drawn
a large arrow on my skin with a marking pen down into my left groin (he said it was to make sure they opened me up on the
correct side) was looking down at me with what I thought was a slightly manic grin. By his side was a very attractive lady
anaesthetist who invited me to think glorious thoughts whilst she put me under - and at the foot of the table was a boy who
looked about sixteen - I wondered why he was there.

I remember looking up at the lights and thinking – “strewth in a minute or so these guys are goin to be cutting me open” and all I
could think of was not the delightful lady anaesthetist’s offer but “oi I’ve got a lot of sailin to do – get it right guy’s” - - - slight
panic, then oblivion.

The sixteen year old boy came round later with the surgeon to see me in the recovery ward and said when he’d opened me up
the repair he’d eventually had to make was almost the size of two regular hernia’s so I’d need to take it really easy over the next
month – seems like trainee surgeons are a bit like policemen getting younger every year.

Now, I’d not been in hospital since I was seven when I had my tonsils out and frankly I didn’t relish the experience and that
moment before I’d dipped into oblivion had concentrated the mind about completing my odyssey before my ageing frame
collapsed altogether. Bit of an emotional exaggeration for someone of 66 - but you know what I mean.

So you see dear fellow members of Marconi (the jury) why I need your help and wisdom in coming to a decision – should I stay
one more season in Scotland overwintering again then moving South in the Spring of 2013 or should I head South this coming
season ?

If you are able to come to a conclusion based on the above facts and emotional arguments and help resolve this thorny case
please send your decision to

I shall offer to Dave Ball to post the verdict of the jury (and their reasons, no names no pack drill) in a future Navigans but in the
meantime - please, nothing comical - - - - - It hurts when I laugh !

p.s. The above infers no criticism of Addenbrookes they were very professional and most caring

- particularly the lady anaesthetist.

David Lakin,
Sadler 26 “Edal”

Fleet Reports

Handicap Fleet
I have recently been appointed as Handicap Fleet Captain
and this is my first Fleet Captains report. Luckily there is a
lot to write about!

Prior to the start of the sailing season, there were two work
parties held at the club. Thank you to all fleet members
who attended one or both of these.

The sailing season started on the 25th March with the first
of the Spring Points Series races. For the first two
weekends we had light and variable winds then last
weekend (15th April) it really blew! Our fleet members have
also taken part in the first of the Bank Holiday Series races.
Results have been posted on the website.
Lark Tuning
On 15th April the Lark Class Association came to the club Dave Russell
to give a training session in Lark tuning. This was enjoyed
and appreciated by all our Lark sailors. We also took the opportunity to promote the club to the
Lark association with a view to maybe hosting a future
Coming soon... open event at the club.

This consists of two pursuit races, great fun and Dave and I
are Race Officers!

distance races:

Ed.

A SAIL WITH Mona
Newer members to Marconi Sailing Club may not know our club members, the Shaft family. They sailed several traditional boats
from the club and loved going off cruising for weeks on end during the school holidays with their children, Laura & Jenny.
Eventually they purchased Mona, an Alan Pape design 33ft Ebbtide, a traditional, steel, long keel boat. After another couple of
years more at Marconi they sailed off into the sunset. Their travels were extensive, traversing the Atlantic, then the Panama
Canal to the Galapagos Islands and across the Pacific to eventually end up in New Zealand, later sailing on to Vanuatu and
Australia, returning to New Zealand another two years later and eventually putting their anchor firmly down in Opua, a village in
the well-known beautiful Bay of Islands on the North East side of North Island. After living on the boat for ten years Mona
required a MAJOR extensive and expensive refit, so this was completed a couple of years ago and now she awaited our arrival!
The Bay of Islands is a New Zealand MUST DO activity. There are over 150 islands in the area and only one has habitation and
that is not with any permanent buildings or residents. We had the pleasure to see it at its best and over several days

23rd January 2012.

We met up with Malcolm and Helen at their lovely house perched on the top of a hill surrounded by a mangrove swamp a few
kilometres outside the small town of Opua. The weather forecast for the week ahead looked really good, so in the morning we
headed off to board Mona just a short journey into town.

24th January 2012.

Opua is a stunning small harbour with clear blue water and a view across to Russell on the other side of the estuary. No Essex
mud to be seen anywhere, just golden sand. Whilst Malcolm and Helen went out to their swinging mooring to get ready for us,
Hilary & I had a walk around the village, stopping to look round the local chandlers! I was quite surprised to see that two stroke
engines are still freely available there as the pollution concerns in Europe seem not to be of importance there, which seems
quite strange knowing how “green” the Kiwis are.

Malcolm duly arrived to pick us up from
the pontoon and off we went to Mona.
She looked wonderful gently swinging
to the warm breeze. It was difficult to
believe that they had sailed so many
miles from Marconi to all those distant
shores over ten years. There appeared
to be some external additions since we
had seen her last, but she still has the
grace and elegance of a long distance
cruiser. After stowing our gear in the
forepeak cabin, we fixed a passage
plan for the first day. The winds were
light as we sailed away from Opua
harbour swinging moorings. Out past
Pahia where all the larger sailing boats
are based we headed East towards
Russell point and on to Takepa Point.
Passing Waitangi on our port we could
clearly see the massive flagpole that
was erected to mark the famous
Waitangi Treaty between the Maori
and Kiwis. The buoyage is fairly
intermittent as the water is so deep in
the main channels. We had a lazy sail
with the main and yankee, as the wind
was light. Also remember that Mona is only 33 feet but weighs in at 11 tons so she is not a racing boat, but a safe, stable
comfortable world girdler), wonderful as it was just so good to catch up on the last 10 years of news with Helen and Malcolm.
Those of you that know Malcolm will know that he always has a number of hilarious and fascinating tales to tell about their
experiences during their world cruisings, so we had numerous tales of their experiences from Vanuatu to Panama and beyond

Our destination was Moturua Island that
meant a turn to starboard as we passed
Takepa Point and a pleasant reach along
the Rawhiti Inlet to find a beach for the
night. After perusing the weather forecast
we found the lovely Otupoho Bay to the
South of the Island where we anchored in
about 5 metres of water. It was an idyllic
situation where the crescent shaped yellow
beach was bounded by rocky outcrops on
the two sides. As this was the middle of the
sailing season we expected it to be busy,
but as Malcolm & Helen pointed out, there
are so many delightful anchorages they are
seldom busy. There was one other boat
anchored closer in to the beach! A pleasant
afternoon swim in the warm water gave us
all a thirst and appetite so Malcolm got
going with the barbeque that Mona now
sports on her stern rail. A couple of
Sundowners were enjoyed as Malcolm
continued to tell us more amusing tales
about their travels to all points of the globe.

25th January 2012.

After a quiet night some physical exercise was necessary so we hopped in the dinghy to go ashore. As mentioned previously
none of the islands are really inhabited and so there are no facilities except for the occasional log drop toilet! Malcolm took on
his official Role sporting his orange jacket, as he now spends time as a volunteer for DOC (Department of Conservation)
policing the Islands’ vermin traps and talking to other visitors about the importance of conservation and keeping the Islands
vermin and rubbish free.

May 2012 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

For interest, animals like stoats and rats introduced by man
only relatively recently, are a real threat to the native
wildlife. There are several species of birds that cannot fly
and thus are at the mercy of the vermin and pose a great
threat. One specie has already been wiped out completely.
The Kiwis are determined to keep New Zealand as natural
as possible not only with the wildlife, but with trees and
plants also. There are some controversial ways of
achieving this and we saw evidence in several places of
what is being undertaken by DOC to reach their goal.

We climbed up the hills and walked through the bush
looking at the most interesting plant and tree life. We could
not name any of the plants or trees as we don’t have any of
the species we saw in Europe at all. Need to buy a book of
plants, trees and birds on our next stop!

A few stops were necessary to cool down and admire the
fantastic view of the many islands stretching into the
distance. We could just make out Cape Brett where you
can go out into the open Pacific and away from the Islands, but our plan was just to enjoy the Bay area.

26th January 2012.

We weighed anchor in 32 degrees and full sunshine with a gentle SW force 3. Now we know why Mona was fitted with full
awnings, to protect us from the sun, high UV in New Zealand, and rain if we have any. We turned north through a very narrow
heart stopping passage between two rocky outcrops and out into the open sea for a good sail. Navigation is quite
straightforward once you get oriented and also helps to have the chart plotter just to be safe. There was the necessary job of the
holding tank that needed emptying and we had to be offshore in specially designated areas to do this, the sail was great. The
aroma from the emptying tank was not quite so good though! A sail back south after rounding Urupukapuka Island to hunt for
another bay was rewarded, but shock horror there were about seven boats already there! It was a huge bay so with plenty of
room we dropped the hook again in Otaio Bay, all of us desperate for a swim.

It also happened to be Pahia Race week – a bit like Burnham Week but with fewer boats- so there was plenty of activity with the
racing fleet dashing between the islands spinnakers flying and they all made quite a spectacle as we watched them rapidly
sailing by out in the main channel.

Hilary decided to try her hand at a bit of fishing off the boat
whilst the rest of us sampled a sundowner or two. Her
persistence paid off eventually after much mickey taking
and she landed a fish!! A Snapper by name and by nature,
as it did get its own back because it bit her with its needle
sharp teeth and even drew blood! Even more mickey
taking! It was just big enough, as measured on Malcolm’s
official fish measure, but the poor thing looked so sad we
thought it better to return it from whence it came and toast
to its recovery. Another bbq expertly cooked by Malcolm
was enjoyed by all, sadly no fish course!

Urupukapuka is one of the larger islands with several quite
high hills and was inhabited (as most islands were) by
Maoris many centuries ago. It is famous for its
Greenstone. On our morning constitutional we came
across a pair of archaeologists on a dig. They had
discovered an old Maori settlement (Pau) which was most
interesting, we climbed a hill to look at some old Maori
water storage tanks and food storage pits.

We also came across a number of American students doing some voluntary work, clearing undergrowth, maintaining pathways
etc. They were camping on the island not far from where we were anchored. The camping is very strictly controlled and only on
a temporary basis through the DOC

The forecast was for it to be windy that night and the following morning so we went for a sail around the island and out to sea
again to do our duty! Also as we were running short of drinking water and there is none available on any of the islands Malcolm
decided he needed to make some! He has a relatively new toy that purifies seawater by high pressure and reverse osmosis.
Unfortunately the engine needs to be run for this, so we motor sailed for a while. After tasting it to ensure the water had cleared
any salt taste we left the watermaker to it. After a couple of hours it appeared we had made 70 litres or so, sufficient to last us
during our stay. Anyhow it was very interesting to see the equipment and watch it all work as if by magic!

We noticed many of the boats heading for shelter due to the forecast of gusts of up to 35 knots with the promise of squally
showers. Malcolm found us a secure spot in Urupukapuka Bay for the night round the back of the island of Urupukapuka, where
we were sheltered from whichever direction the wind chose to come from and indeed true to form the forecast was about as

27th January 2012.

Our last day dawned a bit grey and blustery , so after a hearty breakfast we had a romping sail from Urupukapuka back to
Opua. This was the kind of weather that Mona takes in her stride. Whilst the racing fleet were broaching and tearing spinnakers,
we sailed on steadily without drama at a good speed. As
we rounded the Takepa Point we spotted a white block of
flats – a cruise ship at anchor- off Waitangi. It is a popular
spot for these monsters to ferry their fare paying
passengers ashore in small boats to the town of Pahia to
spend their money on souvenirs. They only spend a few
hours in this beautiful spot, but we were lucky to spend four
days around the islands and be able to soak in the
atmosphere and enjoy the magic of being on a small
sailing boat and choosing where we wanted to go!

A great sail back to Opua moorings and it was with
sadness we left Mona to go back to Helen and Malcolm’s
house where we were to spend another two days enjoying
their company and visiting several interesting places. As
we got in the car it started to rain!

What an amazing place to visit and definitely a MUST DO if
you plan to ever go to New Zealand.

Derek Gardner

On another Tack.
An elongated odyssey around Britain.

Putting up with “the persistence.”
You might remember my last missive when I made a plea to members of Marconi to sit on the jury considering my cruising dilemma of
whether to stay in Scotland cruising it’s delights for another season or head south down the west coast to Cardigan Bay, to continue an
odyssey around Britain.

The case both for and against was I admit littered with emotional debating points - particularly the bit with me whinging on about my
mortality after a hernia operation. How am I now ? – absolutely fine thank you – it’s amazing what they can achieve with modern surgery.
From a distinct bulge in the left groin to now perfectly flat to match the other side – just a sizeable scar and no discomfort whatsoever apart
from an occasional rather strange itch which my wife forbids me to scratch in public!

The other points in the case saw the Marconi jury generate a consensus which could best be summed up as “well dunno really” as the voting
was pretty much split – so as final arbiter I have had in the end to make up my own mind after of course consulting with higher authority.
She, as a final discussion point said “Oh make up your own mind” – I always feel better after a consultation!

Even as late as May when I launched the boat back into the waters of Loch Creran I still hadn’t made the final decision. It’s true to say my
inclination was to head south, but- but- but I’d say to myself, you love Scotland, it’s easy cruising and there’s still lot’s to see.

Before I launched I’d become even more hesitant about turning south when a rather upper crust elderly gent with a walking stick hobbled
across the yard accompanied by his good lady wife and plonked himself on the tree stump I’d been using to sit on to polish the prop and
engaged me in a cruising experience conversation.

He and his wife it turned out had cruised pretty much everywhere, buying their latest boat (a rather nice blue hulled Vancouver Pilot 38) in
the Med then cruising home before taking her to the Baltic for a couple of years then heading to Scotland.

Here was a couple of great experience and modest with it - although they clearly could have been opinionated about their experiences they
were just as interested in what I’d done and where I’d been and happy to share their knowledge to make another’s cruising easier. We talked
for what must have been over an hour, it rained on and off but we didn’t notice such was the quality of the conversation. He asked where my
home mooring was and when I said “the river Blackwater in Essex” he asked if I knew Mike Peyton who he said was a bit older than
himself. I said most people on the Blackwater knew of Mike Peyton and his succession of ferro boats - I knew though he’d now “swallowed
the anchor” as in his eighties his eyesight was failing. He said “oh no, I know Mike and he must be in his nineties because I’m 85!

The thing about our conversation that kept coming back to me though was how this couple with such great cruising experience loved
Scotland because of its scenery, easy distances between anchorages and despite the fact that the weather could sometimes be awful, often it
would change in a moment and become glorious, they described it as “the best cruising ground in the world.” We had also in enjoying our
conversation ignored the rain - something which perhaps in cruising Scotland you have to learn to do.

After launching I thought I’d have a short cruise north to try to get to Sandaig for the silly emotional filming of Edal the boat at anchor in
Sandaig bay where Edal the otter from the book Ring of Bright Water used to play – to be a remembrance for my dottage - - - but the rain,
despite me trying to ignore it persisted, persisted and persisted and looked like it would “persist down” for the next couple of weeks, I also
convinced myself there was important stuff to do at home - so home I went.

Early June came and went and I genuinely got caught up in home stuff till one day the sailing bug crept up on me and bit me hard enough for
me to make a decision. I’d phone the yard at Barcaldine and ask them what a year’s rate would be and if it wasn’t too expensive I’d stay.
I was kidding myself of course I already knew I wanted to stay. The wonderful soft lilt of the nice lady in the yard office came over the
phone “Och halloo David, I thocht you’d be phonin soon” - - am I that transparent I thought – well yes obviously. She worked out if I stayed
for another year, that is summer mooring, lift out, pressure wash, winter storage, lift back in, then a month’s mooring next spring to sort
things out it would cost (if I paid up front) the equivalent of £3 per day for the year - - so the deal was done.

Most of the reasons for turning south had diminished in my mind - I’d recovered completely from the hernia op, the manic surgeon and the
delightful lady anaesthetist were a distant memory, I’d bought an IPod on Ebay to download podcasts for easy listening whilst driving the
long distance to Scotland and I’d convinced myself that the persistent rain was my friend.

Maybe the first cruise of the season would prove if I was right or wrong to stay.

AROUND ARDNAMURCHAN TO MALLAIG AND SANDAIG.
Sunday 24th June the rough plan was to leave the mooring in Loch Creran and be at the entrance to the Sound of Mull roughly LW Oban at
1542 to take the tide up the Sound to Tobermory roughly 32nm. The following day get round Ardnamurchan to Mallaig 35nm, then onto
Sandaig just a short hop of 10nm. After that I’d make the decision on next destination. The wind for the 24th was forecast at N or NW 9 to
11kts with gusts somewhere above that, with some clouds and rain – but hey this is Scotland so who knows.

We left the mooring at 1228 motor sailing out of Creran and into Loch Linnhe. Once round the top of Lismore Island we switched the engine
off and set the main and genoa. Soon over pressed, put one reef in the main and two in the genoa as the wind gusted off the top of the
mountains on the Morven shore – it became quite a boisterous ride down Loch Linnhe.

July 2012 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

A quieter period close hauled down Loch Linnhe.

We turned the corner into Sound of Mull the wind came on the nose and bashing on another 12 miles to Tobermory didn’t seem like a good
way to spend an early evening so we turned into Loch Aline just inside the Sound on the starboard hand and tied up at 1702 in sheltered
water on their pontoons. £16.80 for an overnight stay including water and electricity seemed good value for a nice quiet secure berth for the
night.

Monday 25th we left Loch Aline at 0800 with a couple of hours of flood left to take us up the Sound. Motor sailed all the way and tied up in
Tobermory and making for the showers at 1045 – 2hrs 50 mins later.

Tuesday 26th – At Ardnamurchan the tide turned north about 0600 – it’s about 11nm to the Point depending on how much you cut the corner
in settled weather. Today was to be quiet with southerly winds of 8kts – poss gusts of 17kts – so wind with tide. We left Tobermory at 0600
and were round the point two and half hours later. We motor sailed past the point and once round had one of those no wind moments before
the wind set in again from the NE. We set the main and reefed genoa in 10 to 16kts of wind heading towards the Sound of Sleat and Mallaig.

Coming round Ardnamurchan –
Isle of Muck low in the middle of picture, the Mountains of Rhum behind and the long peak of Eigg to the right.

July 2012 Navigans 16

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Sails set towards Mallaig as the day brightens.

Last time we came round Ardnamurchan heading for Mallaig we called them up and they announced “we’re full” this time, earlier in the
season and with new pontoons in the harbour we expected a berth and sure enough there was loads of space – we arrived 1231 just 6hrs
26mins after a passage in which we’d seen a real mix of wind, rain and shine and some great sailing.
The next couple of days though were forecast to chuck it down with that wonderful “persistent” nature that Scottish rain has – it was also due
to be warm and humid so the midges would be out in force for my sojourn ashore at Sandaig and my new friend the rain was due to test me.

The new pontoons in Mallaig Harbour on the grey morning before we left for Sandaig.

Wednesday 27th - There was no hurry to leave - it was roughly 10nm to Sandaig and the tide would be with us most of the morning. Also I
would have time to make friends with my new chum (the rain) as overnight I’d bent my mind to making the next couple of days as easy as
possible so in looking at tonight’s destination I’d chosen Isle Ornsay as a perfect anchorage.

Ornsay is just one nm across the Sound of Sleat from Sandaig and gloriously the pilot book said you can anchor in 3mtrs into deep mud – oh
how my East Coast heart pounded at the word MUD – a friend indeed to help me defeat the “persistence.”

The trip up the Sound of Sleat to Sandaig was a motorsail – leaving Mallaig at roughly 1130 we headed out into – in local parlance a
“dreich” morning, grey, no real wind, rain slatting down. Despite the climate I felt rather elated and the closer we got to Sandaig a bit
emotional. It’s daft I know at my advancing years to feel like this – but this after all is one of the reasons I’d come to Scotland in the first
place to take my wee boat – the boat I’d lavished all that care and attention on (not to mention all the spondulicks) to the spiritual home of
the otter her first owner had named her after.

July 2012 Navigans 17

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Edal at anchor in Sandaig bay.

If you’ve read Ring of Bright Water you may agree it’s a rather idealised book of its time - one man living in almost isolation creating his
own environment and virtually taming a wild creature to live with all in the most romantic of settings. An idealised existence – yes – but
something I suspect many would like to try to for themselves. On this grey misty rainy day, I was glad the day was the way it was, because it
enhanced the romance of the place in a way that blazing sunshine couldn’t have – it made my visit with Edal more intimate and memorable. I
found everything I wanted to record – the waterfall whose sound Maxwell said was his constant companion, the stone where his ashes are
laid and the memorial to Edal the otter.

Edal’s memorial.

Romance though is one thing “Mudgies” as Para Handy would have it are entirely another – plus not having followed my own advice to
“grease up” with repellent meant the little blighters on this nice humid day were out in clouds and having a field day feasting on me. So
discretion being the better part – I departed on the dinghy back to my Edal gently bobbing to her anchor in the bay. Soon with the rain still
“persisting” we had upped anchor and motored away from romantic Sandaig and were heading the short distance across the Sound to Ornsay
to anchor again for the night.

As the distance was small, engine on little more than a tickover we crept out of Sandaig Bay and two Dolphins (Porpoise ? I can’t tell the
difference) surfaced several times near the boat – before we’d anchored they’d welcomed us in and were now seeing us out. I tried to
photograph them but by the time I’d aimed the camera they’d gone - their presence though added to the experience and memory of the visit.

The pilot book was right and the mud at Ornsay with four other boats at anchor, provided a safe and secure night. Although I’ve yet to
experience more than half a dozen Scottish anchorages this has to be one of the best, not exactly dramatic but pretty in its own way quite
large enough for several more boats and a good area of shallow water with good holding at its head. I ate on board, in the continuing mizzle,
I left the rain to its own devices and watched a DVD on the lap-top, slept late, bacon butties for breakfast.

As I de-rigged the riding light (it’s an all round LED plugged into a 12v socket) I mused on how in most of the anchorages I’d been into
when I’d been up in the night for my usual visit to the porcelain in checking out all was well with the boat – how, most other boats don’t use
riding lights – maybe I’m too much of a traditionalist but I don’t fancy sinking into sleeps oblivion without a nice bright light marking my
presence –
even if it’s just so I can say to the insurance company I’d rigged one.

After several cups of coffee and a discussion with myself the plan now became to return to Mallaig after exploring Loch Hourn then
following day a dog leg to the Isle of Eigg – then back south to Tobermory.

July 2012 Navigans 18

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

We left Ornsay at 1150 made across the Sound towards Loch Hourn which the pilot describes as a fjord like loch with high mountains on
every hand, best seen on a dark day with the clouds spilling off the peaks - - this was such a day and with a good stiff wind blowing directly
out of the loch we tacked in and ran back out again after penetrating about five miles.

Grey and forbidding Loch Hourn, photo doesn’t really do it justice – it was magnificent.

We made out of the loch and miraculously the wind disappeared, the surface of the Sound became glassy and the rain stopped although it
remained overcast as we gently motored the 10 or so nm back to Mallaig. The afternoon brightened as we approached and passed the
entrance to Loch Nevis the twin sister of Hourn. I am told these sisters are known as “Heaven and Hell” clearly with its dramatic peaks
Hourn is hell. Later in conversation with the harbour master at Mallaig he described how as a fisherman he’d worked “at the fishin” during
the night in Loch Hourn and in foul weather when the wind screamed off the mountains it really did sound as if the hounds of hell were after
you – having been there in dark weather I could believe it.
Friday 29th June the forecast was for mixed rain and showers with a mostly southerly wind blowing from 8 to 14kts. The tide in the morning
for going south would mostly be against us but if we were going to Eigg from Mallaig we would have some cross tide. We left Mallaig at
roughly 1100 and into what was then a bright sunny morning with the promised southerly blowing well.

The course to the anchorage on Eigg proved to be pretty close hauled and with some tide against us to the leeway meant we’d not make the
anchorage in one go so we made as best we could on a long port tack before tacking across onto starboard making back towards the
mainland. The little boat looks after herself well in these conditions and with one reef in the main half the genoa and the wind blowing
consistently at 12 to 14kts sometimes more she fairly bowled along under Albert the autopilot with me just enjoying the scene and letting
time slip by.

By 1400 we’d got half way down the last tack towards the Eigg anchorage - I was digesting lunch and the midday forecast on Navtex which
seemed to suggest a worsening of the weather overnight. Did I have a plan B if I didn’t fancy the Eigg anchorage – well not a planned one -
but in this neck of the woods there’s actually several of them depending on direction and strength of the wind. If the wind was going to
strengthen in the next couple of days though I’d prefer to be round Ardnamurchan and not in some anchorage waiting for quieter weather to
get round. The south going tide at the point would start roughly 1600 and it would take me at least two hours to get there so south round
Ardnamurchan it would be.

An hour later and the day had distinctly deteriorated the “heavenly persistence” came on again and the wind got up more - so the second reef
went in the main, she’s got cockpit reefing so fortunately it only took moments – then back on her feet and off we went charging for the point
in 20kts of wind.

It was at this “point” I started to think of all those nice pictures you see in “Cruising Scotland” all bright and sunny with light zephyr’s
swishing you along – this was becoming distinctly different and I muttered “well this wasn’t in the brochure” if I complained to the Scottish
Tourist Board maybe I could get some recompense – at this rate might amount to a pretty penny! I also thought of the tale of the seafarers of
yore who in heavy weather if they happened to be carrying a female aboard would get them up on deck to “bare all” to the foaming brine and
as if by magic the sea would die away. But dammit - I realised I’d left my female at home and even if I hadn’t I could just imagine the
response to my order “Oi get forard and get yer kit off.” If any Marconi member is braver than me I invite them to issue such an order in
heavy weather to their other half and let the rest of us know if it works!

By 1600 we were about three miles off the waypoint for making the first change of course to start coming round the point into the Sound of
Mull to pass about two miles off when the weather closed in and the mainland and its lighthouse disappeared as vis came down to what I
thought was about half a mile. Time to plot – time, position speed and course just in case the vis stayed low all the way round and the plotter
gave up. Cutting inshore blind in Scotland with all those hard rocks is not an option and with the weather the way it was it would be rougher
inshore on the point - so staying a couple of miles off was the best option. With a recent position established and the turn into the Sound of
Mull being deep and wide I’d got plenty of room for error if the vis stayed poor.

Gradually as we came round the sea became quieter the lighthouse reappeared - the wind a little more towards the beam still at 18/20kts as
we turned into the Sound - the rain still stair rodding - the little boat flew towards Tobermory the water fizzing away under her stern as she
went. I found myself on this grey rainy windswept early evening, in the cockpit helming the boat, rain streaming off me - singing my head
off and having a really great time - - strange this sailing lark.

July 2012 Navigans 19

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

We left Tobermory following afternoon with the wind still high from the south and being twisted by the hills to blow up the sound of Mull
we had a tacking passage in occasional rain for the 12nm back to Loch Aline where we again stayed overnight. The following afternoon saw
us back on the mooring at Barcaldine in Loch Creran by 1402.

Over these few days I’d had some terrific sailing and experienced some of the very different moods of Scotland. I’d come to terms with the
rain - in future it won't bother me and I won't bother it - and being Scotland where, as the old gent had said – “you can see all types of
weather in one day” - I'll just get used to treasuring the sunshine when it does occasionally appear.

Thank you to Marconi members for helping with my decision making I know some are considering a trip north, I hope you found this tale
encouraging if I can help with any info then its,

David Lakin,
Sadler 26 “Edal”

p.s. If you want to know what I was singing coming round Ardnamurchan in the murk it was this – not in
anyway Scottish but something you can belt out.

Minutes of the 2012 Fleet AGMs
Combined Cat Fleets Annual General Meeting 2012 – 04/11/2012
Those present; Fenella Miller, Peter Richardson, Rob Clay, Carolyn Warren, Dave Hewes, Kevin Dowley, David Ball, Peter
Tovey, James Tovey, Jenny Ball, Clive Shenton, Simon Plumb, Nick Pavitt, Sophie Hurrell-Smith, Tom Brooks, Neil Pembleton.

Apologies; Steve Glynn, Tom Duckmanton, Andrew and Michaela Glynn, Rebecca Tovey, Lee Harrison. Simon Hey, Kevin
Kirby, Liz Jackson, John and Caroline Nicholls, Steve Cleaver.

Agenda:

1 OVERVIEW/STATISTICS FROM 2012
Discussion took place about the racing at MSC in 2012. Statistics show that the overall numbers of catamaran entries were
down on last year. This was thought partly to be because the bad weather we have had throughout the season. The only
person to have consistently entered all the races needed to count for a series was Jenny Ball.

The question was asked “How do we encourage more to race?”. A lot of clubs having same problems. Dave Hewes asked for
a change in the sailing instructions to allow a boat to enter rather than a helm, but it was pointed out that this would probably
not be acceptable but consideration could be made to allow different configurations in the same boat(Dart 18 only ie. Uni rig-
one helm or 2 sails- 2 crew) This would be taken back to the Sailing Sub Committee for consideration. It was observed that
Wednesday evenings were consistently popular. This was thought to be because it was more family orientated and social,
more relaxed. Clive suggested a series of pursuit races. It was also thought that the Cadets should be encouraged to join in
with catamaran racing as part of their training programme, members of the fleets were keen to encourage the young people
and would help them with starting skills etc if they raced with them rather than separately.

Congratulations were also expressed to Jenny Ball for winning the helm of the year title, and for her constant turn out. It was
agreed that there should be a Cat fleet “come and try racing day” making a direct approach to individuals to invite them along.

It was observed that the Olympics has not made any effect on the numbers racing but the Open day most effective way for
recruitment. Neil told the meeting that they had not planned to have an Open day next year.

OPEN EVENTS AT CLUB
Fenella summarised that there had been a number of successfully run Open events at the club involving Cats. These included
the Sprint 15 TT, East Coast Piers Race, The Junior Cat Championship in association with UKCRA and the Dart18/Shear water
TT. The exception was the Steeple Chase in association with Stone Sailing Club. This will not be run next year as Stone
members were not keen to participate. The Sprint 15 association would like to come again next year and a date has been
booked for 6th /7th April.2 nights camping has been applied for. The Dart 18’s and Shearwaters also said they would like to
come back in the near future.

Piers race report by Clive. Poor weather was forecast but 10 more entries than last year. The Fast Dinghies joining in was
successful. There was a better on-the-day profit. £500 has been donated to the Essex Air Ambulance and £2,353.25. The
Cirdan Trust have raised a further £12,000 so far on the back of the race. Next year the ECPR will be on 30th June. Thanks
were expressed by Clive for the support of the cat fleet.

JUNIOR CAT TRAINING
Fenella told the meeting about the work that Lee Harrison was putting in to encouraging young people into cat racing. He has
become the UKCRA Junior co-ordinator (that is: arranging catamaran training around the UK for young people up to the age of
16). We have 3 Dart 16’s which are RYA/UKCRA owned which are available for the use of any young person to use at the Club
and which can be taken to other clubs for racing events. Peter Richardson is the bosun and responsible for their upkeep.

TRAVELLING ACHIEVEMENTS
Fenella pointed out that one of the reasons why there were not consistent entries in club racing was because a number of
people have travelled to other events.

These events include the Sprint 15 Nationals at which we had 8 boats. The Spitfire Nationals, The Tornado Nationals, Canvey
Cat Open, Grafham Invitation Cat Open, and the Tornado Europeans. It was pointed out that those travelling were good
ambassadors for the Club and the experience gained helps to improve the quality of sailing when back at the Club. Andrew
Dowley has produced club stickers to be stuck on the sails of travelling boats. It was raised that those doing winter series’ and
opens elsewhere including monohull dinghies should all have the opportunity to have these stickers on their sails. Contact
Andrew if a sticker is required.

2 RACING: CHANGES PROPOSED FOR NEXT YEAR.
Fen outlined plans for next year. It was suggested by the Sailing Sub Committee that because Bank Holiday Monday racing is
poorly attended that there should not be any scheduled series racing, but to put in the “one off” races instead like the Pilots Cup,
etc, depending on tides. It was suggested by this meeting that pursuit races could be put on at bank holiday Mondays. A vote of
thanks was made to Kate Williams for working on next year’s programme and for being an excellent results secretary. We all
wish Dave and Kate all the best in their new ventures in Cornwall.

Jenny Ball has agreed to be Trophy co-ordinator.

Peter Richardson will continue to obtain the club’s fuel.

3 CLUB MATTERS:
Neil explained why Terms of Reference for flag officers, fleet captains and sub committees have been defined in order to clarify
the expected duties of each club official. Neil highlighted the Board’s responsibility and liability, and explained that they need to
know what is going on at committees and so have requested that a copy of the minutes should be provided to the Club
Secretary. A new membership data base being designed which will be more interactive. He also told the meeting that money
would be tight next year amongst other things because of rising fuel costs. No major works to the club are planned for next year.

4 WORKING PARTIES
18th November- general tidying up prior to the Winter is planned. Activities will be dependent on the weather.

5 VOTING FOR 2013 FLEET CAPTAINS
Fenella has stood down as Sprint 15 and medium cat fleet captain and Bekki Tovey has stood down as fast cat fleet captain – in
order take over the running of Cadet Week. Fenella thanked Bekki for her help and support to the fast cat fleet. Fenella
proposed Kevin Dowley as joint catamaran fleets captain and he was unanimously voted in.

An assistant to help him is still being sought.

Clive asked that a vote of thanks was recorded to Fenella for her work over the years with the Cat fleets and on other
committees.

6 ANY OTHER BUSINESS
Fenella raised the issue of support boat cover. There is a shortage of support boat drivers. It was suggested that all dinghy
members should do support duties. It was also noted there is a shortage of race officers as well and more volunteers need to be
sought.

Kevin asked that the support boat co-ordinator needs to be made aware of what boats people sail so that clashes are not made
next year (e.g. a cat sailor scheduled for Jack B driver on ECPR weekend).

Clive: Explained why Top Cat was on the grasscrete next to the club - too wet on field.

Peter: stated that it is good that junior cat training is coming to the club. It is an ideal opportunity to encourage them to race with
cat fleets.

Simon Plumb raised cadet fleet starts, there is discussion at the cadet committee for integrated starts with other fleets rather
than their own start to give then better competition on the start line. Fenella added that there had also been some discussion
about moving the cadets to the front of the starting sequence so that the parents could get on the water to race after sorting
their children out.

Dave Hewes is standing down as race equipment bosun. A new bosun is being sought.

Neil summarised that he had heard a lot of positive talk today , especially in encouraging young sailors and in supporting other
cat owners into racing but it was now down to us to encourage individuals. He acknowledges the tremendous support from cat
fleet over this year and for the effort of everyone last weekend at the Dart 18/Shearwater Open. He expressed his thanks for
everything we’ve done as a fleet in contributing to the club as a whole.

Minutes of last meeting: Were approved.

Matters Arising: The Fleet Captain reported that the proposals for changes to sailing format that were objected to, had been
the subject of further discussion at Sailing Sub Committee and not implemented. The decision to recommend disposal of the
Fleet Solo had resulted in it being sold during the summer.

Fleet Captain: John pointed out that he had now completed two years of a one year commitment to fill this role, and
now wished to stand down. He called for a volunteer to take over the role, but none was forthcoming. He advised the Fleet that
whilst he was prepared to carry on for one further year he would definitely stand down thereafter. He will be working to identify
his replacement during the year. The fleet unanimously applauded John for an excellent job over the year and thanked him for
agreeing to carry on.

Review of 2012 Sailing Season: Number of boats competing in all 3 points series was an improvement on the previous
season primarily because of the two new members who joined us at the beginning of the year and were frequent competitors in
the series. This more than balanced the reduced amount of racing of some of the older members. Fleet members commented
that they thought the racing was good, and no particular issues were raised.

Child Protection Policy Statement & Code of Practice
MSCP16 - Issue 02 - 11/12/2012
Policy Statement

The MSC Policy Statement on Child Protection is as follows:

• The child’s welfare is paramount

• All children whatever their age, culture, disability, gender, language, racial origin, religious belief and/or sexual identity,
have the right to protection from abuse.

• All suspicions and allegations of inappropriate behaviour will be taken seriously and responded to swiftly and
appropriately.

• As defined in the Children Act 1989, anyone under the age of 18 years should be considered as a child for the
purposes of this document.

Code of Practice

The MSC Code of Practice on Child Protection is as follows:

• The Club does not at any time act in loco parentis. Whenever activities are organised for the involvement and benefit of
children it is on the clear understanding that their individual parents or guardians have responsibility for the care and safety of
those children.

All training and development activity for children carried out in the name of the Club will be carried out on the clear
understanding that their individual parents or guardians are on site at the time and for the duration of that activity and are
responsible for the care of their children at all times.

• All training and development activity for children carried out in the name of the Club will be carried out only by
individuals (‘Trainers’) who are known to and approved in advance by the Cadet Co-ordinator (supported by his or her
committee). The Cadet co-ordinator will advise to the Executive in advance the names of all trainers to be involved in any
training or development activity.

• Trainers will not take responsibility for activities other than those training and development activities specified by the
Cadet Co-ordinator and specifically will not have any responsibility for children at social events or non sailing related activity.

• Anyone with a complaint about or suspicion of inappropriate behaviour towards children must inform the Club Welfare
Officer immediately

• Club officers in particular and members in general are expected to promote behaviour that minimises the risks of and
opportunities for inappropriate behaviour towards or between children. The Licensing Laws will be properly and full respected in
all regards, including those prohibiting the serving of alcohol to children.

• Parents and guardians are reminded of their duty to care for children in their immediate control. It is desirable that
parents and guardians, when on the MSC site, should be as aware of where children are and what they are doing as they would
be in any other situation.

Note to Parents – for general use.

Marconi Sailing Club is a great place for children and their parents or guardians. The freedom, space, social ambience and
shared activities all give a great feeling of well-being and security. However, this does not mean that parents and guardians
should become inappropriately relaxed about their control of and awareness of the behaviour of their young charges. Parents
and guardians are responsible for the behaviour and safety of their children at all times and should take appropriate steps to
ensure that children are not exposed to inappropriate risk, either through their own behaviour or the behaviour of others.

Parents and guardians should also give thought to the availability and accessibility to private supplies of alcohol that might be
available on site during Camping Fortnight, for example. Experience shows that uncontrolled access to and consumption of
alcohol by children can expose them to unnecessary risk.

Chris Davies on behalf of MSC Board

ECPR REPORT C SHENTON
Clive Shenton ECPR Chairman
This year’s ECPR event was the Jubilee event marking 25 years. The whole club played their part in the event, culminating in it
becoming an excellent Piers Race.

Saturday weather was awful but 73 entries turned up – 10 more than previous year.

Fast dinghies took part this year in the Colne Race – it was very successful. With no problems identified.

ECPR is a charity event, with the charities being theCirdan Trust and Essex Air Ambulance.

Revenue Streams for the weekend where – Raffle/Adnams Beer supplied free/entries/Sale of shirts. Biggest contribution is
sponsorship organised by Cirdan Trust supported founded on ECPR - £15,000.

spaced up the course – providing support and acting as spotters. Thank you to the Cruiser Fleet who provided the mother
boats.

Camping Rules 2013
THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE
DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES.

• All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.
• No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday
• Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.

• Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.
• No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.
• No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.

• No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site at all times.
• The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY. No persons other than
official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.
• All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that guest. Guests may only be
on club property while the member host is present.
• Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.

• Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in the cruiser park area.
This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure that your children are considerate when riding
bikes around the site and playing ball games etc.

• Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to roam freely on
neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.

• Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If you have more cars than
can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-
camping members do require access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers
etc.
• Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are probably not paying
much attention to traffic.

• Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO NOT USE THE
DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.

• The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises vacated. The instructions
of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.
• All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is for the comfort of all
members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left unlocked all night. A clear changing room is
easier for the cleaner to access.

Northey Island Weekend
The big house was built by Sir Norman Angell in the 1930’s
On Friday 12th April the Ball family consisting of Maureen
and has four floors. The ground floor has ample living
and Ray, Jenny and Dave, Gill and David, Becky and Ruth

Dave, who kept us fed and watered for the weekend, were

of the night. A facility much appreciated by the older
members of the group!

There is plenty of time at low tide to visit Maldon and
surrounding areas. For example most of the party went to
Beeleigh Abbey Gardens on Saturday morning and were
back before the tide cut off the causeway. Similarly on
Sunday morning David and the girls had time to cycle to
Maldon swimming pool and Jenny and Dave walked to the
Queens Head at the Hythe for a quick pint and they were
all back in time. Had we wanted to go out for the day we
could have left the island in the morning and returned in the
early evening. What you can do on such a holiday is
obviously dependent on tides but low tide in the mornings
and evenings served us well.

Having suffered from noisy house parties when we stayed
on Osea Island last year we really appreciated the solitude
on Northey. There was something for all the generations;
be it climbing into the tree house or sitting on the seawall
watching the tide come and go. It was so near home and
yet seemed so far away; magic. Definitely a ‘must do
again’.

Ray Ball

Proposed New Fee Structure for 2014
Introduction – The Problems.
In Navigans last month I explained that a financial review undertaken earlier in the year has shown some adverse trends which
will need to be addressed to ensure the future viability of our Club. Our fee structure has evolved over many years, is
complicated and time consuming to administer and has too many loopholes which lead to loss of income due to fee avoidance.

The other problem we face is one of demography. The age profile of our members is increasing and too few of our keen cadet
members transfer into young adult membership.

Possible solutions
In a Club such as ours, where our only source of income is subscriptions & fees, there are only two possible solutions to the
problems; either increase the fees & subscriptions or reduce expenditure. In the opinion of the Board and the Management
Committee a reduction in expenditure would severely affect our ability to maintain and develop the Club and, crucially, would not
produce sufficient funds to safeguard the future. Hence an increase in fees & subscriptions is thought to be the way forward.

Objectives
Our prime objective in introducing the new fee structure is to increase income.

The new system will be simpler to administer and thereby close the loopholes in the present system. Another objective is to
create a fee structure that is fair and reasonable and that keeps our fees in line with our competitors thus promoting recruitment.
A fair fee structure will ensure that present members pay fees in proportion to the load their membership places on Club
resources.

Research
The Board have carried out a comprehensive survey of 12 sailing clubs in our area and compared and contrasted our present
fee system and the new system with that data.

Membership categories
Single full member – Our research shows us to be competitive at the present level and the 2014 fee will be marginally increased
to £175.

Family member (including couples). In all our research we are the only Club that sets family membership at the same rate as
single membership and, of course, two or more people make greater calls on Club resources than one. For these reasons it is
proposed to increase family membership to £210. This is still excellent value, especially for those families with children, and
places us in a good position against our competitors.

July 2013 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Retired single member and retired family member. To address the projected drop in income as more and more of our members
reach retirement age, the retirement discount will be phased out over the next four years. In 2014 it is proposed that single
retired members pay £110 and family retired members pay £120. Most of the Clubs surveyed do not give a discount to retired
members. Those that do place restrictions on that membership.

Young adult members – To address our demographic problem it is proposed to reduce the fee for this category to £40 to
encourage our cadet members to transfer into this category on reaching 18 and to stimulate new recruitment. The age limit of
this category will increase to 18 – 24. (To those that ask why we are reducing fees when the Club needs more income I say that
we only have 11 young adult members at present and that, if this initiative doubles this number, then it has more than paid for
itself).

Junior members will enjoy a reduction to £30 a year. We don’t have any such members at present.

Overseas and Honorary Life Membership levels remain unaltered.

Senior life membership for a one off fee will cease. Members who already enjoy this level of membership will be unaffected.

Boat Permit Fees
Dinghies & cats – Single Full and Family members.

The reduced fee for a second dinghy or cat will be discontinued. The fees of £120 for a dinghy and £140 for a cat will be
inclusive of hard fees, summer and winter storage, trailer storage and apply to each boat owned by that member. To many
members this will be a saving on 2013.

Dinghies & Cats – Young adult members, Junior members.

These members will enjoy reduced fees of £80 & £60 respectively for the same reasons given in the membership categories
above.

Sailboards make few demands on Club resources and a fee of £40 is proposed.

Cruisers
The reduced fee for a second cruiser will be discontinued. It is proposed that each cruiser will pay a fixed fee of £150 plus a fee
of £12 per foot of length. These fees will include hard fees, mooring fees, winter storage, trailer storage, launching, recovery,
travel hoist, tractors, winches, mast derrick, water and power. The effect of these fees will be to reduce charges to smaller boats
with less desirable drying moorings and increase charges to larger boats with deep-water moorings and large trailers.

Even at these increased levels our cruiser fees compare favourably with our competitors and are a fraction of the costs for
comparable professional marina services. This is made possible by our well-developed “self-help” ethos and the fact that,
thanks to the good stewardship of our Board and members over the years, we own our Club, land and equipment.

Existing Loan Notes
The Fee & Subscription discount given in lieu of interest on Loans to the Club will continue as before.

Current status
The proposals have the full backing of both the Board and the Management Committee.

Next steps
I believe that this proposed new Fee structure will achieve the objectives set out above and I commend it to you. On the
following page is a spread sheet that presents the information I have explained above in another format. I invite you to study the
information and understand what the proposal will mean for you and your family. Many of you will be agreeably surprised, others
less so. Either way I invite your feedback by email on

Committee Notes
Commodore’s Notes
I am delighted to be able to bring good news of the sailing kind to my Notes this month.

Members will be pleased to hear that in early July we heard that we have been successful in our application to Sport England
for a grant to purchase a new support RIB. My thanks go to Neil Pembleton, Michaela Dowley, Simon Elwell, Bryan Spencer
and Sue Shenton, all of whom had a hand in the successful application. The grant is for £10,000 and the Club will be required to
add several thousand to this amount. To get the best value for money the new RIB will be built during the winter and we can
expect it to be in service for next season.

Another successful East Coast Piers Race weekend has just passed into history. Blessed by a good sailing breeze on Race
Day, all the competitors went home happy, including the crew of a Prindle who were towed back by one of the big RIBs.

The ECPR was won by Grant Piggott in an F18. Grant was a Club member for many years and in his speech at the Prize Giving
he said he had been trying to win the Race for 20 years and now he had won he could retire a happy man. He also presented
the Bryan Piggott Memorial Trophy to the first Tornado home. Line honours went to Will Sunnocks in his hugely impressive M20
Vampire GBR1 who finished 23 minutes ahead of the next cat, but this was only good enough for sixth place on corrected time.
Steve Glynn & Tom Duckmanton were first Club boat in a very creditable seventh place.

I have great admiration for the crew of the Tornado Sport that won Line Honours in Colne Point Race, not only for their sailing
abilities, but because it was crewed by Nicole Davy who is blind. The Race was won by Robin Leather in a Shadow X. Club
members Michael Taylor & Peter Playle sailing an Osprey dinghy were forth in the combined list and we look forward to
welcoming more Ospreys in 2014. Another Club member, John Pearse in a Sprint 15 was sixth.

While the competitors were racing mother boats deployed, observed, reported and ultimately returned to the Club long after the
Prize Giving. RO Mike Turner and OOD Simon Elwell led their teams on the Committee Boat and in the Bus. Much of the liquid
product donated by Adnams was consumed in the bar; all the souvenir shirts were sold and the first prize in the raffle, a
Wildwind Sailing holiday in Greece, was won by Nick Miller who immediately became the most popular man around as the
holiday is for two.

I am proud to lead a Club that is willing and capable of putting on an Event like the East Coast Piers Race. Around 100
members give freely of their time, expertise and energy to make the weekend successful. From mother boats to competitors,
from Race Committee members to support boat crew, from the hard team to reception and many others, I thank you all. It is too
early to say how much will be raised for the charities that the Race supports but early indications are that the out-turn will
compare favourably with previous years.

The after-glow from the Event was tempered somewhat by the news of the untimely death of Nick Dewhirst from Whitstable YC,
a staunch supporter of our Race, organiser of the Forts Race and UK cat sailing in general. He will be missed.

The week after ECPR the Club hosted a Solo Open Meeting which was well supported on a terrific day for sailing. Thanks go to
John Salmon who organised the event, ably supported by Race Officer Jenny Ball and several more from the cat fleet. See fleet
reports for the whole story.

Now for a word about the new fee structure that I went through in detail in the last edition of Navigans. So far I have only had
ten emails telling me what you think of the proposals. It’s not too late to email me on if you
have something to say.

I wish you all good fortune and good sailing this summer. Let’s hope that the weather co-operates with our plans.

Clive Shenton

Dinghy Cruising
UK WAYFARER ASSOCIATION, TWO RIVERS CRUISE, 1-2 JUNE 2013
Seven months of detailed planning, twenty miles of sailing and a successful crossing of dangerous sandbanks in the North Sea
and there am I, standing on the Outer Crouch No.1 buoy trying to free Myrtle’s reefing line from where it snagged. Whoops, not
really what we had in mind.

A very long time ago the river Thames formed a delta which emptied into the North Sea across much of the east coast. Over
time as man reclaimed the land from the sea with high sea walls, the now distinct Essex Rivers took shape; all parallel to the
Thames and each running about ten or fifteen miles inland. The Blackwater and Crouch are closest to the Thames, separated
by an eight mile wide stretch of mainly agricultural land, the Dengie peninsula.

The intrepid Wayfarer sailors at Marconi Sailing club on the Blackwater had often talked about how it would be great to sail to
Burnham-on-Crouch, a pretty town on the river Crouch; only some four miles away by car but some twenty seven miles by sea.
Some had done the trip, others even there and back, most just talked about it. A UKWA cruise seemed the ideal excuse to just
go and do it.

Our intended passage plan

The major problem (although indeed the secret to a successful passage) is that half way between the Blackwater and Crouch
rivers out in the North Sea lies the Ray Sands, a series of sand banks which dry at low water and block your way. The trick is to
pick a time when low water is around lunchtime, use the ebb in the Blackwater to get you to the sands, wait until the tide turns
and gives you enough depth of water to get over the sands and then allow the flood to carry you up the Crouch to Burnham. The
following day would of course be an almost reverse passage, this time using the ebb down the Crouch to get you to the sands
before using the rising tide to carry you up the Blackwater and home for a well deserved beer. Easy eh! Well not really because
we now throw in the weather. The prevailing wind being south easterly means that you are likely to face a long beat to windward
at some point in the passage, either up the Crouch or up the Blackwater. In strong winds this could be very unpleasant and
tiring, not to mention dangerous crossing the sands at near low water. In light winds (even with favourable tides) we would just
not get there. Throw in a mixture of boats with unknown provenance and skippers with somewhat variable sailing abilities and
there you have the typical UKWA cruise.

In the days leading up to the cruise the forecast had been showing some but not much wind, this was a problem. In some ways
we were happier with strong winds, we would just not go. At a previous UKWA cruise we had just day-sailed in the Blackwater in
winds up to F7. Worst of all would be decent weather on the Saturday but no wind on the Sunday. In this case we would make
the passage but were prepared as a contingency to trail the boats back from Burnham.

Nine boats and nineteen sailors assembled for the 0800 briefing on Saturday morning to hear an unexpected forecast. It was
going to be basically F3 Northerly for the whole weekend, giving us the prospect of a beat both down the Blackwater and up the
Crouch and a nice run through the Ray Sands; the only tricky bit being a beat to windward on the Sunday as we made our way
back northwards. No reefing required.

August & September 2013 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Being in no hurry we managed to get all boats away by 0930 and set off down the Blackwater for the ten mile sail to
Brightlingsea (our lunch stop). As predicted a nice beam reach, leaving the Thirslet spit buoy at leisure to port, past Bradwell to
the starboard and finally making the short tack northwards towards Brightlingsea where we made a stop for lunch anchored at
the Mersea Stone, a shingle beach on Mersea Island. Here we needed to wait sufficient time to allow the now rising tide to
safely cover the Ray Sands.

Brightlingsea for lunch

Eventually we slipped anchors and headed due south, now on a dead run following a series of buoys which would lead us
through the channel. We must have watched the final buoy (the Outer Crouch No. 1) for a considerable amount of time; these
things however have a habit of creeping up rapidly if you day-dream, as I was. I noticed the buoy 20m dead ahead, made a
slight shimmy to avoid it but in doing so Myrtle gybed, the sail came rapidly across and the reefing line snagged on the buoy
(would you believe on a 4mm protruding bolt). Myrtle came to a halt. I had to climb on the buoy unhook the line and jump back
on board as Myrtle dashed away (hoping nobody noticed).

The sail into Burnham in the late afternoon sunshine with the wind on the beam was very pleasant indeed, winding our way
through the multitude of moored yachts, past the posh sailing clubs and by the town quay with its pubs and ice-cream parlours.
Finally we arrived at the marina, paddling, motoring, sailing and rowing to our berths for the night. Some camped on boats in the
marina, others camped at a local campsite, and all met up for well deserved drinks and food later at the Anchor pub on the town
quay.

As promised we awoke to the forecast F3 northerly wind and after much moving of people, boats and camping gear we once
again set off from the marina; an early start this time necessitated by a need to get back across the Ray Sands before low
water. It was a beautiful morning’s sail in bright sunshine as we took the ebb down the Crouch.

Leaving Burnham on Sunday morning

Leaving the dreaded Outer Couch No1 buoy well to port this time, we turned north into the North Sea and once again across
the sands. A long series of tacks into a northerly wind split the fleet even though we tried to keep together; the last of the boats

August & September 2013 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
taking some two and a half hours to cross the Dengie peninsula before finally turning westwards into the Blackwater. The fleet
assembled off Bradwell and headed for Thirslet spit where we anchored for lunch. On a rising tide the Blackwater spits don’t
remain for long and as water lapped our feet we made a timely escape. As the land around us disappeared leaving us in the
middle of the river, the last of our boats actually sailed directly over the spit we had so recently occupied.

Lunch on the rapidly disappearing Thirslet Spit

A short sail later and we were back at Marconi Sailing club, all safe and all accounted for. All that remained was more
movement of cars and gear, a celebratory beer, fond farewells and a good night’s sleep.

In the end we were really ambitious in our plans but lucky to be blessed with ideal weather, some excellent crews and great
company. From all at Marconi Sailing club, our thanks go out to all who helped organise this cruise and particularly to those
who attended and made it such a delightful fifty four mile cruise.
