A TRIP TO SCOTLAND BY TONY WILSON.
On 1st June Colin Leveridge and I started on a journey to Scotland in my boat Moontide to see and go over the Forth road and
rail bridges.We had 1 month to do the round trip, so decided on as few stops as possible. The original plan was Lowestoft,
Hartlepool, Amble and Port Edgar, but after 36 hours from Lowestoft we decided to stop off at Bridlington also.

1st.
We started off at 06.10 and sailed to Walton pier (10.00)where, because of head wind, we took down sails and motored to
Lowestoft arriving at 21.40.

2nd.
Stayed at Lowestoft for the day, looked round the port,marina and town.

3rd.
Leave 06.00 intending to go to Hartlepool. Headwind, so motor till 12.30 then sail. No headway so sails down and engine on at
14.30. Weather kind took forever to pass the wind farm. The sea was like glass in the evening and we passed a number of
anchored ships in the Humber area. Morning came and as neither of us had slept properly we decided it would be safer to head
for Bridlington and a proper rest.

4th.
Arrived 12.15. Entered the marina and promptly went aground and had to ‘walk’ Moontide to a berth as the tide came in.

Moontide is a bilge keeler and as the tide went out the outer keel went into a hole made by bigger boats so we found ourselves
at an angle of about 30 degrees, so it was a case of letting the mooring lines off at intervals! Least said about the marina the
better.

5th.
Left Bridlington at 13.15 and passed a new wind farm, then the Steelworks at Tees side, a blaze of lights on the horizon, then
arrived at Hartlepool in pitch darkness at 02.15. Now, Hartlepool has a light down a long tube to guide you in, but if you don’t
see it you are confronted by a huge wall of blackness and we found ourselves heading for a blank wall of concrete. So a
warning over the radio from the port control and a hurried burst of energy in reverse from my trusty Beta 16 and we were able to
find the guiding light into the lock.

6th.
After a rest went to see a Paddle Steamer and Square Rigger in a museum complex. Had lunch in a pub and we saw a Pound
Shop. Now, I had been suffering with cold hands and needed a form of glove that would slip on and off easily, so £2 bought me
2 oven gloves. Perfect!

When we made arrangements to leave Hartlepool, there was just a gentle breeze, but when they opened the lock at 19.00 to let
us out, the wind was howling a gale and white horses came marching towards us. There was no turning back so on we pressed,
heart in mouths, pulpit dipping under solid water, until we reached deep water when things thankfully calmed down a bit.

We even had a lifeboat escort - don’t know when or why they appeared but they kept station way off to starboard until calmer
water then with a cheery wave they were off to wherever they were going.

The wind and sea soon calmed down and we were able to sail halfway to Amble before again using the engine. We saw, first
time ever, a few Puffins skimming across the water.

7th.
Arrived at Amble 06.30 and had to wait a bit for enough water to cross the bar. Amble is my favourite marina. I wish it was a
weekend jaunt away.

8th.
13.30 Leave Amble and motor overnight to Port Edgar arriving at 11.00.

9th.
After a rest we walked to Dalmeny station and bought return tickets to North Queensferry so had a pleasant ride over the Forth
Railway Bridge and back.

Port Edgar is open to the River Forth but for a wall of floating tyres so there is no protection from the wash or wind, and of
course the visitors moorings are the most exposed. But luckily a large ferry boat came and moored on the other side of our

10th.
On Monday we took a bus ride to Edinburgh and went up Scott’s Monument in Princes Street, all 287 steps high, for a wonderful
view of the City and then went to the Castle for the rest of the day. Had wonderful haddock and chips and peas in a pub, ( nice
local beer too) on our way to the station and came back to Moontide by train.

11th.
Tuesday morning we walked to and across the Forth Road Bridge then down to North Queensferry, had a cup of coffee in a nice
café, then walked up a very steep hill to the station and had our last ride over the rail bridge.

We left Port Edgar at 16.30. Sunny, no wind, then rain and headwind and arrived back at Amble at 13.00 the next day.

12th.
Had to wait for the tide to lift us over the bar (again), had a rest then found a local pub with good food.

13th.
On Thursday we had a bus ride into Newcastle and had a look at the bridges, walked over the Millennium Bridge and looked in
the Heritage Centre where there was a young lady giving a beautiful cello recital. We then went over the Tyne Bridge, along the
embankment and up to the Discovery Museum. This was a fantastic place, where they have Turbinia, the first turbine powered
ship, and hundreds of model ships and boats and all kinds of electrical and mechanical machines and inventions and lots of
things where you can pull and push levers and press knobs etc..

Unfortunately they closed at 4pm so back to the bus for our journey back to the pub for supper.

14th.
10.30. Leave Amble. Motor/sail for 3 hours then motor to Hartlepool arriving at 21.00.

15th.
06.00. Leave Hartlepool. Sailed for 8 hours then ran into thunderstorms all round us so sails down and motored in rain and
wind up to force 7,dodging the black columns where the lightning was coming down. All this with Whitby Abbey on the skyline.
Spooky.

19.00. Into Bridlington, thankfully still in one piece, glad to be on solid ground and ready for our fish and chip supper in a local
fish restaurant.

16th.
Went to York on the bus. Had a walk round and lunch then went to the Railway Museum for the rest of the day. Bus back to a
feast on the boat.

A thing we noticed now and on our previous visit was the number of flags of all sorts and sizes on the boats. I asked someone if
there had been a carnival of some sort. No, he said. It’s to scare the birds! Apart from the ever present gulls there was a great
number of Turnstones on the pontoons.

A mass of them would run along in front of you and would only take off when they reached the very end.

17th.
09.00 Leave Bridlington Engine non stop. Tried jib for short time. No help.

18th.
10.00.Arrive Lowestoft. Have a rest then walk round the town, marina and port. Had Dinner at the Boat Club at the marina.

19th.
Visited a 1960s trawler which is now a museum and had an interesting guided tour and general boating chat with one of the
volunteers.

15.00 Leave Lowestoft. Light mist, no wind, calm sea. I become nervous of what looked like a tsunami wave on the starboard
horizon, it was the only way I could describe it, but when it got nearer, it was no more than a line of foam about 2 feet wide and
as it passed under the boat it was a dead straight line from horizon at the bow to horizon at the stern, to be followed a few
minutes later by another. The mist turned to fog early evening and by 21.00 was thick fog and dark and very still. About 23.00 a
light patch appeared on our port bow, it was the stern of an anchored ship all lit up. It was like passing a big block of flats with all
the lights on. And shortly after we passed a buoy with a green 4 flashing light which suddenly appeared out of the fog on our
starboard bow. Scary stuff. At 24.00 we were at the shipping lane so ran parallel till we came to a buoy then Colin radioed Port

Control, gave our position at the buoy, and asked if it was safe for us to cross the shipping lane. They said yes and requested a
call back when we got to the other side, which we did with relieved thanks. As if to round off our trip nicely the fog lifted at about
01.00, dawn broke to a nice day and we got back to our mooring at 05.45.

20th.
After a couple of hours there was enough water to go alongside the pontoon to unload Moontide of excess provisions, rented
liferaft and dirty washing.

Our trip was over.

Commodore’s Notes
Autumn approaches but at least we can look back on an excellent summer. I hope you, like me, made good use of the weather
and enjoyed your sailing.

The Club has been particularly active over the August holiday period. Cadet Week & Camping Fortnight were a great success
as were the Junior Cat Championships. The Kestrel fleet joined us over the Bank Holiday weekend and seemed to enjoy the
experience. Our cruising fleet went on two cruises in company, one to the Orwell and Deben and another to Ipswich, both of
which were well attended. The vigorous conditions experienced on the return from the Deben brought its own challenges. Club
cruisers have also entered BJRC races with success and one of our number completed the Fastnet. May we have many more
summers like it.

I now need to return to the proposed new fee structure, amendments to which were emailed around all the membership in late
July. The amendments were made in response to emails received during the consultation period. A specimen 2014 Membership
Renewal Form follows so you can work out your Fees & Subs for next year.

I think it is worth restating that the Board and Management Committee have three objectives for the new structure; simplicity,
fairness and to increase revenue.

Simplicity – to make the fee structure easy to understand, and thereby reduce administration and close any loopholes.

Fairness – to ensure that the fees paid by individual members reflect the club facilities utilised by each member, and to
some degree align our fee structure to local clubs which offer a similar standard of facilities.

Revenue – to increase the annual revenue to enable the club to maintain its existing level of service, and to fund
further developments as necessary. The unavoidable running costs of the club have risen steadily over the past few
years, over and above the annual increase in fees, which has resulted in a gradual decline in the cash reserves held
by the club.

I have still only received 26 responses to the new proposals about a third of which are fully supportive. Twenty six is small
proportion of a membership approaching 400 and I encourage you to send me any comments you may have to me at: -

To further help your understanding of the new fee proposals I will chair a meeting at the Club on Sunday 27th October
beginning at 14.00 hrs. My plan is to start by restating the objectives of the new fee proposals before throwing the meeting open
to questions from the floor.

Meanwhile enjoy the remainder of the season.

CLUBHOUSE SECURITY
CCTV evidence shows that at all times of the day and night YOUR clubhouse is being used by strangers such as beach
fisherman and casual visitors. The reason is obvious. Strangers know that the chances are that at least one of the outer doors
to the clubhouse will be open for them to use or abuse as they see fit at any time.

The solution to this is so easy. Always close the clubhouse after you have been in unless other members are using it;
particularly during ‘off peak’ times. Take the trouble to check the other outer doors. It will only take a few minutes. Do not leave
the clubhouse open because you are working somewhere on site and might want to nip back there from time to time.

The answer to all site security is very simple and is just common sense.

FLOOD GATES
The Environment Agency requires that the flood gates must be kept closed from 1st September unless the hard is in use.
Please shut the gates when you come ashore unless it is obvious that another member is using the hard. If in doubt, shut the
gates. They can always be opened again.

PARKING IN CRUISER PARK
At this busy time of boat, boat hoist and trailer movements cars must not be left unattended in the cruiser park or the cruiser
parking area of the cat park. Owners of cars in the cruiser parks must be available at all times and ready to move them at short
notice.

Do not leave your car unattended in the cruiser parks even if you are ‘only nipping out to the boat for 5 minutes’.

CHAIRS ON THE SEAWALL

somebody else to put away.

BOAT DISPOSAL

abandoned on the site by ex-members.

To bring you up to date, the Dart 15 owner reappeared on the scene and has sold his boat to a Club member. Hopefully we will
continue to see this Dart 15 out sailing from Stansgate with the other Dart/Sprint 15s.

The Club has decided to ‘adopt’ the Pico. After some repairs and replacements it will be available for MSC cadets and others to
use.

The disposal notices for both boats are therefore withdrawn. Many thanks to those of you who approached me to show an

Cadet Fleet
JUNIOR CATAMARAN CHAMPIONSHIPS
The weekend of the 17th and 18th August marked the second running of the Junior Catamaran Championships hosted again in
association with the UKCRA (UK Catamaran Racing Association) by Marconi Sailing Club. This year saw eight teams with ages
ranging from 9 to 16 taking part in a hotly contended regatta all sailed in UKCRA owned and borrowed Dart 16 catamarans.
Many of the teams this year determined to show the Multihull sailing skills
have spent much of the summer brushing up on the extra skills needed
compared to sailing a dinghy.

Following the Saturday briefing where teams were allocated boats for the
day. They were then faced with a forecast which saw the wind increasing
throughout the afternoon from a pleasant force 15 to 20 knots, to a
challenging 20 to 30 knots.

The teams ranged from competent club sailors who have done some
multihull sailing to top class Topper squad sailors who have done very little
multihull sailing. Race 1 started with a pleasant 15 knots of breeze, but by
the first windward mark it was possible to see the larger gusts pushing
their way across the race course. David Nickalls and Ben Cross took an
early lead and held this the whole way round, several other team got to
grips with perfecting the technique of right a capsized Dart 16 and how to
hand those challenging mark roundings.

The race team quickly got Race 2 underway as the wind was building there were several more capsizes across the fleet, this
time the two all-girl teams of Emma Crane, Abbie Wallace and Sophie Savill and Hannah Bard put in a great performance, but
team Nickalls / Cross remained untouchable.

With two races under their belt and the wind still increasing, the race team decided to cancel racing for the rest of the day, with
the promised forecast for Sunday looking perfect.

Sunday dawned, with near perfect champagne sailing conditions. The race team were quick to get the teams out sailing again
swapping the boats around to ensure fairness and were able to complete 3 races in the morning and 2 in the afternoon. Emma
Crane and Abbie Wallace quickly showing what she had learnt from the previous day with a very respectable second in race 3.
Throughout the day there was some very close racing and all teams and positions changed dramatically right up to the finish
lines with several occasions the leaders being pipped over the line, simply by missing a crucial tack in the strong tide.

With the fight for 2nd and 3rd place coming down to the last race, Jack Collis and Becki Chapman only lost out to Daniel
Nickalls and William Harrison as Becki lost her footing and was found swimming in the Blackwater, only losing a couple of
places, but it was enough to knock them back down to 3rd on count back.

At the prize giving a new perpetual award was presented, the "Dewhirst
Award" This was presented in memory of Nick Dewhirst the UKCRA
Chainman who sadly passed away in July. Nick's tireless work ensuring that
catamaran sailing received the recognition it deserved among the wider

Sailing on board the Pioneer, Last of the Skillingers
In early July, I had the opportunity spend three days on board the
Pioneer – the last surviving Essex smack of her kind, based in
Brightlingsea. I was accompanying a group of young people on a
Prince’s Trust programme and - for the first, and probably the last time in
my life – I actually got paid to go sailing!

The Pioneer is very special. She is a 64ft Skillinger built in 1864 at
Rowhedge, just up the Colne from her current home. She was one of a
large fleet of Essex fishing smacks that dredged for oysters and scallops
not just around the Essex coast, but further afield off the French, German
and Dutch shores.

Pioneer saw active service until the 1930s when she fell out of
employment and was taken over by the East Mersea Golf Club who cut
out most of her deck to build a shed on top. In 1942, she was towed to
West Mersea and sank soon after. She remained in the West Mersea
mud until 1998 when she was salvaged by a group of professional
enthusiasts with sound financial backing that went on to form the Pioneer
Sailing Trust.

She is now wonderfully re-built, fully rigged and fully employed providing adventurous trips for school children and young people
who would otherwise never have the opportunity for such an experience in their lives. Additionally, the Pioneer Sailing Trust
has a thriving marine workshop in Brightlingsea which employs apprentices in the now re-emerging boat building industry. The
Trust specialises in the restoration of historically significant craft and also the production of beautifully lined coastal rowing
vessels.

For our particular three day voyage, we originally planned to head up
the coast and into the Orwell. However, after crashing into lumpy
seas off the Colne Bar with the wind on the nose, a number of the
young people began to feel the effects of sea sickness – and that was
whilst the wind was still with the tide! Judy, the Skipper, therefore
decided on plan B which was to run back into the Blackwater and
smoother waters. The young people quickly recovered and threw
themselves into all the duties on deck. After a very pleasant sail, we
fetched up off Osea Pier for the night and watched the sun go down in
very familiar tradition to those of us at Marconi!

The next day, the crew arranged for the young people to learn how to
row and to tie knots whilst we waited for the tide to become more
favourable. I was in full Cadet week flow teaching the bowline and
banging on about rabbits, holes and trees when the mate told me with
great consternation that the word “rabbit” was never said on board,
because it was bad luck. He was unable to explain why. I wonder if anyone else is able to tell me? Google and Wikipedia
explanations were not very convincing!!!

We spent the rest of the day beating down the Blackwater getting plenty of practice with all that is involved in tacking a proper
boat (bit more complicated than my Sprint 15) and then moored up for the night at the end of the Mersea entrance, by the Nass
beacon. We then took the young people ashore to stretch their legs and to buy some essential provisions (we had run out of
sugar for their cups of tea) and enjoyed watching all the West Mersea cadets tacking their way back home at low water.

On the final morning, we aimed to head off early – but although we had a good go at creating a new Pioneer channel, we had to
concede defeat and go and have breakfast whilst we waited for the tide to rise. We then had another great beat along the

October 2013 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
length of the Mersea shore before reluctantly turning into the Colne and heading for the mooring. We then spent a couple of
hours cleaning and scrubbing Pioneer so that she looked like new for the next group of people lucky enough to come on board.

If you are interested in finding out more about Pioneer – there is a short book called “Pioneer, Last of the Skillingers” published
by Jardine Press in 2004 and written by Rupert Marks and other.

The Pioneer Sailing Trust is always keen to hear from schools or groups who think their young people would benefit from a trip
on board. They can do day trips or residential for groups up to 10 young people plus 2 team leaders (in addition to the Skipper
and 2 crew). I would certainly recommend it to anyone.

Visit www.pioneersailingtrust.org.uk/ for more details!!

“Like doing Everest without Oxygen”
A classic yacht competes in the 2013 Fastnet
By Tom Anderson

Duet is a 50ft gaff-rigged yawl with an unashamedly beautiful and elegant
shape, designed by Linton Hope and built in 1912 in what proved to be the
zenith of the Edwardian long summer. Classic Boat readers might recollect an
article on Duet by Peter Willis in last year’s “Centenarian of the Month” series.
She is on loan from the Courtauld family (see below) to the Cirdan Sailing
Trust (cirdantrust.org) which now uses her for sailing expeditions, particularly
for disadvantaged youth groups but also wounded service personnel and the
Duke of Edinburgh award scheme. She is a remarkably well-travelled boat,
and her most recent expedition was a circumnavigation of the UK to celebrate
her centenary last year, with assorted groups doing legs of the journey.
Continuing this expeditionary spirit, she was entered for the 2013 Fastnet race
although it was felt that despite Duet having won the MCA and ASTO “Sail
Training Vessel of the Year” this particular event might not be suitable for non-
sailors so the crewlist was opened up by race skipper David Cannell to a few
fortunate individuals who are connected to the Trust.

She certainly was an incongruous entry into the Fastnet. There were a record
number of entries, and almost all the 350 boats taking part were modern
racing machines – their ultra-light carbon-fibre hulls and Kevlar rigs were
manned by sunglass-wearing crews in matching, uniform kits. Something of a
contrast to our teak on oak frames, weighty spars, traditional sails and crew of Corinthian harlequins, let alone the warm
mahogany and brass that welcomes you to her saloon below (and the Baby Blake)…

Perhaps because we rather stood out, many people who were otherwise unconnected with Duet and the Cirdan Trust followed
our progress enthusiastically on http://fastnet.rorc.org/2013-fleet-tracking.html. They may have been occasionally bemused by
our track but our course was heavily dictated by wind and tide as we saw them, which gave us some incredible sails but also
some very frustrating moments. After the start, we struck out into the Channel, thinking that we might get a better breeze out
there, unfortunately (inevitably) it was the other way around and we were almost becalmed for two days, and flushed backwards
and forwards by the tides. It was some consolation to hear that these fickle zephyrs also frustrated the fastest boats on their
return as they were stuck in sight of the finish at Plymouth.

As we passed the Scillies the wind had freshened into a steady westerly, so we punched up to the Fastnet on one tack,
pounding through a confused chop as the Irish and Celtic seas met. We were beating into some lumpy water through the Irish
Sea as we watched other competitors go past us on their reciprocal run home and were also looking forward to a fast sail back
to the Scillies, which would have been a good broad reach if the wind had stayed west. Unfortunately, we got around the
Fastnet and the wind promptly changed north-westerly so having gone around the rock and found the turning mark (laid to
separate the boats coming towards and away from the rock) we were not able to aim straight at the Scillies as it would have
been a dead run and it wasn’t worth risking a crash gybe in heavy seas and growing wind. This was a tough moment for all the
crew as we realised that the best course we could lay would be south which would add miles onto our track, rather than the
direct south-east route that all the other competitors had been able to take.

We were aware that there was a deep low working its way across the Atlantic and the wind and rollers steadily grew as we
gybed towards the Scillies. This gave us some very fast sailing – albeit nerve-wracking – as the swells lifted the counter and

October 2013 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
swung us towards crash-gybe territory. Lots of fighting the tiller, trying to find a balance between going dead downwind on the
straightest route home and going too far off the wind and risking the gybe.

As you can imagine on a classic yacht with no winches every rig change and sail adjustment required extra crew on deck;
whoever went onto the bowsprit to unhank the genoa or yankee would get plunged unceremoniously into the sea at some point
whilst the rest of the off-duty watch fought to get sails up, down and tied away. All kit went slowly from damp to wet, although
we had an afternoon of sun somewhere west of the Scillies so the deck immediately transformed into a Chinese laundry as
socks went back from wet to damp.

Duet was worked pretty hard, but we didn’t break anything that couldn’t be jury-rigged with a bit of imagination and some quick
splicing from one of Duet’s permanent crew, Alex Carpenter. The genoa ripped a cleat off, so we used a pulley system to take
some of the pressure off the sheet which was useful but another thing to remember when we tacked. The bowsprit’s tack
downhaul snapped so a beefier one was put together. The genoa itself also took a bit a battering but nothing too terminal; just a
small tear and some stitches pulled out. Our boathook disappeared somewhere south of Ireland. Bumps and scrapes for the
crew but nothing that couldn’t be overcome by a cup of tea and another sail change to take your mind off the fresh bruises. A
few salient facts picked out from the log show that we raced over 800 nautical miles, and did over 30 sail changes, as well as a
couple of reefs (one of which was completed in a F7). The main was obviously used throughout the race, albeit reefed and
shaken out a few times; we also used the mizzen, mizzen staysail, jackyard topsail, working topsail, staysail, genoa, yankee and
No1 jib. Phew! Just in case the crew of 7 were feeling too relaxed, the bilges required 11,300 pumps and there was also a very
jolly 20 minutes spent using buckets to empty the bilges while we were wallowing mid-channel. Duet is a deeply elegant
Edwardian lady, but she does have a leaky bottom. Having said that, our speed is mentioned several times in the log at around
9 knots, but according to the GPS we topped out at about 11 or 12, which is pretty good going!

However, it wasn’t all hard work and the log shows high levels of morale throughout the race with several mentions of lunch and
the 4th Ashes test, a description of the weather as “lovely”, and (a slightly relieved) “England sighted!!” as we saw Blighty re-
appearing on the horizon… We saw plenty of dolphins, usually in pods of about 6 animals. Although I have to admit that my
ridiculously limited zoological knowledge doesn’t stretch to an ability to identify species, the ubiquitous Google tells me they
were probably one of the genus Delphinus. We saw a very nonchalant sunfish splashing along in the Channel, and a small,
curious-looking, long-nosed garfish was swept onto the deck as we thundered downwind towards the Scillies. It was probably
as surprised to see us as we were to see it, but our miniature Poseidon was returned to the briny without further incident.
During the quiet night watches there was ethereal bio-luminescence which complemented some very clear night skies, giving us
several stars to steer her by.

During the final run in towards Plymouth the wind strengthened, and blew F7. Big rollers, 3 or 4 m high, were sweeping in and
toppling over themselves in a roar behind us. We had our only ‘all hands’ call about 30 miles from the finish to put in a double
reef and dropped to the No1 jib. Difficult with the wind behind but with the indefatigable energy of Gavin Taylor, Duet’s regular
skipper and with the finish so close no-one minded by then, although we were all pretty pooped, as you can imagine.

We had a great welcoming party on the pontoon when we arrived. About 30 people, led by David Cannell’s family, had turned
out and their generous champagne and boisterous hallooing was much appreciated; especially as it was blowing a gale with
horizontal rain and we finished about a day after everyone else, thanks to our little wind-induced detour west of the Scillies. I
think Duet had become something of a talisman for the rest of the fleet, and there was lots of clapping and cheering from the
other boats in the Plymouth Yacht Haven. We had a good supper in the nearest hostelry and then dropped, soggy and drained,
into bed. We later admitted to each other that we had woken ourselves up during that first night ashore, in anticipation of a
whispered “wake up mate, you’re on watch…”

We must thank all those who supported us before, during and after the race. There are too many to name individually but many
people have given generously to support the Cirdan Trust, which uses these donations to provide bursaries to groups who
would otherwise struggle to experience the challenge and teamwork required on board a sailing vessel. One of the things that
surprised us, and the Cirdan team, was the number of sailors who were proudly following Duet’s progress as a classic in what is
a very modern race, posting supportive comments and maintaining a positive online commentary on a variety of sailing websites
and blogs – thank you all.

The 2013 Fastnet was certainly a rigorous test for boat and most importantly, crew. It would have been a real bonus to have
competed more strongly but the weather has a vote and it went against us so we were delighted to have finished, even if it was
behind Jolie Brise! It was a genuinely remarkable experience. Duet’s gear has not been modernised, and there are no nautical
mod-cons such as winches so any rig adjustments require gruntwork. One of the crew described it by saying “doing the Fastnet
on Duet is the equivalent of climbing Everest without oxygen”, which (with apologies to any readers who have climbed Everest)
feels about right. I would strongly recommend trying to do a long-distance race if an opportunity presents itself although during
the race you will ask yourself why you volunteered and after the race you will have to face mystified faces in the office when
trying to explain what you’ve been up to during your hard-earned summer holiday.

By the way, if you see Duet, or the other vessels in the Cirdan Trust’s fleet (Queen Galadriel, a Baltic trader, or Faramir, a
purpose built sail training ketch) on the water do give them a wave – they deserve it!

Duet was built in 1912 and is believed to be Britain’s longest serving sail training vessel. Since she began this role in 1960 she
has sailed more than 250,000 miles and provided a sailing adventure for more than 8,000 young people.

Her involvement with the Courtauld family began in 1931, when the arctic explorer Augustine (August) Courtauld was virtually
buried alive under snow in Greenland but kept himself together by designing a yacht which would turn out to be Duet.

He was a member of an expedition investigating the possibility of an air route to North America via Iceland and Greenland which
involved taking regular weather readings through the darkness of the Arctic winter.

October 2013 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
They established a weather station up on the Greenland ice cap which was to be manned by relays of two men at a time.
Unfortunately, one of these relays was delayed by atrocious blizzard conditions and arrived with rations much depleted and
insufficient for two men to stay the winter. Rather than allow the recording of the weather to lapse August insisted on
volunteering to stay and man the station alone. He was there for five months, cut off with no communication to the outside
world, the last six weeks of which he was actually trapped and buried in his tent under the snow with only a breather pipe for air
and running out of food and fuel. During his entrapment two plans occupied his thoughts, the first to marry his future wife Mollie
and the second to design a yacht.

He was eventually rescued and after his safe return to England and his bride-to-be, scoured the country looking at boats for
sale, until he found one at Burnham-on-Crouch which was so similar to the one he had mentally designed, that he bought her.

He renamed her Duet in honour of his forthcoming marriage to Mollie. They lived in Essex and brought up their six children in
that magnificent county. August, who served on the County Council and as High Sheriff of Essex, sailed Duet until 1955 and
died in 1959. His widow, Mollie, subsequently married RA (later Lord) Butler and they continued to live in the house where
Christopher spent his childhood and where Mollie eventually died aged 101.

August’s son Christopher inherited Duet and in 1960 co-founded the Ocean Youth Club, making her available for young people
to enjoy the experience of sailing.

Although on loan to the Cirdan Sailing Trust, Duet remains in the ownership of the Courtauld family who came over from France
as Huguenot refugees in the 17th century, originally setting up as silversmiths in London and subsequently in Essex as textile
manufacturers.

Pam Davies
I am saddened to write that Pam Davies died on 11th September having been ill for some time. Together with husband Dick and
children Gill, Corrina and Huw, Pam was an active member of MSC in the 1990’s and, through family and friends, never lost
touch with the club. A service of thanksgiving for her life was held at St Mary’s Church, Great Baddow, on the 4 th October. Many
of her friends from the sailing club were present.

I first met Pam when she was Jean Fluke’s galley helper one Sunday just after the Davies family had joined Marconi. Getting
stuck in like this was typical of Pam’s sense of duty and service. Pam was not an avid sailor herself, but she would accompany
Dick for ‘jollies’ on his Dart 15s “Di-Pa” and “Cold Feet”. Back ashore, Dick and Pam forged many firm friendships with fellow
members that continue to this day.

Just over a decade after I first met the Davies clan, Gill and I were married and I was privileged to have Dick and Pam as my in-
laws. I, like so many others, can testify to Pam’s generosity, hospitality and sense of humour – all of which were second to
none.

During 2013 Pam remained active despite her illness, and visited Stansgate several times. She took great joy in watching
grandchildren Becky, Ruth, Jamie and Megan take to the water on my Dart 15 one evening during cadet week.

She will be greatly missed by all who knew her.

David Ball

NSSA Regatta 2013
In 2012 two MSC cadets joined many others at the NSSA regatta in Weymouth, enjoying a great week of sailing. This then
sparked the idea to take a team from MSC to the 2013 NSSA regatta in Bassenthwaite, Cumbria (Lake District). John Nickalls
took on the role as Team Manager and started the many emails to organise the trip. In total 9 cadets were keen, with parents
and brothers tagging along too. I (Richard, brother to Matthew) joined Caroline and John as Team Managers for MSC. The
awkward task of transporting boats was sorted, sweatshirts printed, tents packed, sailing bags overflowing and cars crammed to
the roof, the long journey to Bass was upon us. The MSC team comprised of:

John & Caroline Nickalls – Team Managers
Richard Dixon – Team Manager
David Nickalls – Laser Radial
Dan Bard – Laser Radial
Gemma Clarke – Laser Radial
Beth Spencer – Topper
Sophie Savill – Topper
Dan Nickalls – 420
Hannah Bard – 420 Crew
Olivia Duckmanton – Topper Rookie Fleet
Matthew Dixon – Pico Rookie Fleet

Matthew has written about his Regatta:

Sunday,

We left early on Sunday morning, on our way to the NSSA, which was being hosted by the sailing club of
Bassenthwaite, in the Lake District. First we had to pick up Beth from the Boreham interchange, and then we carried on our very
long journey up North to Bass. Behind us we had a 420, which belonged to the Nickalls. After our 6 hour journey, which included
a lot of sleeping, we arrived at the sailing club to unload the boats and met the Nickalls family who had only just arrived. After
unloading we rigged the boats to make sure it was all ready for the week’s regatta. Then we drove the short distance to the
school where most competitors will be staying on the school's playing field. The first step was to put up the big marquee in our
allocated slot,(R – thanks to the MSC member who offered this for our trip to Bass, it was used daily and invaluable to dry our kit

November 2013 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
and sit under) whilst the Mums went shopping for lunch. David decided to try flying with Beths tent rather than help put it up, he
didn’t get very far! After dinner served in the school canteen, we had the main briefing in the sport hall of the school, where we
learned more about what we would be doing over the week. I was entered into the Rookie fleet which is aimed at sailors who
hadn’t sailed away from their home club, in a Laser Pico. We then played games as a team before heading to bed ready for the
weeks sailing.

Monday,

After having breakfast at the school we then travelled the short distance by car to the sailing club. We rigged our
boats, and then each separate fleet (Laser, Topper, Handicap, and Rookie) had a briefing in the marquee at the sailing club.
Today being the first day of racing many of us were nervous not knowing what it is going to be like sailing somewhere different.
Then the fleets launched one at a time, in order to not cause chaos in the 3 slipways that were available to us, although we
were lucky that we were right next to one of the quieter slipways so could launch easily.

Each fleet had its own race course. The Rookie fleet was close to the shore so didn’t have that far to go, our course was a
triangle shaped, the Handicap had a windward leeward whereas the topper and Laser had odd shaped, but wasn’t obvious from
the shore.

Each lunch was provided as a packed lunch delivered to us. After the afternoon sailing we ventured back to the school to
shower and get ready for the evening entertainment. Tonight’s was a talk by Virtual Rigger who showed us some video footage
and pictures of the days sailing.

Tuesday

After another morning briefing to the Rookies (which was very quiet), we had a rather uneventful days sailing due to
the severe lack of wind on the lake. After the days sailing, and dinner we had an invitation to a game of rounders against the
other teams. This was made a lot more interesting by the fact that the rain had made the field extremely slippery, and so there
were many occasions where a runner slipped over on the mud, with the most spectacular example being when somebody from
the other team ran a rounder and finished it off by falling backwards and sliding into one of their teammates lining up to bat.

Wednesday

Today, we had something different which came in the form of the
Mount Haes event. Sophie and David were chosen to represent Marconi in
the race, which took place in Topper Xenons The race format was similar to
the Football World Cup. To progress to the next round they needed to come
in the top 2 after 3 laps, but unfortunately they only managed to come third,
however this was still a very good result as David and Sophie had never
raced competitively together. Also, there were two other events that were
being held, which was a Topper race, which Daniel and Hannah did, and then
there was the all-comers race, which everybody else did including adult.
Richard and Beth sailed the 420, I sailed the Pico with Olivia and David (who
had finished racing) & Dan sailed their Lasers. This again was unfortunately
met with an even bigger lack of wind than on Tuesday, with an Oppi passing
many boats which started 5 minutes before it. This resulted in a very late
lunch. After the sailing and dinner, we went on a scheduled walk up a nearby
mountain. We met at the sailing club on what was advertised as an easy 1 hour walk. In the heat of the summer evening it
wasnt easy and I soon drank all my drink. The view from the top was amazing and you could see the lake we were sailing on
and also the view far into the distance. After returning to the school we dived into the canteen for a well-earned supper of bread
with jam and hot drink before retiring to our tents for bed.

Thursday

Thursday was a disaster day, we had been using John and Richards cars to
transport all of us from the school to the sailing club, unfortunately his car broke on
the way to the club (R – the flywheel went, AA Tow truck booked for Saturday!).
Everyone had a great day sailing until the afternoon when we found out the 420 was
been protested over a minor incident in what was their best race. After the sailing and
ferrying all of us in Johns car back to school for dinner, we went for a walk around
Cockermouth, which was the nearest village to us. The town has a statue for William
Wordsworth which we discovered, and it was made famous of the flood that
happened in 2009, which was above my head! John then started our Prize giving
giving us each a NSSA Bassenthwaite Mug and Mint cake (that had been to the top
of Everest) and also our virtual prize (as the real prizes were in shops that had shut!)
Mine was a loud hailer, I was the quieter member of the MSC group!

Friday

On friday, I managed to come 1st in both the races of the day which I
believe was down to the heavier winds, which I was used to instead of the light winds
we had been having for the rest of the week (R – it was really down to the excellent
sail training given by John!!). These results along with the re-positioning of previous
results and gaining another discard, I managed to jump unexpectedly from sixth place earlier on in the week to finish the Rookie
Fleet in second place. Once we were all off the water we got the boats loaded up on the road trailers ready for the journey home
on Saturday. The prize giving in the evening was at the sailing club in beautiful sunshine, overlooking the lake. My name was

read out taking 2nd place so resulted in me going up to my trophy. I was really pleased with this as it was my first event outside
of Marconi.

Saturday

Richard’s car was still broken so we had to get up earlier than the rest of our group, so that we would be ready for the
AA man to come and pick us up. However instead of an AA man we got piked up by a local company for the first leg. He then
took us to a very busy services, which barely had enough room for us to manoeuvre around for the changeover to an actual AA
truck. Most of our return journey consisted of us sleeping, being interrupted by the changeovers, which there were 3 of in total.
This along with the fact that the AA trucks could only go 50 mph resulted in a 9 hour journey back to Maldon.

I really enjoyed the NSSA event in Bassenthwaite and would recommend it to anyone, it is friendly and you get to sail against
people of the same ability.

Team Marconi in Ibiza
At the end of September 3 Marconi teams travelled all the way to
the sunny island of Ibiza to take part in the 2013 Tornado World
Championships.

T415 Michaela & Andrew Dowley
T431 Steve Glynn & Tom Duckmanton
T424 Lee & Paul Harrisson

The World Championships were scheduled to be over 6 days with
the practice races starting on the Sunday. We arrived in Ibiza on
Friday evening with Steve, Debbie and the trailer coming off the
ferry on Saturday morning. Saturday turned out to be a boat building
and testing day, we rigged in the harbour so had to sail the boats
over to the private, sandy beach where they would be located for
the rest of the week. Lee had done an excellent job of finding an
apartment which was situated just up from the beach. The 7 of us
had a nice home for the week.

Sunday's practice races had to be cancelled because there was too much wind outside of the harbour. In the evening it was the
opening night with traditional local dancing and formal ceremony where we carried the Union Jack through the town to the
marquee and were presented to the sponsors and crowds.

Monday morning came and we could feel a reasonable breeze from the
is

beach, there was certainly going to be more outside the harbour wall and
onto the race course. Looking back it was probably the windiest day of the
week. Steve and Tom managed a couple of fantastic swims, the 2nd
wasn't their fault as they had a port/starboard with a German team who
didn't give them the right of way.

The second day saw similar conditions and it was questionable as to
whether the breeze was above the 25 knot limit, the race committee
seemed to think it wasn't but they were super keen to get the races

completed. It was Andrew and Michaela's turn for a swim on Tuesday, a
sudden gust downwind after going round the windward mark with the leaders
put us out of the race because the mainsail popped out of the mast track.
Luckily we made it back out for the 2nd race. While all the swimming was
happening Lee and Paul were finishing all of the races and were putting
together a good series of results.

Wednesday was the lay day and perfectly timed after two windy days. It
wasn't just the wind we were recovering from after a heavy night and a road
trip across the island to the infamous Ibiza night spots for some of us.
Wednesday evening we were lucky enough to be able to visit the exclusive
Blue Marlin Beach Club who were a main sponsor of the event for dinner and
drinks.

On Thursday morning the wind had swung round and was now coming from the East bringing some big rolling waves around
2.5m high. Waiting round before the start was very uncomfortable with the boats being thrown up and down. The first race of the
day turned out to be carnage with lots of swims and breakages across the fleet which included Michaela, Andrew, Steve and
Tom unfortunately! The race committee decided that one race was enough for Thursday and send the fleet limping back to the
beach.

Friday was a complete different story with very light winds which continued to drop all day, unfortunately the waves were still
present which made it very hard to get the boats moving, although the Olympians
and Pro's didn't do a bad job of it, more practice is needed for us club sailors.

Saturday and the last day had came around very quickly as it always does when
you're away from work and in beautiful sunny place. Fortunately there was more
breeze on Saturday with between 7 and 13 knots at different times during the day.
The race committee got 3 races in to make the full quota for the week.

With only 1 discard from the 10 races there wasn't much we could do about the
races we didn’t finish, final positions

Michaela and Andrew – 21st

Importantly we all learnt new things about our boats and what to do in different

this level the next World Championships are in Perth over Christmas and New
Year 2014/15, watch this space….

proposed new fee structure has been voted out by a majority of those present at the AGM then the immediate and most

DINGHY CRUISING GROUP - SUMMARY FOR 2013
The dinghy cruising group held a programme of local and away cruises throughout 2013.

We sailed from the MSC every month from March to October on the first Saturday of the month. The only cancellation was in
November - yesterday - when the forecast wind was too high. In the event we walked to Stone, past an idyllic scene with calm
water and warm moderate airs - but it did get windy later. We ended the day with a most enjoyable meal at the Fox and Hounds
in Cock Clarks.

Two high points were our cruises on the South coast and from MSC to Burnham. In May we trailed boats to the Solent and
camped and launched at Eastney, sailing through Langstone Harbour, round the top of Hayling Island and down through
Chichester Harbour to Bosham and back - leaving the boats overnight at Sparks marina at the very tip of the Island - some of
the roughest sailing we have done. We were joined by Andrew and a friend from the Shadwell sailing club, a frequent fellow-
adventurer.

In June we hosted a UKWA event at MSC, sailing round the Dengy peninsular into the Crouch, camping in Burnham and
returning the next day.

In John Eardley's words : Saturday morning saw
9 boats and 20 people assemble at Marconi for a
little return trip to Burnham on Crouch (4 of our
boats; Myrtle, Blue Moon, Nirvana and Samphire)
and 5 visiting.

A northerly F3/4 wind and fine conditions ensured
a swift beam reach down the Blackwater,
followed by a beaching at Brightlingsea’s Mersea
Stone for a lunch stop whilst we awaited the tide
to rise in the Thames - we were to cross the Ray
sands drying channel no earlier than LW+2
(1500). A due southerly course took us across the
sands and we picked up the flood up the Crouch
and into to Burnham. Great early evening sail
followed by a short paddle/row/motor into the
yacht harbour. Lots of transferring people and
gear between marina and campsite, and then an
evening meal in the Anchor hotel.

We woke to a similar forecast on Sunday morning, more movement of people and gear; for some a stop off at the local café for
a full English. A northerly F3/4 in bright sunshine gave us a beam reach down the Crouch on the ebb, before once again
crossing the sands and heading northwards; a two and a half hour close-hauled but pleasant hack.

The welcome rounding into the Blackwater, followed by a quick lunch stop on a rapidly disappearing spit, and we were soon
back at Marconi and saying our fond farewells.

54 miles in total, not bad at all.

For both major cruises we are indebted to John Eardley and Cliff Pountney for the organisation. It is good to combine with other
clubs, extending the network of likeminded sailors.

Our local sails have been up to Maldon, down to Mersea and all points in between, stopping of for picnics on the spits and inlets
around the estuary.

Cruises are generally of between 3 and 10 boats, with 6-20 people, but we are able to mix and match, taking as many or few
boats as the conditions warrant.

We are planning a similar programme for next year and would welcome anyone interested in joining us.

Colin Wardell

Changes to VHF SRC course from 1st January 2014
Do it now on 15th December 2013 if you need it!

The RYA are about to change the procedure for VHF SRC courses and assessments. In a nutshell the current system where
one is trained and assessed on the same day by the same assessor in a one day course will be replaced by the need for an
independent assessor and an increase in the study time to 10 hours minimum. There will also be an increase in the cost of the
RYA fee for the issue of the certificate from £30 to £60 to cover the assessment and this will need to be paid at the time of
booking. The fine detail has yet to be worked though by many schools and an online course is being prepared by the RYA as an
option but the assessment will still need to be done in person at an RYA Training Centre. In short it will cost you more and take
longer after 1st January 2014

Therefore members considering doing the SRC in the near future will find it in their interests to get this under their belts before
1st January. Bob Wale is running a course on Sunday 15th December 2013 and will run at MSC if this is requested. Courses
can be booked and paid for on the Yachtwise website at www.yachtwise.org and the fee remains at £60 for the
course/assessment which includes a light lunch. The RYA fee of £30 for the issue of the certificate is separate and is payable
on successful completion. I have seen that Bradwell are also offering courses in December if mine is not suitable for you
although they are more expensive.

You will need this certificate if you charter or go abroad and it is a legal requirement in the UK so there has never been a better
time to get this done if you need it.

The Honorary Treasurer, Sue Shenton, presented the Financial Statement up to 31st August 2013.

Questions on the Honorary Treasurer's Report:

Referring to the Financial Statement, Kevin Kirby questioned the apparent discrepancy in the information on the
bank loan for 2012 and 2013. Sue Shenton explained that detailed accounts were not available for 2012 only an
overall figure. Detailed figures were available for the end of the 2013 MSC financial year and are reflected in the
Financial Statement.

Bruce Hood asked whether the current Bank Loan had an interest rate collar, possibly transferred from the
previous ‘purchase of club’ loan which he recalled did have a rate collar (as explained by the person responsible for
the financial presentation at that time). Bruce then briefly explained that a collar (also called an interest rate swap)
consists of a defined pair of ceiling and floor limits for the variable rate. A ceiling is advantageous in times of higher
than expected interest rates and conversely the associated floor is disadvantageous in times of lower than
expected interest rates. Since we are in a protracted period of the low interest rates what appears to be a decision
not to continue with a collar is proving to be a wise one.

Sue Shenton replied that she was not familiar with the term but could confirm that the interest rate is variable,
although there was an option to fix it if it thought appropriate in the future.

Bruce then pointed out that one simple measure of financial stability, often used in business, (together with the
cash reserve figure) is to look at the ratio produced by comparing the loan total variable rate interest charges i.e.
£17.7K (re Financial Report Page 4) with the net annual surplus i.e. £20K (thus 1.1 which is adequate/good). This
gives a useful indication of the amount of generated liquid cash likely to be available to absorb future rising interest
rate charges that may occur. In his opinion this is more meaningful and useful than the £227K Total Reserve
figure (i.e. owned Embedded Equity, excluding cash reserve) based on Tangible Asset Valuations.

Sue thanked Bruce for his input and confirmed that the suggestion will be considered.

Graham Cross stated that if the Club has bad debts these could be offset against corporation tax. Sue Shenton
explained that most financial losses were due to members not renewing their membership.

Commodore’s Report to the 2013 AGM

I will now give you my report which I will read so that it can be transferred verbatim into the Minutes of this meeting.

Sailing

I am delighted to tell you that Marconi Sailing Club has been active in its core business of providing facilities for sailing to its
members. I believe we have discharged this objective well and that the Club has had an excellent year’s sailing helped no doubt
by some unusually good weather.

ECPR

I will leave the detailed report on sailing activities to the Sailing Secretary, but as I was ECPR chairman (again) this year, I will
report on that Race. Back in late June all the different sections of the Club pulled together when we staged our “signature” Race
for the 26th time. Good conditions enabled the full course to be run with a minimum of incident. Although entry numbers were
down on last year we were able to donate £400 to Essex Air Ambulance and £2,100 to the Cirdan Sailing Trust who also raised
a further £12,000 sponsorship on the back of the Race. My grateful thanks go to every member who helped in any way,
especially the crews of the mother boats & RIBs that make it possible to control the risks inherent in the Event.

Cadets

Our cadet fleet has gone from strength to strength this year, building on the firm foundations laid by Bryan Spencer and
propelled onwards by the driving force of John Nickalls and his willing team. Not only have the number of training sessions
increased but numbers attending each session have also. All this is in addition to our successful and long running Cadet Week.

RYA Affiliation

We have continued to build strong links with the RYA with regular visits from area co-ordinators whose practical advice has
been helpful and instructive. We have also received valuable advice from the RYA Legal Department.

Sport England Grant

Although not directly connected, I am sure our close RYA relationship was instrumental in our successful application to Sport
England for a grant to purchase a new RIB to support our sailing. We are required to add match funding to the grant and an
order has been placed for delivery in the New Year. My thanks go to the three or four members who pooled their efforts to
complete the lengthy bureaucratic process of the grant application and to the procurement sub-committee headed by Andrew
Dowley.
Training Centre

During the year we took a decision to become an RYA accredited Training Centre. Again, much form filling is required and this
process nears completion. Meanwhile I am pleased to report that we have appointed a Chief Instructor in the shape of Pat Shaw
and he is in the process of gaining the formal qualifications necessary. We have also appointed Bob Collins as the impressively
titled “Training Centre Principal”. The intention is to be ready to train Club members to PB2 level by the start of next season.

Shoreside

Self-help
The Club’s only employee is Joan, our cleaner. All other work at the Club is done by our members. Whether it is Launching &
Recovery of moorings or cruisers; cutting the grass; maintenance of buildings, site or plant and equipment; it is all done by
members. This enables the Club to offer our members (particularly our cruiser members) excellent facilities at lower cost than
anything comparable elsewhere.

January 2014 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Our tight budget dictated that we only carried out one Capital Project this year, the new mast derrick. Much of the work was
undertaken by Club members thus keeping costs down.

A large amount of the work is carried out by the slightly inaccurately named “Wednesday Gang” led by Murray Bates. Inaccurate
because at mooring, launching and recovery times elements of the Gang work up to five days a week. In addition the
Wednesday Gang have brought the new meeting/training room into service and I hear that the long term project to provide a
Club launch for use as a Committee Boat nears completion.

One of the pleasurable duties of the Commodore is to select a member who has given outstanding service to the Club and
present him or her with the Commodore’s Trophy. This year I have selected a long term member of the “Wednesday Gang” who
is always around working hard and giving good advice. As an example, just recently he was on hand to rescue a Club sailor
who was drifting mastless towards Bradwell having ventured out in a Force 7. I am certain he is fully deserving of this award and
it gives me pleasure to ask – Colin Leveridge – to come up and collect it.

Management positions

In several ways it has been an unusual year. It has been a year of mid-term resignations from key positions in the Club
management structure, one of which was my co-option as Commodore back in April.

Both the Cruiser Fleet captain and the Sailing Secretary were unable to continue due to pressure of work and I am grateful to
Roger Camp and to Dave Russell & Jenny Ball for stepping forward at short notice to fill the voids so successfully.

Business of Board and Management Committee

I will now attempt to summarise the main thrust of business within the Board and management committee since the last AGM.

Safety.

Two different events have led us to give particular attention to Safety: -
The accident some 20 months ago to the mast derrick and new RYA Legal advice which was published in autumn 2012. This
has led to a “root and branch” review of all our safety systems with greater emphasis on the assessment of risk and the
updating of our written Codes of Practice. I am particularly grateful for the work of Andy Samuel and Ray Ball who led the
process, but many other did their bit as well.

Developing and updating of our systems to respond to the RYA Legal advice is well advanced but there is still work to be done,
especially with regard to the Club’s duty of care to children entering Club Races. I acknowledge the hard work, drive and
diplomacy of Michaela in the Board’s dealings with the RYA Legal Department and to Dave Russell, Jenny Ball and the sailing
sub-committee to whom much of the work of implementation has fallen.

The process has not been easy; some members have taken the attitude “we have always done it like this so why do we need to
change” and “we are a sailing club why do we need all this bureaucracy”. I think we have made progress in changing those
entrenched attitudes and I also say that any company in the business of providing the facilities and services that we do, must
keep up with changing legislation or face the consequences.

Proposed new Fee Structure

The other main thrust of Board and Committee business has been the proposed new fee structure. This is a summary of the
many historical, current and future problems that led us to embark such a major undertaking.

60 year old fee system.

Our existing fee structure has been evolving for the 60 years the Club has been in existence. It was not updated when we
bought the Club from MASC some ten years ago, nor since.
The current system is very complicated to administer and defies all attempts to use software to ease this burden. The system
has loop-holes that lay us open to both avoidance and evasion esp. with regard to dinghy/cat winter storage payments.
The Cruiser Park is not immune either. There are several “custom & practice” unofficial discounts and underpayments in
operation which do not form part of any fee system past, present or proposed. These unofficial discounts have encouraged a
situation where over 30 cruisers did not launch this year and did not pay a mooring fee.

Our existing By-laws and fee structure did not anticipate this situation and the only rate we have been able to apply for summer
storage is the second boat fee that was only ever intended to be applied to dinghies and cats.

The impact on Club finances does not need further explanation.
On a mitigating note, the Board does have the discretion to adjust cruiser fees when a member hits hard times, for example
serious illness. However few cases of the “no mooring but still storing” cruisers come into that category.

Basic imbalances between dinghies & cruisers.

Our practice over many years has been to apply a “percentage across the board” approach with increases to Fees. This has
meant that any small imbalance set-up many years ago has been magnified. Based on our research the Board believe that a
large imbalance exists between the fees we charge to dinghies and those charged to cruisers. Dinghy/cat fees are amongst the

January 2014 Navigans 13

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
highest and cruiser fees amongst the lowest; a trend that cannot be fully explained by the “self-help” ethos within the cruiser
fleet.

Demographics

Our membership is ageing as “baby boomers” reach retirement age and nearly a third of our membership is now in this bracket.
When this category was instigated all those years ago nobody had foreseen the rise in the active life-span we “oldies” enjoy
today. Unfortunately the discount we have offered for retired members is unsustainable.

We have another problem at the other end of the age range. We have a thriving Cadet Training scheme but, after we have
spent 10 years imbuing our youngsters with a love of sailing, few Cadets transfer into Young Adult membership.

Families

Although we have separate membership categories to differentiate between single and family members, as long as I have been
a member, we have charged the same amount for each, thus keeping the single membership artificially high to sustain the low
family rate. No other Club appears to have a similar practice, indeed many charge for each cadet member in addition to their
parents.

Revenue

The Board and Management Committee are also alert to the need to generate more income to put the Club on a better financial
footing for the future. This will be covered in more detail in the Hon. Treasurer’s Report.

The Board and Management Committee have considered all the above problems, complexities and unfairnesses and reached
the conclusion that they can only be addressed by the introduction of the proposed new Fee structure which is before you in
Resolution 2. I urge you to vote in favour of acceptance.

Thanks

I would like to thank everyone who has given his or her time, resources or expertise to help the smooth running of the Club.
I particularly wish to thank my fellow Directors for their support, enthusiasm and tenacity. They have attended and contributed in
full at often lengthy Board meetings; all fully motivated by our joint objective to ensure the present well-being and future
existence of our Club.
We have one director, Rear Commodore Bryan Spencer, who is reluctantly stepping down from his role after several years.
Bryan’s job takes him out of the country often and unpredictably but nevertheless he has been fully committed and determined
not to become another mid-term casualty. Bryan will join me in the ranks of Vice Presidents next year. I thank him on behalf of
you all.

I must express my admiration and thanks to our Company Secretary, Rall Ball, for the immense work he does for the Club. He is
a totally motivated, tireless and deeply knowledgeable “backroom boy”. He is the glue that holds the Club together.
Thank you Ray and please look after yourself.

The future

There is every reason to be optimistic for the future of our Club.
The new fee structure will be a solid foundation to build on.
Doubtless there will be challenges to come but, with a strong Board supported and advised by an equally strong Management
Committee, I firmly believe that the Club will be able to meet and overcome any challenges that a changing world can throw at
us.

Sailing Secretary Report 2013

Good morning everyone and it is my pleasure to present the Sailing Secretary Report for 2013.

Given we are a sailing club, and a very active one at that, this is the best AGM report to have to present - however,
it also presents some challenges – so I am going to start with two apologies. Firstly, I have endeavoured to cover
the full range of sailing activities in 2013 but if I have missed something out – I am sorry. Secondly, an enormous
number of people give up their time to support the wide variety of sailing activities that we all enjoy. Again, with
apologies, I am not going to try and name everyone as I will only miss people out – but a huge thank you to you all.

2013 has been another very busy year for sailing activity across the club.

In addition to individual sailing activity, the Cruiser Fleet organised a number of passage cruises this year to
Brightlingsea, Heybridge, Tollesbury and Ipswich followed by the Orwell and Stour. The weather was mixed for
some of the passages but the longer passage to Suffolk at least benefited from the positive summer when it
arrived. A number of successful social events were also arranged including the Fitting Out Supper, a visit by Colne
Yacht Club and the Cruiser Fleet AGM – all of which required the Bar Managers to do a full restock afterwards.
Thanks go to Mark Foster, George Male and Roger Camp as Cruiser Fleet captains during the year.

The Cruiser Fleet were also actively involved in racing with participation in East Coast Gaffers, BJRC, local
regattas and offshore races. Among those who had successes in these events were Nick Hillman, Richard
Roberts, Tom Clayton, John Littlewood, Dave Onyons, Peter Ward and their respective crews. Peter Ward and his
crew also successfully completed the Fastnet which is a tremendous achievement. Thanks go to Peter for co-
ordinating cruiser racing activities.

We would also like to register a particular thanks to the many cruiser fleet members who supported the East Coast
Piers Race and made this important event so successful – the safe running of this event depends very much on
this support.

Windsurfing members continued to be very active this year – and, as ever, were seen to venture out when the rest
of us had retreated to the clubhouse to drink coffee. Some of the windsurfers have also entered into the world of
cat sailing – presumably for when the wind is below a Force 6 – and they are welcome additions to those fleets.

Dinghy cruises took place on the first Saturday of every month from March to October and continued to be very well
attended. Local cruises ranged from trips to Maldon and to Mersea and all destinations in between. In June,
Marconi hosted a visit from the UK Wayfarer’s Association with a passage cruise round to the Crouch, camping
overnight in Burnham and returning the next day with a stop off at Thirslet for lunch. In May, the fleet travelled
even further afield, trailing their boats down to the Solent – launching at Eastney, sailing through Langstone
Harbour, round the top of Hayling Island and down through Chichester Harbour to Bosham and back. Thanks to

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Colin Wardell for arranging the cruises and a similar schedule is arranged for next year – do get in touch with Colin
if you want to join in.

The Cat and Dinghy racing season followed its usual full schedule of Spring, Summer and Autumn Points Races,
Bank Holiday Series, Wednesday night races and one off events such as the Jackpot, Marconi Challenge Cup,
Monas Cup, Pilot Cup, Figure of Eight and Last Fling. By my count, that lot added up to 217 individual race starts
over the course of the season – with not too many races lost due to inclement weather. We will celebrate the
successes in the Prizegiving after the AGM – it would be great if everyone could stay to support that and we
promise to keep it short and sweet!

In addition to regular club racing, the club successfully hosted a number of events including the East Coast Piers
Race which Clive has already covered, Open Events for Sprint 15s, Solos, Kestrels, Toppers and Junior Cats.
Away from Club racing, Marconi members represented the club successfully at Bala, Pyefleet Week, Rutland,
Island YC Cat Open, Sprint 15 nationals, Tornado Nationals, Europeans and Worlds. I think it is fair to say that
Marconi enjoys a positive reputation with other clubs and sailors come back and visit us year after year.

I would like to say a particular thanks to John Burgoyne, Dave Clarke, Jemma Clarke and Sally Wilson who have
managed Race Officer rotas, Support Boat rotas, Race Results and the Trophies and Prizegiving. Without their
efforts, the busy racing schedule I have just glossed over would simply not have been possible.

And last, but definitely not least, Cadet sailing activity has continued to go from strength to strength in 2013. Cadet
Week saw around 70 Cadets and 10 adult learners take part in another full week of sailing, racing and fun activities
with the welcome re-introduction of cat sailing sessions and a cruiser session courtesy of Peter Ward. The long
distance race saw well over 100 club members decamp to Thirslet Spit for a picnic lunch in superb weather. The
week ended with the annual Cadet Regatta. 44 young competitors turned out to race in 25 boats – giving the Race
Officer a bit of a headache. Around 60 helpers provided tutoring, support boat cover, launch and recovery and
general support to ensure the Cadet week was a success and we also had a paramedic on site to provide first aid
coverage. Our thanks go to Dave Clarke, Bekki Tovey and Chris Kirby who headed up the Committee which
organised the week. Thanks also to Max Friswell who ended his term as Cadet Fleet Captain and has passed the
baton on to David Nickalls.

In addition to Cadet Week, the cadets have been busy through the rest of the year. John Nickalls co-ordinated 7
very well attended Sail Training days throughout the season supported by an army of helpers including Bryan
Spencer, Lee Harrison, Tom Duckmanton, Rob Bard plus a number of Cadet helpers. The quality of those training
events and our young sailors has attracted positive attention and feedback from the RYA. Marconi Cadets also
performed very well in the Eastern Region Topper Event and Junior Cat Events – both hosted here at Marconi.
Further afield - John Nickalls and team co-ordinated a group of our Cadets to attend the National Schools Sailing
Association nationals event in July and a Team Racing event at the Royal Hospital School in November. And a
couple of specific individual mentions – William Harrison has been selected to join the RYA Topper 4.2 National
Squad – which is even more impressive as he is younger than the usual squad lower age limit. Additionally, David
Nickalls and Sophie Savill competed in the Dart 16 National championships – and not only were crowned Junior
National Champs but also outperformed all the adult competitors as well!

Whilst this is just a whistlestop tour of 2013, I hope it does justice to the full range of sailing we have all been
involved in. I have had the opportunity to visit a number of different clubs this year and it always re-enforces to me
how fortunate we are to have such a variety of sailing activity which many clubs either can’t or won’t do.

In addition to the people I have already mentioned, I would like to thank the remaining Fleet Captains, John
Salmon, Kevin Dowley, Dave Russell and David Bowman; the bosuns Roy Hardwicke and Colin Leveridge for
keeping the support boats in good working order and Pete Richardson for ensuring there was fuel to run them. I
would also like say a big thank you to Bryan Spencer who is standing down as Rear Commodore after several
years of staunch support for sailing and especially cadet training activity at the club.

Finally, whilst this is a report of the past year’s activity – I am pleased to confirm that arrangements are pretty much
finalised for the sailing schedule for 2014. We again have a full range of events planned across the season and
across all types of sailing. We will also be introducing some new activities to hopefully encourage even more
people to get on the water and enjoy the wonderful river and facilities that we are so fortunate to have. I look
forward to seeing you out there.

That concludes the Sailing Secretaries’ report.

BLACKWATER & COLNE COORDINATED CRUISER EVENTS
Q: What is it? A: It's about increasing participation in cruising.

A group of cruising sailors from almost all the clubs on the Blackwater & Colne got together at the end of the 2013 season to
see if it might be possible to organise joint events in 2014. The basis of the idea came from the fact that most of the clubs were
organising cruises to the same destinations, so why not pool and share the organisational effort, whilst many of the clubs were
turning out very small numbers on their cruises. Also, some clubs were only organising 'stay local' cruises whilst some of their
members might have liked to cruise in company to cross channel ports.

Two coordinated cruising events were decided upon and organisers came forward. These events now appear on the cruising
calendars of many of the Blackwater & Colne Sailing Clubs. Any member, from any sailing club is very welcome to participate in
any of the events. They are not races, they are most definitely cruises, but there could be fun prizes awarded by the organises.

Information on how to participate will be circulated later both through navigans, on the club website and through the website of
the Blackwater & Colne Open Sailing Series.

Here's some info to whet your appetite. If you'd like to chat about the events than Peter Ward is the Marconi contact (Yes I know
he's a racer, but these are definitely not races, Peter just has more info about them as he was one of the originators of the idea).

May Bank Holiday Weekend Rally - Pursuit

Date:
Saturday 24th - Monday 26th May 2014

Organiser:
Mel Daniels (WMYC)

Rally Start:
All Blackwater & Colne participants will rally at the Nass Beacon on Saturday morning 24th May.

Rally Format:
The rally will be conducted in the form of a pursuit. All participating boats must complete the registration form in the weeks prior
to the event so that each boat can be allocated a start time. Individual clubs can use the event to award their own trophies and
points.

Boats will sail leaving Bench Head to port and North Eagle to starboard and will take their own finishing times at Harwich
breakwater. The slower boats will start at least an hour after high water, which gives them time to get to Harwich just as the
flood starts, and allows upriver boats to get to the Nass in time for their start time.

Berths have already been booked for our sizeable fleet to enter Shotley marina on completion of the passage and these will be
allocated to participating boats along with their start times. Entrance to the lock will be staggered, so that inside rafted boats are
in position before their outside neighbours enter the marina. We're expecting a big turnout for this event.

Saturday Evening in Shotley:
The rally will hold an informal BBQ ashore at Shotley so boats participating in the rally should take along their own food, wine,
seats, portable BBQ's and stands for the BBQs so as not to burn the grass.

No doubt there will be other impromptu activities to keep everyone amused whilst the wine flows.

Sunday & Monday :
There will be a mini cruise organised for those rally participants able to stretch their time away from the Blackwater & Colne
beyond the weekend, and more details will be available as we firm up the planning of this element shortly. One possible option
