Happy Morning in Barbados
Mike Duckmanton reports on the latest escapades of the yacht “Happy Morning” and her crew in the Caribbean…
Ed

We are sitting on the beach at the Babados Yacht Club resting after an action packed couple of weeks.

We left Rodney Bay St Lucia on Friday 11 Jan to sail across to Barbados. The trip across was our worst. Two friends of David
Onyons members of the Maldon Little Ships Club (MLSC) David and I are all experienced helms and we had a new friend with
us who had never sailed a boat before although he had owned river boats back in the UK.

The wind has been strong around St Lucia and Barbados for several weeks which has increased the wave heights so we had a
rough crossing. Fortunately we were able to take it in turns to be ill or steer the boat. We finally arrived and anchored at Port St
Charles Barbados at 4-30am and managed to sleep until we were able to visit customs and book ourselves into Barbados.
During the trip one of David's friends stated that out of all his ocean experience including the Atlantic twice this was he worst
ever trip.

Later that morning we continued our journey to Carlisle Bay and anchored off shore at the Barbados Cruising Club.

We rested for the next few days visiting Bridgetown to sight see and do some shopping and meeting up with friends at the Club
where we had met and sailed against them.

Other friends of David Onyons and his girl friend had travelled directly to Barbados. Unfortunately one friend Bill who sailed with
us last year had travelled out a week before and had an unfortunate accident. He was found in the sea face down and
unfortunately died. This has put a cloud over our adventure this year.

We took part in the regatta on Friday 17th, Saturday 18th and Sunday 19th. The courses were on the west side of the island in
waters which were much calmer than the seas on the east side. We managed an overal 2nd in our class but because there
were only three in this class we looked at the times of other racing boats and were pleased with our overal performance.

Monday 20 January was a rest day and a day for getting Happy Morning ready for the race around the island.

On the day of the race, 21st January, we were up bright and early so we could load the crew on board.

Our crew was made up with David Onyons Captain, myself first mate and foredeck, David Harris main trimmer, Simon Onyons
genoa trimmer, Ian Gaskell 2nd genoa trimmer, Graham ex pilot and GP now our navigator, one ex Mount Gay Rum girl Belinda
weight on the rail. Two crew members didn't turn up but we were lucky a Canadian Leon was standing on the shore and asked if
he could join us, and it was sooner obvious he was an experienced racing sailer and now a new friendship is begin to form.

We headed off northward to round the island clockwise. Along the west coast the conditions were very good, but that changed
as we sailed round the north end avoiding reefs, no short cuts here. Turning south on the east side we had approximately 3
hours of hammering into Atlantic waves and strong winds. At east point we had to maintain a southerly course until clear of
more reefs. At this point fast boats which started after us this being a form of pursuit race, came past, Idea a 70 footer and also
a Volvo 70. You could hear their sheets groaning as they were eased as we all started to bear off and head west along the
south coast. More reefs to avoid on the south west corner of the island and then a long run to the finish. The tall Hilton hotel
near the finish line was a welcome land mark. Then the finish, and we had successfully and safely completed another Mount
Gay Rum Round Barbados race. Congratulations amongst the crew and promises to do better next year.

No rest the next day we were off for a Safari ride in a jeep around the island followed by the evening party and prize giving. This
year year most of us were in bed before 1-00am.

Simon Onyons had to get back to family and work so we have started to loose crew.

Tomorrow Saturday we go and log out of the island with Customs etc and Sunday up early for the 18 hour or so trip back to St
Lucia.

For now another rum punch and enjoy the cool weather, yes the weather here is not as warm as usual.

Mike Duckmanton

The Continuing Tale Of A Slow Meander Round The UK (part 1 of 2)
THE "LARKS CONTINUE" OR "THE LEAVIN O BONNIE SCOTLAND" SUMMER 2013.
It had become a bit of a tussle - stay or go - stay or go, still so much to see in Bonnie Scotland - this self centred debate swung
back and forth until eventually I could stand it no longer and as we say in the "Sarf" "I ad a word wi me self".

Look - I said, although you aren't getting any younger you are still relatively healthy and once you get round (the UK that is) if
you want to come back you can - you've done it once you can do it again - blimey - look at Malcolm Robertson he does it nearly
every year !

This seemed to settle the debate although the healthy bit struck home when I discovered a lump in my neck and on visiting the
doc - she unhesitatingly referred me to Addenbrookes (again !) where the consultant said "oh we'd better cut it out there's a lot
going on in the neck you know". A couple of scans latter there I was for the second year running being marked up with felt tip to
ensure they applied the blade to the right part of my anatomy. I did start to wonder after being under the knife last year for a
hernia op if these visits to Addenbrookes were to become an annual event as I gradually fell apart with age - but hey ho !

All this of course somewhat b - - - - -ed up my timescales to get South to Cardigan Bay in a nice leisurely way possibly detouring
to Ireland along the way but let's look on the bright side - it was a very happy old sailor who received the news that what they
excised from my person was nothing to be worried about and was just a fatty lump - and as they said at the time "better out than
in".

Nothing but praise for Addenbrookes - all done on the NHS with superlative care both in practice and care of the individual - in
the four clinic's I attended didn't wait more than 10 minutes beyond my appointment time and on the day of the op the consultant
even phoned home to my wife to say "he's OK and all went well but as we operated late in the day he's a bit dozy we'll keep him
in overnight, pick him up tomorrow". She said" he's alway's like that anyway but ok, thanks for phoning".

So what with all that going on little "Edal" wasn't launched till 21st June - and sat on her mooring at Barcaldine till the op on
11th July so we didn't leave our Scottish home of the last two seasons till 22nd July.

The plan was to get to Aberdovey in Cardigan Bay were my brother lives - to lift out in a small boatyard across the river at
Ynyslas - pronounced "Inislas". The passages between Barcaldine and Aberdovey would (all going well) be day sails - potential
ports of call and distances would be as follows,

Easdale - overnight at anchor, distance from Barcaldine 21nm.
Crinan canal - overnight at Cairnbaan roughly half way through, distance 13nm to entry of canal.
Tarbert - East Loch Tarbert, marina with pontoons, distance 10nm from canal exit.
Larg's Marina, distance 23nm.
Troon Marina - distance 17nm.
Girvan - harbour with pontoons, distance 20nm.
Glenarm, Northern Ireland - old harbour with pontoons, distance 41nm
Bangor - marina with pontoons, distance 22nm.
Arglass - old harbour with pontoons, distance 35nm.
Peel on Isle of Man - pontoons in harbour, distance 34nm.
Port St Mary, Isle of Man - berth against harbour wall, distance 12nm.
Holyhead - marina, distance 46nm.
Porth Dinllaen - anchorage, distance 28nm.
Pwllheli - marina with pontoons, distance 33nm.
Aberdovey - harbour wall or visitor buoy, distance 29nm.

You can see - no great long tiring passages in any of the days - fitting with
the ships established principles of sailing being fun, visiting new places,
tieing up in the evenings for a decent meal and a glass of red, enjoying a
good book in the cockpit, maybe stay a day or two if it's nice - all hopefully
after a light zephyr has breathed on the sails to keep to the skippers
immaculately prepared passage plan.

Minimum distance to be covered at sea 384nm, not including the Crinan
canal, nine land miles in length. Would be singlehanded most of the way
except for the legs between Troon and Peel where John another aged
sailor would join me for the trip across to Northern Ireland then down the
Irish Sea. There's also at least nine destinations where if the forecast
looked inclement for a few days I could go home quite easily. In practice I
went home twice once because of "home stuff" to do and once because the It was a beautiful early morning as I left the
weather looked poor. head of Loch Creran and the moorings.

BARCALDINE TO EASDALE 22ND JULY.
The ebb to take me south would start after HW Oban at 0610 and it was with a sad heart I dropped the mooring line in Loch
Creran - what larks I had had going from here round Ardnamurchan to those wonderful anchorages in points north - but for now
- here's to the new.

The wind was forecast to be light so motorsailed main and engine
low rev's out of the loch and past Oban - with tide keeping our SOG
respectable, we had covered the 21nm to Easdale by 1040 - 4hrs 18
minutes later. If you know this neck of the woods you might ask why
Easdale and not Puilladobhrain as a destination - everybody wants
to go to Puilladobhrain don't they ? Well I just fancied, particularly if I
never come this way again the more "gritty" attractions of Easdale
and it's industrial past. You wouldn't think it now but once this was
one of Britian's biggest quarries for slate, shipping it all over the
world from it's pier in the narrows between Sail and Easdale islands
and for a West Midland "Black Country Boy" a bit of industrial
heritage is just the thing for a bit of exploring ashore.

The Island, hollowed out by the quarrying into huge square pits,
flooded by "The Great Storm of 1881" which all but ended quarrying
on the islands and wrecked the local economy so that now the wee
Edal (middle of Pic) from Easdale Island, slate
remnants in foreground - ruined pier to right.

squares of hooses facing each other across their
communal greens are inhabited by a mix of locals and
holiday homes. It's an evocative sort of place with a nice
little local museum and scatterings of it's industrial past.
There's also a wonderful community centre so the locals
obviously think a lot of their "hollowed out" island. We
(Edal and me) had picked up the only visitors buoy in
the bay between the islands and after my history lesson
ashore settled down to an evening meal and some
planning for the easy passage to Crinan early tomorrow.

CRINAN TO CAIRNBAAN IN THE CANAL, 23RD JULY.
It was a peacful night at Easdale - another early start at
0648 to make sure we had the ebb to get through both Northern entrance to Easdale.
Sound of Luing and Dhorus Mhor - know by the locals as
"Big Doris". There's loads written about both of these so I won't go on - but safe to say it needs planning for tide and safe
water. As it dawned the morning was overcast and "driech" grey, grey, grey in a way that only the "hielans" can sometimes be.
Little wind, smooth surface to the sea until the narrow channel by the lighthouse appeared and the surface became troubled,
smooth here, wee whirlpools there, tiny wavelets over
there and patches of bubbling water which twitched the
boats steering and had me correcting to keep her on the
straight and narrow as we sped at over 8kts SOG past
the lighthouse and into the Sound. Completely on our
own in a rather wierd quiet grey morning - on the boat no
noise, little movement - almost like standing still, till you
looked around and saw how far we'd come from the
lighthouse. Passing by the Gulf of Corryvreckan, as we
approached Dhorus Mhor the morning brightened, speed
had slowed in the wider waters of the Sound and after a
slight change of course to head towards Big Doris - the
speed increased again as Doris sucked us in then spat
us out towards Crinan.

Little whirlpools on the water as we approach the
lighthouse on Fladda. Inner harbour at Easdale

The entry into Crinan is a personal milestone for this is
one of the canals Dad had some responsibilty for when
we lived in Scotland over fifty years ago, canals don't
really change that much and whilst I couldn't remember
every detail - it looked pretty much as I remember it.

February 2014 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
We were in the sea lock by 0912
having left Easdale at 0648 - 2hrs
24minutes for the 13nm distance.

It's when you get into inland
waterways that you start to
understand why people cruise there
- no tides, little wind effect, easy
slooooow pace if you want it. The
challenge though if you singlehand
is the locks - particularly going
uphill. Unlike the Caledonian where
the locks are all operated for you

the Crinan maintains a thing called
"assisted passage" which means if
you go through short handed they
will operate the locks for you and
take your lines unless they see you
going through with a couple of other
boats who being yachties all muck
in opening gates etc - the staff will
then stand back and let you get on Edal in Crinan sea lock
with it. At least though one way or
another you know you will get some
help so just have to figure out a routine of handing up your bow and stern line, keeping the boat steady in the lock and getting
the lines back ready for the next time. I had two 15mtr lines which I'd used in the Caley - put a loop secured with a bowline at
one end of each rope made them off fore and aft with the ends draped over the lifelines. As I came into the lock the loop on the
end of my boathook for the stern line
was passed up to a willing helper and
dropped over a bollard - brought the
boat to a halt shortened the stern line
then went forward to pass up the bow
loop and stood by to shorten either
line as she went up in the world - it
worked pretty well. I just made sure I
was last boat of three going into the
lock - felt under less pressure that
way and stayed away from the
turbulence of the sluices as the lock
filled.

Going downhill was much easier -
Bollards on your eyeline, with the
boathook you could slip the stern line
over as you went into the lock - the
bow line passed ashore to a helper
then sit on the coach roof with both
lines in hand as she went down.
Night's berth at Cairnbaan, toilets and showers nearby - it's all downhill from here !

Edal in the basin at Ardrishaig waiting for the sea lock into Loch Fyne.

Introduction
Roger Camp explained that Mark Foster had stepped down as fleet captain mid season due to pressure of work and that he had taken

Brightlingsea some dodgy cider was consumed.

CONDITION OF FIELDS
The wet weather continues at the time of writing and our fields are getting more waterlogged. (We are still better off than some
sailing clubs which have been under several feet of water.)

Until the fields dry out please be extremely careful where you take your car. Bogged down vehicles make a mess of the ground,
leaving ruts that people will be tripping over all season. Don’t think you are safe because you have all-wheel drive. 4 x 4s on soft
ground just dig four holes instead of two.

It is hoped that the fields will have dried out by the start of the season but after one of the wettest winters on record that cannot
be guaranteed. Please park wisely whilst the ground is so soft. If you need to get your boat past the cordoned off areas please
contact Murray Bates ) in advance.

website (see yearbook for username and password) and in hard copy in the clubhouse (upstairs lounge).

lounge in its own folder marked EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN & INCIDENT LOG. A copy will also be found under Operating
Procedures in the members section of the MSC website. Members are encouraged to read this document and remain aware of

BUYING OR SELLING A BOAT?
If you buy or sell a boat which is at the Club you must inform the membership secretary so that accurate records are maintained.
This is especially important now that dinghy and catamaran park spaces are numbered and pre-allocated. If you want to bring a
new dinghy or catamaran to site you must get a boat park allocation first. Don’t just put your boat in the nearest convenient
space as that may already have been allocated to someone else.

If you sell a boat and it leaves site please inform the membership secretary so that the vacated space can be reallocated. If you
sell a boat to a non-member remember you are responsible for it until it leaves the site.

Before bringing a cruiser to Stansgate or changing your cruiser you must first discuss your plans with the Moorings Secretary to
ensure that a suitable mooring is available. Bylaw 3.3 in your yearbook gives useful information on cruisers and moorings.

Dinghy/Catamaran Park Space Allocation Process
If you are buying, selling or changing a dinghy or catamaran dinghy, it is in your interest to follow this process so that you can be
contacted in an emergency about your boat and to avoid the possibility of being charged for a boat which is no longer your
property. To this end please ensure that your boat is located in its allocated position.

The record on Medusa is the Master Reference List of all dinghies and catamaran dinghies registered with the Club.

Dinghy Park spaces are given an identifier of DP followed by three numeric characters and similarly Catamaran Dinghy park
spaces using CP for the initial characters. These locations correspond with physical locations at the Club.

The Master Reference List on Medusa is maintained by the Membership Registrar, Dinghy and Catamaran Dinghy Park co-
ordinators using the process below.

SPACE ALLOCATION FOR NEW MEMBER AND NEW BOAT(S)
1. Membership application received by Membership Registrar who checks information and creates the Boat record assigning
a Z**nnn space location.

2. Membership Registrar contacts the relevant Park Co-ordinator and requests the space allocation.

3. The relevant Park Co-ordinator assigns the space and informs the Membership Registrar.

4. Membership Registrar updates the space location on the Boat record

5. On completion of the membership acceptance process, Membership Registrar informs the member of the space
location(s) and member is free to bring the dinghy(ies) and/or catamaran dinghy(ies) to the Club to store in the assigned
location(s).

SPACE ALLOCATION FOR EXISTING MEMBER AND NEW BOAT(S)
1. Member notifies Membership Registrar of details of the new boat who checks information and creates the Boat record
assigning a Z**nnn space location.

2. Membership Registrar contacts the relevant Park Co-ordinator and requests the space allocation.

3. The relevant Park Co-ordinator assigns the space and informs the Membership Registrar.

4. Membership Registrar updates the space location on the Boat record

5. On payment of any additional fees etc. Membership Registrar informs the member of the space location(s) and member is
free to bring the dinghy(ies) and/or catamaran dinghy(ies) to the Club to store in the assigned location(s).

RE-ALLOCATION OF SPACE ALLOCATION FOR AN EXISTING MEMBER AND EXISTING BOAT.
1. Member discusses and agrees with the relevant Park Co-ordinator the re-location.

2. The relevant Park Co-ordinator informs the Membership Registrar of the space being vacated and the new space location.

3. The Membership Registrar amends the Boat record to show the new location.

4. The Membership Registrar confirms the change to the member and the relevant Park Co-ordinator.

SALE/TRANSFER OF BOAT FROM ONE MEMBER TO ANOTHER MEMBER. (SEE CLUB BY LAW 3.1.4 AND 3.1.4.1)
1. The selling owner informs the Membership Registrar of the sale providing the details of the new owner.

2. The Membership Registrar confirms that the buyer has paid the relevant fees.

3. The Membership Registrar uses the “Transfer” facility in Medusa to update the Seller and Buyer Boat Records
Records

4. The Membership Registrar confirms the transfer to both members, the relevant Park Co-ordinator and the Honorary
Treasurer, who will refund any fees as appropriate.

SALE/TRANSFER OF BOAT FROM ONE MEMBER TO A NON MEMBER. (SEE CLUB BY LAW 3.1.4 AND 3.1.4.1)
1. The selling owner informs the Membership Registrar of the sale providing the details of the new owner.

2. The Membership Registrar seeks confirmation from the relevant Park Co-ordinator that the boat has been removed from
the Club site.

The Continuing Tale Of A Slow Meander Round The UK (part 2 of 2)
EAST LOCH TARBERT AND LARGS. 24TH AND 25TH JULY.
Came out of the sea lock at 1201 into a good 8 to 12kt southerly breeze - which after a quiet time in the canal - was just what
the doctor ordered ! It would mean tacking back and forth across Loch Fyne to get to Tarbert but who cared - we could sail and
we only had 10nm to go. Arrived and tied up on the pontoons at Tarbert at 1525. What made the sail down Loch Fyne
memorable though was the appearance of Waverley coming out of Tarbert on her way up Loch Fyne. No walk down memory
lane for a child growing up in Glasgow in the 1950's could exclude the memory of a trip "doon the watter" on The "paddlers"
Waverley and Jeanie Deans or later on the first Queen Mary. We went on both Waverley and Queen Mary - Mom, Dad and me
from the Broomielaw in Glasgow at different times over the years to Tighnabruaich and other ports of call in the Firth of Clyde -
these delightful old boats provided an escape to paradise for thousands of Glaswegians every summer down to the delights of
the beautiful Kyles of Bute and sometimes further. The old Queen is lying mouldering in the Medway awaiting funding to restore
her - but here is Waverley still plying her trade and as beautiful as ever.

The old Queen will hopefully be restored she's a historic
ship in being one of the worlds first passenger ships to
be turbine driven and of course for famously having
given up her name to Cunard for the later big liner to be
called Queen Mary (she became QM2) then regaining
her original name when the Cunarder was laid up in
America.

As nice as Tarbert was I was keen to go the following
morning as I had a further date with memory lane and a
Knickerbocker Glory in Nardini's Cafe at Largs. The tides

in the big waters of the Firth of Clyde and where Loch Fyne widens
are fairly benign the only part where I wanted to go with flow was
the last part of the passage between the Cumbraes and the SP co a
mainland so we left at 0938 which would allow us the last of the
flood up to Largs. The day was bright and we had a good breeze
until we turned round the southern tip of the Isle of Bute where the
wind died and it started to rain.

In fact it was very odd because the surface of the sea became very
still, wind died, but it absolutely bucketed down for about 15
minutes , greatly reducing visibilty until between the Cumbraes.

From the Lakin family archive Mom and me at
Tighnabruaich the old Queen Mary in the background
around 1960.

Motoring on through Cumbrae Pass Waverley again hove
in view - this time bound for Millport, for an old girl she
certainly gets about.

There is a little sideline to this story apologies if you've
heard it before - but when Carole and I bought Edal, we'd
made the offer, it had been accepted and we knew she was
ours - her previous owners kept her at Wolverstone on the
Orwell - we walked down the pontoon the better to view our
new boat and to marvel at her lines - like you do - and with
our backs to the river talking, after a while I heard this beat, beat, beat of the noise of her paddles coming back to me from over
the years and without turning round to look I said to Carole - I know that's Waverley - and sure enough it was.

We'd covered the 22nm to Largs marina in a little under five hours arriving at 1432 and found the marina a big impersonal rock
wall of a place - can't actually put my finger on it but I just didn't like it - the guy's in the office were fine, the toilets and showers
were too - wasn't too expensive - maybe it was all the jinormous boats - but then I've been in places with them before - strange -
just didn't like it.

So decided to move on to Troon next day which mean't I had to walk into town to Nardini's for my Knickerbocker Glory that
afternoon - I can hereby say Nardini's did not disappoint the KG was fabulous.

March 2014 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Nardini's in Largs is somewhere, everybody but everybody who visits Largs over the years would eventually gravitate to - to sit
in the Art Deco spendour and sample the delights of their ice cream or just "tak a wee scone tae their efternoon tea". I only got
my KG back then if I'd been a very good little boy but today I felt I deserved it again after all these years.

Sitting in Nardini's the years between seemed insignificant and my overwhelming feeling was of being happy were I was - like
being at home - despite the 50 or more years between visits - I also felt grateful - grateful for the parents who brought me here
and for the love and memories they gave me.

I could be accused of being a soppy old sod !

TROON 26TH JULY.
This next leg, small though it was at just 17nm and under four hours duration seemed a bit of a watershed. Most of the way
round (the UK) there'd been a "voyage of discovery" excitement to each days passage. Since entering the Crinan canal
emotionally, because of my family history it had been in the familiar territory of "memory lane". Like most people I'm very happy
with the familiar and would not have missed the days of retracing childhood steps. The "memory lane" phase though sort of
dulled the tingle of excitement that can be had when venturing into pastures new - now though I would be moving south and
starting out of the Firth of Clyde of my childhood.

The passage to Troon was initally a slow motorsail then a brisk sail with full main and genoa of 18nm which brought me into
Troon harbour by about 1445 - aaah this is more like it ! An old harbour with a very sheltered marina in it's far corner - a "comfy"
sort of place.

Here I would stay till August 5th when John would join me for the passsages south - I would use the time by doing a few
remedials on the boat, finish off my book and then spend some time at home. It had only been five days since leaving Loch
Creran, it seemed longer, I hadn't come very far south but the difference in the time to get home compared to being north of
Oban couldn't be more different. The train to Paisley 30 minutes, bus to Glasgow airport 35 minutes, Easy Jet to Stansted
about an hour - ok you have to wait around in the airport but when I came back to the boat I left home about half six in the
morning (I live about 30mins from Stansted) and was back on the boat just before midday - terrific !

My cockpit reading by the way in these five days was Admiral Sandy Woodwards memoirs of the Falklands Task Force - quite
revealing of the internal emotions of an outwardly hard bitten commander as his men die around him and what a close run thing
the campaign was.

One small tale which would interest men from Marconi was of the British warship HMS Brilliant. She left Gibraltar with a Marconi
man still on board (having been kidnapped) working on the Sea Wolf weapons systems radar - this man, David Brean was
described by the captain of Brilliant as having a deep working knowledge of missile computer technology. He became on the trip
south to Ascension and then on to the Falklands a key part of the warships team despite being a civilian.

In the defence of the landings at San Carlos Water, Brilliant's Sea Wolf wiring was damaged and at night as Brilliant was going
round to King George Bay to insert an SAS team David Brean got to work to rewire and reprogramme Sea Wolf. At length and I
quote from the book, he said to the Captain "we have a problem with the radar antenna up the mast" without a thought for the
knifing wind and the cold rain not to mention Mr Brean was not in the Navy the Captain said "better get up there then" David
Brean apparently gulped then said "OK Sir and proceeded to go up the mast in the middle of the night to fix the antenna - - "first
class man" said Captain Coward "best after sales service you can imagine"

The following morning morning HMS Brilliant reported one of her Sea Wolf systems completely operable again and that the man
from Marconi was working on the other.

Although it was gripping stuff I would not finish the book before going home and I would not pick it up again till the longer
passage to Holyhead from the wonderful Isle of Man - an island beloved of the TT enthusiast Murray Bates - in the next
episode of "Continuing Larks".

David Lakin

CAMPING RULES – 2014
THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE
DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES.

 All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.
 No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday
 Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.

 Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.
 No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.
 No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.

 No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on
site at all times.
 The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS
ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.
 All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that
guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present.
 Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.

 Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in
the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure
that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc.

 Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to
roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.

 Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If
you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other
people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require access to the
site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc.
 Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so
are probably not paying much attention to traffic.

 Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO
NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.

 The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises
vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.
 All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is
for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left
unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access.

Tony Benn
Tony Benn died aged 88 on Friday 14th March at his home in west London. He had been President of Marconi Sailing Club
since 2001.

The Benn family have been our friends and neighbours ever since the sailing section of Marconi Athletic & Social Club moved to
Stansgate from Heybridge in the late 1960s.

No doubt newspapers, magazines and historians will devote many column-inches to the life and career of Tony Benn but the
notes below attempt to illustrate the connection between the name of Wedgewood Benn and Stansgate.

Tony Benn (until 1973 Anthony Wedgewood Benn) had a long if controversial parliamentary career lasting from 1950 to 2001.
He stood down from Parliament in 2001 “to spend more time on politics”.

Those who are old enough will remember him as ‘the reluctant peer’ when he inherited the title of 2nd Viscount Stansgate from
his late father in 1960 (William Wedgewood Benn, 1st Viscount Stansgate). At that time peers could not renounce peerages and

April 2014 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
remain in the House of Commons. The passing of the Peerage Act in 1963 allowed Tony Benn to be re-elected as an MP. The
title of Viscount Stansgate still exits and is inherited by his eldest son Stephen who is now 3rd Viscount Stansgate.

Amongst his ministerial positions Tony Benn was Postmaster General (1964-1966). At that time I was a teenage trainee
technician on the GPO (Post Office Telephones). I like to think that it gave him added confidence in his role to know that a
youthful Ray Ball was on his team!

I and other Club members met Tony and Caroline Benn at Stansgate many years ago. They were a very pleasant couple. At
that time he was a minister and asked for permission for a helicopter to land on our field to pick him up the following day. That
was when the cat park was an empty field.

I am sure that other Club members will have met Tony and Caroline Benn and members of their family at various times over the
years.

Sadly Caroline Benn died in 2000. She is buried at the family home at Stansgate. It is understood that Tony Benn will be laid to
rest next to her.

Tony Benn was above all a family man and our sympathies go to Stephen, Hilary, Melissa, Joshua, his grandchildren and great-
grandchildren for their loss.

Ray Ball

STONE WATERSPORTS CLUB – EUROPEAN SKI RACING CUP – 26/27 APRIL
IMPORTANT NOTICE FOR ANYONE SAILING PAST STONE THAT WEEKEND
Stone Watersports Club will be hosting a European Ski Racing Cup meeting on the weekend of Saturday 26th and Sunday 27th
April. The main racing will be on Sunday 27th April between 10:00 and 14:00 but there will be boats and skiers out practicing at
other times.

The racing will take place in the main channel which is why the event has been organised for early season. There will be safety
boats around the course and Nigel Harmer the River Bailiff has been consulted.

The ski racing boats are seriously fast and the dangers to comparatively slow moving sailing boats crossing the course are
obvious. If you are in the area please be advised and directed by the safety boats.

We have a good rapport with Stone Watersports Club and they are very good at avoiding arranging events on ECPR weekend
so please cooperate with them if you happen to be sailing in the area.

As far as MSC racing is concerned we have the Figure of Eight Race and Spring Points 7 on the Sunday neither of which need
go anywhere near Stone.

EARLY SEASON WARNING
As I write this the sun is shining, the tulips are out and spring has (hopefully) arrived.

After the rain we have had this winter it is guaranteed that the water will be wet but also, on a more serious note, for the early
part of the season at least the water will be very cold.

It takes the water a long time to warm up. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and sandbanks before sea water
can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius.

Even if it is warm ashore make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take
inexperienced people afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip
or succumb to the wind chill.

It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm which is not only safer but more fun.

SAIL TRAINING NO1
Saturday 19th April saw a great turnout (26 cadets!) for our first sail training on a cool day, and some real effort and commitment
from everyone! I hope you all enjoyed it…

A few notes about what we learnt below... but before that, a HUGE THANK YOU to all the helpers! We split into two fleets,
which meant we needed more support boats and more people helping, as well as great helpers on the shore (including Davina
and Clare sorting out all the registration forms and who would sail with whom).

May 2014 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
THANK YOU ALL!

Splitting into two groups made a real difference, allowing us to focus on the needs of different sailors, very positive. The new
grant-aided RIB (‘Greygoose’) was a great asset for the training.

In the morning, Bryan helped Group 1 to have a think about the conditions (wind and tide) and how they'd affect the sailing.
Then they rehearsed 'how to tack' on the shore (thanks to David for his great help :-) ).

Sometimes it seems easier not to bother with dagger grip, 'superman' and changing hands after tacking... but it really will make
a big difference as the wind gets up, or as you want to sail faster. And remember, in a boat like a Pico you ALWAYS tack facing
forwards.

Then Group 1 went out and practised their skills just off the hard.

Group 2 crossed the river (wasn't the tide strong?) and sharpened their technique: some focused on gybing, and others on
improving their upwind sailing.

Remember, upwind sailing ('close-hauled') is all about pulling the sails in close and pointing the boat so that the sails just
completely fill with wind (don't flap at the front).

If you can do this, then (if it's at all windy) the sail will make lots of sideways 'tipping' force which you will have tobalance with
your weight. To do this, you need to get your feet under the toestraps, get your bum up on the side of the boat, and probably
even lean backwards ('hike out')... and then you need to steer the boat carefully (small tiller movements) so the boat doesn't tip
up too far but the sails don't start to flap.

This takes practice to do well! And if you find you're having to sit in the middle of the boat to stop it tipping (or 'heeling') towards
you, then probably you haven't sheeted in enough, or you're pointing into the wind.

Have a look through some of the lessons from previous sail training sessions to see some other clues :-). They're
here:http://www.marconi-sc.org.uk/61E54/Members_Area/Cadets/Sail_Training.aspx

In the afternoon we did some racing, over a very short course just off the hard... I hope you enjoyed it!

A key part of racing is the start, and it was great to see how much your starts improved as we went on.

Graham very kindly took some video with the club’s new RYA-helped GoPro camera, which we watched for a while in the
training room. I'll put some clips on Dropbox and send out the links to everyone who put their email address on the registration
forms, enjoy!

That's it for now... next session is Saturday 3rd May (only 2 weeks' time), and there's camping at the club that night. The
weather will OF COURSE be warm, sunny with a lovely breeze*... see you there!

(* Probably)

Marconi SC Sprint 15 TT - 12th/13th April 2014

In unprecedented mild weather for April, 17 visiting sailors joined 6 of Marconi SC’s finest for the first Traveller event and first
Sprint 15 TT event of the 2014 summer season.

Saturday morning started with promise of a consistent breeze that did not disappoint as the day went on. Along with the rain
staying at bay for all three races (although the weatherman did promise sunshine throughout!) the over-cast conditions were
good for competitive racing in April.

In Race One, the majority of the fleet opted to start on port with one or two boats on starboard creating an interesting dynamic
on the start line, that resulted in many boats getting a poor start. The two Sport mode boats, Kevin Dutch and Paul Grattage
battled it out between them all the way round the course with the rest of the pack led by Stuart Snell, Jenny Ball, Chris Tillyer
and Dave Ball chasing behind. At the leeward mark, the fleet split to different sides of the river for the upwind leg which was
against the tide – resulting in multiple changes of positions within the fleet. After three laps, Kevin finished just seven seconds
in front of Paul – but on handicap Paul Craft took first place and Jenny Ball took second place, with Kevin and Paul taking third
and fourth respectively. Down the pack, increasing breeze caught a few boats of guard resulting in a few unplanned swims!

Race Two saw the breeze easing off; again with the majority of the fleet on port dodging those boats that chose to start on
starboard. The ebbing tide had strengthened, combined with the drop in breeze making rounding the windward mark a bit more
challenging for a number of boats in the fleet and a few mishaps occurred! Kevin Kirby had a near perfect start which gained
him an early lead, chased by Dave Ball and Stuart Snell, in amongst the two Sport boats. At the leeward mark, the fleet again
split for the beat enabling Erling Holmberg and Jenny Ball to gain ground over the fleet leaders; a great tactical choice by both
boats. After a closely fought second lap, Kevin Kirby held on to his lead, closely followed by Jenny Ball and David Ball in
second and third place.

By Race Three, the wind had shifted favouring a starboard start at the outer distance mark. Kevin and Paul struggled to pull
clear of the fleet to start with, but on the second lap, with increasing wind favouring the Race Mode boats both managed to pull
out a clear enough lead to put in a first and second on handicap. Jenny Ball, Dave Ball and Paul Craft came in third, fourth and
fifth.

After nearly five hours of exhilarating racing, the fleet and safety boats returned to shore for a well-deserved slap up dinner, a
few (too many?) pints and a chat over the racing in the bar.

Sunday morning saw the weatherman’s predictions came true – glorious April sunshine greeted the fleet as they stirred into
consciousness. Along with the solar rays, a decent breeze rose throughout the morning, presenting near perfect conditions for
the now legendary long distance race around Osea and Northey Islands. The Race Officer set the usual figure of eight course
around the two islands, with an additional lap round Osea Island to ensure a proper long distance race given the favourable
wind conditions. The fleet set off in a good breeze and with a fair tide but shortly after the start, the wind began to be more
fickle with patches of light winds and stronger winds lasting throughout the whole race. Dave Ball led round the turning point at
Northey Island followed by Stuart Snell and Jenny Ball, with a gap to Pete Richardson and the rest of the fleet. However, on the
run back past Osea Island, the wind filled in bringing the Sport boats and Pete Richardson and Chris Tillyer up to the front of the
pack with a tightly fought leg to the turning mark. By now the tide had turned, making for a tougher beat against the tide back
past Osea Island. This leg saw Paul Grattage extend his lead over the water and the front of the fleet spread out with Stuart
Snell taking the lead for the una rigs. Stuart maintained his lead to take overall race win, with Paul Grattage second on
handicap and Dave Ball and Jenny Ball in third and fourth respectively.

After a very enjoyable weekend of racing, Jenny Ball took the overall win with Paul Grattage in second and Kevin Dutch in thi rd.
A big thank you to everyone involved in organising the event and to those who travelled from all over the UK to take part in the
first event of the season!

Jenny Ball

LIFEJACKETS – USELESS UNLESS WORN
Transferring to and from a tender is probably the time when yachtsmen are most at risk; particularly in the MSC moorings which
can be choppy and subject to a fast tide.

A recent incident served to illustrate this risk and the need to be wearing a lifejacket. The member involved was unlucky to end
up in the drink but fortunate that he was seen and an MSC RIB was covering cadet activities nearby and other help was at
hand. This may not always be the case particularly if sailing midweek. Take care when doing familiar tasks which you have
done dozens of times without mishap before.

(By the way, when did you last check/service your lifejacket? Does it hold air for 24 hours, if automatic is the actuator in date
and the CO2 bottle intact and not corroded? Instructions for servicing lifejackets are usually displayed on or in the jacket.)

KILL CORDS – USELESS UNLESS USED PROPERLY
Nearly all outboards whether big or small are now fitted with kill cords. Please use your kill cord attached to your person and not
attached to the boat.

ADDERS
Adders have been seen on site. There is nothing unusual in this; we have always lived with them and them with us. However
care is needed when on site particularly in long grass or when feeling under a boat or cover. Children should be warned.
Obviously if a snake is seen it should be left alone.

VISITORS
Members are reminded that ALL visitors to the Club must be signed in the Visitors Book. The Visitors Book is kept with the other
MSC documentation at the far end of the upstairs lounge.

Members are also reminded that any visitor is only permitted to visit the Club three times in any 12 month period (bylaw 1.1.13.3
refers). If they like sailing from Stansgate that much they are welcome to apply for membership.

‘REGULAR’ VISITORS
Following on from the above, if you bring a visitor regularly to the Club perhaps to crew on your dinghy, catamaran or cruiser
that person must apply for membership.

EAST COAST PIERS RACE & COLNE POINT RACE WEEKEND 5TH/6TH JULY.
The biggest open event in the Club’s calendar is only one or two weeks away. The Race Committee has been busy with the
organisation since January and we only need a decent forecast to tempt potential entries.

The ECPR is a 47 mile course to Walton Pier and back via gates at Bradwell, Colne point and Clacton with entry open to any
catamaran; however the 27 mile Colne Point Race has been open to fast dinghy entries, as well as cats, for the last two years
and this year we have targeted all such fleets. We look forward to a big turnout especially as we are expecting the spectacular
Moth fleet from Thorpe Bay. The length of the CP Race represents an exciting challenge in a dinghy or cat.

I am very pleased to tell you we have recently obtained major sponsorship from ZHIK who, many of you will know already, are
manufacturers of sailing clothing of excellent quality. The sponsorship is in the form of (surprise, surprise) donation of ZHIK
sailing clothing. We will use most of it as raffle prizes including the first prize which will be a ZHIK Isotak 801 Jacket plus other
sailing clothing to a value of £750. ZHIK clothing will also make up some of the lesser, but still high value, raffle prizes. Our
second prize in the raffle will be the traditional and much loved day’s sailing for five people in one of the Cirdan Sailing Trust’s
boats. Of course, to win one of these many raffle prizes you must buy some tickets which will be on sale at the Club before and
during Race weekend. Alternatively you can contact me by email on my address below I will get some tickets to you. Don’t miss
out - these are great prizes!

The Race continues to be supported by Adnams Brewery by the donation of draft ale and draft lager which will be on sale from
the bar all weekend. We have several other sponsors including Yachts and Yachting and one prominent member who sponsors
the Race every year with a tidy sum. Other sponsorship will be raised by the Friends of the Cirdan Sailing Trust using the Race
as a rallying point. Last year all the revenue streams produced a donation to charities of more than £14,000. As always, and
with your help and support, we hope to better that figure this year.

something that all competitors and organisers fully appreciate. Peter Clayton is “filling the slots” this year so please respond

Marconi Sailing Club, Medusa and Dutyman
My apologies as it may have been better to have had this in the last Navigans before implementing DutyMan but I failed to get it
into David Ball in time.

You will be aware that the Club took the decision to invest in the use of proprietary software for its membership database and
selected the Medusa system provided by Sailing Club Software for this purpose. One factor influencing that choice was the
availability of a linked system which is Dutyman also developed by Sailing Club Software.

Dutyman enables the Club to create its duty rotas, such as Support Boat, Race Officer and OOD, and make them available for
all Club members to view. It allows members to confirm that they will be available for their duties as well as being able to swap
duties between each other, at the same time informing the person with overall responsibility. It is expected that the ability for all
Club members to view the rota including any changes will allow Race Officers, OODs etc. to know who has confirmed that they
will be available and reduce the administrative load on the Club volunteer responsible for controlling the rota.

It may be that you are concerned that the Club has made your data available to a third party. This is not the case.

Sailing Club Software simply provide the software, technical expertise to develop and maintain the systems and the data
storage medium. Each club using the facility is set up in its own rights and has its own database. There are various different
levels of access to the system all under the control of the Club.

In our case Medusa can be accessed by myself and Mike Turner as Administrators having access to all the features, members
of the Board whose access does not include those features associated with the technical areas of the system, and currently
David Clarke who has access to the Duty Planning Module. Limited data from Medusa is downloaded to DutyMan under our
control without any involvement of Sailing Club Software personnel.

Within DutyMan I am the only person with access to all the facilities at the present time. Access for the ordinary Club Member
such as you is limited to viewing the rota simply showing the dates of events and the people scheduled for the duties. In addition
you can view your own profile data (taken from the Medusa system) but not other peoples’ although using the Directory feature
you can view their email address and telephone number. In the case of those who are scheduled for a duty, they do see the
email address and telephone number on the rota of others scheduled for duties.

June 2014 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
In addition, you as an individual can limit the data visible to other members, even to the extent of not being visible on the
directory, as explained in the email notifying you that we are using DutyMan.

For your information the email addresses dutyman@marconi-sc-mail.co.uk and administrator@marconi-sc-mail.co.uk are used
exclusively by David Clarke and me respectively. They are not associated with any person at Sailing Club Software.

I can appreciate that the wording in the email, which is coded into the system, can give the impression that Sailing Club
Software or Dutyman are involved in the day to day operation of the rota on our behalf but can assure you that is not the case.

So where from here?

Please log on and take a look at the rota even if you are not a Support Boat Driver or Crew.

Please confirm that you can do the duty as soon as possible so that everyone can see where we may be short of Support
Crews.

If you are a Support Boat Driver or Crew and cannot do your scheduled duty, please arrange a swop with someone else
scheduled to do the same type of duty, and follow the instructions to make the swop on the system.

If you need to swop with someone doing a different type of duty, such as a Greygoose RIB Helm swopping with a Marconi RIB
Helm, you will need to email David and myself to make the change for you. This is necessary as we have set up the system to
ensure that only those authorised by the Club can be allocated to the correct boats but it treats each RIB as a separate entity.

Although the system allows you to simply indicate that you cannot do a duty, please make every attempt to arrange a swop with
someone else and put it on the system. It is only by doing this that the Club will benefit from the potential of the system to
reduce the administrative load on the Support Boat Coordinator and for the Race Officers/OODs to view an accurate list of
those in support boats during their duty.

After an initial “Bedding Down” period, we will be extending the system to cover the Race Officers later this year but OODs will
probably have to wait until next year.

LAaisrrTM Sprint 15s at Carnac, France

Marconi sailing Club was represented by 3 Sprint 15’s at EUROCAT, Carnac, France from 1st to 4th May, a long standing
dream of Nick Dewhirst who sadly passed away last year but would have been proud to see 19 Sprint 15’s lined up on the
beach.

June 2014 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Peter Richardson and Kevin Kirby took the overnight boat from Portsmouth to Caen leaving a 3 ¾ hour effortless drive to
Carnac on the superb French roads, Jon Pease took the more ambitious route via Dover/Calais leaving an 8 hour drive although
he was still there for registration Wednesday evening!

Carnac, in The Morbihan region is a fabulous chic seaside resort with fine restaurants, wonderful shops and beautiful safe
beaches, Carnac yacht Club is one big catamaran club, geared to youth training and a lot of support from The French sailing
system looking at the number of SL16’s and Twinx boats lined up.

The first days racing commenced Thursday afternoon and the fleets were split in to 4 classes;F18’s, all other kite boats, Dart
18’s and our class of Sprint 15’s, Hobie 14’s,and Twinx 2 man youth boats so swelling our fleet to 27.The wind was Force 6
gusting 7 offshore so you really didn’t realize how windy it was until you got 500 yards from the shore but having seen sever al
cats blown over on the beach before launching we had a rough idea what to expect. It seems it’s not the race officer’s decision
weather to race or not, it appears if he can get on to the committee boat its sailable!

After a very uncomfortable sail out to the start line in heavy seas (it made wind over tide off M mark on a windy day a stroll)
Kevin and Peter decided with 3 more days racing in front of them that a swift return to the beach was in order. To his credit Jon
stuck at it and although he had a swim carried on to finish the first race, in the event it was the only race of the day, all the other
class starts were abandoned due to the many capsizes putting the substantial fleet of rescue boats under considerable strain.

Day 2 dawned bright with a F3 / 4, but having lost a day the fleets paid for it with 4 races back to back in short about 7 hours on
the water so by the time we got back to the beach the complimentary drink and croissant was very welcome.

Day 3 was a long distance race, some 40+ miles for the fast cats which included a 20’Phantom, a carbon curved boarded foiling
catamaran (a smaller Americas Cup look a like but with a crew of two) which was out of site of the chasing pack of Tornados,
F18’s and Vipers within 2 legs. For the slower fleets there was a shorter 22 mile course all in all similar to our Piers race. Our
three helms decided to have a day ashore taking in the sites and giving Liz and Fenella a well deserved day off from carrying
and fetching our trolleys.

Day 4 was the final day with no starts after 1pm allowing everybody to get finished and packed up. The wind had dropped to a 2
/3 but we were left with a difficult chop which made for some frustrating sailing at times but it brought to an end some fine sailing
in a lovely location.

The prize giving was conducted in a typical French enthusiastic manner with our class being won overall by Brian Phipps who
not only supports us so well as the UK distributor attending all major events, showed us that he has lost none of his sailing skills
to become the 1st European Sprint 15 Champion, runner up was Stuart Snell the current National Champion, Kevin was 6th,
peter 7th and Jon a well deserved 17th in a very competitive fleet.

The Sprint 15 fleet was singled out for a special mention by Carnac Yacht Club being a new fleet to EUROCAT, purist sailing at
its best with just a main sail and taking the top 10 places in our Class, easily recognizable around the park in our light blue tee
shirts organised by Jon for the fleet and supplied by our very own Dave Clarke.

The Sprint 15 association would like to double the number of entrants for EUROCAT 2015, we have within the class Cheryl
Craft who runs her own travel company and arranges everything, all the little hitches have now been ironed out, there is a lovely
EUROCAMP site a few minutes from the beach so if you are interested keep an eye on the association website or speak to me.

Kevin Kirby

EAST COAST

PIERS |XiRACE
East Coast Piers Race and Colne Point Race 2014
I am pleased to report another successful weekend for our premier open event of the year, the East Coast Piers Race (ECPR)
and Colne Point Race (CPR). The weather was benign, perhaps a little too benign, on the day of the big races while the
Saturday series produced more capsizes than I have seen for many years.

In a growing trend as more dinghies enter, this year the shorter CPR had the greater number of entrants than its Big Brother the
ECPR. While CPR ran its full course, Race Control had one decision to ponder in the gentle winds, which led us to turn ECPR
at Clacton.

I am particularly happy to report that Line Honours, first Tornado home and overall ECPR winner trophies were won by Mitchell
Glynn crewed by fellow Race committee member Andrew Dowley in a bravura performance. It is only the second time that a
Club boat has won the Race. Another headline performance in a generally good showing for Club boats had Jenny and David
Ball claiming third place in their Spitfire.

Mark Bunyan and Andy Bunyan sailing Sprint 15s were first and fourth with the intervening places occupied by ex-member
Simon Plumb and Barry Peters sailing Dart 18s.

The 49er easily won Line Honours in the Dinghy Race with the International 14 not too far behind, but overall winner, as last
year, was Club member Mike Taylor in his Osprey. In a “just for fun” PY calculation Mike would also have beaten all the cats in
the Race on corrected time.

My thanks go to Peter Clayton and all the Club cruisers who turned out as Mother boats and Matriarchs (M&Ms) to provide
essential safety cover for both Races. Coordinated by Roger Camp at Colne Point these boats and their crews provide
invaluable service enabling Race Control to keep close tabs on all competitors. This was especially helpful when one of the
backmarkers set course for the Crouch.

The good efforts of the M&Ms would count for little without the front line RIB support provided by Club RIBs crewed by members
but I acknowledge our friends from Stone, Bradwell Outdoor and Brightlingsea who joined the support fleet to give a high degree
of cover both in numbers and quality. Many thanks to you all. Malcolm Stuart & crew in Jack B were once again placing and
recovering buoys at each end of what is a long day for them and many others in the support fleets.

Shoreside organisation is equally important in a large event such as this and I acknowledge and thank Murray and Mick for
preparing the site & the buoys as well as bossing the hard; Dave Russell & team for scruiteering and beach-mastering and not
least, all my family especially Alex who manned reception, calculated results and organised the Prize Giving.

After our usual Race Officer, Mike Turner, was injured in June, I took on the RO role which meant I spent most of the day on the
committee boat where I was greatly helped by Leonie Golding, Linda Chaplin and more family members Dan, Sue and Marian.
My thanks go to Bryan Spencer, Julie Hawkins and Leonie who picked up the mantle for the Saturday races. They were helped
by Mike & Maggie Boreham who combined their usual Sunday role of running the leader-boards with the noisy Saturday job of
firing the cannons.

Auguest 2014 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Joining OOD Simon Elwell in the Race Control BUS this year was our Commodore who, having only previously seen the Race
from the competitors viewpoint, confessed to be greatly impressed by the level of activity and commitment of the team which
included regulars Barbara Davies and Ray Ball. Another safety feature of Race Control, are the spotters who are based on the
Matriarchs where they gather information and pass it to the plotters in the BUS. My thanks go to Fee Shaw who led the process
and to the spotters, some of whom had exciting RIB rides to and from station.

Finally I wish to thank the core members of the Race committee who meet regularly for some eight months a year to organise
Race weekend. Andrew Dowley; Roger Davies; Kevin Dowley and Ray Ball. It was a hard road and I could not have travelled it
without you. Many thanks.

It is too early to predict financial out-turn but I feel certain our chosen charities, Cirdan Sailing Trust and Essex Air Ambulance
will not be disappointed. We have enjoyed sponsorship this year from a number of sources all of which were gratefully received:
- Adnams for the beer and lager; ZHIK for lots of top quality sailing clothing which made up several raffle prizes; and three Club
members – Andrew Dowley at Dinghy Rope; Mark Foster at AM Safety and Kevin Kirby Ltd. In a sort of “reverse” sponsorship
Cirdan Sailing Trust donate a sailing trip for five in one of their boats. Leonie Back from Cirdan also kindly presented the
Trophies and drew the raffle.

ECPR & CPR 2015 will be held on 12th July. Put it in your year planner please.

Clive Shenton – Race Chairman.

Fleet News

Solo Speak
As we move into the best of the summer weather there have been some good developments in the fleet.

Firstly, we had our first trial of the new short race format in June. This is following up on the RYA recommendation that our fleet
racing would be improved by having shorter races, and more of them, in a day. The Sailing Sub Committee agreed that we
could try this on selected Summer Points Sundays by having an earlier start for the first Solo race such that we finished in time
to join in with the normal 11-o-clock start procedure for a second race on a back-to-back basis. This worked a treat and we are
very grateful to the Race Officer, John Nickalls, and the support boat crew who turned up early to enable this programme. All
taking part agreed that this format was more enjoyable than the normal programme so we are hoping to trial it again in August.

The other good news is that we have a new member of the Solo Fleet. He is Geoff Springett who made his racing debut in July.

The more people racing, the more enjoyment for everyone, so if you have a Solo come and join in the fun. If you do not have
one, we can provide boats that can be borrowed, provided that you are a competent helmsman. Just contact me in advance to
set up a chance to experience the joy of Solo sailing.

A quick reminder that our Solo Open Meeting is coming up shortly (7th Sept) so please support this event if you have a Solo as
we need maximum number of Club boats on the water.

John Salmon

This year’s East Coast Piers Race attracted 55 competitors, 17 from Marconi.

Saturday races were held in gusty conditions, within the River Blackwater.

Sunday’s East Coast Piers Race began at 9am in light wind which built as the fleet moved out of the river. With the wind up and
down it was decided to shorten the course at Clacton Pier. Once the leaders turned they began to catch the stationary Colne
Point fleet.

Colne Point Race had started 20 minutes later in light winds; this became a drift between Bradwell and Colne Point with only the
tide to help. As lead boats turned they struggled against the tide those at the back of the fleet closed in quickly. The rain came in
bringing the wind with it providing a good long beat back to the club.

Tornado’s took the line honours in both races with Kevin Dowley and Tom Brooks completing the 27 mile Colne Point Race and
Mitchell Glynn and Andrew Dowley completing the shortened 38 mile East Coast Piers Race.

Marconi members Mitchell Glynn and Andrew Dowley built a big enough lead to take the victory in the East Coast Piers Race,
only the second time in the club’s history that its own sailors have taken the top spot.

This year again saw dinghies compete in the Colne Point Race.

Commodore
Welcome back from the summer break - I hope each and every one of you has managed to make the most of the fair weather
and wind over the summer and took part in the huge number of activities on offer at MSC over the past few months.

I have a number of positive messages for you in this edition so I have endeavoured to keep my notes as brief as possible!

I am pleased to report that following in the footsteps of his late father Tony Benn, Stephen Benn has accepted our offer to take
on the role of President of Marconi Sailing Club. Stephen is the eldest son of Tony Benn and continues to be our friend and
neighbour at Stansgate. Many of you will have seen the new launch/committee boat moored just off the hard - the Tony B. The
Tony B is named in honour of our late President and a formal naming ceremony is due to take place shortly. I must also
acknowledge here the number of members who have worked tirelessly over the past few years to restore the Tony B to its
current state.

Following in Navigans are a number of reports from our packed events calendar over the summer. Please take the time to read
about the huge amount of activity that has been going on over the summer months. Highlights include a visit from the
Chernobyls Children, the National Schools Sailing Regatta, Cadet Week 2014, successful cruiser racing, topper traveller event,
solo and kestrel opens plus dinghy and cruiser cruises.

Cadet week was yet again a huge success with over 80 cadets taking part this year- thanks are due to the organising team
headed up by Dave Clarke, Bekki Tovey and Chris Kirby. They even organised the perfect weather!

I am also very pleased to be able to tell you that as of 11th September, MSC was accepted as an RYA Champion Club ‘with
flying colours.’ A formal presentation will take place at the Dinghy Show in March 2015 - so don’t forget to book your tickets.
Thanks are due to Lee Harrison for leading this initiative, which means that the club will have access to advanced training and
RYA resources.

I would like to thank the sailing sub committee and social secretary for their efforts over the summer. We have had a packed
calendar with a huge number of successful events. I would particularly like to thank Jenny Ball for the weekly update initiative to
let us know about ‘sailing and other activities at MSC,’ which we all receive by email. It’s amazing just how much is going on at
our club!

For interest - a recent return of information to the RYA has given us cause to look at our membership demographics which I am
happy to report are very healthy. As of the beginning of September we have 392 memberships which totals to 774 club
members - 144 of these classed as ‘junior.’

Finally, and very importantly - in this issue of Navigans you will find the notice of AGM which is being held on 23rd November
2014 and nomination forms for election to the club committees. Marconi Sailing Club only functions because of volunteers fro m
the membership who give their time to keep the club going. I encourage everyone to strongly consider standing for posts on the
Club committees. These positions are not fixed to ‘the same old people every year’ and we welcome new members and fresh
ideas. As well as the Board and Management Committees, there are a number of sub committees that play vital roles within the
Club structure. If you think you have the skills and importantly some time to give to the Club then please get in touch to see
how you might be able to help.

CLUBHOUSE SECURITY
A member who was on site late on the last Sunday of Camping Fortnight after everyone else had gone home found, in his
words, ‘every door and window in the clubhouse unlocked and open’. I will therefore repeat the note I put in Navigans last year
about clubhouse security. It’s YOUR clubhouse and YOUR money that would have to be used to put right any damage.

CCTV evidence shows that at all times of the day and night your clubhouse is being used by strangers such as beach fisherman
and casual visitors. The reason is obvious. Strangers know that the chances are that at least one of the outer doors to the
clubhouse will be open for them to use or abuse as they see fit at any time.

The solution to this is so easy. Always close the clubhouse after you have been in unless other members are actually using it;
particularly during ‘off peak’ times. Take the trouble to check the other outer doors; it will only take a few minutes. Do not leave
the clubhouse open because you or other members are working somewhere on site and might want to nip back there from time
to time. Everyone entitled to be in the clubhouse has an access card so closing the doors is not going to cause problems for
legitimate users.

The answer to all site security is very simple and is just common sense.

Solo Speak

SOLO OPEN MEETING 2014
Our Solo Open Meeting was held on Sunday 7th September when twenty helms signed on including five members of the
Marconi fleet.

The pre-race briefing was held in the club house when the course was described as a triangle followed by a sausage and the
position of the buoys was highlighted. High tide was given as 11:45 and 5-8 knot winds were forecast with a committee boat
start. Each race would be three laps with shortening of the course a high possibility. The scene was then set for races mid-river
between the Steeple shore of the Blackwater and Osea Island.

First Race - There was great enthusiasm in the fleet, dinghies bunched together racing for the line as the count down concluded
and the hooter sounded. As a great number of boats were over the line, too many to distinguish, a general recall was sounded.
While the fleet was regrouping and the countdown restarted rain lashed down but dinghies sped off in a clean start into the first
triangle of the course. The boats rounded the leeward mark and then passed through the start gate with Ewan Birkin-Walls
leading Steve Ede and Mark Maskell. The weather improved, although there was mist and cloud but the rain had stopped. At
the end of the first lap Steve Ede had taken the lead from Ewan Birkin-Walls and Chris Mayhew moved from fifth to third place.
Committee boat members shouted encouragement to Marconi sailors: John Salmon (Fleet Captain), Roger Smith, Mike Taylor,
Bryan Spencer and Gerry Kamstra. Towards the end of the second triangle the shortened course procedure was initiated. The
leading two boats crossed the line within a hair's breadth of each other with the third boat only just behind. The order had
changed again, Steve Ede first, Mark Maskell second and Ewan Birkin-Walls third.

Second Race - Now the tide was ebbing fast so the leeward mark was repositioned closer to the committee boat. The course
was the same. This time it was a very clean start. There was close racing at the front of the fleet, first and second had changed
places to give Steve Ede the lead at the end of the first lap. Some skilful boat handling and buoy rounding saw the first four
boats pull away from the rest of the fleet. With the course shortened to two laps, at the end of the race, Ewan Birkin-Walls
finished first, a good distance from Steve Ede, who was second, closely followed by Mark Maskell in third.

Third Race - Due to the light airs it was decided to run the third race without going ashore for lunch but it was now sunny. The
tide continued to run out strongly and to accommodate the low water the buoys and the committee boat were moved. The race
was about to start, with the countdown under way, when it was decided to postpone as not only was there no wind but most of
the fleet were too far away from the start line. Although this was frustrating the boats floated calmly while the helms chatted.
When a light breeze eventually blew it was fluky in direction which necessitated moving the buoys yet again. A new course was
set and sixteen boats were at the start line. Unfortunately, like race one, many were over the line causing another general recall.

Cadet Fleet
CADET WEEK 2014
Over 78 Cadets took part in Marconi Sailing Club's annual Cadet Week last week to enjoy 6 days of fun and training on the
River Blackwater.

The club caters for sailors of all ages and experience levels and tailors the tuition accordingly. This year a number of new
members took part for the very first time, after
having signed up to join the sailing club after its
successful Open Day back in May. Non-members
were also welcomed to join the fun.

To kick of the week, everybody took to the water
on the Monday morning to sail in some
challenging winds to familarise themselves with
sailing, which for many was their first time. In the
afternoon cadets were invited to take part in the
Capsize Drill, a permanent fixture of all Cadet
Weeks which teaches important boat righting skills
for the remainder of the week!

On Tuesday and Wednesday the groups
separated in to different fleets which allows the
volunteer Marconi tutors to provide specific
training and guidance in smaller numbers. Lighter
winds ensured everybody was able to enjoy a full
day on the water.

Osea Island was the destination of choice this year for Thursday's long distance race where the Cadets competed against each
other with a staggered start from the club's based in Steeple. The stronger winds proved too much for some with a number of
boats ending up capsized, however the training that was given on the Monday certainly gave people a chance to put in to
practice what they had learn to right the boat again! After enjoying a picnic lunch on the South Western area of Osea, the fleets
convened again to commence the second race of the day, against an ebbing tide for the trip home.

After another eventful summer of sport with the Brazil World Cup and the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, event organisers
decided upon the them of "Countries of the World" for Friday's fun day. After a morning of Pico Water Polo and Dinghy based
Basketball the groups joined together after lunch to take part in "The World Class Competition." Cadets split in to different
country groups to help assist "Captain Graham Cross." of the World Navy who had become stranded on Osea Island with his
fleet of 12 Laser Picos. Working as a team, the cadets had to find their respective country flag and the pieces of the boat that

Extreme 40 Sailing Series
August Bank Holiday saw the return of the Extreme 40 sailing series to
the UK for some spectacular close quarters racing in Cardiff Bay.

For those who are not familiar – Extreme 40s are cats which are a
scaled up version of something between a Tornado and a Spitfire –
complete with asymmetric kites. They are 40ft long so they can fit into
a container. They are very light and very fast and can do up to 30
knots. They also fly hulls, pitchpole and capsize (and crash) which
makes for good spectating and film footage so long as no-one gets
hurt.

Some of the world’s top sailors have been attracted to the series
which sees 10 – 12 teams competing at 8 events around the world.
More recently, it has become part of the training and recruitment
ground for America’s Cup teams. As such, this year’s teams include
JP Morgan BAR skippered by Ben Ainslie and Emirates Team New
Zealand skippered by Dean Barker. Former Marconi SC member
Mark Bulkeley is on board with Red Bull Sailing Team. Additionally, teams are required to have a crew member who is either
female, under 25 or an amateur sailor so it is becoming a great training ground for new talent.

A core element of the Extreme Sailing Series is that it is accessible to public spectators – as opposed to other events which take
place offshore. The venues are, therefore, chosen to support this and the race courses are very tight and compact – particularly
for boats of such size and speed.

Cardiff Bay is a perfect setting – an enclosed sailing arena and anywhere the
spectators stood around the bay gave them a perfect view of the racing. The
official spectating area was freely accessible to the public. Corporate and
hospitality clients got the opportunity to go on board the boats during each race
as Guest Sailors (subject to weather conditions) – which is a pretty unique
opportunity!

The format is multiple races each lasting around 10 minutes and the race marks
are about the same length apart as our club marks. The finish line is shorter than
the club start line and was just off the harbour wall in full view of the spectators.
Additionally, the sailors are often around the public spectating area as they attend
race briefings etc and were very open to requests for photographs and
autographs – even when about to go off racing. The atmosphere is very
accessible and family friendly.

Having followed the series on the web and Youtube for some time – I decided to
sign up as a volunteer for this year’s event. Over the three days I got to help guest
sailors get into sailing gear, ambush members of the public with leaflets and
information they may or may not have wanted and on the last day, I was in charge
of the finish hooter and the big clock that counted down to each start!

We were able to attend the skipper’s briefings and try to overhear the redress
hearing between Team New Zealand and SAP. We were lucky enough to get out
on a RIB to watch two of the races and, thanks to the rainy weather, some guest
sailors did not show up so we got to be Guest Sailors for the final race of the
series! I was lucky enough to be assigned to Red Bull so got to sail with Mark
Bulkeley again – I reckon the last time that happened was 25 years ago in a Mirror
…….

And – as some of you may know, I am a massive fan of Team New Zealand so rounded off the weekend with a picture with my
all time hero Dean Barker!

The Extreme 40s are at Istanbul, Nice and Sydney for the remainder of this year – and the series will return again next year with
an event in the UK (Venue and dates to be confirmed). See www.extremesailingseries.com for info and some great footage.

I can highly recommend going along for some or all of the next UK event – it is refreshingly geared up to the fans and if the
breeze is up, it is fascinating viewing for anyone, even a non-sailor. I also bumped into a number of sailor friends – either

have a support boat duty, do read the guidance notes. Even if you have driven or crewed on support boats before it is worth
reading the latest version of the relevant notes; they do get updated from time to time.

Winches, tractors, mast derrick and boat hoists also have their own codes of practice and user guides. Please read them. Their
relevance to the operators of the equipment is obvious but it is also useful for boat owners to be familiar with the codes of
practice. You will have a better understanding of the operation of the equipment, which is satisfying in itself, but also appreciate
the operators’ point of view and the codes of practice under which they work to ensure the safety of all involved.
