Mike Smith 1929 - 2014
LT.CMD. M.A.H. SMITH (SCC) R.N.R M.B.E.
In 1959, aged thirteen, a school friend suggested that I ‘try’ the Sea Cadets. Yes, I thought, a sailor’s suit would be irresistible to
attract the girls, as I cycled from Billericay to Brentwood one summer’s evening.

This was the first time that met Mike Smith; He was a young C.P.O. Instructor, having recently come out of the Navy where he
had served as a P.O. Telegraphist / Yeoman. This would explain why anyone making a faux pas with their flags was firmly
corrected by him! Unbeknown to me this was the beginning of a life long association with sea cadets and with Mike Smith, who
became my instructor, mentor and then to lifelong friend.

In the early 1960’s he built a heron dinghy in his garage and I could only marvel at his carpentry skills. It wasn’t long before he
was teaching many of us to sail on the River Crouch, in the Heron.

Mike’s drive and enthusiasm for Youth work took up nearly all his spare time and he was soon promoted to become the
Commanding Officer of Brentwood unit.

Following a disastrous fire in the old unit it was due to Mike’s motivation and the aid of his highly qualified committees, as well
as the parents and friends that the new unit was built in 1966. Alongside this construction he also instigated and fulfilled his
dream of a Boat Station on the River Crouch. There must be many hundreds of people who have fond memories of weekends
and weeklong courses afloat at the Boat Station, learning to sail.

I recall one occasion when we were both examining candidates afloat in the Walton Backwaters; each of us in a 16 foot six open
dinghy , with six cadets in each . One candidate froze on the mainsheets! The boat slowly heeled over to 90 degrees and Mike
in equally slow motion entered the water with his clipboard held aloft and was heard to say ‘You’ve failed son!’

After more than the usual period of ten years in command, Mike was promoted to District Officer, for the eleven units in Essex.
His enthusiasm and leadership was then transferred to all these units and he was greatly respected throughout the area.

Mike’s commitment to youth work was recognised, in June 1980, when he was awarded an M.B. E. which he proudly accepted
at Buckingham Palace; not that this altered his down-to-earth attitude to life. It was about this time that his serving Sea cadet
career was coming to a conclusion. He then devoted his time to management committee work with the Sea Cadets as well as
becoming a member in the Royal Naval Sailing Association, sailing under the blue ensign.

Mike’s love of boats meant that he bought a succession of small craft, in varying states of repair, and was always at his happiest
using his restorative skills to make the current project sailable; until the next acquisition appeared.

Working for Marconi ,at this time, he decided to join the M.A.S.C. and M.S.C. and many of you will know that he always had time
for a yarn and a joke or two. Those of us that went aboard his boat were never allowed to leave without sampling his ample
supply of rum and hospitality.

His presence of 33 years, with the M.S.C., has been and will continue to be felt within the club not least because of the various
projects that he undertook. He instigated and designed the Dell Bar, now the Managu bar, where club members meet and
socialize today which he built and equipped almost single handed.

We will all be aware of Mike’s love of dogs and he rescued more than I can remember. I have fond memories of many of them,
not least Hobi. This dog was well known at the sailing club; he also loved boats but more than that he loved jumping off of them!
Many was the time that Mike was seen chasing after Hobi, in a dinghy. But the frustration of ‘first catch your dog’ resulted in
Hobi being confined to terraferma .

Mike told me that his claim to fame, in his opinion, was that in 1940, as a spotty schoolboy, he organised a petition to start a
Sea Cadet unit in Brentwood. The list of names he collected was treated seriously and as a result 1941 saw the inaugural
meeting of Brentwood Unit Number 52. The one thing that upset him, as the first member, was that his name was not the first in
the ship’s books. Smith will never be first in the register. At that time the corrugated iron building was being used as a Soup
kitchen and subsequently shared its use with Unit Headquarters. Interestingly the new unit, still in use, was built on the original
site.

Mike loved sailing and was seen sailing a week before his death. At the grand age of 85 years, I can think of no greater tribute
or inspiration.

Derek Hall

Fleet News
420 Open Residential Class Training at Rutland
The 420 is a great boat to sail: it's challenging, with a
traditional symmetric spinnaker and a much more tunable rig
than many other boats... and it goes really well in a breeze.

Hannah Bard and I, and Jack Collis with Jack Wardell, seized
the chance to join 4 days of 420 Class Training up at Rutland
Water (the week following the Laser Inlands). It was a
residential course, staying in the clubhouse bunk-rooms with
all the other sailors. The group was very friendly and got on
well; most of us were in Yr 11, with some as young as 13 and
up to 18.

After a hot breakfast (three hot meals a day!) Hannah was
delighted that each day started at 8:15 with a warm-up /
fitness work for an hour, then we had a briefing on the day's topics. Boat handling was covered, including trim/balance etc., roll
tacks, roll gybes, spinnaker work and double tacks; other sessions included rig setup, race tactics, starting skills, team racing
and many others.

The 13 boats were coached (often in separate groups) by three top-end coaches (Steve Irish (470 Olympic coach), Tom
Mapplebeck and Sam Brearey) so we had great inspiration as well as feedback on all our faults! We had two on-the-water
sessions each day, with the final debrief usually finishing after supper around 7:30.

Overall it was a great 4 days: Rutland was perfect, it was great socially and we had a lot of fun learning a lot about high
performance sailing. Thanks to everyone!

Dan Nickalls

MSC at Laser Inlands
The number of Lasers sailing at MSC is rising, and looks set to rise further, so we thought it would be interesting and fun to take
up the challenge of the Laser Inlands at Rutland on 25th - 26th October. We sailed in different fleets: Dan in the Radial (with 103
others) and David in Standard rig (with 43 others); with the 4.7s, there were nearly 180 Lasers on the water, sailing off the same
line but with inner and outer loops to keep us reasonably separate.

It was windy! Finding a good slot on the line had to be balanced against getting clear air and staying out of trouble. Loads of
boats capsized (including us) in the strong gusts. It was impressive to see the leaders sailing radical angles downwind, including
by the lee, to take advantage of shifts and the waves that had built up at the bottom end of the enormous reservoir.

The weekend was exhausting, but we learnt a lot and could clearly see the difference between the top sailors and club racers.
We're looking forward to the next chance!

David and Daniel Nickalls

Ron Greygoose
As this edition of Navigans was going to press we learned with deep regret that Ron Greygoose had passed away in Broomfield
Hospital on Saturday 15th November.

Ron had been a member of the Club for many years. The records of the early MSC days are incomplete but records from 1970
onwards show that Ron occupied the following positions in the Club:

Sailing Secretary 1971 & 1972

Vice Commodore 1975 to 1977

Commodore 1978 to 1980

Vice President 1981 to 1992

President 1992 to 2000

Solo Fleet Captain 1982 to 1984

This is truly a remarkable record of service to the club and until fairly recently, although no longer sailing himself, Ron was still
prepared to take his place in the race box as Race Officer.

Ron compiled the Club History with pictures for the MSC website which is well worth reading.

The Club was pleased to name the new RIB Marconi Greygoose after Ron; which was a fitting tribute to his years of service to
the Club and now a fitting memorial.

Above all Ron was a true gentleman in every sense of the word with a smile and a friendly word for everyone. His passing is a
great loss to those who had the pleasure of knowing him.

Our sympathies go to Ron’s family and friends at this sad time.

Ray Ball

Saltmarsh 75 – An alternative way to see the River!
Saltmarsh 75 is a long distance event which (as its name suggests) covers the 75 miles of sea wall from South Woodham
Ferrers, through Fambridge to Burnham, turning left along the Dengie peninsular to Bradwell, along the south bank of the
Blackwater to Maldon, then along the north bank past Tollesbury and finishing in the village of Salcott.

And you do all that in a weekend. And some people are mad enough to run it – although you can also walk it or even enter as a
relay team.

As many of you will know, walking along the sea wall by the River Blackwater or Crouch is one of life’s great pleasures and over
the past few years, I have walked virtually the entire route albeit in much smaller chunks. I therefore recognised some of the
challenges that the Saltmarsh 75 organisers warn you about – eg. that stretch between Burnham and Bradwell, the weather, the
terrain and the psychological challenges of seeing your destination quite close as the crow flies, but having to walk a lot further
as the sea wall twists and turns around various creeks and inlets. I knew that I would not be able to do proper 8 hour training
walks as I was sailing every Saturday and Sunday in the run up to the event in early October. I also noted how many
competitors had dropped out after the first day at last year’s event.

But I decided to give it a go anyway with the target of at least completing the first day. I did not manage to convince Dave to join
me – but I did sign him up as my pit crew for the day.

The next stretch was 13 miles from Burnham to Othona (Bradwell) which is one of the most isolated walks you can do in Essex
– plus the forecast was for the weather to deteriorate significantly. About an hour into this leg, the wind swung from southerly to
a strong north westerly and it poured with rain. Unhelpfully, this was as the walk turned northwards along the Dengie peninsular
– meaning three hours directly head on into cold, driving rain. One of the advantages of sailing is being used being soaked to
the skin and walking around all day in wet boots – which is just as well. Even so, I got very, very cold and by now my legs and
feet were tired and sore. However, I decided not to risk stopping because of the cold and ploughed through the whole four
hours from Burnham without a rest. Unexpectedly, I started catching up a lot of the groups of walkers who had taken rests and
who looked pretty miserable – clearly not sailors!

Dave met me at Othona with some welcome additional jumpers and food! I wrung out my socks and boots as best I could. A
number of walkers had got so cold and miserable that they decided to call it a day at Othona – including some who had
managed the whole event last year. I was not inclined to give up although I was so cold, I could not do my boot laces back up
and I was getting concerned I would not be able to complete the walk before the 9.30pm cut off.

Helpfully, the rain cleared and it was a beautiful walk in autumn evening sunlight to the next checkpoint at Bradwell Marina
where Dave was kind enough to meet me again with a steaming mug of coffee!

walk!! By this stage, I was having to stop every few minutes because of muscle pain in my right hip so I was also not particularly
quick! The last stretch was from Stone Sailing club, through to Marconi, along the access road and then across the fields to
finish the day at Steeple Village Hall. Dave met me at Marconi and then escorted me along the sailing club road to the footpath.

Peter advised that there are plenty of drying moorings available however deep water ones are all allocated. There have been
two breakaways this season and they have all been above the Buoy. He stated that everybody should have two strops and
advised that one of these should be a chain. The breakage occurs when there is no swivel as the strop always turns with the
tide in the same direction and this causes it to unwind.

CRUISER RACING DEVELOPMENT
In the last season through my involvement in the clubs management committee I became aware that the club has an ambition
plan.

The plan has been in place for a number of years and many of the developments we have seen i.e. opi club, new rib, support
boat containers, changing facilities upgrade, barn e.t.c. can be linked back to ambition plan objectives.

On the plan are statements relating to racing such as:

Status

We will be recognised nationally (and in Europe) as a club that hosts well – run open events (national and
international) and sends competitors to open events across a wide area.

As a consequence of all of the above and our own self-promotion we will be known as one of the premier sailing clubs
in the UK

Activity

The Club will promote a strong racing calendar for its major fleets, will encourage members to compete nationally and
internationally and will seek to attract Open event activity.

With regards cruiser racing, there have been a number of small initiatives and achievements by club members that help the club
towards achieving its goals, but this has mainly been unplanned and coincidental. There are clear signs that Marconi are
becoming recognised as a cruiser racing club locally for a number of reasons, and this provides us with the opportunity to build
our reputation further. We are a long way off being one of the premier cruiser racing clubs in the UK, but I’d like to think that we
could become in the very near future, the premier cruiser racing club on the Blackwater, if not Eastern region.

When cruiser racing issues have been discussed at both the sailing sub committee and management committee meetings in
recent years, there has always been enthusiastic support and I am in no doubt that any development plan that we might put
forward for cruiser racing, will receive support and encouragement from these committees.

A meeting has therefore been arranged for existing members with an interest in cruiser racing, to discuss topics that might be
used to formulate a development plan for Marconi cruiser racing.

Topics for discussion might include:

Club Members only racing.
Increasing numbers of Marconi boats in races.
Cadets racing on Cruisers.
Marconi cruiser racing Open Regatta.
Club owned Keel Boat Fleet Acquisition.
Promoting a Marconi Offshore Open Race.
Attracting Racers to join from other clubs.

The meeting will be held in the bar at 2pm on Sunday 11th January.

I look forward to hearing your ideas.

Ron Greygoose - A Tribute
In last month’s Navigans Ray Ball marked the sad passing of one of the Club’s longest serving members, and listed the many
offices that Ron held going back to the Club’s formative years. His service to the Club has been outstanding, and it can truly be
said that he has contributed in no small way to shaping the Club that we enjoy today.

January 2015 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
But Ron’s passion was dinghy racing. When I first came across him in the early 1970s he was one of the helms in the very
strong Enterprise fleet that Marconi had at that time, competing in Club, Area, and National championships. He subsequently
moved on to a 420 with daughter Louise as crew, and briefly a Laser, before buying his first Solo in about 1980 when I also
joined the Solo Fleet. Ron and I must have been racing each other in
Solos for at least 25 years, and he was one of the people who gave
me the most help while I was learning to sail the boat. Ron was

2014 Commodore’s Report - Michaela Dowley
AGM 23rd November 2014
I will begin by commenting on the main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season.

Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board, and for the previous financial year has comprised six directors:

Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site

Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment

Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing

Graham Cross - Rear Commodore for events

Sue Shenton - Treasurer

Myself, Michaela Dowley - as commodore I am managing director and chair

We welcomed Graham and the return of Pat to the Board this year both of whom have hit the ground running and ensured a
balanced representation across the fleets at Board level.

Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of
the administrative burden of the Club.

The Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like to extend thanks to all who take
the time to serve on the main and various sub committees to enable the Club to continue to thrive.

I would like to review with you the subject of memberships and fees - the new fee structure voted in this time last year had been
the subject of much debate and I must extend thanks to Clive Shenton for steering the Club through a difficult yet essential
process. As a reminder, the introduction of a new fee structure had 3 aims:

1. Simplicity - bringing in a fit for purpose, sensible charging system

2. Fairness - to address the basic imbalances between dinghies and cruisers

3. To generate more income - accounting for our aging demographic

I am delighted to report that at this point in time, there are 400 members of Marconi Sailing Club. This compares to 399 at the
same point last year. This stands us in a very positive position in light of the following facts:

1. We are holding our own at a time when clubs in our local area see membership numbers declining.

2. Some considered that the new fee structure would drive members away and this has simply not been the case.

3. The demographic of the membership is encouraging in that 25 of our members are young adults and 152 are families.

4. The Clubs financial position is sound - the details of which I will leave to the Treasurers report. However I will say that
the Club is in an improved financial position as a result of the new fee structure. This will allow us to invest in capital
improvements and maintain our site and facilities.

This past year has seen the embedding of our new membership system, Medusa and the use of dutyman which is software that
allows the coordination of support boat and race officer duties. As with all new systems there have been some teething issues
but I thank all the administrators who have made the systems work for us.

As many of you are aware, unfortunately in March of this year our Club President, Tony Benn sadly passed away. Tony Benn
had a long, if controversial Parliamentary career spanning from 1950 - 2001, when he then became President of Marconi Sailing
Club. The Benn family have a long history with our Club both as friends and neighbours and I am pleased to say that Stephen
Benn, Viscount Stansgate and eldest son of Tony has agreed to be our next President. Later in the agenda you will have the
opportunity to vote Stephen in as an honorary member of MSC and as President.

Moving onto sailing, and without treading on the toes of the sailing secretary, I have to say that 2014 has seen a new breath of
life come into the sailing calendar. Thanks to innovative thinking from the sailing sub committee, we have seen the introduction
of a number of new activities on offer - all designed to encourage members who are perhaps less confident on the water or wish
to hone their skills.

I have to add sincere thanks here to Jenny Ball who has again continued to demonstrate her commitment to our Club. Jenny
proposed and implemented initiatives such as the Friday free for all sessions, revised the sailing programme to incorporate
more popular styles of racing and has been instrumental in driving an increase in dinghy sailing participation. She is also the
mastermind and author behind the sailing activities emails that grace our inboxes weekly. Like me, many of you were probably
unaware of the extent of all our activities. So Jenny, thank you.

Turning to cadets - the future lifeblood of the Club. Cadet week, in its new format was yet again a tremendous success. Sail
training continues to go from strength to strength and this year has seen the addition of ‘Oppi Club’ aimed at our members as
young as 2.

January 2015 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

It is here that I would like to take a moment to recognise the contribution of John Nickalls to the development of our cadets.
John has worked tirelessly over the past few years particularly in driving sail training with an incredible 409 individual cadet
sessions delivered this season. This year John has also been involved in coordinating other events and activities such as the

The sailing secretary will cover the various opens and training events hosted at Marconi this year, however I will report on the

The dinghies, catamaran and cruiser racing fleets have also travelled the length and breadth of the UK and even into Europe to

I would like to reflect on one particular race where there was an incredible achievement for an MSC crew.

The Round Ireland Race is run by Wicklow Sailing Club every two years.

The 2014 Race attracted 36 starters including McGregor IV from Marconi. The crew included Marconi members Peter Ward,
Tom Clayton and Derek Brown with a number of other members involved as delivery crew.

The Race is a course of 704 nautical miles and the Race instructions are very simple – leave Ireland to starboard. Any crew
completing this course has exhibited seamanship of the highest standard.

McGregor IV finished 2nd in Class and 10th overall in a time of five days 11 hours 18 minutes and a few seconds.

For this achievement I ask the owner and skipper of McGregor IV Peter Ward to come forward to receive the Seamanship
Trophy.

Hosting opens and large events have been supported by access to the Tony B and our new support boat which took to the
water in February of this year. Marconi Greygoose is a 5.5m rib and is the result of a successful Sports England grant. She

very poignant at this time to say were pleased to name the new rib Marconi Greygoose after Ron. This is a fitting tribute to his
years of service to the Club and is now a fitting memorial.

The Tony B took to the water late this season and is named in honour of the late Tony Benn. This has been project over a
number of years, with all renovation work carried out in house, mainly by the Wednesday gang. The Tony B has a number of
functions, serving as a support to mooring parties and also as a committee boat.

As well as on the water, there have been many shoreside activities and developments.

MSC is ‘on the map’ more than ever before thanks to our new website, open day and numerous publicity opportunities with
regular articles in yachts and yachting and the local press. We have also seen improved links into the RYA with Marconi now
recognised as a Champion Club and RYA training centre.

dinghies provided 100 individual sailing trips whilst the children’s activities and Pimms Tent were very popular onshore.

Social events in general have been a huge success this year with a number of new ideas and wider participation. Events have
included Morris Dancing, Bands, theme nights and quiz evenings to name a few. Social events have helped to drive up the
revenue generated by the bar - so I thank you all for helping on that front.

The bar has also been open more frequently this year, often on a Sunday to help hydrate members after a days racing or
working around the site. We all know serving behind the bar can be a thankless task. Although not purely for her barwork, it is

opinion she is a truly deserving recipient of the Commodores trophy for 2014.

presentation of accounts by various suppliers which will now be met in 2014/2015. Social and publicity showed an increase of

Marconi SC Sailing Secretaries’ Report 2014
AGM 23rd November 2014
Good morning everyone and it is my pleasure to present the Sailing Secretary Report for 2014.

I am pleased to advise that 2014 has been another very busy year for sailing across the club. I will endeavour to do justice to
the range of activity but I apologise in advance for anything I may have missed.

With support from the Board and Management Committee and encouragement from the RYA, the Sailing Sub-Committee set
out to enhance sailing participation during 2014. There were four strands to this:

1. continue improving the club’s sailing equipment and capability

2. support activities to recruit new members;

3. introduce some new activities to encourage wider participation

4. make our sailing activities more accessible for existing and new members to join in

We were fortunate this year to have some welcome additions to our sailing related equipment. The new RIB, part funded
through a grant, has been a valuable add to our support cover. The club has recently bought a new Laser and Topper thanks to
proceeds from Cadet week and a generous individual donation. And 2014 saw the launch of our very own purpose built
Committee Boat – the Tony B – which was officially baptised at the Helm of the Year event. A big thank you to the many
people involved in making these projects happen and continuing to build our sailing equipment and capability.

This was also our first season as an official RYA Training Centre which means we can now deliver RYA accredited power boat
training – thanks to the efforts of Bob Collins as Principle and Pat Shaw as our qualified instructor. We have taken this
opportunity to train club members to RYA Powerboat standards and Bob and Pat will continue to expand this offering going
forward. The club was also awarded RYA Championship Club status this year in recognition of the club sail training and racing
activities. Thanks to Lee Harrison for co-ordinating this with the RYA.

In May, we supported the Open Day which Michaela has already covered – with cruisers, cats and dinghies providing 100
individual sailing trips, alongside the shore based activities.

With new or recent members in mind, we introduced Friday Free4All evening sailing sessions. We provided safety boat cover
and offered support for people who wanted to build on their sailing skills or just go for a sociable evening sail. These sessions
were very well received and with the galley providing an evening meal after sailing – it was pretty much the best way to start a
weekend! Based on the popularity of Wednesday night pursuit races – we also included some Sunday pursuit races to
encourage people who prefer racing from the hard. Both of these formats will be continued next year.

We also reviewed the communication of sailing activities in the club. The year book and website continue to be the main source
of information about club activities. However, they do not necessarily explain what a particular sailing activity is or how to get
involved which might deter some members from joining in. We therefore introduced a Sailing Information leaflet to supplement
the year book – by explaining how the different activities work (eg. dinghy cruises, cadet training, cruiser events, club racing etc)
and who to get in touch with to find out more. In a similar vein, we also introduced the weekly email to remind people of
upcoming sailing activities and encourage people to join in. We hope members have found these to be positive additions to
club communications.

And we have had plenty of activities to talk about in the weekly emails!

The Cruiser Fleet organised a number of passage cruises including Brightlingsea, St Katherine’s Dock, Ipswich, Tollesbury and
the Watercress Run to Heybridge. Annual social events included the Fitting Out Supper, visit from Colne Yacht Club and
Cruiser Fleet AGM. On the racing side, Woozle Hunter netted 14 trophies in the East Anglian Offshore Racing Series including
winning their class and coming 2nd in the overall series. Caroline and Blue Moon posted consistent top 3 placings in the BJRC
races and McGregor IV competed in the Royal Ocean Racing Club Series coming second in class and fourth overall amongst
an international fleet in what is a very challenging series. Congratulations to Ian Ivermee, Andy Ellis, Richard Roberts, Peter
Ward, Derek Brown and their respective crews. Thanks go to Roger Camp as Cruiser Fleet Captain and Peter Ward as Cruiser
Racing Rep.

We would also like to register a particular thanks to the many cruiser fleet members who supported the East Coast Piers Race
and made this important event so successful – the safe running of this event depends very much on this support.

Dinghy Cruises continue to go from strength to strength with cruises on the first Saturday of the month from March to November
and taking part in the UK Wayfarer Association Rally over the late May Bank Holiday weekend. The dinghy cruise schedule for
next year is being expanded with cruises in January and February and the introduction of some weekday cruises – so watch this
space! Thanks to Colin Wardell and the team for co-ordinating the cruises.

Windsurfing members continued to be very active this year – and, as ever, were seen to venture out when the rest of us had
retreated to the safety of the clubhouse. The windsurfing fleet have been successful in recruiting new members and the club
has recently purchased some windsurfing equipment to encourage people to give it a go. See fleet captain, Nick Miller if you
are interested!

The Cat and Dinghy racing season comprised a full schedule of Spring, Summer and Autumn Points Races, Bank Holiday
Series, Wednesday night races and one off races. It would be remiss of me not to report that, with the exception of Wednesday
night races, participation in racing was down this year vs last year. We are not unique in this and some of it is due to individual

January 2015 Navigans 20

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
circumstances – but it is an area that we will review to see if we can improve racing participation next year. Nevertheless - we
had a total of 221 fleet race starts over the course of the season – with very few races cancelled due to wind or participation.
We will celebrate this season’s successes with a short Prizegiving after the AGM – we would appreciate if everyone could stay
to support that.

The club hosted a number of events including the East Coast Piers Race which Michaela has already covered, Open events for
Sprint 15s, Solos, Kestrels, Toppers, Junior Cats and the Dart 16 Nationals. Marconi members also represented the club at the
Sprint 15 Nationals, Tornado Nationals, Grafham Cat Open, Maylandsea Bay and Thorpe Bay Winter Series – and we will be
represented this Christmas at the Tornado Worlds in Perth!

Marconi was also well represented at the Barts Bash – an event involving 600 clubs around the world in memory of Andrew Bart
Simpson, Olympic Sailor and to promote the Andrew Simpson Sailing Foundation. We joined forces with Stone, Blackwater,
Maylandsea, Bradwell Cruising Club, Goldhanger and Harlow Blackwater Sailing Clubs to put on this event over three race
courses. 54 Marconi cruisers, dinghies and cats took part raising over £1000 for the charity – many more club members were
involved as support boat crews and race support and we also organised the Guinness World Record witnesses! It was a
wonderful event and the sight of 200 boats racing together on the River is not one that any of us will forget in a hurry.

And last, but definitely not least, Cadet sailing activity has continued to go from strength to strength. Cadet Week saw around
80 Cadets and adult learners take part in another full week of sailing, racing and fun activities. The long distance race saw well
over 100 club members decamp to Osea for a picnic lunch in superb weather. The week ended with the annual Cadet Regatta
with 42 competitors turning out to race in 25 boats. Around 60 helpers provided tutoring, support boat cover, launch and
recovery and general support to ensure the Cadet week was a success. Our thanks go to Dave Clarke, Bekki Tovey and Chris
Kirby who headed up the Committee which organised the week. Thanks also to David Nickalls who ended his term as Cadet
Fleet Captain and has now passed the baton on to Beth Spencer.

In addition to Cadet Week, the cadets have been busy through the rest of the year. John Nickalls co-ordinated 8 very well
attended Sail Training days throughout the season supported by an army of helpers. Attendance ranged between 12 and 40
cadets split into two groups so training could be tailored based on experience levels. This was supplemented with the new Opi
Club run by Fee Barnes for cadets who may not feel quite ready to join in the sail training – providing a welcome addition to our
training provision. Further afield - John Nickalls and team again co-ordinated a group of our Cadets to attend the National
Schools Sailing Association Regatta event in July. Marconi Cadets also performed very well in the Barts Bash, Eastern Region
Topper Event, Topper Nationals, Junior Cat Event, Laser Inlands – and David Nickalls and Sophie Saville are this year’s Dart 16
National Champions.

In addition to the people I have already mentioned, I would like to thank the remaining Fleet Captains, John Salmon, Kevin
Dowley, Tom Brooks, Rob Bard; the bosuns Dave Clarke and Colin Leveridge for keeping the support boats in good working
order and Tony Goode for maintaining the race marks. Additionally, John Burgoyne, Sally Wilson, Dave and Jemma Clarke
have ensured that Race officers and Support Boats were rota’d, that results were calculated and trophies organised.

Whilst this is just a whistlestop tour of 2014, I hope it does justice to the full range of sailing we have all been involved in. I am
pleased to confirm that arrangements are progressing well for the 2015 sailing schedule. We again have a full range of events
planned across the season and across all types of sailing. I look forward to seeing you out there.

Employment of Contractors by Members 16/01/2015

1. Introduction

This Code of Practice covers the employment of contractors by members at the Marconi Sailing Club site.
This Code of Practice MUST be followed when any contractor is employed by members to work on their boats or equipment.
It is recognised that members may be assisted by relatives and friends when working on their boats and other equipment, who
receive no financial remuneration. In such cases it is the member’s responsibility to ensure their safety and well being.
Under no circumstances will the Marconi Sailing Club, its officials, employees and other Club members be held responsible for
any injury incurred by any person working on a member’s boat or other equipment.
At all times any equipment supplied by the Marconi Sailing Club may only be used under the supervision of an Authorised User
and in accordance with the appropriate Code of Practice.

2. Definitions

Club Member: - Any individual member or group of members of the Marconi Sailing Club.

Contractor:- Any person, company or organisation employed by a Club member to carry out work on the member’s boat, trailer
or any other property for financial gain.

3. Member’s Responsibility

1. To ensure that the contractor is given a copy of this Code of Practice.
2. To ensure that the contractor has current Third Party Public Liability Insurance (minimum recommended amount
£5,000,000 Five Million Pounds).
3. To ensure that any equipment supplied by the member for the use of the contractor is safe, correctly installed and fit for
purpose. For example that any ladder is adequate and suitably fastened to the boat.
4. To obtain the agreement of the relevant Board member if the contractor will be using any Marconi Sailing Club
equipment. (Contractors are expected to use their own tools and equipment as far as possible. This benefits the
contractor who knows their own tools and equipment and minimises the use of MSC equipment. However it may be
necessary to use MSC equipment, an example would be the mast derrick, where it is impractical for the contractor to
supply their own.)
5. If MSC equipment is required, to make the necessary arrangements with an authorised user of the relevant Marconi
Sailing Club equipment to attend at a mutually convenient date and time. The contractor and others may assist but
only under the Authorised User’s supervision.
6. To ensure that they or their representative (who must be an MSC member) is present at the Club at all times when the
contractor is on site. To record all such times in the MSC Log Book which is kept in the upstairs lounge in the
Clubhouse including any damage/incident occurring. Any damage to other members’ property must be recorded in the
logbook and reported to the owner of the property as soon as possible. Similarly any damage to Marconi Sailing Club
property must be recorded in the logbook and reported to a member of the Board.
7. To ensure that the clubhouse and site are securely locked when the contractor leaves the site.

4. Contractor’s Responsibility

1. To comply with this Code of Practice.
2. To furnish to the Club member a copy of their current Third Party Public Liability Insurance (minimum recommended
amount £5,000,000 Five Million Pounds).
3. To ensure that any tools/equipment they supply and use on site are fit for purpose and used in a safe manner.
4. To only use Marconi Sailing Club equipment in the presence of the Club member and a Marconi Sailing Club
authorised user.
5. To ensure the safety and well being of any other persons on site who may be affected by the activity. For example
ensuring that adequate shielding is in place to protect others when arc welding etc.

5. Member’s and Contractor’s Joint Responsibility

1. To act at all times with due regard to current Health, Safety, and all other relevant legislation.
2. To record any Dangerous Occurrence, Accident or other situation in the relevant documentation in the Club House.
Completed sheets must be sent to the MSC Safety Officer.

Club Notices
Commodore
Welcome your March 2015 edition of Navigans.

At the recent RYA dinghy show at Alexandra Palace, Marconi were presented with our RYA Championship Club Status. As a
Champion Club we can look to enjoy the support and help of the RYA in achieving our aims in youth training and development
including advice and support from our local RYA High Performance Manager. Thanks are due to Lee Harrison for driving
forward this development with the RYA.

I would like to update you on some applications for external grant funding that the Board of Directors have been working on over
the winter months.

In 2013 we were successful in obtaining a £10,000 Sport England Grant for a new safety boat - the Marconi Greygoose. In
February 2015 we submitted a second application for £10,000 towards a rowing gig. The rowing gigs are built by the Pioneer
Trust, based in Brightlingsea where young apprentices learn the boat building trade. We were fortunate enough to have a
rowing gig on site during camping fortnight in 2014 where a number of our members showed an interest in rowing and had a go
themselves. There is a very active gig community on the Blackwater and we believe the gig will be a great asset to the Club,
allowing more people access to activities on the water. We hope to hear soon if our bid has been successful.

We are also in the process of compiling an application for the Sport England Inspired Facilities fund. This is a fund where
awards of up to £50,000 are made to aid in the renovation and modernisation of local sports facilities. Marconi SC will be
submitting a bid to support the development of a permanent covered area over the patio at the rear of the Club, plus a viewing
platform or veranda extending from the clubhouse towards the BBQ area which incorporates a secure storage area beneath.
These are exciting projects, which will allow us to improve our training facilities and enhance the experience for members.
However, these projects are dependent on the success of our grant application. The deadline for applications is at the
beginning of June 2015 so I hope that we will have more news to share with you towards the end of the summer.

You may have seen recent emails regarding the cat and dinghy parks. I would like to thank Jenny Ball and her team who have
taken on the mammoth task over the winter of reconciling our membership database records with boats in the parks. It is
absolutely essential that all boats in the parks can be identified for a number of reasons, one of which is to ensure that all fees
have been paid. Please take note of the information contained in the emails and ensure that your boats are clearly labeled with
your information.

I would also like to remind you that the Spring working parties are scheduled for the Sunday the 8th and Sunday 15th March -
please do support the Club by attending to help get us ready for the new season which is now rapidly approaching!

Michaela Dowley

OODS & INFORMATION
If you have an enquiry or a request for something to be done at the club when there is an OOD on duty, the OOD should be
your first port of call. They have experience at the club and access to keys to just about everything.

If you become aware of an emergency on the water the OOD has contact with the race officer and support boats. If there are no
club events taking place the OOD has access to the small RIB.

Committee and board members are happy to talk but remember that the chances are that they are at the club for the same
reason as you and that is to go sailing. To get stopped when just about to get changed for a race or about to hop into a tender to
go cruising can get a bit tedious.

Of course this is not to say that committee and board members shouldn’t be approached but you are just asked to choose your
times.

SOLO FLEET BOWLING EVENING
As you may remember from previous reports the Solo Fleet are keen bowlers (well once a year).

So eight, with three supporters, descended on Madison Heights Bowling Centre in Maldon on Friday evening February 20th. As
usual we played two games with a snack in between.

All bowlers, including the two ladies, showed real skill in the first game and although there was one bowler well ahead, the
scoring was very close.

There was a good choice of snacks which was served on a long table to take all eleven of us. This was very much enjoyed .

The snack must have fired up some people for they seemed to have their eye and arms co-ordinated (if that’s the right
expression ) afterwards. This resulted in some good total scores.

The first lady was Julie Spencer (214) and she was awarded the trophy and a bottle of wine. I think it may have been a little
overwhelming for the men as Julie’s score was 13 higher than the highest man. That was Mick Taylor (201) (presented with
trophy and wine). Next was Dennis Dear (187) followed by Geoff Josey (175). A good night was had by all, with the supporters
sitting by the two lanes adding their encouragement.

Dennis Dear

WINTER DINNER DANCE REVIEW
The new venue this year for the Clubs Annual Dinner Dance, proved to be a success!

Over 100 people began the evening at the Orsett Hall, by enjoying a cocktail reception listening to concert harpist, Danielle
Perret playing a selection of popular music for all tastes.

Caricaturist Paul Gurney provided amusing likenesses of many of the guests (hopefully, no-one was unable to recognise the
person looking back at them on the page!)

Good food and good service was provided by the chef and the waiting staff. I know at least one guest who required a special
diet,who said the staff couldn't have been more helpful.

The D.J. Russell Frost seemed to please the majority of revellers with a wide selection of music.

I do hope that Clive Shenton, who won a raffle prize of a (model) combine harvester, appreciated the Wurzels playing "I've got a
brand new combine harvester" as he walked back to his table!! I know I did.I used to love that song!

The Clay family had a field day with their photography. Rob tells me they took about 250 photos!

All the feed back I have had was very positive. If anyone has any further constructive comments, please contact me at
. I really want to build this event up and encourage as many members as possible to enjoy, what really
is a great evening out of wetsuits and buoyancy aids!

Sorry for those of you who weren't able to get tickets this year. There was quite a waiting list of hopeful people. Tickets sold out
relatively quickly. So remember for next year, buy your tickets early!

I may look at a larger venue if early indications suggest this would be beneficial.

CAMPING RULES – 2015
THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE
DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES.

 All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.
 No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday
 Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.

 Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.
 No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.
 No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.

 No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on
site at all times.
 The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS
ONLY. No persons other than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.
 All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that
guest. Guests may only be on club property while the member host is present.
 Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.

 Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in
the cruiser park area. This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure
that your children are considerate when riding bikes around the site and playing ball games etc.

 Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to
roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.

 Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If
you have more cars than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other
people’s pitches. Please be aware that other non-camping members do require access to the
site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and trailers etc.
 Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so
are probably not paying much attention to traffic.

 Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO
NOT USE THE DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.

 The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises
vacated. The instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.
 All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is
for the comfort of all members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left
unlocked all night. A clear changing room is easier for the cleaner to access.

EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD
The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and
sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius.

On sunny spring days it is easy to be fooled but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim.

Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people
afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the
wind chill.

There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm.

Cruiser Fleet
As the season approaches, thoughts turn to the laying of moorings and the launching of boats. We have the usual reminders
about not leaving your car unattended in the cruiser park or in the vicinity of the gap in the sea wall. We had a few problems last
year with unsuitable and badly maintained trailers and owners being unprepared and without a suitable number of helpers to
launch their boats. Whilst the duty tractor drivers will help if they can, they are primarily there to operate the machinery. The
launching list is now on the club notice board so, after you have put your name down, please make sure that you contact the
designated tractor driver for the day.

If anybody has any questions or queries about launching their boats, especially if they haven’t launched before, please ask any
tractor driver for advice. Although this will be freely given, it is the owners’ ultimate responsibility to carry out the operation in a
safe manner. Make sure that the warning signs are in use, be aware of the winch cable and make sure that nobody is between
a boat launching and the sea. Non cruiser owners may not be aware of the loads and dangers involved and although dinghy
members are meant to use the west side of the hard when launching operations are in progress, they tend to wander to the east
side sometimes, especially when coming in from a sail. If this happens, politely ask them to move over and point out the
dangers involved.

We have our fitting out supper on Saturday the 18th April 7.30 for 8.00 and the cost per head will be £16. Please make cheques

Cadet Fleet
MARCONI AT THE 420 INLANDS
After a balmy trip to Rope Runners for the cadet social last weekend, this week’s weather was just the opposite at Rutland
Water for the 420 Inlands. A strong, gusty north-easterly, 4-6C and intermittent rain from threatening grey skies set the scene for
a challenging weekend for Hannah Bard and Dan Nickalls.

With easily the oldest boat and sails (leading to the class association’s dusting-down of a little-used ‘grandfathering’ rule!) in an
intensely-competitive fleet (with squad selection at stake, and with personal on-
the-water coaches at the top end), the scene was set for some challenges. Whilst
Dan and Hannah didn’t win the event (by admittedly a significant margin) they
had a great time (especially after they’d defrosted). They came away with some
really good learning experiences (including an understanding of the dramatic
difference between how you start in top-end 420 and Laser fleets), some stories
of success (a great improvement in first beat performance was one of them) and
a firm belief that you can keep a positive attitude and enjoy yourself even when
any sane person would find the going very tough.

Great to see the Marconi flag flown again on the circuit, especially with our new
Champion Club status.

John Nickalls

CADET SOCIAL MEET UP TO ROPE RUNNERS
On the afternoon of Sunday 8th march, the cadet fleet went to Rope Runners for two hours of adrenaline, excitement and
competition. We got kitted up in our harnesses ready for the unknown. There were six courses, two bottom, two middle and two
top, the hardest being the top right. So it was unsurprising that most of us went for the hardest courses first, a bit of competition
came through here and a large amount of screaming.

I was the only one who had been before, so I thought I would find it easy, but on the first course Olivia Duckmanton and I went
on (the hardest one of course) and I got stuck. Left hanging for a while was not just painful but very embarrassing, especially as
my legs were too short to reach the platform. It was certainly funny for everyone else who stood there laughing at me. I believe
that I will never live this down now…. that teaches me for being so cocky.

Along with the course there was a climbing wall, which a few of us (Jason Clarke and Dan Nickalls) took part in. It was neck and
neck all the way to the top of the wall but with Dan’s advantage of height he was able to reach the bell first, taking the win.

Within the Marconi cadets the fan drop was very popular. It involved jumping off of a platform to the floor. Our youngest
participant was Alex who landed on the ground with a great smile on his face. He seemed to be the bravest throughout the
whole afternoon, questioning those who didn’t want to do certain courses, asking why they were so scared.

Marconi’s new Racing Coaches
Sorry about the dramatically deteriorated weather for Mothers’ Day, it
was our fault.

As part of our efforts to develop the sailing and racing at Marconi (which
is mainly focused on our youngsters, but a number of slightly less young
members have joined in over the years… and they’re always very
welcome), we ran an RYA course over the weekend for a disparate half
dozen of keen instructors / coaches / mentors. With an intense mixture
of sailing and coaching theory, briefing / debriefing skills and practise at
running exercises on the water, the course (thanks to coach Bruce
Bonar) was excellent. The challenges of a strong north-easterly,
unreasonably low temperatures, intermittent rain, RIB problems, 4
broken spars (from 5 boats), unreasonable sailing brilliance from some
and grumpy ineptitude from others (well, just me really) were overcome
to leave us with a great learning experience and inspiration to pass on
what we’ve learnt through the season.

Our new ‘Racing Coach Level 2’ skills will help improve our Sail Training
sessions. We also plan a programme of mentoring or more personal
coaching for any of our cadets who are thinking about coming to NSSA with us, or who would like to develop their sailing in that
direction even if they can’t do NSSA… more of that later.

Thanks from me to Fia, David, Tom, Andrew and Lee… as well as Bruce… for making the weekend so much fun, and
committing to help us build the skills in our club, especially with our new ‘Champion Club’ status!

Edal's continuing meander around the UK summer 2013
Troon to Isle of Man.
Apologies to one and all but it's taken me a while to get round to updating this continuing tale but there's been a lot going on -
particularly 2014 on the sailing front - more on that later. Previous logs detailed how we set out Spring 2010 up the East coast
through the Caledonian, spent two seasons and three winters on Scotlands West coast then turned south in 2013 through the
Crinan Canal into Firth of Clyde and in this episode are about to leave the Firth bound for Northern Ireland. We'd made it to
Troon harbour in the south of the Firth by 26th July when I decided to spend some time at home before getting back to Edal on
the 2nd August.

TROON TO GLENARM.
The marina at Troon is just one of those places that feels "comfy" - set behind it's old stone harbour walls which still has some
trade and fishing plus the high speed ferry that berths on the outside of the wall. Maybe it's this mix that makes it to my eye's
"comfy" I was always a bit happier with a bit of industrialisation and mix of different craft plying their trade. Coming up the East
Coast the mixed harbours of Lowestoft, Wells, Grimsby etc were much more interesting than harbours where it was just leisure
craft.

The other thing I really like about Troon is it's transport links - getting back from home in deepest Essex to unlocking the boat
hatch took just about five hours - I could hardly believe I was in Scotland and back on the boat in such a short time after the 11
hour drives I'd previously done to get back to Loch Creran north of Oban.

Before I'd got back to Edal on the 2nd I had been communicating with my soon to be crew John about where and when he
should join. The favourite seemed to be our next port of Girvan but it seemed the wind direction and strength would not be kind
on the 3rd to allow me to get there. Come the 3rd and I did actually leave and started beating into a wind over tide but after a
couple of hours I felt discretion was the better part and turned back and berthed again in Troon. Interestingly it's only the first
time I've ever turned back after setting off and on reflection I think it was the best thing to do as it was not so much the
conditions in beating into the sea but what I'd face when I got to Girvan as it has a shallow entrance which by reputation could
cut up rough.

Let John know I would be another day in Troon and he said - "no worries I'll come to Troon anyway and that will give the
weather another day to go down". So in the event we left Troon together on the 5th in a light clement wind on which we sailed
and motorsailed the 20nm to Girvan. The entrance to Girvan is shallow and best entry is 3 hours either side of high water - high
water on the 5th was 1204 so last entry would be about 1500 - we left Troon at 0728 and were in the harbour at 1203 just about
high water. Roughly four and a half hours for 20nm a pleasant easy trip.

Girvan is another old harbour which the local authority has spent money on in the hope of improving both the environment and
local income. There are super new pontoons with electricity and water and a very welcoming harbour master who can't do
enough to help. The only negative are the facilities - at the time of our visit they were "public" and only opened restricted hours
so if you wanted to leave early as we did, the "facilities" would not be open. The HM said as visiting craft numbers go up they
expect to be able to justify building dedicated loo's and showers but at the moment they were "spent out". Despite this I'd
recommend using Girvan as a passage port - in clement weather it's easy to get into and a very welcoming place.

Edal on the new Girvan pontoons. Girvan beach and southern breakwater of harbour entrance
- Ailsa Craig on horizon.

The next day was to be a milestone passage leaving Scotland and across the North Channel bound for Glenarm in Northern
Ireland. The North Channel has a bit of a fearsome reputation particularly in bad weather, when you look at a chart of Ireland
and the Irish Sea you can understand why. As the tide floods a huge amount of water in the Atlantic squeezes in towards the
land between Scotland and Ireland then turns 90 degrees south and squeezes up even more to rush into the Irish Sea down the
North Channel towards the Isle of Man - so it's best to plan to go with the flow. As we would be crossing the channel, most of
the time we would be across tide with a couple of hours at the start of the passage with tide against.

Passage distance to Glenarm is just short of 41nm so at our usual plan speed of 5kts the crossing should take a little over eight
hours. Girvan high water on the 6th August was at 1245 and we could leave three hours before but in consultation with the
harbour master he said with our draft we could get out much earlier at 0800 so eight to leave it would be. Leaving then would
mean we would punch the weak tide in the remainder of the Firth for about three hours before we got into the stronger tide in
the channel and I wanted to take the strong tide more on the beam so the plan on leaving Girvan was to head south of the

March 2015 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
straight line to Glenarm. The tide in the main channel was calculated to be 2,2kts going to 4.6kts when it went north so we
needed to use it if we could but certainly we didn't want any part of it against us. The forecast said the wind would be in the
south with a touch of west at 12/16kts for the entire trip so if the plan worked we would be a little slow to begin with but as we
shaped more for Glenarm we should get a cracking sail.

In owning Edal I'd done a fair few passages to get where we were now - but I can't remember one which came together and
provided such a brilliant passage - this one was my highlight in owning her. We cleared Girvan harbour just after eight and
motorsailed for a couple of hours as we were just off the wind and to make more south before gradually in the next hour coming
round further west to make a course just south of our line direct to Glenarm - I wanted to be south of the line so we had the
option of ending with tide to our destination.

Before we left Troon I'd rigged the new No3 instead of the big genoa as it sets much better than the reefed 150% genoa and
with a few tweaks to iron out the wrinkles (suggested by John) as we came onto the long tack of five hours towards Glenarm the
little boat picked up her skirts and flew. The day was mostly bright with scudding white clouds - the wind stiffening to middle
teens often higher, boat well heeled, autopilot steering we sat in the cockpit drinking coffee, eating, chatting, occasionally
tending the boat and just enjoying the thrill of a sailing boat going so well.

The only slight "jar" in the day was a minor disagreement with the crew about the course being kept as I still wanted to be with
tide to our destination so we didn't have to punch it into Glenarm - but as is the way of these things it was soon forgotten as the
excitement of going so well continued.

Some shore side folk may wonder what all the fuss is about it's only a big piece of plastic being blown by the wind - but sailing
and it's different experiences good and bad - stir the soul and this day was one of the best. Geoff Pack the old Yachting Monthly
editor said in one of his last articles before he died "there is just nothing like getting your old boat sailing as best she can" I
couldn't have put it better.

We made it into Glenarm and were tied up at 1628 - eight and a half hours for 41nm not bad for a wee boat with a 20 foot 6 inch
waterline.

Glenarm was delightful - easy entrance - an old harbour with new pontoons and a welcoming HM both of the skippers on board
would recommend it. We ate on board with a few glasses of wine before a walk then bed anticipating after such a great day the
passage to Bangor tomorrow.

Glenarm Harbour

GLENARM, BANGOR, ARDGLASS THEN ONTO THE ISLE OF MAN.
The next few days would see us covering shorter distances in very mixed weather although the forecast was in the main for
fairly light winds. The plan was to make for Peel on the Isle of Man by day sailing south down the coast of Northern Ireland to
Bangor, then Ardglass before striking out for Peel across the Irish Sea.

Our next port would be Bangor only 24nm away and on the 7th August the tide would start south from 0620. The wind would be
light so we would motorsail. With such a short trip we could afford to have a bit of lie in so agreed to leave about 0830. In truth
after yesterday there was nothing spectacular about a motorsail down the NI coast there are a few hazards - - a cluster of off-
lying rocks known as The Maidens and inshore of them the Hunter Rock. There is a lighthouse on The Maidens and the Hunter
is marked by a North Cardinal at it's seaward end with a clear channel between them - we chose the channel rather than stand
out to sea and go round. Just south of them is The Isle of Muck which if you are relatively close in the pilot warns it looks like
you can go inside between the Isle and the mainland but don't as there's a drying causeway so we passed outside about a mile
off.

Leaving the Isle behind we were soon in Belfast Lough and several big ships came and went as we made the six nm from Black
Head to the marina at Bangor, arriving at 1210 - only 3hrs 40min to complete the passage of 24nm - the tide had rushed us
south.

March 2015 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
After Troon, Girvan and Glenarm all relatively small harbours with pontoons - Bangor seemed massive, friendly enough, very
nice facilities, everything you could want, a very good passage port but for me lacking in character. Leaving following day would
be interesting as to get to Ardglass we had to pass through Donaghadee Sound between the mainland and Copeland Island
and it's one of the places where the tide rushes through so you have to "go with the flow". The south going tide on 8th August
would begin about 0651, we had 34nm to reach Ardglass and just under 5nm from Bangor to reach the Sound. We left just on
the turn of the south going tide following a larger boat out of the marina who also turned to make for Donaghadee Sound - - - it's
always reassuring when you see another sailor executing the same plan as you!

The Sound although appearing quite wide has a fairly narrow buoyed channel which shallows then doglegs south to avoid a
series of rocks called the Deputy Reefs. Both boats were rushed through on the south going tide, our companion with her longer
waterline out distancing us quite easily. The remainder of the passage was an unremarkable motorsail on a mixed weather day,
a little rain mainly overcast but sometimes a little brighter. It was also unremarkable due to my habit of preferring to be well off
the coast to clear any off-lying dangers. Down this part of the NI coast if you stay well in there are quite a few and you'd be
dodging in and out to miss them - I prefer to set a good long distance between waypoints so we can relax and just manage the
boat.

Arrived Ardglass just after 1300 having left Bangor 0651 just over six hours for 34nm another fast passage for such a little boat
showing the power of the tide and Edal's speed using the Bruntons propeller to motorsail.

The entrance to Ardglass and it's small marina is easy to get into and the town and harbour much more my cup of tea - with a
working fish quay and modest boats on the pontoons - we were to stay here two nights due to some higher wind forecast next
day. The elderly Harbour Master with his gentle Northern Irish accent was helpful and welcoming and at £21 per night with
electricity, water, and showers was good value. The village and it's main street echoed it's past as a fishing village with grey
fronted houses and small shops, some modest pubs and an excellent fish and chip shop where we dined one early evening.
John also found himself a little local pub where he could satisfy his long held need for a couple of pints of draft Guinness on the
island of Ireland.

The dogleg entrance to Ardglass harbour at low water - it goes down a long way in these parts

During our one day stay we fell in with a couple on a 30ft Jeanneau a boat we'd spotted leaving Bangor over an hour before us
previous day - they cruised the Irish Sea from their base in Holyhead and when the wind had blown through were headed back
there following day. For a time I was tempted to ask if we could sail in company with them as Holyhead was where I intended to
eventually make landfall back on the mainland. I dissuaded myself from asking them though as if I never pass this way again I
would be sorry to have missed what I'd been told by Murray Bates about the delights of The Isle of Man. When we got to Peel I
was very grateful to have made the decision - would not want to have missed seeing the IOM.

Friday 10th August we left Ardglass 0629 to make the 32nm to Peel a simple passage gradually losing sight of the Irish coast
astern then seeing the bulk of the IOM come up ahead. It was a misty start gradually brightening but remaining overcast. We
sailed most of the way and were tied up in the harbour by 1328, seven hours for the crossing. The approach to Peel harbour is
easy with it's large outer mole protecting the gate to the inner harbour which only open certain times to allow boats to enter and
berth on protected pontoons. The object of the gate (it also has a companion bridge) is to retain the water in the inner harbour
so the boats and pontoons stay afloat - before the gates were installed most of the harbour dried. We were approaching at one
of these opening times and after calling up the Port of Peel they advised we could follow an old gaffer into the harbour. As we
passed through the entrance the HM called out our berth number and gave us directions to the bottom of the harbour.

March 2015 Navigans 9

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Aerial picture of Peel harbour.

My immediate impression of Peel was - I loved it - here was an old port surrounded by it's town a busy bustling sort of place
unspoilt by new developments, with a wonderful mix of different craft - - the Old Gaffers were visiting on their Round Britain
adventure so they with their varnished spars, bowsprits and bunting made the old port look very gay. The tourists thronging the
quaysides and going in and out of the shops, cafes and restaurants added to the bustling scene - it was wonderful just to find a
seat at a waterfront cafe and watch the world go by.

The harbour is very sheltered from the weather and an ideal place to leave the boat for a time. John and I had been considering
best place to get home from and after looking at transport links - this was to be the place - we would both fly, him to
Northumberland me back to Essex. A conversation with the Harbour Master said he was happy for me to leave the boat there
for up to a month if necessary and he would keep an eye on her.

In the event I would be away for just about a fortnight - it was a sad to say goodbye to John at the airport - he had been a good
companion - in truth though we weren't fully compatible shipmates there were things he did and said which sometimes grated on
me - probably due to us both being skippers on our own boat and having slightly different personalities - his glass always half
empty, mine always half full - so although grateful for his companionship I would be happy to be back on Edal on my own.

Sunday 12th saw us both flying home - I would be back on Saturday 17th to continue my protracted "lark" round Britain.

David Lakin

SAIL TRAINING #1
What a great start to the Sail Training season! It was lovely to see the club packed and full of action on a Saturday, especially
on a very breezy day which didn't start very bright. But when the sun came out it was smiles all round and some great sailing!

Thanks to all the parents and helpers who got the paperwork done and provided so much vital help on and off the water :).

Before we started, we did a quick recap of important things when it's windy...

Preparation:

May 2015 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk
Tie a knot in your mainsheet so the boom can't go out more than about 80°. (Then tie another knot in case the first comes
undone!)

Flatten your sails as much as you can before you set out: kicker, cunningham / downhaul and outhaul all on tight

Upwind:

Hike hard to make sure the boat can keep moving

If you can't keep the boat flat, let the mainsheet out until you can (but keep pointing close-hauled). Be ready to react
quickly!

Bearing away:

This is the most tricky bit, and caused most of the capsizes yesterday.

As you come up to the windward mark:

o Ease off your kicker so the sail twists and
the boom rises a bit (this can be tricky on a
Pico  )

o If you can, lift your daggerboard to about
halfway

Then KEEP THE BOAT FLAT as you steer smoothly
away from the wind around the mark, easing the
sheet out as you go.
Keeping the boat flat is really important, otherwise it
will just turn back into the wind and you'll have to
start again.

As the boat accelerates, the rudder will get much
more sensitive, so steer smoothly and firmly.

Finally, as you approach downwind sailing, the tipping force on the boat will suddenly disappear: you need to be ready to
get in towards the centre of the boat to keep it flat (and the right way up...).

We did the first few races of the 2015 'Sail Training Series' at the end of the afternoon session. Success mainly meant getting
round the course without capsizing (or capsizing fewer times than others), but we saw a variety of results and some excellent,
fast sailing.

We'll take all the results forward to an end-of-season celebration!

Well done yesterday, everyone who sailed should be very proud about their performance... it was solidly windy and very gusty,
and we saw great sailing and great determination. Well done!

Saturday 2nd May 2015 at 10:00am
