I would like to pick one cruise in particular to tell you about, which was taken by one of our newest members, Tim Wood. I’ve
been provided with a short account of Tim’s epic 8000-mile journey across the Atlantic in a Sadler 34.

Their voyage started in 2012 from Mersea. Thinking they had run aground, they actually hit a whale in Biscay and continued to
the Canaries. Crossing the Atlantic they had a knockdown but arrived in Antigua just 12 hours before the flight home. They left
Antigua in May 2015 for Bermuda, travelling back across the Atlantic with a total of 40 days at sea. Another knock down had
damaged the engine so they had a non-stop voyage from Bermuda back to their Marconi mooring completely under sail. So I
would like to award the seamanship trophy this year to Tim Wood for his amazing achievement.

The catamarans, dinghies and cadets have also been hard at work representing the Club at local, national and international
events as well as competing in our own regular racing schedule. More information to follow in the Sailing Secretary’s report.

I would now like to award the Commodore’s plate, and this year it is going to someone a little different. As I’ve been forcibly on
the sidelines for much of this season, I’ve watched with great admiration all of the cadets that are regularly out racing when the
‘oldies’ are sat upstairs complaining of cold, too much or too little wind, whilst nursing their hot cup of coffee. For me, Jason
Clarke has stood out in particular. Jason is always there, eager to help and never gives up. If he isn’t out racing, which is rare,
then he’s on a support boat or doing something else useful around the Club such as waiting at the gate for over 2 hours for an
ambulance to arrive during cadet week. I remember one very windy Wednesday night race this year, one of the first races back
in my laser and I was ready to call it a day. On my way back to the hard I saw Jason, still struggling along in his Topper after his
umpteenth capsize and he just wasn’t giving up - that day I turned myself around and carried on racing because lets be honest,
no cadet in a Topper is going to out-do the Commodore! I’m pretty sure he beat me by a country mile in that race. So Jason I
think you are an inspiration to the many cadets coming through the ranks so please accept this years Commodore’s plate.

Moving onto the East Coast Piers Race. As always, thanks are due to Clive Shenton and his huge team, which will include
many of you sat in the audience today, for organising another superb event. 2015 saw an impressive increase in entries with 76
dinghies and catamarans on the start lines. Yet again we had some excellent results from Marconi teams in the race itself. I am
sure you will be interested to know that the Friends of Cirdan Sailing Trust have had an exceptionally good year for raising
sponsorship in the name of the ECPR, in that we have just presented the Trust with a cheque for a staggering £33,850. On top
of this we have also donated £500 for the Essex Air Ambulance.

Sail training and Oppi club have seen a steady growth this year and we had another busy and successful cadet week. Thanks
are due to John Nickalls, Fia Barnes, the cadet week committee and their extensive teams for providing such great training for
our young people. They are the future of our club.

Another important development this year has been the purchase of MSC’s very own rowing gig. Elettra was specifically built for
us by the Pioneer Trust and was funded by a £10k Sport England small grant. We hope this gig will enable more members to
take to the water and that the opportunity to race in local competitions will encourage the growth of paddle sports at Marconi.
As sports with no harmful conflict of interest to sailing, we feel that rowing, stand-up paddle boarding and canoeing for example
are great additions to the Club’s offerings and may encourage new members who would relish the opportunity to row or paddle
on tidal waters. Elettra will be taking to the water after the AGM with a short naming ceremony for those who wish to see her
afloat. A more high profile, formal launching event is planned for the summer months where the aim is to ask Princess Elettra,
Granddaughter of Marconi herself to formally name the gig.

Shore side the bar has seen record takings, especially over ECPR weekend, so thank you to all for contributing. Another
successful and varied social calendar, including the open day has meant there was rarely a dull weekend at MSC this year. It
has been great to see all the fleets socialising together and I look forward to seeing many of you at our annual winter dinner and
dance in January.

I would like to end my report by sharing some of our plans for next season. I will describe our ambitions for capital development
later in the meeting, where we aim to grow and improve our facilities for training, safe storage for club equipment and
spectating. Most of you will notice that the galley has grown in size this season and there is a total refit planned over the winter
to ensure this facility is fit for purpose. In terms of sailing, we intend to initiate the rowing section of the Club and are also
considering the concept of a Club owned Robber. We plan to continue with our annual open day and also to hold fewer but
bigger events, such as a 29er Open that is taking place in March 2016. This coming season will also see a change to Club
racing, for example with retimed and fewer starts, which is all part of the process to reinvigorate dinghy racing. As always
training takes a prime position in our objectives and we will continue to deliver and develop sail training as well as offering
formal courses throughout the year for skills such as power boating and first aid.

Overall Marconi Sailing Club has had a successful year and I look forward to the year ahead.

Thank you for your kind support this year and for listening to this report.
I am happy to take any questions.

Michaela Dowley

FINANCIAL SUMMARY
ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING 29th NOVEMBER 2015

As Finance Director of Marconi Sailing Club Ltd, I present a financial summary along with the accounts for the year ended 31st
August, 2015, for approval by the members. The accounts as distributed to the members are set out in the prescribed format
ready for submission to Companies House and to HMRC.

Independent Review
The accounts have been reviewed by John Bird, Chartered Management Accountant (former member and Treasurer).

Income (top half of page 4)
Overall income from subscriptions and fees stands at £137,654 (£142,879 less Member Loan Discounts of £5225) as against
last year’s income of £141,801 (£147,651 less Loan Discounts of £5,850). Although the level of membership – 401 -is nearly
same as last year, the income has reduced. This is partly due to the lower proportion of cruiser members and also to new
members joining the club later in the year.
Surpluses on the bar, social events, camping fees, open meetings, Cadet Week and other activities amount to £13,123 (last
year £15,541). Camping revenue has increased but the surpluses from Open Meetings have decreased. A straightforward
comparison for the bar income and expenditure is not possible, as the amounts paid in and expended can fall just outside the
accounting period, as is the situation this year.
Overall therefore the club’s revenue has decreased to £150,777 (last year £157,342).

Expenditure (lower half of page 4)
Spending has been a little higher for sailing activities (up £459), representing necessary maintenance on the club’s fleet of
dinghies. Spending on club and precincts (up £343) includes major improvements to the First Aid Room and the construction of
a mezzanine floor in the Barn. This was offset by significant savings on cleaning and waste collection costs. There was an
increase in rates but expenditure on electricity, gas and water were minimal notwithstanding higher charges. Social and
publicity showed a decrease of £2,457 as there were no setting up costs for a new website this year. Administration expenditure
no longer includes the income and expenditure relating to training.

Net Surplus (bottom of page 4)
Therefore the club’s surplus before interest and tax was £62,495 (last year £69,218).
This amount includes contingency amounts for major repairs to the approach road, potential insurance claim and refunds for
boat fees payable in December each year. It also includes a Sport England grant of £10,000 towards the purchase of a rowing
gig which was awarded in April 2015.
As the end of the financial year falls on 31st August, and subscriptions and fees are not due until 1st January thereafter, it is
essential to ensure that club retains about £30,000 in the bank account to meet unavoidable expenditure for those five months
(September to mid January) where little or no income is received.
The annual budget plan is set to create a small surplus annually which can be put towards minor capital projects for improving
the club infrastructure and/or as seed money to be used to secure grants such as the Sport England awards.

The club continues at present to benefit from the historically low interest rates in the repayment of its development loan, but it is
important to bear in mind that even a small increase in interest rates of 0.5% would amount to at least £3,000 p.a. extra per
annum.
There have not been any significant changes to the balance sheet during the year and the overall Net Asset Value of the club
improved to a sound £352,571 (last year £319,026). This is approximately £881 per member!
It is worth drawing members’ attention to the following areas:

Capital spending (note 2, page 2):
This has been fairly low this past year and includes £3,600 deposit for the rowing gig, £1,000 for a new club dinghy and the
purchase of new mowing equipment. However some significant areas of expenditure have already been assigned this autumn

Marconi SC Sailing Secretary’s report 2015

Good morning everyone and it is my pleasure to present the Sailing Secretary Report for 2015.

I am pleased to report that 2015 has been another very busy year for sailing across the club. I will endeavour to do justice to
the range of activity but I apologise in advance for anything I may have missed.

With support from the Board and Management Committee and encouragement from the RYA, the Sailing Sub-Committee set
out to enhance sailing participation during 2015. There were four strands to this:

To continue improving the club’s sailing equipment and capability

To support activities to recruit new members;

To introduce some new activities to encourage wider participation

And to make our sailing activities more accessible for existing and new members to join in

Throughout the year we have been having discussions about how we can improve racing and to try and encourage more of our
members to get out there and to use those fantastic craft that populate the fields outside. The changes are still being refined but
ultimately there will still remain similar fleets, however the number of starts will be reduced & the sequence will changed to 5,4,1,
GO, to be more in line with the ISAF recognised sequence. The aim of this is to create busier start lines and ultimately to
improve racing.

This was also our second season as an official RYA Training Centre we have been delivering RYA accredited power boat
training – thanks to the efforts of Bob Collins as Principle and Pat Shaw as our qualified instructor. We have taken this
opportunity to train club members to RYA Powerboat standards and Bob and Pat will continue to expand this offering going
forward. The First aider training is also going well, and next year we will be going into the next stage of getting those with
certificates issued, renewed qualifications to keep them up to date.

The open day was once again a great success, as Michaela reported, and saw many people sampling sailing for the first time or
returning to a sport they once loved.

The Friday Free4All evening sailing sessions continued this year, with the aim of easing the new members and less confident
sailors into sailing the fantastic water we have just off the club, although they might not seem quite so appetising today. Next
year they shall be known as Sunset Sail and Supper and with the galley providing an evening meal after sailing – it was pretty
much the best way to start a weekend! The Sunday pursuit races continued again this year, an easier form of racing with starts
from the hard, this saw good turnouts with 22 in one race.

The weekly emails have continued this year, with Jenny kindly doing them until June when she handed over that responsibility
to me, I hope you have found them both informative and enjoyable and have had as much fun reading them as I have had
writing them. The idea of the emails is to keep you informed of both what to look forward to and what you have missed. And we
have had plenty of activities to talk about in the weekly emails!

From the cruiser cruising fleet there were many trips starting off in a shake down to Brightlingsea, The watercress run to
Heybridge, A jaunt to Tollesbury. The summer cruise was across the Thames estuary to Ramsgate and then on to
Queenborough, Chatham and finally Brightlingsea. The bank holiday cruise was to Ipswich, onto Wrabness, Walton and finally
Brightlingsea. And one final cruise to Brightlingsea, just to make sure it was still there. The racing cruiser fleet had just as much
fun travelling around the country, starting with the BJRC series, Blue Moon was the highest finishing Marconi boat, coming in
2nd in IRC and 4th in BJRC handicaps. Woozle Hunter was the highest finishing Marconi boat in the EAORA, offshore series,
2nd in class 3 and 4th overall. In the Fastnet Race, Woozle Hunter finished as 1st Marconi boat and in 188th position from a
fleet of 309. Closer to home, Caroline competed at the prestigious Ramsgate Week, were she finished 4th in class.

New this season, the highly successful Marconi Autumn Series saw 6 boats competing, with a further 4 in the Bart’s Bash event,
4 x boats were still in with a chance of winning come the medal race. Unfortunately the wind died on us, which saw Woozle

Schools Sailing Association Regatta event in July. Marconi Cadets also performed very well in the Bart’s Bash, Eastern Region
Topper Event, Topper Nationals.

In addition to the people I have already mentioned, I would like to thank the remaining Fleet Captains, Bryan Spencer, Kevin
Dowley, Tom Brooks, Rob Bard; the Bosuns Dave Clarke and Colin Leveridge for keeping the support boats in good working
order and Tony Goode with support from the Wednesday crew for maintaining the race marks and the mooring teams for laying
and recovering them. Additionally, John Burgoyne, Dave Russell, Dave & Jemma Clarke and Sally Wilson, have ensured that
Race officers and Support Boats were rota’d, that results were calculated and trophies organised.

Whilst this is just a whistle-stop tour of 2015, I hope it does justice to the full range of sailing we have all been involved in. I am
pleased to confirm that arrangements are progressing well for the 2016 sailing schedule with many events such as the 29ers
visiting in mid-March and Larks and Lasers visiting along with the traditional opens. Many thanks to Jenny Ball who has been a
great help in my Inaugural year as sailing secretary and has kindly put the schedule together. We again have a full range of
events planned across the season and across all types of sailing. I look forward to seeing you out there.

CLUB ROBBER
A number of you may know that in recent months MSC has purchased a small racing cruiser of the Robber 1/4 ton class. This
is an addition to the fleet of club owned boats which to date have been limited to dinghies. As you might expect the
arrangements for use of the Robber are slightly different to our other club boats in that there is a cost associated with the use of
it. Members wishing to use the club Robber are paying a fee for the use of the boat, which over time will cover the purchase
and running costs. The boat is currently undergoing some major renovation and repair works which are being carried out both
professionally and by those members who are signed up to sail her during the year. This scheme is being co-ordinated by Peter
Ward, the Club is fully insured for the intended use of the Robber and there will shortly be a specific code of practice available.

As detailed at the Club AGM in November, MSC has applied for a £75k grant from Sport England to make capital improvements
to the Club. Our bid was submitted on 9th January 2016 and we await a decision in April. Many thanks are due to our
Treasurer Sue Shenton for putting the application together and working tirelessly to improve and provide evidence in the areas
on which our previous application was rejected. For more information on our proposed project, see the AGM minutes in
January 2016 Navigans and on the members section of the website.

MSC Photo Competition
MSC will be holding an ongoing monthly Photo Competition throughout 2016 and whilst we finalise details of how you can
submit your iconic photography (we’ll let you know in due course), here’s a heads up and some guidance for all you budding
photo journalists and visually creative masters out there.

Categories to enter images into include:

1. Serious sailing - racing, race box madness, open meetings, competitions, safety boat operations etc.

2. People at work - unsung heroes involved in running the club events or site and boat maintenance eg. launching
cruisers, laying moorings, OOD, race officers, galley staff, cadet organisation, management etc.

3. People at play - e.g. relaxed sailing and cruising, social events, camping, fishing, BBQ’s, walking the dog, chilling…..

4. Landscape and Seascape - beautiful scenes at all times of the day and night, all seasons.

5. Candid Camera! - those classic moments that make us laugh.

6. Memories of Marconi - images from the archives. Dig deep and even scan old prints that show how much our great
club has evolved over the years.

Images may be posed portraits, classic landscapes, action shots, close-up macro shots, abstract art, snaps of funny moments,
reportage….pretty much anything goes.

Rules:

Two age categories, under 16 and adult.

A single winning entry from each age group plus commended images will be chosen from entries across all categories
each month. (This may be subject to change depending on number of entries received). Prizes TBD.

All entries to be your own photographs (no video at this stage) in compressed digital format, eg. high resolution jpegs
(or other compressed format) and emailed / uploaded (details to follow) and labelled in their appropriate categories. No
large uncompressed files such as TIFs please.

Please try to caption your images using appropriate image software or send an explanatory email (address to follow)
with your contact details.

Up to 5 entries from any one individual may be submitted in each of as many categories as desired.

All entries for each month to be received by the end of the first week of following month. Eg: January entries to be
received by 7th February.

Limited but not excessive digital manipulation is permitted where it reasonably enhances an image but remains true to
the subject within.

Agreement from participants that any submissions be made available externally e.g. on the club website, social media,
and for promotion via press and publicity for MSC marketing purposes, (subject to prior parental agreement where
children under 16 are featured within images).

Full copyright will remain with the creator of the photograph.

Overall annual winner and runners up will be announced at the end of the year / laying up supper.

Judges decision is final.

open to fast dinghies and catamarans, there are three different course options of different length with the longest being 48miles.
Along the course are a number of mother boats who are able to provide support with no penalty so the course is easy to follow.
It’s a challenge but a manageable one. The race will be held over the 9th and 10th July in 2016.

Marconi take part in the Burnham Gig Race
This weekend Marconi Sailing Club made it’s world debut into the rowing scene, by entering our Harker’s Yard Rowing Gig in
the Burnham Gig Race!

Not one, but 2 races in fact, due to a last minute practice session of commands and technique organised by Tom Clayton on
Saturday, we were able to add a “Mixed Crew” to our Men’s entry.

There were 12 boats entered, 2 GRP Thames Class 4 man boats (which run in their own class) and 10 Harkers Yard class Gigs.
We had set ourselves the task of “looking neat from shore” and “actually finishing” as being fair targets.

The men’s race started at 12.45

Crew:-
No.1 – Lee Hooper (Bow)
No.2 – Roy Hardwicke
No.3 – Steve Cleaver
No.4 – Kevin Stubbs (Stroke)
Cox’n – Tom Clayton

It soon dawned on us that a race start would be more difficult than a sailing one, as with 12 boats mean 48 Oars to also keep
clear of. The tide was due to turn 4 minutes before the start and we chose to get out early (avoiding the crew change on the
pontoon from the first “Ladies” race). Our cox’n chose the far bank to start and we set off at a steady pace (so we had some
hope of being able to last the distance)

February 2016 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

As we only had one or two practice sessions each, we had not really tried a race pace, concentrating on basic technique first, so
to me keeping breathing in time with rowing movement was the first challenge as we headed out to No. 3 buoy, seaward of the
start.

Fortunately for us Tom’s metronome had a miraculous improvement and we were heavily encouraged by Tom to keep going,
time seemed to slow down and it seemed some while before we had even got 1/3 of the way to the turn. We could see the worry
on Tom’s face as we closed on the turn, realising he would not want to be in the middle of the bunch for the turn around the
buoy.

For the return towards Crouch Y.C. we were pushed along by
Tom, and managed to stay fairly close to the main bunch, and
followed the north shore, it was certainly getting to the point for
me not to be able to pull much faster when encouraged by the
cox’n, but we were soon finishing about 15 seconds or so after
boat No.11, with some strong encouragement from the
supporters ashore (thankyou).

After a quick crew change, the Ladies race started at 13.30

Crew:-

No.1 – Rhiannon Hitt (Bow)
No.2 – Lucie Walker
No.3 – Tristran Hutt
No.4 – Tom Clayton (Stroke)
Cox’n – Kevin Stubbs

As tide was building, about 2 knots pushing us over the start line, the start became more complicated to manage for me as
Cox’n, plus the poor mixed crew (2 ladies,2 men) had me to drag along plus more work pre-race stemming the tide

I decided we would row a 360 and then along the line for the start, and follow the deep water, we made a fair start, our rowers
kept good time and we stayed relatively close to the bunch all the way downstream to the turn, where we arrived last but made
a fast turn (“bow side” “ hold water”, “stroke side” “pull hard” and made up a length or two. Tactics split here and I decided to
head close to the south bank against the tide going back, as the north side seemed a lot farther away. I did not get us over quite
as far as I should but managed to tuck in eventually (the support Rib said by tucking in we gained a knot in boat speed to 3.5
Knots over ground against the tide. Our younger crew had great stamina here, credit especially to Rhiannon and Lucie, and by
still responding to my gentle encouragement and “10 Good Pulls” (several times!) they gained over a boat on the North bank
and we were not going to be last, the crew agreed to go harder and we finally crossed the line on the opposite side to our
supporters AHEAD OF THE LAST BOAT!.

(I have attached some “before” and “after” photo’s from the Mixed race, unfortunately the cameraman was busy rowing on the
Men’s one).

Immediately after the finish, having stopped rowing, we realised the full strength of the tide, and the distance to row back, so
called on the services of a support Rib to tow us back. By the time they had tied us alongside we were halfway out to sea again
but were glad of the tow. We have also noted that the last boat to finish can easily be a long time awaiting a trailer on a narrow
slipway, waiting turns with a large fleet.

We received some post race tips from other crews, some who have been
racing 2 seasons now – interestingly one was “Why are you using your
practice oars?” – it turns out that our “One Class” Harker’s Yard boats can
be used with hooked blade oars, which can give 10% more efficiency (they
say…..), so our 12/12 and 11/12 was perhaps more respectable than we
thought. – the bad news is we’ve now got to raise £2,500 ish for a set of
Race oars!

So, well done both teams – a respectable first outing, a few blisters to show
between us and certainly a few aches already for me tonight.

- a challenge is now set for at least a couple more ladies to come forward so
we can field 3 crews at the next event (Maldon) 7th Feb – or Stone – 21’s
Feb

(Practice next weekend needs a careful eye on the weather plus how to fit around the Dinner Dance Saturday night too!)

Thank you especially to Roy Hardwicke for fixing the roof of the Gig container mid week, and to Peter & Sandra for towing the
boat both ways and providing invaluable support plus linking us in with the race schedule organisers.

Elettra signing off now ._.

Kevin Stubbs

Club Notices
Frank Bennett
Frank Bennett passed away on 22nd January 2016. His funeral, which was attended by club members, was held in Chelmsford
on 2nd March.

This tribute to Frank was put together by Ray Ball with contributions from Marconi Sailing Club members who knew Frank at
work or at the club or both.

………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………..

No doubt Frank had a long career behind him before joining the Marconi Company but club members who knew him at work
recall that he was a research engineer in the Radar Research Laboratory at the Marconi Research Centre at Great Baddow.

He is remembered as cycling from his home in Old Moulsham to work in Baddow wearing shorts whatever the temperature. We
are told that he continued wearing his shorts even in the office or laboratory. To those who remember Frank at the club that will
not come as a surprise. He was well known for wearing shorts when others were shivering with cold.

Frank joined Marconi Sailing Club from the Royal Burnham Yacht Club.

He built his Solo sailing dinghy which he sailed at the club for many years He also bought a Halcyon 23 called Sundowner in
which he ranged far and wide on the East Coast; often on his own.

It was typical of Frank that instead of putting up with what he saw as shortcomings in the way Sundowner handled, he decided
that the designer did not know his business and removed the keel and moved it back by 6 inches. Apparently this modification
was successful.

Frank was treasurer of MSC from 1989 to 2002. During that time Marconi Sailing Club was the sailing section of Marconi
Athletic & Social Club and was not allowed its own bank account. Frank spent many hours at Beehive Lane ensuring that the
interests of the sailing section were given due consideration.

He was a supportive and loyal member of the committee. When, at the start of this century, there were some doubts about the
future of the sailing club at Stansgate Frank gave his full support to the small group who got together to form what became
known as the Lifeboat Committee. The Lifeboat Committee ultimately arranged a members buy out creating the independent
Marconi Sailing Club that is enjoyed by members today.

Frank stood down as treasurer in 2002. At the annual general meeting in November 2002 the commodore, Neil Pembleton,
thanked Frank with the following words:

(The first paragraph is a little ‘tongue in cheek’ as Frank would have been in his mid-50s in 1989.)

[Quote from AGM, November 2002]

Finally, before I close the meeting, I must return to Frank Bennett. It was just over fourteen years ago that I stood down from the
post of Treasurer and was introduced to a young lad wearing shorts, quite obviously fresh out of school. In the last fourteen
years this lad has blossomed into the fine figure that we know today.

I cannot believe that there is an area of the club which has not received his magic touch, be it from chucking lighted paper into
the hole we dug to replace the water main to check that we had not punctured the gas pipe, designing and building the gate and
clubhouse locking system, maintaining the sewage system and many other jobs. At the same time there cannot be many
members who have not benefited from Frank's knowledge and experience.

I personally, and I am sure that all other previous Commodores, members of the Executive and main committees, have
welcomed his calm, careful analysis and advice over the fourteen years.

In addition to this he also found time to carry out the duties of treasurer, a role mainly in the background but most essential to
the wellbeing of the club. Without his careful husbanding of the club's finances we would either be paying very much higher fees
or be unable to renew and develop the facilities the way that we have. The fact that we are able to move forward with the
replacement of the electrical system, whilst reducing our reserve for the next two or three years, and not had to take the
alternative route of closing the site, is largely due to his skill in making every pound that we pay, stretch and work for all our
benefit.

On behalf of those people who have worked with you on the committees over the years, I would ask you to accept this gift. (A
barometer and watch were then presented to Frank by Murray Bates on behalf of present and past Committee members.)

Neil Pembleton

[End of quote]

Frank was an MSC vice president in 2003.

March 2016 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

He was elected an Honorary Life member of Marconi Sailing Club at the 2008 AGM in recognition of all his contributions to the
club.

As well as being treasurer, which is a demanding and time consuming task, Frank was involved in the club in many practical
ways. From the heavy engineering of repairing tractors to printed circuit boards and many things in between Frank was
involved.

Frank designed and built the club’s gate and clubhouse electronic access system which served the club for some 20 years. He
also produced the swipe cards issued to every member to access the site and the clubhouse. Those who visited Frank’s house
will recall the home built box connected to an elderly computer which sat on his dining room table and produced the cards.

Visitors who went into his conservatory would have noticed shelves full of items either repaired or waiting repair. Frank was the
exact opposite to the ‘throw away’ society and if a thing could be repaired why replace it?

I recall that when presenting Frank with a receipt for a broken item replaced on one of the club boats, Franks response would be
‘We could have repaired that’. However he always paid without delay, usually in cash.

Although he lived and often sailed alone Frank was a sociable person. Peter Clayton and Sandra took him mince pies at
Christmas. Derek Kirby recalls Frank visiting him and Doreen on Happy Medium for a chat and a cup of tea. He also went
aboard Amyjack to visit us. Maureen was impressed by the way Frank would tie his tender to the stern of Amyjack and just hop
over the rail. Frank was very agile.

He also sailed with John Todds on Chimo and Dave Steward on Swiftsure.

Things changed when Frank had an accident on his bike in April 2012. After a spell in hospital he went into the nursing home at
Howe Green.

In the contributions made to this tribute by club members Frank is summed up as clever, inventive, a touch eccentric,
interesting, unconventional and always a pleasure to know. That is how he will be remembered.

Ray Ball

BUYING OR SELLING A BOAT?
If you buy or sell a boat which is at the Club you must inform the membership secretary so that accurate records are maintained.
This is especially important now that dinghy and catamaran park spaces are numbered and pre-allocated. If you want to bring a
new dinghy or catamaran to site you must get a boat park allocation first. Don’t just put your boat in the nearest convenient
space as that may already have been allocated to someone else.

If you sell a boat and it leaves site please inform the membership secretary so that the vacated space can be reallocated. If you
sell a boat to a non-member remember you are responsible for it until it leaves the site.

Before bringing a cruiser to Stansgate or changing your cruiser you must first discuss your plans with the Moorings Secretary to
ensure that a suitable mooring is available. Bylaw 3.3 in your yearbook gives useful information on cruisers and moorings.

Cruiser Fleet
As I write this mid February, the sailing season starts in six weeks so now’s the time to check your mooring tackle ready for the
coming season. ‘ C’ row goes down at the beginning of April with the rest every two weeks after that. Frank’s chain store is
open every Sunday until the end of April, although if you are making a special journey it might be best to ring him beforehand on
either or . He has stock of ground and riser chain, shackles, anodes and rings. I believe he also
has a couple of second hand moorings for sale. Whilst we are talking moorings, a personal plea from the telehandler drivers -
would people please have the slots of the pallet (the bit where the forks go in) facing the road or accesses point with the
anchors on the bottom stocks towards the telehandler. The ground chain should be on top of each anchor with the riser on the
ground chain. This should be topped off with the mooring buoy. This makes it easier to pick up the pallet and pull out the
mooring for inspection on the hard.

We have a club working party on Sunday 6th March starting at 0930 and one on the13th March. This is to get the club ready for
the forthcoming session so if you could make one of these days it would help, as many hands make light work.

On the 9th of April we have the fitting out supper in the upstairs lounge of the clubhouse with a 7pm for 7.30pm start. I will be
putting the list on the clubhouse notice board in the next couple of weeks. The cost will be £16.50 a head and the menu is to
follow.

The summer cruising programme is now posted on the club website and in the year book. If you have any good photos of last
year’s cruising, please send them to Peter Booth to add to the cruiser gallery.

CAMPING RULES – 2016
THE MANAGEMENT & EXECUTIVE COMMITTEES ENDORSE AND ARE
DETERMINED TO ENFORCE THESE RULES.

 All Marconi Sailing Club rules are to be adhered to during camping fortnight.
 No camping on site OR in the access roads before 8.00a.m on the first Saturday
 Maximum of 6 people allowed to camp per pitch and must be pre-registered and fees paid.

 Noise is to be kept to a reasonable level at all times, so not to annoy other members.
 No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.
 No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.

 No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is on site at all times.
 The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS ONLY. No persons other
than official cadet week tutors may camp in this area.
 All guests, including those under 18, are to be signed in by the member responsible for that guest. Guests may only
be on club property while the member host is present.
 Parents and guardians are responsible for their children at all times.

 Please ensure that you know where your children are at all times and that they do not play in the cruiser park area.
This area is not a safe place for children to play in. Please also ensure that your children are considerate when riding
bikes around the site and playing ball games etc.

 Dogs are to be kept on leads at all times while on club property. Dogs must not be allowed to roam freely on
neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be respected.

 Cars are to be parked safely off the road in case emergency vehicles need to access the site. If you have more cars
than can be parked on your pitch, please find a place away from other people’s pitches. Please be aware that other
non-camping members do require access to the site at all times and indeed will expect to be able to access boats and
trailers etc.
 Please drive slowly around the club, at all times, as there are lots of children playing and so are probably not paying
much attention to traffic.

 Chemical toilets must be emptied in the septic tank as marked, and washed out at the tap. DO NOT USE THE
DRINKING WATER TAPS TO RINSE CHEMICAL TOILETS.

 The Licensing laws are to be obeyed. The Bar is to be shut at closing time and the premises vacated. The
instructions of the Bar Manager or his deputy must be followed.
 All personal property is to be removed from the changing rooms immediately after use. This is for the comfort of all
members and also for the safety of your property as the clubhouse is left unlocked all night. A clear changing room is
easier for the cleaner to access.

EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD
I issue this warning every year but it may be useful for new members and perhaps a timely reminder for older hands.

The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and
sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius.

On sunny spring days it is easy to be fooled but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim.

Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people
afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the
wind chill.

There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm.

TENDERS ARE OFTEN JUST THAT!

Every year it seems we have at least one incident when someone is either going from tender to yacht or vice versa. It’s easy to
get complacent (well we do it every weekend, right) but probably most of us have had a near miss at some time but got away
with it. Some are less fortunate and end up in the drink.

Please take care in your tender where you are probably most vulnerable and possibly alone. As the man said, lifejackets are
only useless ornaments unless they are worn (or words to that effect).

As the season approaches, thoughts turn to the laying of moorings and the launching of boats. Please remember to not leave
your car unattended in the cruiser park, even if no boats are launching there may be boat movements in the cruiser park, for
example moving under the mast derrick. We had a few problems last year with unsuitable and badly maintained trailers and
owners being unprepared and without a suitable number of helpers to launch and recover their boats. Whilst the duty tractor
drivers will help if they can, they are primarily there to operate the machinery.

I appreciate that some club members are new to launching and may be unsure of how to go about it, even after reading their
cruiser notes. Please ask any tractor driver for advice and, although this will be freely given, it is the owners’ ultimate
responsibility to carry out the operation in a safe manner. Everybody is responsible to operate safely when launching
operations are in progress. Make sure that the warning signs are in use, be aware of the winch cable and make sure that
nobody is between a boat launching and the sea. Non cruiser owners may not be aware of the loads and dangers involved and
although dinghy members are meant to use the west side of the yard when launching operations are in progress, they tend to
wander to the east side sometimes, especially when coming in from a sail. If this happens, politely ask them to move over and
point out the dangers involved.

There have been occasions recently when members have come on site early in the morning to find the front and back doors of
the clubhouse unlocked. The doors may have been unlocked overnight or even for several days.

ensure that all the exterior doors are locked. It is worth checking the back door and the external doors to the changing rooms
even if you haven’t used them yourself. It only takes a minute or two.

Lock up even if there are still members on site. Anyone entitled to be in the clubhouse will have their own access card.

MAMGU BAR SECURITY

Users of the bar are asked to ensure that the external patio doors are properly closed and locked. The leaver needs to be
pushed fully down (to at least 45o or more) before the key is turned. The last centimetre or so is quite stiff. Double check by
trying to lift the lever after the key has been withdrawn.

If the leaver is not fully down it is easy to open the door from the outside with obvious potential consequences.

RHS TEAM RACING APRIL 2016
On Saturday 23rd April Marconi sent a group of six cadets to a team racing regatta hosted by the Royal Hospital School on
Alton Water. This was a competition in which our team of three Fireflies sailed against a series of other teams in races where it
was often more important to slow down the opposition than to sail fast ourselves. The team consisted of Dan Nickalls, Will
Harrison, Jack Collis, Charlie Collis, Hannah Bard and Sam Featherstone.

A total of 12 teams from various clubs and schools competed in group stages, with the top four teams in each group then going
through to knockout stages. Through the day we raced five races, winning two of them – a great outcome for such an
inexperienced group of team racers. This meant we were fourth in our group and qualified for the silver sail-off, but unfortunately
a scoring error meant we did know this until some of us had left for home.

The team had a great experience in some fiercely competitive and very enjoyable racing, as well as learning a lot about the
tactics involved in team racing. We will definitely be returning for another go next year!

John Nickalls

SPRINT 15 TRAINING DAY – MARCONI SC
Saturday 16th April 2016

Six local sailors and eight visiting sailors arrived at Marconi SC on a decidedly chilly Saturday morning for a Sprint 15 Training
day at Marconi Sailing Club led by Howard Hawkes.

A pre-session briefing took place over coffee and bacon rolls which is, as we all know, a mandatory part of any proper training.
Participants had been asked to pre-register to give an idea of the range of experience and what people wanted to gain from the
day. It was quite a diverse spectrum from learning how to tack/gybe effectively, some racing practice, how to return to shore in
an onshore breeze plus a slightly more broad comment of “why am I always at the back of the fleet”.

The training started in earnest with a shore-based session running through boat set up, the importance of having a very tight
trampoline and talking through how to tack without stalling. All of which is a lot easier to do when everyone is stood around a
boat on dry(ish) land.

The fleet then took to the water for the morning session. The wind had eased from quite strong to fairly light and the water was
flat – making for nicely manageable conditions for the first sail.

A proliferation of Go Pros on the RIBS meant that (a) we would be able to review the sessions when we came off the water (the
reason we gave to the participants), (b) everyone was on their best behaviour and (c) potential opportunities for future website /
magazine / blackmail material were maximised (the real reason but don’t tell them).

A triangular course was set to provide tacking, gybing and three points of sail practice with the RIBS following and filming. The
fleet came ashore for lunch and took the opportunity to review some of the footage from the morning session – particularly
around tacking and trim when sailing downwind.

After lunch, the wind had freshened making for ideal sailing conditions on the flat water. A committee boat and race course
were set up and a series of short one lap races were run to give a good opportunity for practice starts and sailing in fairly close
quarters. During the first race, Rob Bailey from Thorpe Bay kindly provided excellent footage by turtling in the middle of the
river, which Howard naturally filmed for future training (blackmail) purposes.

With some cajoling from the team on the coach boat and the committee boat – participants were encouraged to keep a very
tight pre-start sailing area and after a couple of races, the start line was nicely busy and competitive. The coach boat also took
the opportunity to follow different participants to film and offer some tips. After a good afternoon’s sailing, the fleet headed
ashore to debrief over coffee and cake.

The majority of visitors left their boats at the club to take part in the Traveller Event the following weekend which was fantastic.
Unfortunately, we forgot to film the sailor who got his Transit stuck in the mud in the cat park (until a tractor was arranged to
come to his aid) – so I can’t officially use that for blackmail material.

A big thank you to our guests – Paul Shields (Seasalter), Andrew Berisford, Gordon Deuce (Brightlingsea), Donald Sloane,
(Felixtowe Ferry), Chris Tillyer, Steve Healy, Rob Bailey and Darren Fitchew from Thorpe Bay. Well done also to Andy Perks,
Dave Clarke, Antony Bailey, Nick Pavitt, Dani Pavitt and Steve Thomas from Marconi who are all very welcome additions to our
fleet!

SPRINT 15 TRAVELLER EVENT 2016 – MARCONI SAILING CLUB
21 competitors took part in the first 2016
Summer TT at Marconi SC on 23rd and 24th
April. We were particularly pleased to
welcome a number of new faces – who had
participated in the Association Training Day
run by Howard Hawkes the previous weekend.

A decent northerly breeze and cold
temperatures meant it did not feel very
summery but did provide great racing
conditions across both days. Race 1 was a
round the cans and the breeze fell away to
fairly light conditions to start with. Jenny Ball
led round the windward mark, closely followed
by David Ball, Paul Grattage and Liam Thom.
Paul and Liam pulled ahead on the downwind
leg and led for the next two lap followed by
Jenny, David and Chris Tillyer. For lap 3 a strong breeze filled in with a shift making for multiple changes at the front of the fleet
- although Paul's lead was unassailable - Chris came in second followed by David and Kevin Kirby.

Race 2 was the now legendary long distance figure of eight race around Osea and Northey Islands. With a strong if
inconsistent northerly breeze, this proved to be one of the fastest round the island races with a fetch for much of the race. Paul
Grattage took an early lead, chased hard by Kevin Kirby, David Ball, Chris Tillyer and Liam Thom. Stuart Snell soon caught up
the pack and was in the front runners at the turning point at Northey Island. The rest of the fleet were close behind with a lot of
position changes on the leg back round the back of Osea Island. After a real blast of a race, the fleet finished pretty close
together with Paul Grattage leading followed by Kevin Kirby, Stuart Snell, David Ball and Liam Thom. The fleet headed in to
thaw out over a well-deserved evening meal.

Sunday morning saw another day of strong northerly breezes and flat water. The start of race 3 saw a bunching at the pin end
of the line and a couple of boats tacked off from the rest of the fleet to get into clear air. Paul Grattage who went left up the
course rounded the mark first followed by Jenny Ball who had gone right with the rest of the fleet close behind chasing down the
reach. Paul Grattage continued to lengthen his lead with very close racing between Jenny, Steve Healy, Stuart Snell, David
Ball, Kevin Kirby and Liam Thom. Wind shifts made for some interesting tactics particularly on the windward legs and very
competitive racing throughout the fleet. Paul Grattage took
first, followed by Stuart Snell, Kevin Kirby and Jenny Ball.

For Race 4, the wind had strengthened including the odd
Force 6 gust. Line bias again meant that the fleet bunched at
the pin end, and this time a larger number of boats tacked off
up the right hand side of the course with Donald Sloan and
Erling Holmberg making good gains and coming in with the
front of the pack coming in from the left hand side. David Ball
led off on the reach closely followed by the rest of the pack.
By the second lap, David had pulled out a decent lead with
Paul Grattage and Liam Thom chasing – whilst Chris Tillyer,
Kevin Kirby, Stuart Snell, Jenny Ball and Daren Fitchew battled
out behind. Paul managed to work his magic again and
eventually got past David to take the win, with Liam in third
followed by Chris, Stuart and Kevin.

The fleet headed home after an exhilarating weekend of
sailing! Big thanks go to the Race Officer, Race Committee
and Support boat crews who had a very cold time of it whilst
we all enjoyed ourselves. Congratulations to the newer
members of the fleet who found themselves sailing in breezier
conditions than they were used to – but got on really well
anyway! And Thorpe Bay made an impressive start to the
newly introduced Traveller Team Trophy with a turnout of six
competitors.

Results: 1st – Paul Grattage, Shanklin, 2nd – David Ball, Marconi, 3rd – Kevin Kirby, Marconi, 4th - Stuart Snell, Grafham, 5th
– Liam Thom, Shanklin, 6th – Chris Tillyer, Thorpe Bay.

Club Notices
Commodore
I write this the night after our open day, held on 21st May, which was another resounding success! Many thanks are due to the
army of volunteers, headed up by Graham Cross who helped to show our Club at its absolute best. 65 families signed in at our
registration desk with plenty of people taking advantage of trips out on the water on a variety of boats. Our artistic youngsters
created a beautiful mosaic in the arts & crafts tent, whilst the bouncy castle provided entertainment for the little ones and a
Pimms tent for the older. It was also a lovely day for our members as all fleets really pulled together during the day and enjoyed
a social event with BBQ in the evening. As you know, membership is our only real source of income so it is vital to the future of
the Club that we proactively look to grow our membership - please keep supporting events such as open days in the future.

Unfortunately I have to report that we were unsuccessful in our recent attempt to win a Sport England Inspired Facilities grant
for £75,000 to invest in capital improvements to the clubhouse. There was fierce competition in this, the final round of funding.
Although the outcome is disappointing we have a sound idea of what our priorities should be for capital improvements and I
thank Sue Shenton for putting in a huge amount of time and effort into making our bid as strong as possible. Also thank you to
all the members who engaged in discussions at the AGM and through our online survey earlier this year. We will continue to
seek out grant funding in the future so please let us know if you hear of any potential funds we can apply to.

In response to a query at the 2015 AGM, over the past couple of months we have carried out a survey of cruiser owners
providing options for the development of mooring laying/retrieval at MSC. The results of this survey, which have been
communicated to the cruiser fleet, include increasing mechanisation of the process in the near future and the potential to move
to a 3-yearly cycle of laying/retrieval. These proposals will be discussed with the moorings sub-committee and at the cruiser
AGM.

We have also been discussing plans to build a ‘bridge deck’ above the western end of the support boat containers. The
purpose of the bridge deck is to provide options for race control for opens hosted at MSC, including the East Coast Piers Race
and also for one-off races in our own sailing calendar in the future. The plan is to begin construction over the winter season so
keep an eye out for developments.

Our calendar is packed over the remainder of the season with events such as the ECPR, cadet week and camping fortnight to
look forward to. Please refer to our excellent website for up to date information on upcoming events and reports.

Happy sailing!

WOOZLE WINNING WEEKEND
The East Coast offshore racing season got off to a good start over the May bank holiday weekend with the traditional Burnham
– Mersea back to back races.

Woozle Hunter was Marconi’s only representative in a fleet of 7 boats, but they set off out of the Crouch racing against some
very experienced crews, which included one other closely matched Sigma 33.

The Pattinson Cup race saw the fleet taking the tide up the swin in an attempt to beat the tidal gate at the North East Gunfleet
mark. As was the pattern of the day, the wind was sometimes none existent and at other times saw boats heading down the
wallet to finish at Mersea, some with kites up, others hard on the wind.

After 48 miles of racing, Ian & Laura Ivermee and the Woozle Hunter crew finished in 9 hours and 14 mins, which on corrected
time gave them their first overall victory of the season.

The following day the fleet did it all again in the Ralph Herring race back to Burnham, but with slightly better winds towards the
end of the race, Woozle was able to finish a little quicker in 8 hours and 37 mins. Their competitors also recorded faster times
on the return, but it wasn’t enough, Woozle had done it again! 1st overall and of course the class 3 title as well which puts them
in a great position to challenge for the 2016 series.

NORTH SEA RACE WINNERS – WOOZLE HUNTER
The RORC North Sea Race, the most prestigious Offshore Race on the East Coast, has been won by Marconi boat, Woozle
Hunter in 2016.

Ian & Laura Ivermee, joined by their Fastnet race crew from last season, set off from Harwich last Friday morning in a fleet of 30
IRC racers which included the best from Holland.

The race, 180 miles offshore is a real test of seamanship, stamina, concentration and persistence and this year was no
different, in what turned out to be a light airs race with very little shelter from the sun.

Woozle, the slowest boat on handicap rating to finish the course, pressed on as they chased the fleet out to the South Galloper
before turning North around the windfarms to head to Smith Knoll off Great Yarmouth, before turning to cross towards Holland.
It wasn’t until 5:30 in the morning on Saturday that they managed to pass this most Northerly mark of the course, and as they
were now way out of signal range, they had no idea of their position.

Those ashore watched the race play out on the online tracker, which you can see here, and looking at the weather forecast, it
seemed that the bigger boats would have light airs all the way with the possibility of slightly increasing wind later in the evening
for Woozle.

As it turned out, Woozle was still racing into the dark of Saturday evening when for a moment the wind died bringing the
possibility of ruining their chances whilst the rest of the fleet had made Scheveningen. But the hole in the wind didn’t last long
and at 10:30 in the evening Woozle finished after 36 hours of racing, to win the race outright, over 1 hour ahead of their nearest
competitor on corrected time.

A truly remarkable and well deserved achievement
for the Woozle team, in particular skipper Ian who
has spent many hours preparing both the boat and
assembling his crew over the past 2 years. This
must rank as one of the best, if not the very best
achievement of a Marconi racing member from any
fleet.

The crew are seen here collecting the Goeree
Challenge Cup and the Jan Moreton Salver, after
the race. Later this month, they will be awarded with
the Royal Ocean Racing Club Medallion at a
ceremony on the 19th May at the clubs HQ in St
James’s.

Well done guys.

You can see the full result here - http://www.rorc.org/raceresults/2016/ircoverall04.html

CRUISER SPRING SERIES – WEEKEND 1 RESULTS
Six Marconi Cruiser racers set off early on Sat 21st May on leg 1 of the Spring Cruiser Series. Caroline, Woozle Hunter and
Crazy Suzy, all sailing short on crew opted to race without spinnakers, and on the gusty passage to the finish line off Batemans
Tower this proved to be a good decision.

Crazy Suzy was first across the line, putting her new main sail to good use, whilst the rest of the fleet crossed closely bunched
together. Ned Kelly, having issues with her main sail retired and took the short route inside Bench in order to get to the line in
time for Leg 2 which started at midday.

Leg 2 was a joint race with the Colne YC fleet and the 16 boats tacked out of the Colne, over the shallows to try and beat th e
flooding tide. After Bench Head, and then on the return from WMYC No:10 where kites could have been flown, almost all opted
to keep them in their bags. On corrected time Caroline, was highest finishing Marconi boat, 3rd overall in the LH class, with
Woozle Hunter in 7th and Blue Moon in 10th. Crazy Suzy, Ned Kelly and Monkey Business were in 13, 15 and 16th place
respectively.

After a great social evening with the Colne YC fleet on saturday, the Marconi boats started leg 3 of their series in very light
winds and against a strong flood tide. Once around the East Mersea point, the boats skimmed the bottom along the Mersea
shore before finally making it out and around Bench Head. Monkey Business was having a great light airs day but as the tide
turned and the winds died off Bradwell, all boats eventually retired, some after a long wait at anchor. Not the Woozle team
though. After initially anchoring in 13m in mid channel, and then taking a very slow passage along the St Lawrence shore that
saw them kedge another 3 or 4 times, they eventually crossed the line jubilant having beaten the conditions after 6 and a half
hours of racing.

There’s just one time that needs to be confirmed in leg one, but the current standings in the series show Woozle Hunter leading
both the Local Handicap and the IRC classes.

media (25,000 responses on Facebook!) and local press for
this year’s event, MSC was pleased to host around 100
families and other visitors to their Open Day on Saturday
21st May as part of the RYA’s “Push The Boat Out” event.

It was all hands on deck as guests received a warm
welcome from club members who gave tours of the club’s
facilities and arranged joyrides on the beautiful River
Blackwater. Rear Commodore Graham Cross was in charge
of proceedings and laid on a fleet of boats for guests to try,
from wayfarers to twin trapeze racing catamarans and
yachts. MSC’s active windsurfers were also on hand to
demonstrate their skills. Plus a beautiful sailing mosaic was
created by children for the clubhouse in the Art Generation
tent as a memento of the special day. Publicity Secretary
Christopher Kirby commented “The Open Day has provided us with a real opportunity to showcase the very best that our club
has to offer and we were so pleased that we were able to welcome so many guests on a day when the forecast was not looking
particularly favourable.”

Getting to a World Championships
At the end of 2014 we made an epic trip over to Perth in Australia to take part in the Tornado World Championships. This
involved two road trips (there and back) to Southern Germany to load and unload the boat into a container, then of course th e
flight to Australia (with a 3 month old baby).

At the time I never wrote anything down about our preparation of getting to a World Championships and the logistics around
attending. I thought this might be a useful read, whether you’re thinking of travelling to your first open meeting down the road or
you’re looking at attending a World Championships. We’re in no way pros but we love our sailing and we like to sail with the
best, watching and learning from further back!

This year in early June we’re off to the 2016 Tornado World Championships in Lindau, Southern Germany. No flights involved
this time, just a long road trip with a trailer (again), a toddler and a 3 month old (again!).

So here are some tips on how we go about preparing for an event.

FIRST STEPS
Where is the event? What’s involved in getting there? What are the dates? Where is the notice of race? Sailing instructions
published yet? Who are you sailing with?

Collect all of the necessary information you need and start planning early.

LOGISTICS
With logistics, it could be an easy trip or it could be long and painful.

This year getting the boat to the World Championships is in our own hands using the trailer we have, no containers, far away
loading destinations or customs.

Although in our own hands there are two boats travelling; Steve Glynn & Tom Duckmanton and Michaela & Andrew Dowley.
We’ve also got the pleasure of bringing a new boat back for John Nickalls – welcome to the fleet John! Or maybe the boat is for
David and Daniel?

You really need to think about your timing with logistics, how long will it take you to get to the event? Although Google maps is
useful, you usually hit traffic so make sure you leave plenty of time. I would recommend arriving a day earlier if you can,
although that’s with a Tornado which takes some time to put together. I find if you build the boat the day before you can at least
relax knowing you don’t have to rush before the first race the next morning because the boat is ready to go.

Looking ahead to Germany, our friends at Google tell us it’s an 11 hour drive down to Lake Constance and we know it involves
the M25, a ferry and a very long drive in Europe, probably around Brussels which isn’t great for traffic.

TRAILER AND CAR
My first thoughts always fall to equipment and prep for a road trip – the car is booked in for a service, the trailer has been
checked over and we roughly know how we’re going to carve up the journey over the days depending on progress. Steve is
towing the trailer and will leave on Tuesday morning, we will follow on Wednesday morning with the kids onboard (wish us luck).
The first measurement day is on Friday so this leaves at least 2 days to get there which is plenty of time and allows for an
overnight stop.

Another important thing to always remember is a spare wheel for the trailer. If you buy me a beer in the Mamgu bar one night I’ll
tell you the story of chasing a trailer wheel down the M3 at 11 o’clock at night. Buy me two and I’ll name the driver of the car.

I would always make sure you secure the boat properly, get straps or non stretch ropes and plenty of padding. Make sure you
also check your knots and straps every time you stop, it’s surprisingly easy for them to come loose on a long drive.

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

ACCOMMODATION
Where to stay? Our most useful tool in previous years has been Airbnb, we found our accommodation for Ibiza and Perth here.
Simply punch in the address of the sailing club and look for nearby places to stay. This year we’ve ventured elsewhere to book
because there are no apartments around the area listed on Airbnb. We’ve managed to find an apartment 450 yards from the
sailing club this year which is ideal. There’s also a pub less than 100 yards from the door – very important with us being sailing
athletes!

We’ve always had a few people travelling to the events over the years so we’ve gone for apartments which work well although
they are self catering. Sometimes a hotel can be nicer but it’s obviously your choice. B&B’s are fantastic in the UK and are worth
searching for, especially for a short stay. Of course, most events also allow camping in a tent – the Commodore (Michaela) isn’t
too keen on this option.

The key with accommodation is to work it out and book early, especially if you’re going to a big event. I’ve came unstuck
previously at a large catamaran event where we had to stay quite far away from the club. Another useful tip is to speak to the
locals and check out the club website for recommendations.

BOAT AND EQUIPMENT
One thing I’ve learnt is to make sure your boat is in the best condition it can be. Failing to prepare is preparing to fail and all
that….. We took a boat to Perth which wasn’t in great condition, the World champion commented on the bad condition when it
went back into the container to come home. The first thing I did when we got it back to the UK was took it to Graham Eeles, it’s
amazing how a polish and small tidy up can make it look like new again.

SIMPLE CHECKS
Some of you may have seen me spending some time on the boat over the early May bank holiday. Okay, yes it was most of the
weekend but we did hit some issues….

Make sure you spend the time, check each rope from end to end, your rigging, your sails, your blocks, shackles etc etc – the list
is endless but just take some time to look in detail – it could save you an embarrassment when you get to the event.

By typing this I’ve just jinxed us and something is going to break!

SPARE PARTS
Although it would be ideal you simply can’t pack a spare of everything! You know your boat, you know the bits you replace
frequently and you know what could happen. Invest some money and get some spares. If you are short on cash to carry spares
then there will always be a Chandlery locally, it might just mean you miss some races – not ideal if you only have one discard for
example. Another option is to borrow, there are plenty of people who have the odd spare block hanging around they won’t mind
you borrowing for a weekend or so.

Along with spare parts make sure you have some tools with you, a small tool box with basic tools can really save your event.

With some boats it’s also wise to carry some Gelcoat, filler or epoxy resin – a small dent or crack could be repaired at the event.

INSURANCE
Check your insurance paperwork – are you covered to sail where you’re going? You might need to pay a little extra if you’re
going far away. Is your boat also insured while in a container? It’s worth speaking to your insurance company.

PACK YOUR SAILING KIT
First of all check you’ve got the essentials but then my advice would be to pack as much as you can (depending on the length of
the event). You can never have enough gear, the more warm layers the better because at championships you’re going to be out
on the water for lengthy periods of time. Try and find somewhere on your boat where you can store an extra layer, just in case.

GOALS
Ahead of arrival set your goals for the event. If you sail by yourself then you will know what you want to do and achieve. If you
sail with a crew/helm then make sure you talk about it. Maybe it’s not to come last, or maybe you don’t care where you end up
as long as you learn something new to bring back to Marconi.

AT THE EVENT
STUDY THE SAILING INSTRUCTIONS
This document you get given is your bible for the event! The organisers have spent a lot of time gathering the info and pulling it
together for you – make sure you read it along with your crew/helm.

MEASUREMENT
If your boat and sails need to be measured then it’s likely the organising committee will want the boat in bits again. Work out
what’s needed and where you have to go. You may also need the boats original measurement certificate so make sure you
pack that before your trip.

TEST THE SAILING AREA

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Go out ahead of the event (if you can) and go exploring, wind patterns are often similar in the same conditions. If you’re sailing
on a lake or pond then work out if there is a big tree that’s going to give you a nasty shift or lack of wind.

GET ON THE WATER EARLY
If you can push past the other boats it’s worth getting out on the water early. Go out, test the conditions, set the boat up as it
should be for those conditions and practice, practice, practice. Think about how you’re going to start, where and what your
tactics might be for the race. BUT make sure you also keep an eye on the committee boat incase the warning signal goes.

TALK TO OTHERS
I attended the 2010 Tornado World Championships to do some work for the organisers of Travemunde Week and the Tornado
Class Association. Although frustrating not being on the water it was nice to be in the background driving a rib around the race
course – you see things from a different angle.

One of the best things I did that week was introduced myself to people and talked to the sailors about their race, why they made
decisions and why they have their boat set up in a certain way. I learnt so much! I also ended up filming a Tornado tuning gu ide
with the Greek Olympic team which has been viewed on YouTube nearly 8,000 times.

ENJOY YOURSELF
The most important thing is to go and enjoy yourself, there is no point putting in the effort if you don’t enjoy yourself.

If you did have any questions, I would be happy to have a chat about this in some more detail. Sharing is caring!

Andrew Dowley

Although I have headlined this piece “ECPR weekend” I think it is worth reminding members that we now run three separate
races on Sunday these are: -

East Coast Piers Race (cats only) 48 Nm
Colne Point Race (cats & fast dinghies with PY with 944 or faster) 27 Nm

It takes a devil of a lot of work to make the weekend successful, so if you are not racing I would very much appreciate your help.

The object of the weekend is both to put on a top class sailing event which puts the Club on the map nationally and also to raise

With your help by entering the Race, drinking a pint(s) of Adnams, buying a raffle ticket or a polo shirt we can keep up our
donations to our chosen charities.

With your help and support it promises to be another great weekend.

All we need is for the weather to deliver some wind.

Rubicon (8 metre yacht) from Stansgate to Dunkirk – June 13 through 20, 2016
Skipper: John Walker (JW) Crew: Richard D Wood-Kneller (RDWK)

DAY ONE SUNDAY 13 JUNE
We loaded our belongings at the Marconi Sailing Club, Stansgate at 16.00 hours and set off for a one hour sail down the River
Blackwater to Bradwell Marina. We stayed there overnight and checked all the rigging and chart courses for the following day.

DAY TWO MONDAY 14 JUNE
We left Bradwell at 05.30 hours and set sail due East for the Eagle at the entrance to the Spitway. We passed South West
through this narrow gap in the sandbanks and then headed due east again for Barrow Number 2. We passed over the Sunk
Sand sandbank and continued South West to Foulger’s Gap. This entailed sailing through one of the multitude of Wind Farms in
the Thames Estuary. We met all our Waypoints without difficulty up to Long Sand Inner at the entrance to the gap, but instead of
Long Sand Outer we found Long Sand Middle. Our chart was a few years old, but this was one of only a couple of changes we
encountered. From there we had a long run to North Foreland. A couple of hours later found us in Ramsgate Harbour at 13.30
hours. We had planned the tidal assistance carefully and this paid dividends.

Our arrival at Ramsgate produced the first “incident” of our cruise. RDWK went to step down from Rubicon to make her fast at
our pontoon; in doing so he looked down and his spectacles fell into the harbour and slowly disappeared from view. As these
had cost over £500 a short time ago he was upset! A fellow seaman came over to enquire about the fuss and immediately
suggested that we contact Terry Vickers, the local diving instructor. He quoted £175 and RDWK agreed. After a short while
below at 8 metres in total darkness Terry found the glasses and handed them over to a much relieved RDWK. Terry reported
that he had all but given up when his hand touched something and thus the day was saved.

DAY THREE TUESDAY 15 JUNE
We left Ramsgate at 11.00 hours with overcast skies and a wind forecast of force 5 gusting 6. Almost immediately we had
doubts about continuing, but having started on the main reason for our cruise we were reluctant to turn back. We followed our
SatNav course on the screen as there are no buoys between Ramsgate and Gravelines to act as waypoints.

For a few hours the seas were large and the wind force six as forecast, but Rubicon seemed comfortable even if were not.
About midway across the wind increased and at times was probably force 6 gusting 7 and this made life really uncomfortable.
RDWK attached his lifeline to the boat, but the skipper’s was below and it was now impossible to leave the cockpit. We rigged a
rope to act as his line and we both felt safer.

We had been warned about heavy traffic in the shipping lanes, but saw only half a dozen ships and none of them threatened our
progress. Needless to say, we did not see any other yachts from start to finish.

By now the waves were considerably bigger than forecast and seemed to come from several angles making the helm hard to
manage and it was difficult to keep our course. At one point Rubicon broached to and this was by far the most exciting moment
of the whole journey. If we were alert before we were doubly so thereafter. To say we were concerned would be true, but
Rubicon shewed her true worth then and throughout. She quickly lifted her skirts and righted herself much to our relief and we
continued at a good pace on our way.

Some while later the wind eased a little and this gave us a much needed respite and easier sailing. It was still too rough to leave
the cockpit and so we had nothing to drink or eat throughout the crossing. It also meant certain other functions were more
difficult than normal and left us with some amusing images of our epic voyage! JW found it less amusing, but that is another
story.

We had hoped the better weather would last until we reached Gravelines, but it was not to be and the last part of the journey
was again hard work demanding 100% concentration at all times and no small amount of physical application as well. Changing
helm was a particularly difficult operation.

After about eight hours sailing the Skipper noticed that our SatNav was indicating a course that led us several miles up the
coast and into Belgium instead of Gravelines in France. We could not alter the settings because of the weather and so
abandoned it. As we could see the land in the far distance we decided to sail due south until we were near enough to the coast
to locate our position. RDWK called the French Coast Guard on channel 16 and asked for our position. They replied that we
were due north of Dunkirk and should call the latter on channel 9. We attempted this, but found that the radio would not stay on
any station except channel 16. The coast guard than told us to call Dunkirk on channel 16, but there was no reply. In order to
alert them we made a PAN PAN PAN call and at last they responded. Before they offered any advice they pointed out that there
were dangerous shoals between us and the port and that they would only continue if we accepted full responsibility should we
go aground. As we only draw just over a metre the Skipper decided to proceed. Finally, we spotted the harbour entry lights, but
they were reversed, i.e. red was where green should have been and vice versa. Later, we found that this is due to the fact that
entry to Dunkirk is along a coastal channel and not directly from the North.

After some nine hours at sea we entered the marina in Dunkirk and tied up at the fuel pontoon for the night.

DAY FOUR WEDNESDAY 16 JUNE
Samuel awoke us at 09.00 hours and politely asked us to move as others wish to refuel. We did so and spotted numerous small
boats flying the red duster. It transpired that a $150 million film was being made about Operation Dynamo and the “Little Ships”
that transported tens of thousands of allied troops off the beach at Dunkirk in 1940 to avoid capture by the Germans.

We spent the day sightseeing in Dunkirk and generally recuperating from our bruising battle with the waves the day before.

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

DAY FIVE THURSDAY 17 JUNE
We cleaned up the boat and studied the operation of the SatNav until we mastered its somewhat complicated menu system.
After various discussions with Little Ship Captains and local yachtsmen we decided on our course back to Ramsgate and
entered it into SatNav. We also listed the headings, waypoints and timings on paper in case of any further machine difficulties.

Most importantly we checked and found a loose wire on the radio which was easily fixed and meant we had no further radio
problems. We also charged and tested our back-up radio.

In the afternoon we hired a car to explore Gravelines and Calais. We missed the turning on the way home and only just returned
the car in time.

The weather forecast for Friday was good and we decided to head back to Blighty on the morrow, as did most of the Little
Ships.

DAY SIX FRIDAY 18 JUNE
We were up early to refuel and fill up with water. Having made sure we had food and water easily accessible and the chart in
the cockpit, we set off for home at 10.00 hours. The tide was against us as we sailed towards Gravelines and we were
concerned that this might affect our timing later in the day. About two miles short of Gravelines we swung away from land and
headed back across the Channel which had given us such a rough ride coming over. On this day the weather was perfect and it
all seemed so easy. The only real risk was sunburn and we applied lotion early to avoid any problems. The equipment worked
faultlessly and we only had to take avoiding action twice to give the big ships crossing in front of us a wide berth.

We hit all our waypoints exactly on schedule and the passage was so calm the crew was able to sleep below for a couple of
hours well-earned rest.

Great care was taken as we moored in the harbour to avoid losing any spectacles and we celebrated the completion of our
crossing with a good meal in town.

DAY SEVEN SATURDAY 19 JUNE
The weather forecast was bad and we decided to explore Broadstairs before making our way home on Sunday.

In the evening we set up the SatNav and plotted our course for home. The engine was checked, minor repairs effected, the oil
topped up and food prepared for the last leg.

DAY EIGHT SUNDAY 20 JUNE
The weather forecast was good and we set off at 11.00 hours. Again we suffered a small adverse tide to begin with, but
benefitted later from a strong assist for the last leg home. We found all the waypoints without trouble except for one that was
concealed by a wind turbine in one of the many wind farms that litter the Estuary now.

It had taken us nine hours to reach Ramsgate from Bradwell on day two and we did as well on our last day, reaching the
Marconi Sailing Club at Stansgate after ten hours. After unloading we shook hands on a mission accomplished and headed for
home.

Richard D Wood-Kneller
