East Coast Piers Race sponsored by Zhik
67 boats made their way to Marconi Sailing Club for
the annual East Coast Piers Race over the
weekend of the 9th and 10th July.

The East Coast Piers Race is a long distance race
weekend for fast dinghies and catamarans raising
money for The Cirdan Trust and Essex Air
Ambulance.

East Coast Piers Race 2016With free camping
available from Friday through to Monday many
competitors arrived on Friday to get their boats
rigged.

After morning registration and a good breakfast on
Saturday there was a midday briefing for a 1pm
start with windy conditions forecast for the
afternoon of racing where the race officer was
hoping to get two races in.

A course was set which took the sailors up and down the River Blackwater to give them a healthy warm up for Sunday. It was a
breezy start to the weekend with a few capsizes in the first race, mainly around the windward mark in the larger chop.

Many of the competitors thought it would be best to sit out the second race and prepare for Sunday.

August & September 2016 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

At 6pm on Saturday the official race briefing was held in the marquee, with Adnams as a race sponsor it was rude not to have a
beer in your hand during the briefing. As soon as the briefing finished the BBQ was ready and the sailors and their guests
tucked in! After the BBQ the bar was continuing to sell beer where the visitors and Marconi members were making their
donation to charity by drinking. Later in the evening a band came on and entertained everyone until very late.

As per usual, and not at the request of the usual person, the camp site was woken at 6am by the sound of Sweet Caroline and
Neil Diamond through the PA system. A firm favourite with many of the competitors, or maybe not but it’s becoming tradition.
With the first race start scheduled for 8am an early start was unfortunately needed
to match the tides.

The East Coast Piers Race which takes sailors 48 miles to Walton and back was
the first to start at 8am. Due to the wind forecast and possible force 7 gusts it was
decided on Saturday that the course would be shortened to Clacton, making the
race around 38 miles.

The Colne Point Race (27 miles) started at 8.15am and then the Bradwell Race (13
miles) for fast dinghies at 8.30am.

In the full ECPR race it was the Dinghy Rope Tornado which had the best start
flying off the line with the Marconi Commodore at the helm. As the fleet reached
Thirslet Spit they were over taken by John Gimson and Pete Jary sailing the big
pink Nacra 20 Carbon. Closely behind were the Hurricane and Windrush Tornado
followed by a fleet of F18’s.

Through the Bradwell gate and out towards Colne Point the wind was building and
the waves were getting bigger making a 2 sail reach very tricky! It was at this point
that the foiling Nacra F20 overtook the Tornado and started to catch up the non
foiling Nacra 20 Carbon.

The two Nacra 20’s then started to pull away through the Colne Point gate and up
towards Clacton pier which was the turning point. All the way back from Clacton it
was a long beat with only 12 tacks made along a distance of 19 miles.

As the ECPR fleet were heading back from Clacton they came across
the Colne Point race boats which were going around the Colne Point
marker and heading for home. This meant the fleets were arriving back
in mass at Marconi after a long beat back.

First back in the Colne Point Race were Kevin Dowley and Tom Brooks
from Marconi sailing a Tornado. First back in the ECPR in a time of just
over two hours were John Gimson and Pete Jary who took the line
honours trophy.

Due to the quick race the prize giving was held at 1.15pm, much earlier
than usual meaning the sailors could head off home early. First up was
the raffle where our race sponsors had donated some fantastic prizes.
William Harrison was the lucky guy who took home the top prize of £750
worth of Zhik sailing gear.

BROWN CUP
MCGREGOR WINS BROWN CUP. BLUE MOON & MONKEY BUSINESS 2ND & 3RD IN THRILLING IRC RACE.
19 cruisers passed the club on Saturday lunchtime, in what turned out to be a thrilling and close Brown Cup race between the
Marconi representatives.

Crazy Suzy and Monkey Business were at the head of the fleet with Blue Moon and McGregor 3 in hot pursuit. Sailing the
longest course on the card, Ned Kelly had a close boat race towards the back of the fleet, whilst Caroline swapped positions
throughout.

After the turn at Wallet No3, Crazy Suzy took the lead all the way home on the windward leg, whilst McGregor 3 got ahead of all
the other IRC boats on the water. Blue moon remained close on her transom, always close enough to be ahead of her on
corrected time and approaching Colne Bar the team on Blue Moon looked as if they might have overhauled series leader,
Absolution.

Monkey Business then started her charge back up the Blackwater in an attempt to claw back her time, and by the time she had
rounded No12 off Bradwell she had passed, Behave and McGregor. Absolution had got back into the groove on the homeward
leg and was now 2nd on the water behind Crazy Suzy, it was now all about, how much time Monkey Business might get ahead
of McGregor and Blue Moon whilst Triton, not far behind, would also have a say in the final positions of this exciting IRC race.

Absolution (Eric Reynold – Maylandsea) finished 1st on corrected time after more than 6.5 hours of racing.

Blue Moon (Richard Roberts – MSC) had a super race in 2nd place, beating Monkey Business (Dave Onyons – MSC) by 1:47
mins who were 3rd. Triton (Peter Copsey – BSC) was just 62 secs back in 4th place whilst McGregor 3 (Steve Purdue) was a
further 70 secs behind.

All 7 IRC rated boats finished within 20 minutes of each other on the water, and on corrected time, the first 5 boats were
separated by just 7:48 mins

Using the BJRC local handicaps on which all 19 boats in the fleet are scored, Steve Purdue and Monica Wolff racing McGregor
for just the 3rd time, came out on top and are this years winners of the MLSC Brown Cup.

The full results and report can be found here on the BJRC website.

IONIAN ODYSSEY 2016
Holiday booked through Sailing Holidays that provided
us with a very useful and comprehensive marina guide
including excellent photographs of the majority of the
marinas in the whole region.

An enormous thanks to Jackie and Roger Camp for
organising the most exceptional Summer Cruise. What
an amazing fortnight. The scenery, the sailing, the
weather, the food, the drink, the company. And of
course an extra large portion of laughter. I can’t think
of any way of improving it. Here is my diary style
record of our two week holiday in Greece, starting in
the Northern Ionian sailing to the Southern Ionian and
back stopping at many wonderful places along the
way.

The Fleet:

August & September 2016 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

KALAMAS (Lead Boat) Skipper: Kit, Hostie: Ellen, Engineer: Richard

CORDELIA: Roger & Jackie Camp

ISIS: Steve & Margaret Golding, Robin & Diane Good

Plataria Our first taste of the Ionian. A beautiful bay skirted by mountains with a lovely shingle beach with restaurants spilling
out onto it. We enjoyed our first meal at Olga’s on the marina. One of the local cats decided to pee through the pergola roof onto
Jan causing much mirth and an interesting aroma. It was great to all be together if the restaurant had a problem with dealing
with the volume of dinners ordered. We stayed another day in Plataria due to strong winds and rain in the morning. We gathered
for a quiz after lunch then went out for a sail round the bay in the afternoon. We had a lovely dinner on the beach. It was q uite
difficult sitting on chairs on the shingle beach and there was a dominos effect moment when Mike Cutmore toppled over and he
and Cheryl tipped off their chairs. Was the wine to blame?! A great place to watch the sun go down and see the stunning
sunset.

Gaios Fabulous sail over. Gaios has lots of restaurants which early in the evening started to release the ever tempting smell of
bbqed meat and many different shops selling a wide variety of goods. Somewhere that might be worth staying for another day.
We had dinner at Genesis overlooking the the bay. Enormously pretty. All sorts of different craft moored against the long
winding harbour wall with a pretty little beach tucked round the corner that was ideal for a cooling swim.

Spartatahori Early start and big swell to Lefkas Canal where we were able to stop for lunch moored against the quayside
before going through the canal and on to Spartatahori, Meganisi, Steve and Gerry’s Quay. – totally beautiful spot. Dinners were
usually dip style starters, grilled cheese or stuffed vegetables. Fresh fish, squid and mussles could be had as well as popular
favourites such as mousaka, kebabs and spicy meat balls. Spartahori was surrounded by stunning pine covered hills. We swam
off the boat after mooring up and all got together for a joint meal. Walk up to cliff top in the morning before leaving to see view of
the whole Ionian. Really beautiful (but isn’t it all!)

Kalamos Georges restaurant – dinner on the beach with stunning backdrop of the distant misty mountains. Great sail down
alongside Richard and Margaret. Did not find the bay with the church that was recommended for lunch stop. Lunch for us was
usually local produce such as Feta cheese, olives, enormous fresh ripe sweet tomatoes , stuffed vine leaves with crusty freshly
baked bread dipped in olive oil. A naked girl on the beach rather startled Richard when he swam ashore. He believes she may
have had an accident with the strimmer. We swam off the boat and snorkelled round rocks. Later we all met in the local cocktail
bar for pre dinner drinks.

Vathi On our way to Big Vathi on Ithaka we raced to One House Bay. Had our usual lunch, snorkelled and fed fish. Woke to still
flat calm and immense heat! Wide populated bay. Rafted on quay. Delish yoghurt with honey and fruit for breakfast. Some took
20 minute walk into village. It was way too hot so we made off and welcomed the cooling sea breeze.

KionI Made off early for Kioni. Lunch stop then early in to port to
find good spot and avoid mooring away from the quay and using
tenders. Had to moor out with stern lines which made an interesting
muddle to negotiate in the tender to get on and off. Punch party on
the quay. Really good dinner at Three Windmills right by the beach.
Had enormous fun attempting to get back on board the boats after
a wine or two. Lots of shrieks of laughter from Sue Arnold and Sue
Booth finding keeping dry impossible. Lunch stop in a pretty little
bay just before Frikis. Moored up and got in the water for a swim
and snorkel. As we entered the bay a young woman was waving at
us. To our surprise the police turned up and moved us on due to
mooring too close to the beach and being a danger to swimmers. It
would appear the waving young woman was telling us to go away
and called the police!!! Totally mad!! We moved onto an adorable little bay that was perfect.

Decided to stay another day in Kioni to chill. All the fleet got spaces along the quay. Sampled the yoghurt and fruit and walnut
for breakfast. A new take on delicious! All swam off the quay from steps down the rocks. Enormous racing yacht came into the
bay and anchored but neglected to secure the anchor and the whole lot fell to the sea bed! Peter Clayton, in swimming at the
time was asked if he could dive down for it. Naturally de didn’t! All met up for pre dinner drinks at Derek and Hillary’s boat. All
had dinner at Avra. Lots of feline friends came to share with us! The wind got up and blew strongly all night. And kept blowing
the following day.

August & September 2016 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Sivota was the next stop. Sailing holiday base. Lots of Tavernas and shops fringed by wooded mountains. Small beach for
swimming. Could buzz over the harbour in tender. Lunch swim in bay by Frikes avoiding nutty sunbathers.

Preveza Stopped at Goat Bay for a swim. Went through Lefkas Canal 4pm opening. Wind speed had gathered. Great sail up to
Preveza on foresail only. Moored on the quay. Very hot. Good town with lots of tavernas and shops. Great meal. Enormous
mullet – delicious cool spot outside the restaurant and inexpensive. Busy night. Sue Arnold’s anchor was not holding and had to
be relaid. Next boat to us decided to run engine at 11pm! Hot night had to spend time in the cockpit cooling off.

Parga Early start for Parga. Possible stop at Two rocks bay.
The bay was stunning. We swam snorkelled and had lunch.
We were moored grounded on the beach at Parga and had
fun on the paddle board. We caught the ferryboat into town.
Large bustling town with Venetian fort on the hilltop. The
majority of us went up for dinner in a restaurant by the fort
with spectacular views over the bay. Bit of a challenge getting
off the boats and shopping in the morning.

Stopped at Emerald Bay for lunch on the way to Mongonisi.
The bay seemed deserted then we were joined by a pleasure
boat overflowing with people. The bay was transformed from
a tranquil paradise to the local lido! Had a great evening in
Mongonisi Greek dancing which started with a demonstration
given by the locals after which we were all pulled up to have a
go ourself. Much to all the ladies delight the local lad performed stripped to the waste exposing a gorgeous muscular torso that it
would gave been rude not to have gazed at.

Sivoter Muertos We hugged the coast of Mongonisi then took a 45 degree course to SM which enabled a sail over. There
being no opportunity to stop in a bay to lunch and swim we had our lunch whilst under sail. This seemed rather decedent and
definitely rather clever!

We all assembled for a briefing ashore and Jan got a tart with candles for Ellen our hostess who was 29 that day. The girls
donned wacky glasses and we were given ‘viagera’ shots by the bar
owner. A few jokes were exchanged.

We had dinner at George’s which was superb. A few shops to wander
round and daft hats to try on.

Plataria Dropped off for a swim after a yoghurt honey and fruit
breakfast. Nice little beach just before Plataria then into Plataria stern
to by Olga’s. The last evening of the most amazing holiday we all got
together for dinner on the beach.

There was some concern as it had rained earlier but the skies had
cleared and we decided to take a chance. Was the most perfect
evening. Food was fabulous. The restaurant put out oil filled torches to light the table then we dined and watched the most
wonderful display of the day turning to night and the sun slowly sinking into the sea creating the most wonderful orange glow.

Happy sailing

Cheryl Cutmore

As in the previous two years, MSC once again played host on Tuesday
5th July to twelve special youngsters from Ukraine, giving them an
unforgettable lifetime experience, which for most of them was their first
time on the sea. The children: six boys and six girls aged between 8
and 13, are on a one-month recuperative holiday organised by the
South Essex branch of the Chernobyl Children’s Lifeline charity. They
have all grown up near the ill-fated Chernobyl nuclear power plant,
where local communities continue to be affected by health problems
thirty years after the nuclear disaster. The children visiting are being
treated at home for a range of health issues, and their time in England
enables them to enjoy uncontaminated food and fresh air, whilst
experiencing wonderful activities thanks to the generosity of
organisations such as Marconi Sailing Club.

Our young cadets (and slightly older volunteers) did a fantastic job of
entertaining their visitors with a warm welcome which was reflected
in the gradually emerging sunshine. The day started with a trip up
the river on Top Cat, Jack B and the RIBs past Mundon Point to
hang out with curious seals popping up for a peek at these young
visitors from afar, and everyone enjoyed an exciting ride back for
lunch… all against the backdrop of the beautiful Essex coastal
landscape so utterly different from their home hundreds of miles
from the coast in Ukraine. Not all could be persuaded to taste the
salty water! The afternoon was spent in exciting sailing conditions in
the club’s smaller dinghies, all the children were soaked but the big
grins remained and they even tried their hand at crabbing.

The youngsters, still excited by their adventure on the high seas,
then treated the Marconi volunteers to a lovely rendition of a
Ukrainian folk song as a thank you. They will go home refreshed,
healthier, and with memories to last a lifetime.

Thanks to all those that volunteered their time, energy and boats,
and for giving our visitors such a great day.

SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITY ON THE COAST
I recently received the following request from PS Ben Felton who is a sergeant at Maldon. Ben is also a yachtsman who has an
interest in local sailing clubs and marinas.

Dear all,

Sorry I have not been in contact for a while. It has been very busy so far this summer. Luckily I haven't had any intelligence to
share with you all which I guess is a good thing.

I am emailing today to ask for your continued vigilance around suspicious vessel or persons. In this time of heightened threat it
is vital you are the eyes and ears of the coast. You know your area better than anyone. You know what looks out of place.
Please don't hesitate to report anything suspicious to me or the marine unit, no matter how small.

Today we had information regarding a yacht entering Tollesbury at night and the crew acting suspiciously. Luckily after checks it
turned out to be a false alarm and the crew were in order. But that is exactly the sort of information we need. I would rather
every call turns out to be a legitimate yacht rather than miss that one vital piece of information so please keep it coming.

You can visit the Project Kraken website for more information. Please use my email or contact the Essex Police Marine Unit via
the 101 non-emergency phone number. If you believe it is an emergency please dial 999 and let the call taker assess the
information and respond accordingly.

Thank you for your support. I hope you are all having a busy and profitable season.

TEAM MARCONI AT THE SPRINT 15 NATIONALS!
The Sprint 15 Nationals were held over the August Bank
Holiday weekend. Kevin Kirby, Pete Richardson, Jon
Pearse, David Ball and myself - with support crew of Liz
Jackson and Fenella Miler made the journey up to
Pwllheli in North Wales - which is a beautiful sailing
location with sandy beaches and the back drop of
Snowdonia. And, defying all known precedent, we had
dry and warm weather and plenty of sun across the
three days! We found ourselves sharing the boat park
(not as big as we are spoilt with at home!) with 120 RS
Teras, their sailors, parents, RIBS etc So it was a bit
cosy for the 40 Sprint 15s but we all fitted in somehow.

Racing:

Racing format was a practice lap followed by two races
on Sunday, three races on Monday and two races on
Tuesday - all sailing back to back out in the bay.

Sunday was fairly breezy with a solid force 4 and some
stronger gusts blowing through.

Monday dawned with no wind so the racing was postponed until the afternoon when a light but sailable wind filled in. The thr ee
races were mentally taxing as it required a lot of concentration to try and find the best air and get ahead of the other boats.

Tuesday had a lovely force 3 - 4 breeze with some larger waves that Pwllheli is famous for from previous events! A cracking
two races saw strong placings from all Marconi boats.

With all 7 races sailed, there are two discards so the best 5 results counted.

SELLING BOATS AT STANSGATE

If you sell your boat to a non-member you remain responsible for it until the boat leaves site or the purchaser becomes a
member of the Club. A member’s responsibility does not just end when the deal is done (bylaws 3.1.4 and 3.1.4.1 refer).

Members’ gate cards are personal and must not be loaned to others; for example to a non-member who may want to gain
access to work on the boat that they have just bought.

If a non-member has bought a boat on site and wishes it to remain at Stansgate for a relatively short time they may apply to the
membership secretary for Short Term membership. They will be granted Short Term membership for a length of time and for a
fee which will be agreed in advance.

If a non-member buys a boat at Stansgate and wishes to keep it at the club permanently they may apply for membership by
completing and submitting a membership form. Copies of the form are kept in the clubhouse and are also available on the MSC
website.

If they have purchased a cruiser they should speak to the moorings secretary. Buying a cruiser from a member does not
automatically mean that a mooring will be immediately available. There is sometimes a waiting list especially for deep water
moorings.

If they have purchased a dinghy or catamaran they should agree a dinghy or catamaran park space with the membership
secretary and the appropriate boat park co-ordinator. All dinghy and catamaran park spaces are allocated to particular boats
and members. It is essential that all information is kept up to date when boats change hands.

Contact details for all club officials will be found in the yearbook or on clubhouse notice boards.

OPERATION OF CLUB BOATS AND EQUIPMENT

For information for new members and a reminder to older hands, there are detailed codes of practice and instructions for most
activities at Stansgate from procedures for a flood alert to the operation of machinery.

It is essential for the efficient and safe operation of club boats and equipment that users are familiar with the guidance. If you
have a support boat duty, do read the guidance notes. Even if you have driven or crewed on support boats before it is worth
reading the latest version of the relevant notes; they do get updated from time to time.

Winches, tractors, mast derrick and boat hoists also have their own codes of practice and user guides which are regularly
updated. Please read them. Their relevance to the operators of the equipment is obvious but it is also useful for boat owners to
be familiar with the codes of practice. You will have a better understanding of the operation of the equipment, which is satisfying
in itself, but also appreciate the operators’ point of view and the codes of practice under which they work to ensure the safety of
all concerned.

A paper copy of the codes of practice and user guides is kept in the upstairs lounge in the clubhouse but you can also
familiarise yourself with them at your leisure in the members section of the MSC website. Go to Members Area/Document
Library. The password for the Members Area will be found on Page 2 of the 2016 yearbook

Helm of the Year
This annual sailing event sees the “winningest” sailor
from each of the cat/dinghy fleets based on the
Spring and Summer points series do battle for the
coveted title of Helm of the Year. In recent years, this
has also included a representative from the cruiser
fleet. The event is completed in a one design class
which is not regularly sailed by any of the competitors
– as such, the “class of choice” for several years has
been the Pico.

The event was scheduled for Saturday 17th
September but competitors arrived to a very blustery
morning. The forecast was for the wind to decrease,
so the Race Officer, Dave Clarke, very sensibly
posptoned to the afternoon. However, with boats and
competitors rigged and ready for a 1pm start,, it
became clear that the conditions had not subdued at all. Eventually, it was decided to postpone racing until the following
morning, ahead of Barts Bash.

Sunday morning dawned with much lighter breezes and the fleet hit the water at 10am to give enough time to run the series
before Barts Bash in the afternoon – plus one of the competitors had a county level football match he needed to compete in the
afternoon. The Race Officer laid on five races – starting from the pontoon – with each competitor swapping boats in between
races to ensure the playing field was as level as possible. The younger competitors Jack Collis (Cruisers) and Jason Clarke
(Cadets) made an early impression scoring 1, 2 in the first race followed by consistently good positions in the remaining four
races. The monohull sailors Bryan Spencer (Solo Fleet) and Rob Bard (Handicap monohull fleet) also seemed pretty
comfortable in the Pico – whilst arguably the cat sailors (Steve Thomas, Medium Cats, Jenny Ball, Sprint 15s and Steve Glynn,
Fast Cats) had a bit of a disadvantage sailing very small monohulls in light winds. But we were all particularly impressed when
Steve Glynn (Fast Cats) not only capsized in Race 2 but also managed to go turtle! The racing was very closely fought with
short races, light winds and a relatively strong tide – and the downwind leg against the tide from the penultimate mark to the
finish line proving to be very tactical. After an extremely close series, the top two competitors – Jack Collis (Cruisers) and Jenny
Ball (Sprint 15) had identical race results meaning that it literally came down to the results for the last race. A coming together
on the start line between Jack Collis and Steve Glynn, allowed Jenny, Jason and Rob to get ahead of the fleet and, as a result,
the final race and, the overall series went to the Sprint 15s by the skin of their teeth.

As always, a great event! Many thanks to members who lent their boats – (David Ball, Dave Russell, Dave Clarke, Graham
Cross, Sam Flaherty), to all the Support Boat crew and to Dave Clarke and Rory Thomas as RO and Assistant RO for running
the event so efficiently.

Commodores Notes
First of all, apologies for not writing in Navigans since the summer - I have been just a little occupied with baby number 2 and
also busy sailing when possible! Hopefully you have been able to keep up to date with major news and events at the Club via
our website and weekly emails.

For those of you who were able to attend the Club AGM on 4th December you would have heard the various yearly reports,
which are available in this edition of Navigans. We have had a fantastic season of sailing, racing, social and training events at
Marconi. The Club have hosted a number of very successful open meetings for our regular fleets such as the Sprint 15’s,

Toppers and ECPR but also new ones such as the 29’ers who visited early on this year. Although these events had varied
requirements and demands on the Club, feedback was consistent and hugely positive so thank you to all those involved.
Training has again been hugely popular with the biggest attendances ever at Sail Training days and another huge success with
Cadet week 2016.

Our own sailors have demonstrated some great results when attending other open events and championships including Sprint
15’s, Tornados and cruisers (not an exhaustive list). There are a couple of major highlights to mention here - Woozle Hunter

Topper Squad - congratulations Charlotte, Ian and crew!!

As well as being good at sailing it appears we are also pretty good at partying!! Thanks are due to our Social Secretary trio of
Sara, Claire and Julie who have organised some brilliant social events from a Barn Dance to 80’s disco and a Mexican night to
name a few! Thank you also to all those members who have supported these great events - the outfits have been amazing and
plenty of people have had lots of fun! Don’t forget the annual dinner and dance which is being held at The Lion Inn (Boreham)
on 4th February - grab your tickets ASAP if you haven’t already.

I am also pleased to report that our membership stands at 430 (as at 14th November). This is great news as membership has
been at or around 400 for the past few years. Membership subscriptions and fees are our only real source of income so please
make all new members at Marconi feel welcome and keep spreading the word about our fantastic club!

Marconi Sea Wall Challenge and Winter Walks
Following the news of a Marconi members breast cancer diagnosis some of us ladies came up with the idea for a sponsored
walk for breast cancer charities. Our first idea was for a group of us to do the Moon Walk in London next May but felt this was a
challenge too far for some and administration for a group was difficult to organise.

We would therefore like to organise a walk of approximately 14-15 miles from Maldon to the club along the sea wall on 27th May
2017 (the Saturday of the 2nd May Bank holiday). The exact route is still to be determined. I intend there to be a small entrance
fee to cover costs in organisation, donation to the charity and a t-shirt. Greater donations and individual sponsorship would be
up to the individual taking part. The walk will be open to both men and women and youngsters over the age of 14 as there is
rough and exposed ground to cover.

I am hoping to arrange refreshment and loo stops along the way and there are a number of pick up points along the route if
people are getting tired.

I would be grateful if interested people contact me by email even if they can’t finally manage it on the day – no commitment is
needed but I would like to have an idea of numbers and t-shirt sizes. I am also looking for non-walking volunteers with cars to
act as taxi’s to drop people off at the start point and pick up stragglers along the way if needed, but also to run a registration
process on the day.

In preparation for the big walk I am hoping to arrange some monthly Winter Walks on a Sunday and would like to know who
would be interested in these as well. I think it will be a nice way of keeping fit over the winter and keeping in touch with our
sailing club friends. Hopefully we will be able to do circular walks along the shores of the Blackwater with a Pub or refreshments
at the end. I am aiming for the first walk to be Sunday 27th November, meeting at Bradwell Marina car park at 10am to leave by
10.30.

Looking forward to hearing from you with your contact details and t-shirt size.

2016 COMMODORE’S REPORT TO THE AGM
Michaela Dowley
4th December 2016

Good morning and welcome all to the 2016 Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting. This report will comment on the
main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season. As usual I will award a few coveted prizes and
hope to enlighten you on our plans for the year ahead.

Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board of Directors, and for the previous year has comprised these six people:

Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site

Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment

Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing

Graham Cross - Rear Commodore for events

Sue Shenton - Treasurer

Myself, Michaela Dowley - as commodore I am managing director and chair

Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of
the administrative burden of the Club.

I can report that the Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like to extend thanks
to all those who take the time to serve on the main and various sub committees.

Usually I would move straight onto the main business of the Board over the past year, however I would like to pause for a
moment to acknowledge the people here at the front with me today. Many of you know that I have been lucky enough to have
two children over the past couple of years and although they are a joy it has also been hard work. I want to thank the rest of the
Board for their support in allowing me to continue as Commodore during this rather hectic time and ensuring the club has
operated as usual. It must be said that shouldering responsibility for a Club of this size is no small task and we each have
commitments outside the club, whether it’s a full time job or family. I would like to give you an idea of what these people do;
Murray is our go to man for everything around the site and probably drives more miles on the club tractor than in his own car.
Peter leads on administering all things mooring related, health and safety and still finds time to tutor our smallest cadets during
cadet week. Pat looks after all things sailing, is our power boat instructor having qualified 32 new rib drivers since the inception
of our training centre, he’s carried out at least 21 support boat duties this year alone and is also administrating our club
membership database. Graham coordinates our hugely successful open day, oversees our marketing strategy and all things
social as well as helping to tutor during cadet week. Sue can tell us where each and every penny of club funds is, she has

Club racing cruiser. In response to a need generated by new members who joined as a result of last years 1st Autumn cruiser

THE RORC NORTH SEA RACE BY LAURA IVERMEE
After a great start to our season the previous weekend, winning the first two races in the East Anglian Offshore Racing
Association series, our 2015 Fastnet crew was reunited and hopes were high for the 180 mile RORC North Sea race to
Scheveningen in the Netherlands.

The conditions were good for a Sigma 33, light airs and good weather, which suited the smaller boats, but we were competing
against a lot of very fast people! Delayed in the lock leaving Shotley Marina, we headed for the start line as fast as we could,
other latecomer boats speeding along with us.

In the distance the start line was a mass of boats on the horizon, milling around. Once checked in with the committee boat, we
headed for the port end of the line and got a great start, working our way amongst many larger boats up to 1st place on the
leader board. Then we tacked losing places to the faster boats.

Most boats went around the Cork Sands, but as one of the smallest boats, we were able to sail over them, gaining back a few
positions.

Fantastic sailing weather for us and our colourful kite. Approaching the Black Deep Buoy, to round it to Port, the tide was
against us, and the wind died. We dropped our kite too early and nearly failed to reach the mark, along with a couple of other
boats with the same problem. We inched slowly towards the buoy, considering dropping the anchor at one point, finally rounding
it after a very unwelcome delay. Once round, however, the tide was in our favour and we made great pace.

We stayed in sight of the pack for many hours, though gradually the faster competitors disappeared into the distance.

Another boat had a medical emergency during the night, and a helicopter was sent to airlift the casualty off.

Night watch and a totally clear sky. Millions of stars, shooting stars, and a phosphorescent boat trail, until 3am and skipper
wanted the kite up!!

Kite flying in the dark? Fun!!

A stunning sun rise, and other yachts amazingly still in sight as we made our way towards our Nemesis, Smith’s Knoll, a buoy
notorious for problems rounding it, and which has cost us this race in a previous year!!

Approaching Smith's Knoll, (also known as 'The Bastard'), this time, we carried a good speed to it with our kite flying and round
beautifully at 5.45am.

Now to head for Holland.

One of the best sails in a long time. The boat behaved like a little darling.

Still boats within sight after 24 hours!! A rare sight for us in other years! This year the boat was performing superbly, and was a
pleasure to race.

Eventually Holland appeared out of the murk, and we fought for every second in the final leg.

At one stage, the wind dropped within sight of land, leading to much blaspheming!!

Out came the Haribo, then kite up, and so far forward it was a real challenge to keep flying.

11pm (local time) and one mark to go. Round the NAM 22, kite up again and a flying dash to the finish. One of the best night
kite sessions ever. We flew in the dark, heading for the lights of Holland.

Every second counted, as much faster boats than us had already finished.

And, across the line. Just over 36 hours of racing and a hyped, but weary crew.

Sails down and into the marina. Heading for beer and results!! Boat tidying could wait!!

We were met on the way to the bar by the RORC officials with the results, and .... we did it. We won.

Beating over 30 boats to an overall win, and sailing less miles than anyone else.

What an amazing result for a bunch of misfits in a 30 year old Sigma 33.

The Woozle Misfits are:

Financial Summary

As Finance Director of Marconi Sailing Club Ltd, I present a financial summary along with the accounts for the year
ended 31st August, 2016, for approval by the members. The accounts as distributed to the members are set out in
the prescribed format ready for submission to Companies House and to HMRC.

Independent Review

The accounts have been reviewed by John Bird, Chartered Management Accountant (former member and
Treasurer).

Income (top half of page 4)

Overall income from subscriptions and fees stands at £145,628 (£150,678 less Member Loan Discounts of £5050)
as against last year’s income of £137,654 (£142,879 less Loan Discounts of £5,225). The level of membership of
430 is higher than last year (401) which has helped to boost income, although a substantial part of the increase is
represented by new members joining the club later in the year on reduced fees.
Surpluses on the bar, social events, camping fees, open meetings, Cadet Week and other activities amount to
£15681 (last year £13,123). Camping and Social Events revenues decreased, but the surpluses from Club
Training and Open Meetings have increased. Bar Income shows an increase of over 14% but a straightforward
comparison for the bar income and expenditure is not possible, as the amounts paid in and expended can fall just
inside or outside of the accounting period, as is the situation again this year.
Overall therefore the club’s income has increased to £161,309 (last year £150,777).

Expenditure (lower half of page 4)

Spending has been significantly higher for sailing activities (up £4117), representing necessary upgrades on the
club’s fleet of dinghies used for training and specifically on the introduction of a club cruiser for use by members.
This outlay is offset by income generated by training and the costed use of the cruiser.

tools and container unit, offset by savings in some areas.

the travel hoist, and the payment of the insurance claim for the ‘Tony B’.
There were small increases in rates, electricity and gas, with a more significant increase in the water rate.

in December each year, resurfacing works in the Cat Field, mechanisation of lifting/laying of moorings, construction
of an equipment store for club boats and a bridge deck, and towards major improvements to the clubhouse.(See

Sailing Secretary’s Report

Good morning everyone and thanks for the other reports, it’s good to hear from the other people that keep the club
going. And now for the one you’ve been waiting for, the Sailing Secretaries report for 2016.

This has once again been another bumper year, membership numbers are up and participation numbers are also
up. We’ve seen a more that 50% increase in participation both through the training we are laying on and the racing
that is happening at the club. Our thanks must go out to Dave Russell for both collecting and sending that data off
to the RYA, and it clearly paid off as in April we were pulled out of the monthly prize draw by the RYA for returning
our participation data! We spent our prize on some useful race training marks.

Last season we set about making changes to the racing that would hopefully improve the experience for those
already racing and to try to encourage more people to use their dinghies in a racing environment. The number of
starts was reduced down to 3 and the start sequence was changed to a 5,4,1, go system. So far it seems to have
been a great success. We also introduced a mini closed regatta for the final bank holiday weekend which kept the
racing really close and the prize-giving afterwards made sure we hadn’t forgotten why we were picking up trophies.

The training centre side of things is going well, we have now trained up lots of eager RIB drivers and First Aiders to
help save us when things sometimes go a little wrong. We are looking to expand this going forwards and hopefully
will be running RYA sailing courses soon to teach, and to qualify those that already know how to sail.

This year’s Open Day seemed to be even more successful than ever, there were lots of new sailors that came
along on that day, took part in cadet week and have joined us again and again for our Sail Training days. Which
have also seen record numbers this season, with the adults joining them for the first time, hopefully these are good
signs for the future.

The Weekly emails have continued in their interesting, informative and hopefully amusing vein. I hope you have
enjoyed reading about everything that’s been going on in the Club.

The Cruiser sailing fraternity have had a busy year starting with an early cruise in the Ionian Sea, exploring the
Greek islands. It’s like the Walton Backwaters, but slightly warmer! They have also been on their traditional
voyages up and down the east coast, with trips to Ipswich, Brightlingsea & beyond. Some of our members have
ventured further afield and as mentioned previously, Antigua Kiss 2 has completed two Atlantic crossings,
Locomotion is currently en route to the Med, and Woozle Hunter has racked up many miles offshore as well.

This brings us nicely onto the cruiser racing side of things, Woozle Hunter have had a stellar year winning the
EAORA championship. More locally we have had the BJRC championship and Marconi boats did well under the
IRC handicap with finishers in 3rd, 4th & 6th place. The Autumn series was once again a great success, with many
new people introduced to sailing and a tight series of races was enjoyed by all who took part. Those that joined last
year had the opportunity to crew & maintain our new club yacht, Ned Kelly. They have had a fantastic year and
have hopefully learnt a lot about racing.

Colin’s dinghy cruises are still a popular feature of the sailing calendar. They’ve been on voyages from the club to

2. REVIEW OF 2016

(a) Cruise to Brightlingsea on 28th May was reported as fantastic but a bit windy. About six boats went.

11. RACING PROGRAMME – PETER WARD

A successful season for Marconi cruiser racing, saw club boats racing locally, inshore, offshore and the club organising a spring
cruiser regatta to compliment the 2nd running of the Autumn Series from the club line.

The winners of the Spring and Autumn series who received their trophies at the cruiser racer forum held immediately after the
final race, were Woozle Hunter (Ian & Laura Ivermee) for the Spring series and Blue Moon (Richard Roberts and the pink polo
team) in the Autumn series.

Once again the Autumn series went down to the final medal race and Crazy Suzy (John Littlewood and his reprobates) was just
pipped at the post. An equally close battle was had between the 1st year teams on Monkey Business (Brian Pearce) and Ned
Kelly (Lydia Coffey) the latter losing out. In all 5 boats completed the Autumn series but a total of 9 different boats participated in
at least one event.

In the BJRC series, once again Blue Moon was the highest finishing Marconi boat. 3rd in IRC and 9th in BJRC handicaps.

In the team race, Marconi were well beaten by Blackwater SC and just managed to hold off Maldon LSC to grab 2nd spot. But
there were wins for Marconi boats.

McGregor 3 (Steve Purdue & Monica Wolff another 1st year team) won the Brown Cup, and Caroline (Andy Ellis) were the
winners of the Marconi Cup, these trophies to be awarded at the BJRC dinner in February. Many thanks to Richard Collis who
put on an excellent race as race officer, and to John Nicholls, Andy Dowley and Sophia Barnes, who excellently conducted
protest proceedings after the race.

Offshore, Woozle Hunter was again the highest finishing Marconi boat in the EAORA offshore series and had a truly remarkable
season finishing as EAORA offshore champions overall and in class 3. Not only did they win the prestigious 180 mile North Sea
Race against a fleet of 31 NED & GBR boats, but their list of offshore race wins this year is impressive. Pattinson Cup, Ralph
Herring Trophy, Houghton Cup, and Walker Challenge Trophy as well as the North Sea race, and what's more single handedly
took Marconi-SC to 2nd place in the EAORA offshore team result.

Last Autumn in 2015, at times we had more people (guests) wanting to sail at the club as racing crew, than we had spaces
available and every boat that sailed was fully crewed almost all the time. In 2016 this resulted in the club obtaining Ned Kelly
and making it available for club members to sail which has been a great success. This Autumn we turned people away, as once
again we had more people wanting to start cruiser racing with us than we had crew spaces available. Since we stopped sailing
we have signed up 5 new members from these guests, who have committed to learn to sail as race as crew in the BJRC series
next year. Our challenge next year, is not to find a boat for these people to race on, as we're able to do that from our existing
fleet, but it's to find a way of increasing yet again the number of boats racing, so that come the Autumn series of 2017, we can
invite yet more people to come and experience cruiser racing with us and then turn those into members and crew. Interestingly
many of these new members are female and when we look at the make up of the active cruiser racers in this Autumn series
33% were female.

In rounding up the 2016 cruiser racing season, there are many club members to thank many of whom are neither racers, or
cruiser members. There is no doubt that without the support and commitment of these other members, cruiser racing at Marconi
would not be as strong as it currently is. From the Wednesday gang, to the rib drivers, race officers, committee members and
other willing volunteers, we thank you.

In 2017 Marconi will once again be represented in EAORA offshore racing, as well as the BJRC inshore series. A complete race
schedule of dates has already been circulated amongst the racer members.

On the 2017 calendar Marconi will be organising a Spring Bank Holiday Regatta, where we'll race to Brightlingsea on the same
date our cruisers will be on passage, and then race against the Colne fleet. Before racing back on the Sunday.

We are also planning a long distance inshore race for early September, and as a club are aiming to enter as a fleet into both the

And finally, a request from the sailing sub. To those cruiser members who feel uncomfortable when it comes to mooring laying

The Blackwater as a London Airport
The following is an article by Kevin Bruce published in The Essex Society for Archaeology and History, Summer 2016
Newlsetter. It was spotted by club member Jenny Ball, also a member of the society, and is reproduced here by kind permission
of the original author and publication. Ed.

Following the 2nd World War, the Government sought to improve transatlantic and long distance air transport. FLying boats
were considered suitable and Saunders-Roe were approached in 1945 to design a suitable plan. The following year they
received a contract for three of what were to be the largest flying boats – the S.R. 45 “Princess”.

Steps were taken to find a suitable site for a Flying Boat air port to serve London. The Chichester Area and the Blackwater
were the two suggested locations and assessments were made in 1947 of their suitability.

Initial conclusions stated:

“At Chichester, the ideal terminal cannot be provided without the engineering difficulties of building on reclaimed land. At
Blackwater, it cannot be provided without a larger terminal basin and mooring area than is proposed in the Blackwater Survey
Report. IF neither of these courses should prove practical, then, in terms of taxying distances, Blackwater, with a terminal at
Bradwell and Maintenance and M.O.S at Ramsey, would be preferable to Chichester.....

Extendability of Alighting Area - Chichester, once built could not be extended, whereas the length of run at Blackwater is
practically limitless.

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Availability - Chichester would not be available for use until the end of a lengthy development period. On the other hand, most
of the alighting area at the Blackwater is available now and would be so during the development period.”

The three terminal sites suggested were at Osea Island, Ramsey Wade between Stansgate and Ramsey Island, St Lawrence
and Bradwell Creek. The Bradwell basin would have utilised an enlarged creek. At Ramsey, it would have occupied the Wade,
previously sealed off from the Blackwater in 1815. Both basins would have been deepened by excavation and at Ramsey
Wade, the sea wall demolished to gain access. The plans do not indicate where the Osea basin might have been but the
terminal would have been on the island itself with a new causeway constructed to give road access towards the A12.

It was envisaged that the then redundant Bradwell Bay aerdrome could act as a feeder airport for the south bank sites. They
estimated that the road journey from these two sites would take 3 hours compared with today’s 1 1/2 hours. Consultations were
held between several government ministries and local authorities. Maldon’s MP Tom Driberg also requested to be kept
informed. One consultee put forward the Medway Estuary as a better alternative. A precursor to Boris Island?

The scheme came to nothing as it became obvious that the land based airfields would cater more economically and safely.
Only one of the Princess aircraft ever flew, in 1952. Small sea planes did operate on the Blackwater during the First World War
in conjunction with HMS Osea fast motor boat base. Sea planes may still return to the Blackwater as there is currently a
proposal to operate a service between Osea and small airports around London.

Kevin Bruce
The Essex Society for Archaeology and History, Summer 2016

Club Secretary
SECURITY OF YOUR CLUB
I recently had a call from an ex –member who was out for an early morning walk and noticed that the clubhouse door was open.
He was good enough to phone me and offer to make the clubhouse secure. I gratefully accepted his offer.

Unfortunately finding the clubhouse door and/or the gate open when there is nobody about is more common than you might
think.

It is essential that your sailing club site and clubhouse are secure. Do not assume that someone else will lock the clubhouse or
close the gate if you don’t.

A convoy of vehicles will drive through the gate and the driver of the last vehicle will assume that the gate should be open
because that is how it was when they followed the other vehicles out. If in doubt close it.

Generally the gate will only be tied back for open meetings or if a trades vehicle is expected.

EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD
I issue this warning every year but it may be useful for new members and perhaps a timely reminder for older hands.

The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and
sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius.

On sunny spring days it is easy to be fooled but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim.

Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people
afloat with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the
wind chill.

There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm.

LaisrrTM Sprint 15
MSC SPRINT 15 OPEN
29 competitors took part in the first 2017 Sprint 15 Summer TT at Marconi SC on 8th and 9th April including an impressive home
turnout of 14 boats. We were pleased to welcome a number of new faces – who had participated in the Association Training
Day run by Howard Hawkes the previous weekend and also the local new fleet from Stone SC. We were also pleased to
welcome Nigel and Fiona Denchfield as guest Races Officers for the event.

The total absence of wind on Saturday morning resulted in a postponement until after lunch and even then, most of the fleet
were towed to the start area where they beached on Osea Island and chatted in the sunshine waiting for some wind. But fill in it
did and provided an afternoon of great sailing
conditions.

Race 1 saw the majority of the fleet start on starboard,
enjoying a decent blast off the line. A closely fought
race at the front quickly emerged between Liam Thom,
George Love and Paul Grattage. The beat on the
second lap saw the fleet split, with some of those
tacking off to the left hand side of the fleet making
better progress than those who stood on but the run
also proved very tactical, managing the impact of the
tide and positioning coming into marks three and four
vs the rest of the fleet. After four laps, George Love
just pipped Liam Thom into first place, followed by
Paul Grattage, Chris Tillyer and David Ball.

On Race 2, Chris Tillyer and Jenny Ball managed a
clear port hand start, regrouping with Liam Thom,
George Love and Paul Grattage at the first mark. On
the second lap, Jenny benefitted from tacking off to the left hand side, coming into the windward mark in second place behind
George and just ahead of Liam and Paul. At the end of the downwind leg, Jenny managed to establish a lead which she held
onto for the rest of the race, followed by Liam, Paul, George and Chris.

Race 3, with the main fleet sliding down to the favoured pin end on starboard, the port hand starters did not fare well, having to
duck most of the fleet. Paul Grattage quickly established a clear lead chased by Liam, Kevin Kirby, David Ball and Andy and
Finley Webb. The tide had just turned seeing the fleet split much more on the beat and the downwind legs. Paul's lead was
unassailable and he took the win followed by Andy and Finley, Kevin, Liam, David and George.

The fleet headed in after a thoroughly enjoyable afternoon's sailing for a well-deserved evening meal.

Sunday morning's weather was even more unseasonably warm and sunny, which was very pleasant but again, the wind
delayed its appearance. The Race team headed out anyway and after about an hour's delay, the wind appeared - fairly light
from the south but enough to get decent racing. The fleet were joined by four additional sailors lured out by the sunshine.

Race 4 – was another trapezoid course, watched by lots of spectators moored off Osea Island beach. Liam, Paul and David got
off to a good start with the rest of the fleet taking different routes up the beat, trying to find the best wind and cross the incoming
tide. Liam managed to hold off Paul to take the win with David in third, followed by George Love and Peter Richardson.

May 2017 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

The final race was the now legendary long distance race round the islands. This was shortened to just Osea Island as the
delayed start meant there was not enough tide to go round Northey as well. After a reaching start, the fleet headed downwind
to the western end of Osea Island, trying to position themselves for the best of the wind but out of the ebbing tide. Liam
rounded the end of the island first, closely followed by Paul, Kevin, Andy & Finley, David and Jenny with the rest of the fleet
bunched closely just behind them. The wind round the back of the island was a little more shifty causing the fleet to split across
the river, depending on the lifts or headers they were able to take. At the eastern end of the island, some of the locals tacked
across to get into the main tide and try to gain an advantage on the way up to the turning mark. A number of visitors followed
the locals but those who stood on were benefitted with better breeze and made significant gains by the time they reached the
turning mark. Liam and Andy & Finley led round, followed by Paul, Bill Hurr sailing sport mode, David, Jenny, Andy Perks and
Jim Bowie. On the final leg back to the committee boat, it was definitely a case of following the breeze rather than worrying
about the tide and heading over to the left picked up the best of the wind. Liam picked up his second win of the day and the
overall TT, followed by Andy & Finley, Jenny, David, Jim and Paul.

The fleet headed home after a great weekend of sailing! Big
thanks go to the Race Officer, Race Committee and Support boat
crews who had to set up and deliver 5 races in difficult conditions
whilst we all sunbathed waiting for the wind. Congratulations to
our youth helm, Jason Clarke from Marconi and to Andrew Perks
from Marconi winning the Chairman's Award for an impressive
long distance result, despite only starting to sail a Sprint 15 last
year.

Fleets:

The club is divided into fleets – each with its own Fleet Captain elected by their fellow fleet members. The Fleet
Captain co-ordinates matters relating to their fleet (e.g. racing and sailing, boat storage etc) and also
represents their fleet on the Sailing Sub Committee. Each Fleet holds an AGM (see Yearbook for dates).
These are informal and sociable meetings and all are encouraged to attend to review the prior sailing season
and make recommendations for the following year.

The Fleets are as follows and further information for each fleet is included on the following pages:
 Cruiser Fleet
 Solo Fleet
 Handicap Fleet – representing all monohull dinghies
 Cat Fleet – representing Sprint 15s, Medium and Fast Cats
 Windsurfing Fleet
 Cadet Fleet – representing club members aged 18 or under.
 Rowing Gig Fleet – a new fleet following the purchase of Elettra, our beautiful new gig.

Cruiser Fleet - Sailing:

The Cruiser Fleet organises a number of events throughout the year normally starting with a Fitting Out Supper
followed by a number of “cruises in company” over the course of the season. The season finishes with a Fleet
AGM and fish and chip supper.

We normally have several weekend/long weekend cruises which are an easy day sail away and often include
venues from Heybridge to the Orwell, plus longer cruises which could be farther afield and/or to continental
destinations. The cruiser fleet also supports the ECPR by supplying the mother boats and crews for the course.

Before each cruise, the bar should be open on the Friday night for a get together and to sort out any last minute
queries. All skill levels are catered for and friendly advice and guidance is freely given by the more experienced
members.

There may also be occasional joint cruises with other clubs on the river – please see the Year Book or
clubhouse Notices.

The fleet has, with the correct instruction, access to travel hoists, tractors, jacks, pressure washers, mast
derrick and scrubbing posts (the last two require pre-booking).

Dates: Please see year book. (see “Cruiser Events” column in the schedule)
Contact: Robin Good – Cruiser Sailing -

Marconi cruiser members participate in races organised by the BJRC throughout the year – a great way to

The racing is both very inclusive and competitive and all are welcome to participate. Crewing opportunities on

Cruiser members also race in events further afield ranging from Burnham Week to the Fastnet race! And in

provides a small swell for some bump and jump fun. Sailing between Osea Island and the shore provides mirror
flat shallows for smooth gybing and epic freestyle manoeuvres.

Dinghy, Cat and Cadet Racing:

Spring, Early Summer, Late Summer and Autumn Points Races:
Take place on Sundays – morning races start at 11am. Afternoon start times can vary.
Six fleets three combined starts: 1. Cadets, Solos & Monohull Handicap. 2. Sprint 15s 3. Medium Cats and Fast
Cats/Moths. Start from the Race Box line using the RYA 5,4,1 sequence. Each race lasts around 60 minutes.

Bank Holiday Series:
Take place on Bank Holiday Sundays and Mondays. Two races back to back in the morning (1st race start at
11am) followed by one race in the afternoon.
Three fleets with separate starts: Slow, Medium and Fast Handicap (Cats and Monohulls combined).
Start from the Race Box line using the RYA 5,4,1 sequence. Morning races will be 45 mins, afternoon 60 mins.

Pursuit Races:
Take place on Wednesday evenings in the summer and on specified weekend dates – (see Year Book).
All in races with Cats and Monohulls combined.
Start from the hard – starts are staggered with slowest boats going first in line with a scheduled set of start times.
Race finishes at a set time – whoever is in front, wins!
Wednesday evening – first start is 7pm. Race finishes at 8.10pm.

Individual “One Off” Races:
Jackpot – Helms aged 40 or over. Race to Heybridge. Stop for lunch. Race back! (under 40s welcome to sail)
Pilot Cup – Race to the Nass (near West Mersea) and back.
Marconi Challenge Cup – A one day event comprising 2 pursuit races.
Figure of Eight – a figure of eight course, ideally round Osea and Northey Islands.
Mona’s Cup – a race to Heybridge/Maldon and back again.
Last Fling – the last race of the season! An all-in handicap race with a Race Box start.
Ladies Series – a one day event for female helms, comprising 3 handicap races.
Helm of the Year – a one day event where a representative from each fleet competes in a series of races in one
design dinghies for the Helm of the Year title.

Other Racing Events:
Marconi will also be hosting the East Coast Piers Race, Sprint 15 Traveller Event, Lark Open, Laser Open,
Topper Summer Champs, Tornado event and Skiffs Open.

General Comments:
All races are listed in the Year Book in the Sailing Schedule.
Support boat cover is provided for all scheduled racing – although competitors enter solely at their own risk.
Competitors are required to sign on/off for each race for safety purposes.
Cadet helms under the age of 18 require a parent or guardian to countersign the signing on sheet for each race.
All race information and signing on/off is located in Race Reception (far end of clubhouse on the ground floor).

RATS & ADDERS
A reminder to be careful of some of our local wildlife. We need to be aware of rats and adders.

If adders are left alone everything should be fine but all members, especially children, need to be aware of them particularly in
long grass where they may not be seen or when reaching under boats.

Rats will occasionally be seen running around the site. Care should be taken particularly with standing water for example in boats
or on boat covers. Rats urine can convey Well’s disease so standing water and puddles may be contaminated. Cuts and grazes
should be covered to minimise the risk of infection.

BRITISH KEELBOAT TEAM SELECTION
Marconi’s inaugural Keelboat League Selection Regatta, took place on Sunday 7th May. 3 teams of 4 sailors took part in three
identical Robber 3E Quarter Tonners, the Club’s own Ned Kelly, Ian Carruth’s Sundance & Raffles who’s owner Charlie Ball had
sailed a tough 8 hour passage from Fambridge to help the club pull off the event. The three teams selected for their racing skill
and sailing pedigree from across the club, had, on the previous weekend, participated in the clubs keelboat race training day,
facilitated by the RYA and senior race coach Ian Patience, where they honed their crewing skills, mixing it with our cruiser racing
members, on an extremely windy day.

June 2017 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

In the Keelboat League Selection Regatta, race officer John Burgoyne set a
course in steeple bay to replicate what the winning team will sail when they
progress through to the regional British Keelboat League regatta at Burnham-
on-Crouch on June 3rd-4th. The Marconi teams competed in 9 x 15 minute
races on the course, with crew changing boats every third race in order to
counteract any affect that a lighter faster Robber might have on the overal
result.

The racing proved to be very tight and highly competitive particularly in the
pre-start area, which saw the teams challenging for position on the line. In
the earlier races, those teams more used to asymetric kites, had to work hard
on their sail handling skills in order not to loose time rounding the windward
mark and after the first set of 3 races, Sophia Southgate’s team had recorded
3 wins sailing on Sundance. The next three races also went to Sundance,
this time in the hands of Tom Clayton’s team. In race 7, once again
Sundance came home victorious now sailed by Steve Glynn’s team. At this point the Race Officer and organising team were
beginning to get worried about the way this was panning out, it could come down to second places. However after an on course
side (OCS) start for Raffles in race 8, saw Tom’s team pushed over by their competitors and having to recross the line, but soon
after they managed to pick up a wind shift and made some massive gains to come home in first place to break the sequence.

By the start of the final race all three teams were still pushing hard to play out their intended strategy which resulted in two teams
OCS, the only one clear being Tom’s team by the smallest of margins being called by the race officer. Soon after they were
quickly protested for infringing a boat to leeward of them and had to perform penalty turns, which put them back into the middle of
the fleet. The race wasn’t over for any of them though and Raffles (Tom’s team) sailed through to take victory and the regatta win.

The full results:

Tom Clayton, Tristan Hutt, Bryan Spencer, Jack Collis. 5 wins + 3 x 2nds + 1 x 3rd = 22 points

Sophia & Oliver Southgate, Andrew Dowley, Luke Lazell. 3 wins + 3 x 2nds + 3 x 3rd = 18 points

Steve Glynn, Tom Duckmanton, Jenny Ball, Michaella Dowley. 1 win + 3 x 2nds + 5 x 3rd = 14 points

At the regatta prize giving, the three onboard coaches revealed Luke Lazell, as their selection for the 5th member to join the
winning team that now moves forward to represent Marconi Sailing Club at the British Keelboat League in Burnham.

Well done to everyone who participated in the selection regatta and a big thank you to our on board selectors, race officers and
organisers.

Marconi sailing clubs keelboat champions, competed in the British Keelboat League competition this weekend at Burnham.
Racing in a fleet of 5 teams, the Marconi sailors were aiming to come out on top to secure a place in the National final late r in the
season.

Marconi’s team, supported by local companies Dinghy Rope, Billericay Heating, and TCS Chandlery, comprised of Tom Clayton,

represent the club in the British Keelboat

team prepared with a series of training events
on the river crouch to familiarise themselves
with the Hunter 707 keelboats that were used

Club Notices
Commodore’s Notes
Dear all,

Firstly, apologies for not having written much for Navigans of late. I find that most of the information I would like to update you on
is covered by our weekly email and news articles on our website, which I would direct you to for the most up to date information.

Now we are past the peak of the season I am pleased to report that we have an extremely buoyant membership this year so
please make all of our new members feel welcome to the MSC family. Not only is membership high, we also have a huge amount
of activity going on at the Club whether it be training, sailing, social or paddling sports. This is an excellent achievement in light of
the decline in membership and/or activity of a number of our neighbouring clubs. Our healthy membership allows us to invest
more in our club and you will have seen a number of improvements to our site and equipment over the year with more planned to
come. Of note is the new boat store for club boats and equipment, the purchase and re-fit of the UKCRA rib to support our
training activities and the erection of the Bridge Deck above the support boat containers which will enable improved control for
opens and events such as ECPR. We have also received another Sport England £10k grant to improve our training offering. The
Board of Directors will be meeting over the summer to discuss plans for further capital improvements specifically to the clubhouse
- more to come on that in the autumn.

2017 marked the 30th anniversary of the East Coast Piers Race, which was held over the first weekend in July. 86 competitors
took on the challenge of the ECPR or CPR, the highest number of entries for a number of years. Competitors, their families and
club members were treated to a fantastic weekend of wind, sunshine and entertainment with overwhelmingly positive feedback
from many visitors. Congratulations to Clive Shenton and team for not only keeping this amazing event going during a period
where others are struggling with entrants, but for making it better year on year.

Our open day in May was another resounding success and has definitely contributed to our peak in membership. We were lucky
enough to be visited by Olympic Gold medallist Saskia Clarke on the day who was very happy to hand her Rio gold medal round
to members - a amazing inspiration for our young (and not so young) sailors!. The RYA also filmed much of their publicity for
Push the Boat Out at MSC this year and you can see this footage on their website. Again, many thanks to Graham Cross and all
the club members who made this day such a success.

At the time of writing this, cadet week is about to begin but I have no doubt that it will be about fantastic week of learning, fun and
socialising. I would like to give my thanks to Bekki Tovey and Chris Kirby who are standing down from the cadet week organising
committee this year. Bekki and Chris have been involved in cadet week for over 15 years as tutors and organisers and have
made some very positive changes to the way the week is run.

For the first time ever MSC has entered a team into the British Keelboat League. Selection races were held in April with the
winners competing in our local leg in June. Although not successful, the RYA were so impressed with the team that they have
been given an invitational place to a further leg in August and also to the final due to be held at the end of September in Cowes -
good luck to team Marconi! Thanks to Peter Ward for driving this initiative forward.

Marconi has been ‘on the road’ during the season with good attendance at Tornado, Sprint 15, Moth and Topper Opens and
Nationals to name a few. We continue to be well represented in the BJRC and other cruiser racing series and our cadets are
flying the flag at the NSSA as I write this.

Our RYA dinghy-training centre is pretty much up and running and we expect to be offering dinghy sailing courses by the end of
the year. Congratulations to Pat Shaw, Bob Collins and Rhiannon Hitt for making this happen.

Unfortunately it is not all good news. I have had several complaints recently from members, pedestrians and neighbours of the
club regarding poor and dangerous driving down Stansgate road. Although it is a fairly low traffic road, it is narrow and there are
several blind corners. Please drive slowly and take care when driving down Stansgate road for your own safety and that of other
members, pedestrians and our neighbours.

Wishing you all the best for the rest of the 2017 season!

Michaela Dowley
Commodore

SECURITY – OF YOUR COASTLINE
I recently received the following request from PS Ben Felton who is a sergeant at Maldon. Ben is also a yachtsman who has an
interest in local sailing clubs and marinas.

Dear all,

I apologise for being quiet recently. Due to operational matters and high demand I have been very busy. Now summer is well and
truly under way it is a good time to re-establish contact.

With better weather and longer daylight hours can I ask everyone to remain vigilant. People smuggling and drugs and weapon
importation through small ports and marina's is most likely during July and August. You may have seen or heard items on the
news highlighting this issue. It is happening around our coast.

As professional water users who know your area's well, you are best placed to notice any unusual or suspicious activity. Please
report any suspicious boat movements or activities to Essex Police or the UK Boarder Force. If the activity is happening in front of
you, please dial 999 in an emergency or 101 for police.

Any 'slow time' intelligence can be emailed to me, the Essex Police Marine Unit or UKBA. We share intelligence between
ourselves so please be assured it is taken seriously and acted upon.

In other news, we have suffered a small rise in thefts in marina's and boat yards. Brightingsea had several outboard engines
stolen overnight a week ago. One boat owner also had his Dory taken and towed towards the Blackwater.

I have continued my overnight patrols of your premises, particularly around high tides. I also spend a number of days out on water
as a Marine Unit officer every month.

Most of you will have met the new Marine Unit special constables during the day. They have been very proactive getting to know
water users in the whole county.

My work is focused on the Dengie and Tollesbury area's only and provides a uniformed presence out of hours to deter thefts and
detect overnight suspicious activity.

I hope to get round to visit you all again soon.

Stay safe.

Regards,

Sergeant Ben Felton

SECURITY – OF YOUR CLUB
Finding the clubhouse door and/or the gate open when there is nobody about is common and should not happen.

It is essential that your sailing club site and clubhouse are secure. Do not assume that someone else will lock the clubhouse or
close the gate if you don’t. Remember, it’s your property which is just as likely to go ‘walkies’ if you leave the site unsecured.

A convoy of vehicles will drive through the gate and the driver of the last vehicle will assume that the gate should be open
because that is how it was when they followed the other vehicles. If in doubt close it.

If someone is following you through the gate they should at least be able to show you their access card which they would have
used to open the gate if you were not in front of them.

Generally the gate will only be tied back for open meetings or if a trades vehicle is expected.

Even during the day strangers have been challenged wandering around the site. They had got in by following a member or
because the gate had been left open. Having had a good look round, they might come back when its quiet ………. .

the hard is in use. Please shut the gates when you come ashore unless it is obvious that another member is using the hard. If in
doubt, shut the gates. They can always be opened again.

The gap in the seawall is vital to our club but it is a privilege not a right. We must be seen to be doing the right thing by keeping
the gates shut which as well as meeting EA requirements also protects our club and our neighbours.

PARKING IN CRUISER PARK
At this busy time of boat, boat hoist and trailer movements cars must not be left unattended in the cruiser park or the cruiser
parking area of the cat park. Owners of cars in the cruiser parks must be available at all times and ready to move them at short
notice.

Do not leave your car unattended in the cruiser parks even if you are ‘only nipping out to the boat for 5 minutes’. There is a very
real risk of damage to your vehicle and inconvenience to others.

MARCONI CRUISER LONG DISTANCE INSHORE EVENT
9 boats came to the start line at Radio Caroline and Sue Carroll (1st time Race Officer) got the fleet underway, downwind to
Thirslet. Pinocchio (Colne Yacht Club) led the charge turning onto a very shy kite leg to Stone mark No9. Blue Moon (Marconi SC,
late to the start) selected their headsail after a drop at Thirslet and rapidly overhauled Skylark and McGregor 3 (both MSC) who
left it too late to change down in the shifting winds and then struggled to round the mark.

Charlie Don’t Surf (CYC) gradually took the lead as the light winds got even lighter as the fleet rounded further Stone marks on
their way to the Marconi buoy. Stone No3 (a virtual mark it seems) missing from the river caused some confusion as Charlie
searched for its location, while others used the marks coordinates as a rounding. Charlie back tracked to put themselves over the
same ground as Pinocchio and the fleet behind followed a similar course. From the Marconi Buoy, kite packers had much more
time as the fleet worked their way through the light NE’rly back across the line to complete the ‘Sprint’ leg of the course.

Shearjoy (winner LH) chases Flyer soon after the start. Pre-Start chill out on IRC winner Pinocchio

The three Dehler 34’s, Shearjoy (Dabchicks), Flyer & Radiance (CYC), were now doing close battle while Charlie tried to work
their way back into handicap order on the long legs to WMYC No1 & No10. At the back of the fleet, Monkey Business (MSC, also
a late starter) had sailed high up Goldhanger creek in search of Stone No3 and the failing breeze back at Marconi caused Monkey
and Skylark to retire as the tide ebbed against them.

The course was shortened by the race officer twice, missing Wallet Spitway and then C8, but the breeze held, encouraged by the
black clouds and a weak sea breeze, sufficient to cause some spinnaker control problems on McGregor and Charlie as they
spinnaker reached down to Inner Bench head. Most controlled kites much better, with one applying a not too often seen technique
of attaching the clew to the halyard and hoisting. A happy snapper afloat captured the moment, which by now should have done
the social media rounds, but we can’t possibly reveal the crew involved here!

Meanwhile, Blue Moon was working their way ever closer to the boats ahead and it was looking difficult to call the winner from the
view on the water. With over an hour between the first and last finisher and after 8 hours of very challenging sailing in light wind

delighted that his wife Jackie Camp was able to join us for part of the trip. An enormous ‘thank you’ to Robin Good, Vice Fleet
Captain, and his First Mate, Di, for stepping up and planning an amazing Summer Cruise to Holland. We saw some beautiful
places and had some great experiences. Thank you also to Roy Bellord for the benefit of his experience and advice.
