The following is a brief log of our journey, some of the experiences we had and entertainment. I have written a separate piece
describing the places we visited.

Sat: 5.30am depart for Ramsgate from various home ports as some of us are now at Bradwell Marina and others from the
Crouch. Arriving approx. 12.30. Those arriving alongside us joined us for G&T on Last Orders to celebrate (any excuse!). I
actually wanted to show off my newly found ice making skills.

Excellent meal at ‘Bon Appetite’ overlooking the marina booked by Robin. Wonderful hot summer’s evening. After, we retired to
The Royal Temple Yacht Club for a Passage Planning Meeting and a cheeky nightcap.

Sun: 9am Channel crossing and onwards to Ostend. Depending on weather conditions we were heading for a) Dunkirk b)
Nieuwpoort c) Ostend. Fabulous conditions! HOT HOT HOT! Beautiful calm blue sea, a light breeze and the tide under us, we
pushed on to Ostend. Arrived just as the sun was going down. We had the pleasure of encountering a number of porpoise on
the crossing and thankfully not too many large ships.

Mon: Depart Ostend 7am arriving Middelburg 13.45. Locking into the Dutch canal system at Flushing to encounter locks lifting
bridges traveling along the prettiest of tree lined canals. Allure came to a shuddering halt as the prop had been fouled by fishing
net. Richard had to take a swim to free it aided by Roy. Luckily he removed the problem and caught up fairly quickly. We all sat in
the shade on the quayside ‘borrowing’ cafe chairs. Later we had an excellent meal in the pretty town square. HOT HOT HOT!

Tues: Middelbury to Veers Meer – Haringvreter Island. Michael and I entered the lock and the far end of the run of bridges and
tied off our lines neglecting to notice that the lines had to be loosened manually when the water lowered. Our fellow yachtsmen
called to us to let off our lines but the one round the winch would not budge. Michael vanished below and returned wielding a knife
to cut the line unfortunately not in time to prevent the winch from being wrenched from its holding and propelled upwards into the
air at some velocity! Fortunately nobody was hurt apart from our bruised pride! We continued rather shaken to Haringvreter Island
where we all tied up on a beautifully appointed pontoon. The Island was wooded and uninhabited apart from numerous wildlife
including what we thought were very shy deer. Later we all enjoyed a BBQ when the ‘shy’ deer very soon became curious and by
the end of the evening came right up to us to see if there were any pickings. It was a really magical and very special evenin g with
a beautiful sunset sitting in the midst of the wild deer.

Wed: Woke up to a welcome cool breeze that did not stay for long and the temperature soon rose to it’s familiar blistering level
(no complaints!) We all loaded onto GEM and went to the pretty little town of Veere for a look round and a spot of lunch. After
Pete took us for a sightseeing trip round the Meer before returning to our births.

It was mega hot so we all decided to take a swim in the Meer accompanied by a fair few jelly fish! They did not seem to be of the
stinging variety but were pretty revolting to the touch. We had all swam round from the pontoon into a small marina where we all
struggled out of the water not wishing to have to encounter our slimy friends again! Nigel and Richard having blown up their
tenders decided to have a race with extra power provided by their respective passengers, Nicki and Di. Lots of cheating and
corner cutting went on! After drying off we all gathered again (including the deer that became even more familiar – not to forget
their friend the seagull) to another BBQ and game of Frisbee. Another wonderful evening.

Thursday: Under Zeeland Bridge to Zierikzee. Lovely harbour overlooked by beautiful restored windmill. Girls went for a look at
the market and drinks were had on the cafe outside until the skies opened and we had a summer storm. Torrential rain and
thunder & lightening! Trapped us in the pub for a while.

After a refreshing G & T on Gem we went to the square to have dinner on one of the restaurants that boasted ‘best’ mussels. W e
made our choice and we’re rewarded with an enormous bucket of fresh new season mussels. Totally delicious!!! After we had a
group gathering to plan the next few days.

Friday: 10.30 for Goes – Beautiful town harbour surrounded by pretty traditional Dutch terraced houses with stepped gable
houses. Drinks on board Allure before group meal in steakhouse selected by Robin. Mine was great. Enormous plate of ribs for a
October 2017 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

starter and a delicious burger to follow. Some others portion sizes were not so good but good atmosphere and friendly staff. A
rather good bar/pub was discovered on the way back to the boats. Singing, dancing and much merriment. Needed further
exploration tomorrow!

Saturday: Rainy day was not to deter us! We decided to do some stocking up of provisions and made off to the supermarket with
a plan to meet up in the afternoon for a Crazy Golf challenge! Before golf we took a look at the delightful ‘De Werf’ with the marina
bar where your helped yourself and paid by leaving your money in an honesty book. A delight!

After we went for an exciting round of Crazy Golf. There were some very challenging holes!! It absolutely poured with rain the
whole time but undeterred we fastened our wet weather gear and carried on! The score cards varied massively but it was great
fun. After we consoled ourselves with delicious hot chocolate drinks – chocolate chips given separately to stir into the hot milk
yourself. After a meal on board we all met up at the ‘Party pub’ that had been discovered the night before and all joined together
for plenty for singing and dancing. Some of the songs were in English and we knew them others were in Dutch but we weren’t put
off and joined in all the same! Another great evening.

Sunday: Goes to Flushing. It was decided not to stop at Middelburg but to push on to Flushing. Too many bridges and locks!!!
Lucy B and Seremban went on to Breskens but the remainder of us had enough and ducked into Flushing where there were good
showers, and lovely little restaurant and most importantly diesel. It had become very windy and Allure and Last Orders did some
spectacular mooring bouncing off a few posts!! No damage done though – surprisingly. Harbourmaster was HM and Chef! After a
busy time directing boats into moorings he had to rush back to the restaurant and cook dinner for everyone.

Monday: 5am start for Ostend after night of tummy problems!!! It was quite lumpy but rain and wind cleared and the sun came out
again to welcome us into Ostend. Gem for drinks then all off for a chicken dinner. A speciality that had to be experienced. Half a
chicken each and fresh bread. We samples other delights of Ostend namely the delights of McD! Early night after an early start.

Tuesday: Bruges for the day. 15 minute train journey from Ostend. We started with waffles with fresh strawberries and ice cream
sitting in a cafe on the square. Belgian waffles were a very fitting start to the day. We decided on a city tour bus trip. This was
ideal for the time we had available followed by a boat tour so we experienced Bruges from all angles. A very beautiful city with
marvellous architecture. We then had the tourist special lunch of mussels or an excellent beef stew. This was followed by
purchasing a great deal of chocolate that we all claimed was bought for our families!? Meeting in Bar of Royal North Sea Yacht
Club to decide what we should do tomorrow.

Decision made to for an 8.30 start for Dunkirk.

Wednesday: Off we went at 8.30 for a very bumpy passage to Dunkirk! And a slight run-in with a rather large ship meandering
into Dunkirk. We decided it had the size/weight advantage and let it through. Arrived Dunkirk 13.00 bedraggled from a sudden
‘welcoming’ downpour! Unperturbed Di invited us all aboard for a cheese and wine party. We spent a marvellous afternoon
drinking eating and exchanging yarns. The party concluded with enough time to have a quick freshen up and then we made off I
find a restaurant that served mussels. The old favourite was closed so we chose L’edito that had been recommended to us. It was
great. We all then retired for the night ready for our Ramsgate passage tomorrow.

Thursday: 9.30 we were off. Forecast indicated not so good on leaving with a chance of rain but improving about 13.00. Indeed it
was very grey and a little bouncy and dark rain clouds swept through fortunately missing us. We all safely navigated the shipping
lanes and the sun shone. We were all very pleased and made lunch and relaxed looking forward to an easy run into Ramsgate.
How wrong we could be! One minute 9 knots of breeze the next 26!!!!!!! All I can say is the last leg of our passage was
‘interesting’! We all pretty much surfed into Ramsgate and were very happy to have arrived in one piece. Last Orders, Gem and
Chemma all managed to get mainsail halyards caught round radar reflectors so Chris was sent up the masts to unravel – what a
hero! Margaret and Roy invited everyone on board for drinks before heading off for fish and chips.

Friday: We all said our farewells and congratulated Robin for his good planning and ourselves for completing the course and
departed 8.30am start for home ports. All said a prayer for good conditions. Our prayers were answered with a stunningly
beautiful clear blue start. The day continued to go well. Everyone was a little undecided as to which course to take back over the
sandbanks but there was plenty of water and no need for concern. We attempted a little sail but the wind dropped, a few
threatening clouds were gathering and we did not want a repetition of yesterday’s experience. Arrived back at Bradwell approx.
17.00. We finished our adventure with a very welcome dinner with Jan and Pete in The Green Man.

What shall we do next year?

Cheryl Cutmore

British Keelboat League Team Training
Marconi Sailing Clubs British Keelboat League Team (BKL) were invited to train in a J70 on Solent Water by UK J Boat distributor
Key Yachting this weekend.

October 2017 Navigans 12

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

As part of their preparations for the next leg of the British Keelboat League in Cowes in two weeks time, team captain Tom
Clayton, Michaela Dowley (helm), Bryan Spencer (mainsheet), Luke Lazell (trim) and Jack Collis (bow), familiarised themselves
with the planing asymmetric J70 keelboat in a very exciting 20+ knots wind.

(l/r, Luke Lazell, Michaela Dowley, Bryan Spencer,
Tom Clayton, Jack Collis, Charlie Marchant)

Charlie Merchant, J Boats UK Brand Manager provided boat specific coaching from a support rib, and the Marconi team were
super impressed by the efforts of Charlie to help them very rapidly get up to speed with the J70, the boat of choice for the
European Champions League of Sailing which the qualifiers in the British Keelboat League will progress to.

The J70 training came at the end of a week of continued preparations by the Marconi BKL team which saw them sailing a series
of match races during the evenings of their clubs cadet week held during the first week of August.

Three challenger teams came from a mix of experienced dinghy, catamaran and cruiser racers who lined up to put the BKL team
to the test during the pre-start that saw the crews manoeuvring in very close quarters in an attempt to get the other boat to foul, or
push them over the line prematurely.

The Marconi BKL team came out on top after two days of racing the clubs Robber 3e keelboats, comprehensively leading 6 – 0 as
they entered the final evening of races as the spectators gathered on the sea wall. This time the competing team managed to put
the BKL racers under real pressure and both boats were required to perform penalty turns as they raced within inches of each
other around the three 15 minute windward leeward matches. On the very final downwind leg of the series, just 100m from the
finish, the competitors managed to get an overlap on the BKL team which resulted in a foul by the BKL team and as the
competitor team lead by Tristan Walker – Hutt crossed the line to win, the BKL completed their penalty to finish with a series
score of 8 – 1 and victors in this very local version of the Americas Cup competition.

The team will travel to the Royal Yacht Squadron in Cowes for the next leg of the British Keelboat League on 18th August.

Many thanks to the sponsors of our team, who are helping to promote keelboat and match racing on our East Coast, river
Blackwater.

OPERATION OF CLUB BOATS AND EQUIPMENT
For information for new members and a reminder to older hands, there are detailed codes of practice and instructions for most
activities at Stansgate from procedures for a flood alert to the operation of machinery.

It is essential for the efficient and safe operation of club boats and equipment that users are familiar with the guidance. If you have
a support boat duty, do read the guidance notes. Even if you have driven or crewed on support boats before it is worth reading
the latest version of the relevant notes; they do get updated from time to time.

Winches, tractors, mast derrick and boat hoists also have their own codes of practice and user guides which are regularly
updated. Please read them. Their relevance to the operators of the equipment is obvious but it is also useful for boat owners to be
familiar with the codes of practice. You will have a better understanding of the operation of the equipment, which is satisfying in

Cadet Fleet
NOTES FROM SAIL TRAINING AND OPPI CLUB 2017
The weather could hardly have been kinder to us for the final Sail Training and Oppi Club of 2017. The sun shone, the
thermometer said ‘July’ rather than ‘October’, the wind was F3-4 from the southwest (and I’m sure everyone kept this direction at
the front of their mind for the whole day) and the water was gloriously wet. We had a wonderful turnout, and having counted 69
tallies out onto the water, we were fortunate enough (as we try to ensure) to be able to count them all back again. Of course they
had to come back, because the wonderful, ever-present supporter of sail training Tina had prepared the now traditional Sail
Training Laying-Up Buffet, and all could eat their fill and dream of next sailing season.

We’ve had a great year, and have issued tally numbers to a record 176 different participants since the first session back in March.
Many of you are new to MSC as well as to Sail Training, it’s great to see you and you’re very welcome. In very large part these
numbers have been down to Bryan’s fantastic encouragement of the new group of adult sailors, some of whom haven’t sailed
before, others who’ve crewed but not helmed, and yet others who are more used to cruisers and have enjoyed having a go in a
boat that lets you know when you’ve got it wrong. Dan Bard has been fantastic with our intermediate group, rising above the
chaos of boat choice, sailing partner choice and multiple explanations of what we’re doing and where we’re going, to deliver a fun
and educational session for all. At the top of our experience range it’s been a real pleasure for me to shout, whistle and hoot at
some great sailors doing some great sailing. Underpinning it all, and getting the next generation of Marconi cadets to love being
cold and wet, has been Fee Southgate, standing or paddling in a kayak in the mud while Oppis flit to and fro to the delight o f all
involved. Behind those who do the shouting are an army of helpers picking up a myriad of pieces, from sorting the important
paperwork through fixing all the boats on the hard (where do all those bungs go?) to crewing RIBs so we can have buoys to go
around and are able to do so in safety. THANK YOU ALL SO MUCH!

But my biggest thanks have to go to our fantastic cadets, young and ever-so-slightly-less young. You turn up every month full of
energy, you’re kind enough to listen and respond to whatever point it is I try to make, you get the boats out (and usually put them
away again), you encourage and help others, you smile (even when I’m shouting at you...) and you are BRILLIANT!

Have a lovely winter, before you know it I’ll be promising you balmy breezes and bath-temperature water in March and we’ll start
all over again.

MARCONI INLAND KEELBOAT CHAMPIONSHIPS 2018 – ENTER EARLY!
April 14th is the date set for Marconi’s start to the 2018 keelboat racing series.

Next season we’d like to offer a greater number of Marconi members the opportunity to participate in the exciting racing format of
the British Keelboat League. In order to do that we have teamed up with the Royal Thames Yacht Club, one of the key drivers
behind the increasing interest in this form of racing in the UK, and have pre-booked the clubs fleet of J80’s that are afloat at
Queen Mary’s reservoir near Staines.

As part of the collaboration the Royal Thames have agreed to provide the race officers and umpires to run a full day of 15 minute,
windward leeward races that will culminate in the crowning of the Marconi Keelboat Champions of 2018.

The event is open to teams made up solely of club members and we’re able to have as many as 9 teams doing battle throughout
the day as we’ll be swapping out boats and crews to ensure that every team sails each boat, against all the other teams. What a
great way to start the 2018 season, strong competition on the water and quite a bit of banter in the club house afterwards.

Sailing Instructions

The Sailing Instructions can be downloaded from the Marconi SC website:
http://www.marconi-sc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Marconi-J80-keelboat-regatta-Spring-2018.pdf

But don’t wait until the Spring to put your team together, we need to firm up the booking with the Royal Thames by Christmas.

Skippers / Team Boss’s can build a team of their choice, so we’re expecting some pretty strong haggling, persuasive tactics and
inducements offered, to come into play during November and December as teams are formed. We’ll have prizewinners for the
cadet team, ladies, over 50’s, mixed and mens as well as the overall champions, and what’s more, we’ll be taking the results into
consideration as we once again select sailors to compete for a representative place in Marconi’s team for the 2018 British
Keelboat League.

Question: What should I do next?

Answer: If you’re a potential skipper / team boss, then start chatting up your preferred crew members and get them to commit.
Once you have your team, register it with the organiser (Peter Ward). If you’re an individual who would like to participate, let the
organiser know, so that we can make the potential skipper / team boss aware that you’re available.

We can guarantee that this will be one of the most exciting days of sailing organised by the club in 2018, so get your name on the
list before the places are all gone!

BRITISH KEELBOAT LEAGUE CAMPAIGN REPORT
It was done. The sailing sub had pre-selected the 12 most competitive sailors in the club that might be able to represent Marconi
in a series of very long race days of, physically and mentally challenging keelboat races.

Our entry was in. We were going for it. Let’s test
ourselves as a club, against some of the best teams of
sailors from across the UK in the 2017 British Keelboat
League (BKL).

The prize was clear. Increased profile for the club,
involvement in a format of racing that we’d very little
experience in, a great experience for the 12 selected
sailors and the opportunity to learn from the events that
we were to organise and be involved in, that would inform
our decisions about how we develop club racing and our
racers in future years.

April: We were off. Not having keelboats other than
cruisers available to us, Ian Caruth, owner of Robber 3e Sundance, offered his boat to match up against the clubs own Robber,
Ned Kelly. Hearing of our plans, Charlie Ball of North Fambridge yacht club made a very difficult 8 hour passage from Crouch to
Blackwater, so that his Robber Raffles could also be used in the selection races between our 12 sailors that would determine the
team to represent Marconi in the British Keelboat League.

Replicating the format of the BKL, John Burgoyne and Sally ran a day of 15 minute, windward / leeward races that saw the 12
sailors swapping boats until a winning team was identified. The onboard coach / selectors which included Dave Onyons,

November 2017 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

experienced racer on Ned Kelly and the other owners, Ian and Charlie, selecting the 5th member to join the winning team that
would progress to the regional leg at the Royal Corinthian in June.

Our sponsors were now onboard, Billericay Heating, TCS Chandlery and Dinghy Rope provided support for our team to prepare
themselves for the competition.

May: Tristan Walker – Hutt (helm), Tom Clayton, Bryan Spencer, Jack Collis and Luke Lazell embarked on a series of training
sails on 707’s on the Crouch as they prepared. When it came to race weekend their training paid off. Quickest out of the blocks
they made their mark in the first 3 races, but the more experienced teams from the Royal Thames YC and Queen Mary’s SC,
soon got up to speed with the 707’s and targeted Marconi in pre starts and 1st beats, forcing penalties using there better
application of the racing rules. Mental note 1 made.

June: Our team didn’t go unnoticed. Their commitment to the event, boat handling skills, 4th position and the exemplary way that
they represented the club, resulted in them receiving an invite to the next leg to be held in Cowes organised by the Royal Yacht
Squadron.

July: Training continued. Key Yachting, the distributor of the J70 yacht in the UK, provided Marconi with a training boat for a day
from their base at Hamble point. Charlie Marchant coached the Marconi team, which now included club commodore Michaela
Dowley as Tristan had to drop out because of other commitments. J70 training was followed by three evenings of match racing
during the clubs cadet week, where teams of challengers put our BKL to the test in our Robber 3e’s.

August: Off to Cowes. The Royal Yacht Squadron (RYS). What a
fantastic weekend. Not just because of the close fought fleet racing in
J70’s in Osborne Bay, but the very warm welcome that was provided
by the staff and officers of the Royal Yacht Squadron and the super
professional way that the event was run on the water. Not only did
they relax their dress code to invite our team for dinner (not quite as
relaxed as Luke’s Board shorts), but they provided a tour of the
Castle. Surrounded by Ainslie’s Americas Cup challenge trophies, and
ship fittings from King George V’s yacht Britannia, and the library of
‘First Editions’ lodged by the members, the clubs team of catering
apprentices served a fantastic supper. ‘And those showers after the
sailing were just the most luxurious surroundings you can imagine’,
reported Bryan who was in there for quite a long time.

The competition at the Royal Yacht Squadron leg was strong. Not
much time difference between first and last boat on the water, but the
university teams both from the UK and the OSC who were well
practised in team racing, where noticeably towards the head of the J70 Training thanks to Keyachting
fleet in many of the races. Mental note 2 made. Our Marconi team,
now helmed by Michaela, consistently finished in the mid to lower half of the fleet, but things were much closer than their position
might suggest with just a few boat lengths between positions.

September: Next an invite to the final. This time organised by the Royal Thames Yacht Club, who like the RYS, have a fleet of
J70’s dry sailed from Shepards Wharf in Cowes.

Once again the event was run like clockwork, with the well practiced race officer team from the Royal Thames supported by Jack
Fenwick, RYA keelboat development manager and his team of umpires buzzing around the fleet in their ribs. Three days of racing
in warm and sunny conditions saw the Marconi team change things around a bit as they searched to build on what they’d learned
last time out. Both Bryan and then Jack spent a day on the helm, adding to the experience that we were building within the team
as our crew swapped roles.

Itchener Sailing Club came out champions, lead by Ben Saxton, Nacra 17 Olympian and just back from an 8th position in the J70
Worlds. Itchenor were worthy winners and the only team that at times could put distance between their boat and the rest of the
fleet. Marconi finished in 15th position, a solid performance for our team and as they came off the water on completion of their
campaign, wide smiles on their faces, Jack Collis was heard to say ‘I nearly had him, there was less than a bowsprit between all 3
boats in that race, I nearly had him.’ Such was the spirit and friendly competition in this hottly contested championship which now
sees Itchenor to represent Britain in the European Champions League in 2018.

What an experience the BKL had been in 2017, but no sooner were our team back in Essex, our thoughts began to turn to the
2018 event and the first leg of that was to be the Youth leg of the competition in October 2017.

Cruiser Fleet
The cruiser Autumn Series ended with the double points, no discard race, sailed in a westerly 25 kts gusting beyond 30 at times.
A simple course of Marconi (P), Thirslet (S) increased in difficulty as the tide began to flood in opposition to the wind.

4 Boats came to the line, and Ned Kelly fully reefed and sailing much flatter than the others controlled the conditions best. Blue
Moon, looking to wrap up the series was the only one to risk flying a kite. Although small, once it got to the masthead it remained
under control until the first gust, after which it provided a great spectacle for those who dared take their eye’s off their own
mainsail.

Monkey business tried hard to keep ahead of the others but sailing safe by tacking to prevent spinning out on the gybes with their
overpowered main allowed Ned Kelly to stay close astern. Sundance improvised at the back of the fleet. With all headsail
halyards lost to the top of the mast, they reverted to using the spinnaker halyard to hoist their smallest headsail.

The crews were relieved when Nick Miller finished the race after two laps, who was out of the race box and onto his board like a
shot to enjoy the challenging conditions with the windsurfers.

Congratulations to Vy Trans. 1st Year skipper on Ned Kelly who steered his team to claim their first ever race victory, not only on
local handicap but on IRC rating also. Well done.

Richard Roberts Blue Moon had an equally impressive series, winning both LH and IRC for 2017.

2017 COMMODORE’S REPORT - MICHAELA DOWLEY - 3RD DECEMBER 2017
Good morning and welcome all to the 2017 Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting. This report will comment on the main
business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season. It has been an exceptionally busy year so I have
plenty of good news to report on, as well as awarding the Club’s most coveted prizes.

Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board of Directors, and for the previous year has comprised these six people:

Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site
Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment
Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing
Graham Cross - Rear Commodore for events
Sue Shenton – Treasurer
Myself, Michaela Dowley - as commodore I am managing director and chair

January 2018 Navigans 2

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and shouldering the bulk of the
administrative burden of the Club.

I can report that the Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I would like to extend thanks
to all those who take the time to serve on the main and various sub committees.

This AGM sees a few key individuals leaving their posts so I would like to give our sincere thanks to Chris Kirby and Bekki Tovey
who have been organisers of Cadet Week for the past 5 years. Chris has also served as publicity officer on the management
committee for a number of years. I am pleased to say we have filled these vacant posts with younger members Dan Bard and
Jemma Clarke stepping up into the cadet week committee and Sophie Hurrell-Smith and Nicola Jacobs standing as publicity
officers for this coming season.

Unfortunately, after 4 years as rear Commodore of Events, Graham Cross is standing down at this AGM so I would like to thank
Graham for the time, effort and commitment he has given to the Club. Although we are losing Graham, I am pleased to report
that we have proposed Liz Kirby to join the Board as Rear Commodore of Events.

Graham has made a huge impact since joining the Board; providing serious business acumen and his vast experience of PR and
marketing have been invaluable in helping the Club to move forward. One of Graham’s main roles has been the organisation of
our annual Open Day and I am sure you will agree that they are in a totally different league compared to 4 years ago - they’ve
given us great publicity, new members and improved our links with the RYA. In fact, this year Graham managed to pester the
RYA PR team people so effectively that we were honoured by a visit from Saskia Clark, Olympic Gold medal winner, along with
the RYA media team. Not only did some of our cadets get to meet an inspirational Olympic hero and hold a Gold medal, but
Marconi SC featured heavily in the RYA social media and video outputs which raised our profile once again.

Peter Ward, who unfortunately cannot be here today has been in touch with the RYA about something unrelated and provided me
with this quote from one of their team who attended our open day in 2017 -

“What a fantastic friendly club, we had a wonderful time with you and I had been wondering if you might apply for Club of the Year
as you made a big impression on us. From arriving at the gate to be met by the meeters and greeters, and through the whole
time we spent with you there was a super friendly buzz around the Club, even though the weather wasn’t brilliant. What a great
day.”

So it looks like we’re sticking in the minds of people who a few years ago would not have known who or what Marconi Sailing Club
is. Whilst the Open Day is a result of a huge team effort it needs a flamboyant mastermind to drive it forwards and bring everyone
together - so Graham in light of all your work over the past four years, but especially for your amazing positive impact in
organising open days I would like to award you the Barograph trophy for outstanding commitment to the Club.

Membership

Moving on to membership, in 2016 we had 430 members and since then there have been 50 resignations. It is important here to
remember membership is our only real source of income and the Board and committees have been working hard to deliver
improvements to the Club and it’s activities to attract and retain new members. Along with successful Open Days, our website is
current and still a leader compared to other sailing clubs, our training programme is growing and our sailing activity is becoming
more varied with the addition of keelboats, dinghy courses and paddle sports to name a few. Because of this we have welcomed
56 new members into the Club this year. This means that we now have a membership of 436, which is an incredible
achievement and as far as we can work out, a record high. This is of course equates to a lot more people, probably around 950
taking into account family memberships.

As detailed at last year’s AGM we have now switched to a new club membership database called Sailing Club Manager and will
be offering membership renewals online. Payment can be made via a payment portal linked to our database with members able
to pay via cheque, BACS, debit card or credit card.

In line with a healthy membership I can report that our finances are in a good position. I will leave Sue to take you through the
statutory accounts a little later in the agenda.

The remainder of my report will focus on the highlights from this year and our plans for the year ahead.

Keelboats

One of the biggest highlights for the Club this year has been the introduction of keelboat sailing, which has been driven
completely by Peter Ward. Peter isn’t in the audience today but it is hard to describe how much thanks he deserves for the time
and effort he has put into driving this initiative forward for the benefit of the Club and it’s members. From personal experience, this
time last year I was someone who had barely set foot on a cruiser before but by September I had been out practicing and racing
on several Club keelboats and found myself competing on the Solent in the British Keelboat League. Peter has an infectious
enthusiasm, which has meant that a large group of members had the opportunity to take part in an RYA keelboat training day,
selection races, training races and then finally an adult and youth team competed in their respective British Keelboat competitions.

It is here that I would like to award the Mamgu trophy to David Nickalls for his write up of the Marconi Youth team’s baptism of J80
sailing when they travelled South to compete in the Youth Keelboat finals in October. It’s a good read and available on the Club
website.
January 2018 Navigans 3

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

2018 looks even more exciting for keelboat sailing as the Board have agreed to support the purchase of at least 2 keelboats,
likely to be SB20’s. Peter is also organising the Marconi Inland Championships, an event on 14th April hosted by Queen Mary’s
where members are invited to enter their own teams to race in a BKL style event. There are still a couple of team spaces
available for anyone who is interested. We will also be entering the BKL again in 2018 and invitations to compete for a position in
the Club’s team will be sent out before Christmas.

I am pleased to report that we have been entered into the RYA Club of the Year competition as a result of our innovative activities
in Keelboat sailing this year. Winners are announced at the RYA dinghy show in March.

Sailing

I am going to leave nearly all of the sailing achievements for the Sailing Secretary’s report. All I will say is that we have had a
brilliant year for Marconi sailors in club racing, travelling to opens, nationals and other events from both the dinghy and cruiser
fleets.

However, I would like to just mention one of our young sailors who has really been doing us proud over the past few years.
William Harrison has been involved in the Topper Eastern squad, the Nacra 15 youth squad and has travelled to Lake Garda and
Holland this year and achieved a 3rd place in the Nacra 15 Nationals sailing against much older crews. William has recently been
selected for the Nacra 15 youth National Squad, so I would like to award the seamanship trophy to this incredible young sailor.

Training

Cadet week and sail training have once again had a fantastic year with record turnouts and a healthy flow of volunteers working
under Dave Clarke and John Nickalls. Congratulations are also due to Bryan Spencer whose Turtle group of adult cadets has
grown considerably. In fact Bryan has instilled such a love of sailing in some people that a group of Turtles have been out sailing
over the past few weekends when most of us are at home hiding from the cold.

Providing training for adults is something that we have been keen to build on as we broaden the Club’s training programme. I am
pleased to report that at the end of October we ran our first RYA dinghy sailing course, which is a huge achievement and
something that seemed almost unobtainable a few years ago. Thanks are due to our Senior Dinghy Instructor, Rhiannon Hitt, our
RYA Training Centre Principal Bob Collins, and of course Pat Shaw for getting us certified as a centre to run dinghy courses. We
have a number of qualified dinghy instructors within the Club and we will be looking to invest in more instructors as we begin to
offer formal RYA courses on top of our current successful Sail Training programme. We will continue to run powerboat courses
and look to expand this to safety boat in the future, but the ability to offer dinghy sailing courses is a really important step forward
for the Club.

Events

2017 saw the 30th anniversary of The East Coast Piers Race and it was another resounding success with 86 entries, 22 more
than last year. This year we saw improved Saturday night entertainment, the introduction of GPS tracking and some more
strategic marketing, which all helped to swell the number of competitors over the weekend. As always, thanks are due to Clive
Shenton and his team, which will include many of you sat in the audience today, for organising another superb event. It is thanks
to this army of selfless volunteers, from those scrutineering boats onto the hard, driving ribs, laying race marks to manning mother
boats and race committees that make this iconic event possible and I wish to thank you all.

Looking forward to 2018 our provisional sailing calendar is looking packed with sailing and social activities. I would like to mention
that we are hosting a Topper National Championship event in early September 2018, which is likely to be an event on the scale of
the ECPR. This event has the potential to really raise the profile of MSC and also raise some funds and will require a number of
volunteers to help the organising team over the weekend, so look out for more information in the New Year.

Social

We have had an active and well supported social calendar throughout 2017 thanks to our social diva team of Sara, Julie and
Claire. I would encourage you all to attend the annual dinner dance on 3rd February at the Lion Inn with tickets still available.

Rowing

Kevin Stubbs joined the management committee this year as our first rowing rep to represent this growing area of activity. Gig
rowing is building in popularity and has enabled us to provide access to a water sport for people who are not necessarily
interested in sailing. Marconi are hosting a leg of the Harkers Yard gig racing series on 7th January so please come along t o
support the event and our team if you can brave the cold.

To further encourage paddle sports, the Club purchased another 2 kayaks this year, taking our total to 4 along with 2 stand up
paddle boards. On certain days in the summer there have been queues of members waiting to use these, making them a great
addition to the clubs offering.

Projects

Now I would like to talk about capital projects that have been a focus in 2017. As we’re a sailing Club I am really pleased to report
that we have spent a chunk of capital expenditure on buying boats and items related to boats. In order to support our training
provision we have purchased 2 wayfarers (named Skylark and Swallow via public vote), 4 pico’s (taking the total to 6), 2 optimist

January 2018 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

dinghies and a Hartley 10. With the aid of grant funding we have also gained another support boat, the cat rib, complete with new
engine, 2 further kayaks, 2 paddle boards and a full complement of hand held and support boat mounted radios.

Projects have included the construction of the Bridge Deck, which is almost complete and will act as a control hub for events,
OOD’s and race management in some instances. The road at the far end of the catamaran field has been completely replaced,
mechanisation of the mooring laying and retrieval process has been improved, we now have a third container for storage of club
boat equipment and some remedial work has been carried out to the approach road.

Going into next year we plan to complete projects currently underway as well as making improvements to the upstairs lounge.
We are conscious that we have now outgrown our social space and plan to knock the bar through into the training room and
provide training space elsewhere.

As a club we rely on some key pieces of heavy plant and equipment and maintaining these could probably be a full time job. W e
are very fortunate that within the membership we have some skilled individuals who selflessly give their time and expertise to
keep the Club and its equipment running. Here I would like to award the Commodores Trophy to a very deserving individual -
Mick Richardson. Mick was instrumental in the mammoth and very frustrating task of returning the big tractor back to health last
winter when it suffered a catastrophic breakdown. We have purchased a dumper truck to reduce our reliance on the big tractor
and Mick is stripping down and rebuilding that engine as well. On top of being a master of engines, Mick is also our sewerage
system expert and has spent too much time with his head in the sewerage system changing pumps and ensuring that it continues
to function. He has also produced a detailed analysis of what is wrong with our current system and planned a simple and cost-
effective way forwards. In addition, Mick is often in the background doing unseen, useful tasks such as preparing and laying race
marks for ECPR, training Teleporter drivers and scrubbing the hard.

Challenges

I will end this report with a note about the challenges we face as the club moves forwards and develops within a changing
environment. I am fortunate as Commodore to be able to spend nearly all of my report talking about the positive achievements
and progress the Club is making each year, however I am mindful that with success can come problems. For instance, as a Club
we need to be thinking about efficient usage of space. As one of the largest Clubs in the South East we have always had the
luxury of space for boat storage, parking and camping. As our membership and the popularity of our events grow, we need to be
smart about the way we use space and may have to change some of our existing conceptions about how the Club is laid out.
Other examples of challenges for the Board include our obligations for data protection, finance and safeguarding of children and
adults which is something we must be as vigilant of as general Health and Safety. The world of social media, digital media and
reaching new members is always changing and we need to make sure we stay ahead of the rest of the field if we want to continue
to grow and cement our place as a premier sailing Clubs. Within the Club we have some very experienced professionals to call
upon and I am entirely sure we can meet these challenges head on with the team I hope you will elect during this AGM.

So, in conclusion, Marconi Sailing Club has had a resoundingly successful 2017 and I look forward to the year ahead.

Thank you for your kind support this year and for listening to this report.

I am happy to take any questions.

Michaela Dowley
Commodore, Marconi Sailing Club

RNLI Quiz Night
What?

It’s quiz time!

In the bleak Midwinter it would be good to get together, remember all those heady summer days!? MSC are having a social quiz
night in Maldon for everyone to meet up, keep those grey cells active and to raise money for the RNLI!!!!

Ably guided by the brilliant Tony and Sally Ferguson, renowned for their Cadet Week Quiz’s, this will be a night of testing trivia
and jovial festivities.

When?

Saturday 13th January 7 for 7.30

Where?

Maldon Little Ship Club at the Hythe Quay Maldon.

Why?

To raise money for the RNLI by supporting the Marconi rowing gig at the RNLI Rowing Race.

We’ve already raised a lot through many members generosity, but are aiming to be the Rowing Gig that raises the most this year!

How?

Marconi Sailing Club Quiz Night

Book your table fast to guarantee your place, as we the club can only accommodate 8 tables of 8 people. Contact Sandra Clayton
at or via phone: / .

It’s £5 per head with all proceeds going to the RNLI and of course a raffle!

Bring your own wine and nibbles, cask beer and bottles can be bought from their well-stocked bar.

The Marconi Sailing Club have rowed in the RNLI Rowing Race since 1979, when Mike Turner and Pete Clayton first rowed and
raised money for the RNLI. There have been many memorable fancy dress costumes particularly during the years when the Ball
family and more recently the Claytons and Ashes took part. This is our second year with the Gig Elettra and we are hoping to
encourage the Gigs to raise more money!

The race is now in its 41st year and still going strong. This year due to tides and lack of light it has shifted from its traditional
Christmas/New Year slot and will be held on Saturday 20th January.

Sailing Secretary’s report for 2017
Hi all,

Well another year has passed and another season is over as I find myself once again in front of you to deliver my report as Sailing
Secretary.

It’s been a fantastic year to be involved, once again, in sailing at Marconi Sailing Club. That’s a lot of sailing to be saying, but it is
now my pleasure to share with you all that has been going on.

There have been less changes this year to the way we’ve been running things, which has been nice. We rolled out the Bank
Holiday regatta prize-givings over all the bank holiday weekends to encourage more to take part in the mini-series. The long
Summer Series was split into two and the other series shortened to make space for an Early and a Late Summer series so that
the holidays would have less impact on the competitor’s results & discards.

The dinghy and cat racing fleets are still well supported and the extended season has meant that we’ve all had some good racing.
The Solo fleet is still quite strong and the Sprint 15 fleet continues to grow, the medium cat fleet have also had a few Dart 18s out
racing which is good to see.

This year’s Open Day was once again steered by the masterful Graham and seemed to be even more successful than ever.
There were lots of new sailors that came along on that day and also Saskia Clarke who got a few tips about cat sailing with
Andrew Dowley. Many new members took part in Cadet Week and have joined us regularly for our Sail Training days. These have
also seen record numbers attending this season, with the adults joining in as well; all these are good signs for the future.

The Training centre side of things continues to progress. We have trained up yet more Powerboat drivers under Pat’s careful
tutelage and we have now expanded into dinghy courses. Last month saw our first RYA level 2 dinghy course, with three of the
Turtles or adult learners to those uninitiated, Our thanks to Gemma and Rhiannon who put on that course.

On the subject of Turtles, these are a rapidly expanding group of adults who are showing great enthusiasm for learning to sail
later in life. They are so enthusiastic that they are even seen during the winter months honing their skills. We have had many
graduates of this programme throughout the years and it really looks like there is a bright future for them, and the club going
forward.

The Cruiser sailing fleet have had a full season of trips, this year venturing across the North Sea before the borders come down!
Thankfully they made it back in time to provide their invaluable help with the ECPR as Mother Boats keeping an eye on the Cats &
Dinghies as they race to Walton pier and back. There have also been the traditional rallies around the East Coast to Brightlingsea,
to Ipswich and beyond.

The Cruiser Racing fleet have seen a buoyant year of racing in the BJRC championship, which has seen a good turn out from
Marconi boats with Blue Moon taking first in the IRC championship and Monkey Business coming home in second place. There
were even a couple of race wins for John Littlewood and crew on Crazy Suzie. The Autumn series was also well supported and
went to Blue Moon The competition saw the first win for Vy Trans and the crew of Ned Kelly, the club Robber; what great progress
they have made!

This year also featured for the first time a Marconi entry in the British Keelboat League or BKL for short. This is a new competition
with the aim being short quick-fire races in keelboats around the country leading to a final in Cowes. Lead by Peter Ward we held
a qualifying competition to select the team to represent MSC at the local round of the BKL. I was lucky enough to be selected and
went off with my team to Burnham to race against 5 other local teams. This then lead to an invite to the southern qualifier and
even to the final where we finished a respectable 15th place. Jack Collis who had been bowman and helmed for us during the
finals then took a crew down to the Royal Southern Yacht Club for the youth BKL as none of the other crew qualified, Jack had to
find 3 other crews.

As a result of the interest drawn by the BKL Peter Ward has organised a Keelboat championship for next season. It kicks off with
a one day event Saturday 14th April, currently there are 7 teams that have registered an interest with a capacity for 12. So if you
are thinking that a day of keelboat racing on J80’s around the Queen Mary Reservoir in balmy April conditions then please get in
contact with Peter and get your team together!

There have been a number of opens held at the club this year, with Sprint 15’s visiting in March, the Tornadoes visiting for a
training day in May, The Larks in June, a Laser open in July and the 18’s visiting for the first time for a round of their Grand Prix
circuit which was quite a spectacle. Of course we also had the East Coast Piers Race, another good year with great conditions for
both Saturday & Sunday which lead to course records in both the full and the dinghy course.

Bart’s Bash once again was a huge inter-club success; it’s great to see so many boats out on the water even if the Race Officer
didn’t want to wait for everyone to start proceedings.

Colin Wardell’s dinghy cruises are still a popular feature of the sailing calendar. They’ve been on voyages from the club to any
pub that is willing to serve them, their quest was almost curtailed by the weather but a detour to start their east coast cruise from

The windsurfers continue to venture out when most have given up all hope of sailing, and they have been using the excellent club
kit to train up others in the hope that they also get the bug! These training sessions have been oversubscribed throughout the

USE OF SAFETY HARNESSES
This report was copied from MAIB Safety Bulletin 1/2018. The full report is available on the MAIB website www.gov.uk/maib

BACKGROUND The sailing yacht CV30 was taking part in the third leg of the Clipper Round the World Yacht Race having left
Cape Town on 31 October 2017 bound for Fremantle, Western Australia. At about 1414 local time on 18 November 2017, the
yacht was in position 42°30.3’S, 087°36.3’E, approximately 1500nm from Fremantle, when a crew member, Simon Speirs, fell
overboard. He was attached to the yacht by his safety harness tether. The hook at the end of the tether that was clipped to a jack-
line, deformed and released resulting in him becoming separated from the yacht. Simon Speirs was recovered unconscious onto
the yacht but sadly could not be resuscitated.

INITIAL FINDINGS Simon Speirs was using a three-point webbing tether attached to the integral harness of his lifejacket that
allowed him to clip on to the yacht with a short or long tether. A safety issue identified during the investigation was that the hook
on the end of Mr Speirs’ tether had become caught under a deck cleat (see Figure 1), resulting in a lateral loading that was
sufficient to cause the hook to distort (see Figure 2) and eventually release. The harness tether was certified under ISO12401
(Small craft – Deck safety harness and safety line – Safety requirements and test methods), which is the international standard
applicable to this equipment. The standard contains detailed testing requirements that assume the tether and its hooks will be
loaded longitudinally rather than laterally. The tether hook was of a conventional design and quality of build, and was commonly
used by manufacturers of safety harnesses and tethers that were certified under ISO12401. When loaded longitudinally, the
tether can withstand a load of over 1 tonne. However, when loaded laterally a tether hook will deform at much less load. It is
important that tether hooks remain clear of obstructions and are free to rotate to align the load longitudinally.

SAFETY LESSON To prevent the strength of a safety harness tether becoming compromised in-service due to lateral loading on
the tether hook, the method used to anchor the end of the tether to the vessel should be arranged to ensure that the tether hook
cannot become entangled with deck fittings or other equipment. Issued January 2018 4 Figure 1: Tether hook under deck cleat

Marconi Sailing Club Recognised For Excellence in Innovation
__$_—___
Marconi Sailing Club (MSC) has been announced as a finalist in this year’s RYA and Yachts
and Yachting’s Club of the Year. An award that recognises and celebrates the outstanding
achievements of UK sailing clubs.
RYA YAGIS
CLUB OF THE YEAR
MSC is one of the South East’s leading sailing clubs, and has been selected as a finalist 2018
because of its innovative approach to making sailing accessible to all – enabling its new and FINALIST
existing members to get on the water no matter what.

One of MSC’s top initiatives, which has led to its nomination is associated to its Keelboat fleet. In 2015, the Club recognised that
an increasing number of new members wanted to learn to sail yachts and participate in racing, but the Club had insufficient boats
to cope with demand. To overcome this, the Club formed the Keelboat programme – investing in a number of boats to increase
capacity.

Fast forward to 2017 and the Club’s Keelboat programme has proven so popular it has seen the formation of Club Keelboat
racing. This has led to the Club building a competitive team that entered the British Keelboat League (BKL) and participated in the
BKL Youth Event on the Solent in October 2017.

Peter Ward, who initiated the Keelboat programme says: “The Club’s involvement in BKL has provided great opportunities for
members to gain race experience and develop their skills in numerous ways, including as race officials and umpires. It has also
introduced 50 non-sailing adults to big boat sailing and developed regular race crew for new members in 2017. As a result, 21
new members have joined the club from this initiative alone and now race regularly.”

Alongside the Club’s keelboat success, 2017 also saw it become an official Dinghy Training Centre. This has further boosted the
Clubs ability to get people on the water – making sailing more accessible than ever before.

Michaela Dowley, Commodore of MSC commented “We are absolutely thrilled to be a finalist for the innovation category, and to
be in with a chance of being crowned the RYA Club of the Year. We’ve run many initiatives over the year, but the Keelboat
programme is by far one of our most successful. A few years ago, keelboat sailing was non-existent at MSC so we’ve made huge
progress. We are now working towards starting our own keelboat fleet and organising a competitive league with local clubs. What
is of equal importance to me is the success keelboat sailing has had with our members. Whether they are new to sailing or more
experienced, it has attracted new members, created a degree of competitiveness and brought all our fleets together. It is
something we are all excited about growing in the future.”

The winner of RYA Club of the Year will be announced and presented with their trophy at the RYA Dinghy Show on Saturday 03
March 2018.

To vote visit http://awards.yachtsandyachting.co.uk/marconi-sailing-club/

Andrew Dowley

 No generators are to be used by camping units whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club site.
 No camping units may plug into mains electricity whilst on the Marconi Sailing Club
site.

 No one under the age of 18 may camp unless an adult with responsibility for that child is
on site at all times.
 The camping area at the far end of the catamaran field, is limited to cadet week TUTORS

and playing ball games etc.

allowed to roam freely on neighbouring farmland. All footpath restrictions are to be
respected.

EARLY SEASON WARNING – THE WATER IS C-C-COLD
As I write this there is snow outside and the daytime temperature is 0oC so it’s not difficult to imagine the water temperature being
very low. When the sun does come out and Spring finally shows itself, as surely it must soon, it is easy to be fooled by feeling
warm ashore but a serious risk of hypothermia exists especially if you take an unintended swim.

The water has been cooling down all winter and is now very cold. Many tides need to flow over sun warmed saltings and
sandbanks before sea water can be coaxed into gaining a few degrees Celsius.

Make sure that you are dressed appropriately when going afloat. (Don’t forget your head.) If you take inexperienced people afloat
with you make sure that they are fully protected against the cold should they take an unplanned dip or succumb to the wind chill.

There is no fun in being chilled to the bone. It’s easier to think straight and react properly when warm.

on the blind bends are particularly vulnerable.

Please drive carefully on the club road and remember that the vehicle approaching you may not be as careful as you are.

New Arrangements for Dinghy Racing
With the new season comes some new arrangements – it’s only a few minor tweaks to keep things fresh and hopefully find some
new ways of making things better.

The headline change is probably that this season the Fast Cats will be starting first.

FAST CATS STARTING FIRST
This means our order of starts will be:

1. Fast & Medium Cats

2. Sprint 15s

3. Mono-hulls

A number of factors contributing here but probably the two most noteworthy are that we wanted to give the newer and younger
sailors a clearer starting area and less boats to deal with whilst launching and that clearing the line of the faster boats early means
we can set them a longer course with less impact on overall race management times. The real focus here is to make racing as
accessible as possible to as many as possible.

SHORT COURSE HANDICAP
The other big change seems a little more complicated but actually is very simple.

We won’t be setting a course called “Cadet Course”.

We will be setting a course called “Short Course Handicap”

Told you it was simple………………

(The only complication is we might not have caught up with changing the signing on sheets yet:-)

The short course handicap course is intended to be sailed by anyone of any age in any boat that wishes to sail a short course.
This course is ideal for anyone wishing to concentrate on improving their sailing, or that simply wishes to sail a shorter course.

We expect to see a mixture of cadets and adults sailing this course with plenty of coaching going on and top tips being
exchanged, the application of the “outside assistance rules” will be relaxed for this fleet, particularly if you need a little help
righting your boat after a capsize (It happens to all of us – you could take the view that if you don’t capsize every now and then
perhaps you are not pushing hard enough —- maybe that’s just me 🙂

Cadets Aged 14 & Over

We are removing the requirement for a Cadet to get a parent to sign them on for a race. We should point out that parents are
responsible for their charges at all times at MSC, but you all know that already.

In addition any cadet aged 14 or over can now race in any fleet.

SPRINT 15 TEACH IN AT MARCONI – APRIL 2018
Nine boats took part in the Sprint 15 Teach In at Marconi on Saturday 7th April led by David Ball and Chris Tillyer. We were
particularly pleased to welcome Armin from Brightlingsea who has just bought Gordon Deuce’s boat and ventured to Marconi for
his first ever Sprint 15 sail. Also joining us was Jemma Clarke from Marconi who had her first proper sail in a Sprint 15, alongside
her Dad and her brother and we hope she will join the fleet too! Donald Sloan travelled down from Felixtowe Ferry as did Rob
Wilson from Stone – together with a home fleet.

Once the boats were rigged, the team retired to the
galley for a briefing and bacon rolls. After a session from
Chris and David on key aspects of sailing a Sprint 15
and race starts – the fleet took to the water.

Pausing briefly to wait for Nigel James to right a capsize
- a series of committee boat races were run by Jenny
Ball and Rob Wilson in near perfect sailing conditions.
Starts were filmed and Go Pros were deployed on RIBs.
Which would have provided really useful training material
if only Chris knew which way round a Go Pro works.
Instead, we ended up with multiple videos of half of
Chris’ face resembling that film, the Blair Witch Project.
David briefly crewed for Armin to help him see the key
differences with his previous boat (a Wayfarer) – but it
was not long before Armin was comfortably sailing round
on his own and getting to grips with the boat. Donald
put in some great races and showed the way round on
multiple occasions with Jason Clarke putting in some
great starts. Once Jenny and Rob had finished the
Easter Egg they brought out with them – they decided it
was lunch time, so the fleet headed ashore.

Over lunch, it was discussed that the fleet were very polite pre-start and needed to (a) get much closer to the line and (b) exercise
their windward boat keeps clear rights. So with words about positioning for the line, coffin corner and getting rammed into the
committee boat ringing in their ears – the fleet set off again in slightly breezier conditions.

Pausing briefly to wait for Nigel James to right a second capsize – the first race got underway with fleet members positioning
themselves much closer to the line, clearly taking on board the feedback over lunch.

Pausing briefly to wait for Nigel to right a third capsize and for the Rib to tow Antony Bailey’s boat back when his forestay rope
broke and the mast came down – the next race got underway. Andy Perks led the race from start to finish with a convincing win
– particularly as a number of the fleet experienced that great thing when its breezy enough for a Sprint 15 to be difficult to tack
and duly get parked up.

Moving into the last race – the fleet were regaled with Donald calling “up! Up!” really loudly on the rest of the fleet just as he had
been taught to do at lunchtime. Unfortunately, he got so carried away that he sailed straight over the line 10 seconds early so
had to go round again. Jason got a split second perfect start and led all the way round to win the race. Most importantly, he
beat his Dad. The fleet then headed home for a final de-brief over tea and cake and a short lesson in tacking and promises that
any footage not basically just featuring Chris’ right ear would be posted somewhere for forensic review and homework for all
participants at a later date.

And as an aside, Nigel rather nobly makes a donation to the RNLI every time he capsizes. Based on today’s performance, we
can expect to be invited to the launch ceremony of RNLB The Nigel James at some point prior to the end of the season.

Thanks to David and Chris for leading the session, to the support boat crew and galley team and to everyone who took part in the
day – it was a fantastic day on the water.

Jenny Ball

WILDLIFE AT STANSGATE – RATS
For your own protection against being bitten be very careful when moving anything that could be hiding a rat’s nest. Obvious
things are upturned boats, boats themselves if hatch covers have been left off, boat covers, piles of wood, trailers and anywhere
else that might form a cosy nesting place for rodents. Warn your family, particularly younger members, who may move a boat
without thinking.

As well as the risk of being bitten the other danger when rats have been near standing water (puddles on boat covers or on the
ground for example) is Well’s Disease. Well’s Disease is caused by rats’ urine in water. (There is a lot of information about Well’s
Disease online.)

Where there is water that has a high risk of rat infestation take great care not to ingest the water or let any wounds come into
contact with it.

The most effective way to protect yourself from Weil's disease is to avoid contact with infected water. However, there are steps
you can take to lower your risk of infection.

if you have cuts do not allow them to be submerged in the water;

never swallow water unsuitable for drinking;

wash all equipment and clothing in clean water;

clothing that can survive bleaching should be disinfected or bleached to kill the bacteria;

if you have a wound always use clean fresh water to clean wounds as soon as possible

MAaiesrrTM Sprint 15
Sprint 15 Traveller Event 2018 – Marconi Sailing Club, Essex.

27 competitors took part in the first 40th Anniversary Sprint 15 Summer TT at Marconi SC on 14th and 15th April including an
impressive home turnout of 13 boats. We were also pleased to welcome Nigel and Fiona Denchfield as guest Races Officers for
the event.

In addition to the racing, we welcomed the winner of our competition at the RYA Dinghy Show for a cat coaching session with
Brian Phipps from Windsport International.

As forecast, there was no wind in the morning but with a light breeze forecast for later in the afternoon it was decided to postpone
racing for an hour. With the AP dropped ashore, the fleet headed out to the race area off picturesque Osea Island in a pleas antly
mild afternoon with a light breeze.

With the ebb now running, a number of the fleet managed to get caught in the “coffin zone” behind the committee boat, but with
the breeze strengthening, the fleet headed off to the windward mark. Paul Grattage established his lead at the first mark which
proved unassailable. Meanwhile, Liam Thom, Chris Tillyer, Stuart Snell, Jenny Ball and David Ball battled it out for the “next”
positions. Chris only managed to knock into Jenny’s shiny new boat once and Liam only managed to slightly insult Jenny by
comparing her to the age of the Thames Sailing Barge that sailed by during the race. As a result of which, whilst Stuart came
second, Jenny made sure that Liam and Chris came 4th and 5th respectively behind her.

May 2018 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Race 2 saw a number of boats get pushed over the line by the ebb tide. All but one (Jenny) re-cleared the line to continue the
race. Uncharacteristically, Paul managed to knock the windward mark and had to do a turn. Jenny, David, Liam and George
battled round the course with David taking the win (due to Jenny’s OCS) followed by Liam, George and Stuart. Meanwhile Jon
Pearse had endeavoured to sail the race with a broken universal joint on his tiller extension which, even with the aid of some
string from Chris, did not prove sustainable – but did earn him the GJW Direct Insurance spot prize – see below.

By Race 3 – a sea breeze was starting to build – unusual in April but reflective of the cold water and unusually warm air
temperature which was, frankly, a welcome return after the cold and wet winter/spring we have all endured! Any original planning
thoughts of deferring race 3 to Sunday were re-evaluated and it was decided to stick with the original NOR plan. Which proved to
be the right call as a decent breeze accompanied the race. Stuart and Paul broke away with Stuart building enough of a lead to
take the win. David. Jenny, Liam and Kevin Kirby battled out behind – who managed to hold off Ed, Jim Bowie and George
snapping at their heels.

The fleet headed in for a well deserved dinner – accompanied by champagne and cake as the Events Assistant had managed to
coincide the event (at her home club) with her birthday.

On Sunday morning, the forecast was for a decent breeze coming in at about 12 noon As such, the plan was to fit in a “round the
cans” race from about 11 – and then the legendary figure of eight round the islands race to follow. The weather decided to
continue its fickle record this winter/spring by providing lots of mist, although this had cleared by the time the fleet launched mid-
morning. Patiently expecting the forecasted 11 knot breeze, the fleet sailed about but the winds remained fickle and not possible
to race in for a further hour. Eventually, a light breeze came in and, with a slight tweak to the marks, the Race Officer set the
fleet off. In a fluctuating breeze of anywhere between 2 and 7 knots, the fleet set off round the course. Some had been delayed
getting to the course, having opted to park on the beach and some got delayed by the strong tide. Andy Perks led round the first
mark, pursued by Paul, Stuart and Nigel James – with a group of Jenny, David, Kevin, George, Jim Bowie, Will Harrison and Jon
Pearse battling out behind. The wind held out enough to complete a proper two lap race with Paul taking the win, followed by
Stuart and Nigel and Andy putting in really impressive third and fourth place results given they both only recently joined the fleet.

As a result of the delay, but with the light breeze holding, the fleet decided to go ahead with race 5 but a shortened versio n of just
Osea Island, (rather than the full course including Northey Island). given the state of the tide. With an interesting downwind start
(!), the fleet headed diagonally across to Osea Island. By now punching an ebb tide – it was an interesting decision whether to
hug the Osea shore out of the tide but risk an element of wind shadow by doing so. Chris managed to do this successfully whilst
Liam headed out into more breeze / more tide and the pair converged ahead of the rest of the fleet just before turning at the head
of the island. As the fleet reached the turning point, the wind filled in with good strength creating a fantastic beat behind Osea
Island. Those who stood on further to the Goldhanger shore benefitted those who had tacked earlier but it was a great beat to the
turning mark at the end of the island. At this stage, Liam had consolidated his lead to take the win, followed by Ed Dalton, Paul,
George, Jenny, Jim, Stuart and David.

The fleet headed home after a great weekend of sailing! Big thanks go to the Race Officers, Race Committee and Support boat
crews who had to set up and deliver 5 races in some unpredictable conditions whilst we all waited for the wind.

Commodore’s Notes
Welcome to the July edition of Navigans, and apologies for not writing for some time. You can find most of the Club news on our
website and weekly emails which I recommend to all current members.

Its been a really busy year so far both on and off the water with plenty of work going on ‘behind the scenes’ so I have a couple of
things to tell you about.

MEMBERS DONATION SCHEME
At the AGM in December 2017, a donation scheme was suggested (by Kevin Kirby, a member) and supported in principle by all
the members present.

The Sailing Club has outstanding debt to NatWest bank (approximately £330k) as a result of loans taken out to buy the club site
from MASC and to extend and refurbish our changing rooms. MSC is in a sound financial position - repayments of the loans are
factored into our financial planning.

Members present at the AGM were overwhelmingly supportive of an initiative that would offer the general membership an
opportunity to donate money to the Club in order to speed up repayment of this loan. Thus enabling us to strengthen our financial
position and drive more of the clubs revenue into improvements and sailing activities. We make repayments of approximately
£2700 per month to the bank. If we didn’t have to make those repayments we could spend more on driving the club forwards and
funding our massively important projects.

This initiative is likely to be discussed at the next AGM however we are keen to hear what the feeling amongst the general
membership would be before we try and put a scheme together. The scheme could take the form of a £1000 one off donation or
perhaps £250 per year over 4 years. We would only need 330 members to subscribe to this scheme to then completely clear our
debt. If a smaller amount is raised we may be able to significantly reduce the term of our loans. Please feel free to talk to any
member of the Board if you would like some more information or to give some feedback.

OPEN DAY 2018
We held our annual open day on Saturday 26th May where we welcomed 218 visitors to the Club. We offered opportunities to
have a go at sailing a variety of dinghies, catamarans and cruisers as well as windsurfing and kayaking. The Pimms tent was well
supported by the adults and a bouncy castle and arts and crafts tent kept the smaller people entertained. It was a fantastic day
that allowed us to showcase our wonderful Sailing Club to the general public. As a result we welcomed 7 new members on the
day and several more are likely to join us in the near future. As well as providing opportunities for non-sailors to enjoy our
facilities it was an excellent day for current members as well. A Club BBQ and band in the evening with plenty of members
camping rounded off a top event. Congratulations and thanks go to Liz Kirby for heading up the organisation and also to all those
volunteers who helped make the day possible from meeting and greeting at the gate, taking visitors out sailing to manning the bar
and giving tours of the Club. Our members are one of the best selling points for the Club and it makes me very proud to hear the
feedback around how welcoming and friendly visitors found us to be, so thanks to you all!

SUCCESS!
MSC is going from strength to strength at the moment with many positive initiatives and activities taking place. Sail Training is
thriving with a growing adult section and huge numbers turning out to sessions. Our RYA training centre is also gaining
momentum as we welcome Jen Miller as Chief Instructor working with Rhiannon Hitt and Bob Collins to deliver dinghy training
courses which is a massive step forwards for the Club. Membership numbers are holding if not increasing year on year which is a
great achievement when we compare ourselves to other sailing Clubs. Our fleets continue to be active with the Sprint 15’s
travelling on mass to Weymouth for their

Nationals and MSC is again well represented in the BJRC series for cruiser racing. Keelboat racing suffered from a lack of wind
early in the season for the regatta day at Queen Mary’s, even so, 45 of our sailors, umpires and race officers travelled to try and
compete. This shows a great enthusiasm for keelboat sailing and we plan to try and acquire our own fleet of these fantastic
racing boats to further develop the activities we offer at MSC.

Of course success in activities and membership comes with some complications. As the number of boats on site increases (which
is good) we will need to think about the way we do things. Over the coming seasons you will notice changes to the layouts of boat
parks, initially rearrangement of the dinghy park which is planned for this winter. Every camping weekend seems to be busier so
please be mindful of the amount of space taken up by each unit. This is especially true for ECPR where all members and visitors
will be asked to squeeze up to make sure we can accommodate everyone (tents, caravans, campers and boats!).

SUMMER 2018
Its now the busiest and most active time of the year at MSC - ECPR is just around the corner as I write this. ECPR is the biggest
event in our calendar and its set to be another busy one. Thanks are due to Clive Shenton and his team of organisers who have
been meeting throughout the year to deliver this event on behalf of the Club. Clive is due to stand down as ECPR chairman after
14 years at the helm so I would like to extend my gratitude on behalf of the Club and past competitors for the blood sweat (and
tears) Clive has poured into this event.

Cadet week and camping fortnight are due to take place at the end of July/beginning of August. Please note that camping for
these 2 weeks must be pre-booked and paid for. Week 1 has already sold out and there are a couple of spaces still available for
week 2. Contact the camping manager for further details.

We have a growing fleet of Club boats, from optimists and Hartley 10’s for the little ones to Sprint 15’s and lasers for the bigger
sailors. These boats are available for use by club members. Please see the club website for more information and guidance on
how to access the club boats.

DATA
Thought you had heard the end of GDPR? We take your information and the use of your data very seriously at MSC. We will
shortly be circulating our Privacy Policy which details how and why we use your personal information. I would encourage you all
to log into the members portal where you can amend your own personal information, pay invoices and communicate with the
Club. This is really important as we need to hold current and correct information for members, and it helps us when we come to
renewals in January.

Wishing you all a great summer of sailing,

COMMUNICATION WITH MEMBERS (1)
Most communications from the club are now via email whether they are invoices, messages from club officials or routine sailing
updates. It is important that the club has the correct email address for you.

Emails from Marconi Sailing Club (including the membership database – Sailing Club Manager) can have a tendency to go into
recipients SPAM box which can mean that members miss out on club information. This has caused a lot of extra work for Mike
Turner when dealing with 2018 subscriptions and fees. The problem is being addressed but, in the meantime, please check your
SPAM regularly. If you are satisfied that a message is genuinely from the club please declare it as NOT SPAM; or whatever the
equivalent is on your system.

(If your system gives you the choice of not sending MSC emails into SPAM, that’s even better.)

COMMUNICATIONS WITH MEMBERS (2)
Under the new data regulations members have the choice as to whether or not to receive routine emails from the club. Members
now need to opt in. About half of the membership have not opted in and are missing out on club information which is a pity.

Those who have not opted in probably will not have received this Navigans. If any of your fellow members complain that they
have stopped receiving club information please ask them if they have opted in.

The new data regulations give people more control over their personal data but it does mean that they have to be proactive to
ensure that they receive wanted messages.

The two items above on COMMUNICATIONS WITH MEMBERS have been written by a layman but I’m sure that members will get
the general idea.

CRUISERS MAY NOT BE LEFT ON MOORINGS OVER THE WINTER
To leave a boat on an MSC mooring over the winter is bad for the boat and possibly bad for the club’s reputation if damage
results in an insurance claim.

At a meeting on Tuesday 22nd May the Board passed a resolution which adds the following bylaw.

Bylaw 3.4.4 No cruiser may be left on a mooring between 1st December and 1st March

This bylaw is effective from 1st June 2018. Please put this notice in your 2018 yearbook.
