SPRINT 15 NATIONALS RACE REPORT
With much positive anticipation – the Sprint 15 fleet
descended on WPNSA, the Olympic Sailing Venue, in late
June for our 40th Anniversary National Championships
and general celebrations.

With support from an array of fabulous partners – GJW
Direct Insurance, Kevin Kirby Limited, Windsport
International, Hyde Sails, White Formula, RWO, English
Braid - and welcoming longstanding supporters of the
Association, including past Chairs and the founder of it all,
Ian Fraser, we were all set for a great weekend. And what
a weekend it was.

A fantastic venue under any circumstances, we were
blessed with blazing sunshine and beautiful conditions at
WPNSA all weekend.

Some of the fleet arrived early on Friday to take advantage of a coaching session provided by Brian Phipps from Windsport
International and Stuart Snell, multiple National Champion to help them get to grips with sailing in these waters and in fleet racing
conditions. Amusingly, the lake sailing contingent left their trolleys at the waters edge, only to find them floating off on the
incoming tide – earning them the first of the weekend’s spot prize awards (of which more, later).

Friday night saw a gathering of fleet members for an evening meal – enjoying a fantastic sunset and general catch up on the
balcony overlooking Portland Harbour.

Saturday launched the event with GJW Direct Insurance Race Day and time to get into some serious racing. The forecast was
not hugely promising (blazing sunshine, blue skies, riviera conditions - but Sprint 15s get nervous if the forecast in anything below
15 knots). However, under the expert supervision of the WPNSA team plus Race Management team of Fiona and Nigel
Denchfield and Henry Wright - we were in great hands and got four Championship races in the bag.

July 2018 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Race 1 – set off in relatively light conditions. In what turned out to be the general rule of thumb for the weekend – those who
stood on closest to the WPNSA end of the harbour picked up the favourable wind and despite the risk of coming into the
windward mark on port, this approach generally paid off. Stuart Snell rounded in first place, followed by David Ball, Jenny Ball
and Liam Thom who pointed out that Jenny’s old boat was faster as he sailed over the top of her new boat to reach mark 2
ahead. By the end of the second lap, this had been addressed – with Stuart taking the win, followed by Jenny, David, Gary
Sverdloff and Liam.

Race 2 – was definitely dominated by the younger end of the fleet. Stuart Snell took an early lead but Tom Gurney and Hector
Bunclark showed everyone else the way round for much of the race – whilst Gary S had another great race, fighting it out with
George Love and Jenny. Stuart went on to win, followed by Jenny, George, Gary, Tom and Hector.

Race 3 – Team Shanklin decided to put in their normal appearance with Liam taking the lead and showing Stuart a pair of
transoms for a change. Paul Grattage and Jenny also battled it to take fourth and third place – with Hector taking fifth and Mark
Aldridge finally remembering how to sail a Sprint 15 again and coming in sixth. Steve Healy had to retire due to a broken tiller
extension but was back out in time for Race 4.

Race 4 – Liam decided once was not enough and established a substantial lead which he maintained to the end of the race –
thereby proving how good you can get when you spend eight days a week sailing rather than working. Stuart picked up another
second, followed by George, Kevin Kirby, David and Gordon Deuce.

Aside from significant trolley support, Windsport International also supplied all returning sailors with Pimms and Lemonade. As
well as being very welcome, we all decided the garnish constituted one of our five a day, so obviously all good for the serious
athletes among us.

Following racing, the promise of free drink and cake saw a well attended and brief AGM which is exactly as it should be.
Formalities dispensed with, the fleet enjoyed a 40th Anniversary Drinks Reception to celebrate the past 40 years and plan for the
next 40 years – courtesy of GJW Direct Insurance – supporting the fleet for the second year. We then adjourned for dinner –
followed by a celebration Anniversary cake – ceremoniously cut by John Tuckwell from GJW Direct and Ed Dalton, our Chair.
And without entirely crashing an unconnected event being hosted by WPNSA, we enjoyed another beautiful sunset from the
balcony.

Sunday dawned with blazing sunshine and an even less promising wind forecast – but local expertise from WPNSA suggested we
would get four races in so that was the plan. Sunday was Supplier Race Day – supported by Windsport International, White
Formula, Hyde Sails, RWO and English Braid who collectively make up a Sprint 15.

With such support and such idyllic conditions (on land at least) – its hard not to be positive so the fleet set off out into the harbour,
trying not to think about the Force 3 at 7am in the morning followed by a forecast to drop to not very much at all.

And, to be fair, the first race was a light one ……

Race 5 – the fleet set off in light but sailable conditions. Standing on to the WPNSA end of the harbour provided slightly more
breeze and Jenny led round the first mark followed closely by Liam and Paul. With more tension than the conditions warranted,
Jenny managed to hold off Liam and Paul to take the win – with George in fourth and another fantastic fifth place for Tom Gurney.

Race 6 – Chris Tillyer decided to try a port hand flyer which he pulled off brilliantly to take a clear lead off the start. After a bundle
at the windward mark, filmed by Brian Phipps drone, port hand boats did not do well. But Chris led the way – pursued by Stuart in
what turned out to be a closely fought fight to the finish that most of the fleet spent more time watching, rather than concentrating
on their own race. Chris took the well deserved win, followed by Stuart, Mark, Liam and Gary.

Race 7 – Chris took another port flyer, and surprisingly, the fleet let him get away with it for a second time. Liam and Paul not far
behind for the first lap. On the second lap – Stuart and others took the left hand side of the course which paid off massively with
the build of the sea breeze. The race positions shuffled considerably as a result with Stuart taking the win, followed by Paul,
Gary, Peter Slater and Ed Dalton.

Race 8 – Jenny and Jan Elfring decided to join Chris for another port flyer although the rest of the fleet had had enough and slid
down the line making ARO Henry Wright mildly apprehensive about the pin end committee boat. Ducking a few boats proved
worthwhile as it got the pin end starters to the favourable winds on the right hand side of the course giving a good advantage.
Jenny led round the windward mark followed by Paul and David. Jenny held on to the lead to take the race win, followed by Paul,
David, Peter Slater and Ed Dalton. Jason Clarke’s mast had come down in race 7 – but he still managed to make it out in time to
finish race 8 in a credible mid-fleet place.

The fleet headed ashore and got glammed up (ish) for the Class Association Dinner celebrating our 40th Anniversary – supported
by Windsport International, Hyde Sails, White Formula, English Braid and RWO.

We were delighted to be joined by Ian Fraser, originator of it all – together with Pat Oxley, Jim Jeffrey, Cissy Dewhurst, Chris
Tillyer and Ed Dalton representing Association Chairs for the vast majority of our 40 year history.

Courtesy of Morrison Design Ltd and George Love (current Vice Chair) – a million wonderful memories were relived courtesy of
fantastic picture boards sharing events, sailors and boats – both past and present - who make up the fleet’s past and future. We
hope we can share these again at a future opportunity.
July 2018 Navigans 6

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

After dinner, Chris and Jenny (Events Secretaries), presented the spot prize awards supported by GJW Direct Insurance and
Fernhurst Books. Each winner was presented with a Fernhurst book and a 40th Anniversary commemorative glass trophy
produced by our very own Fenella Miller as follows:

Team Draycote – who fielded an impressive 9 competitors. But more importantly, as pond sailors had left their trolleys by the
waters edge, only to find them floating in the harbour when they came back from sailing. Collected by Owen Jones because none
of the rest were brave enough……

Steve Pell – another pond sailor who jumped off his boat too far off the beach and had to be rescued by Stuart Snell.

Tom Gurney – our youngest participant for putting in some stellar results and showing the rest of us the way round

Jason Clarke – another junior competitor, whose mast came down but was ashore, fixed and back out for a mid fleet finish in the
next race.

Daren Fitchew and Jim Bowie – for promptly forgetting directions to their accommodation on Friday night and dragging the Events
Assistant out of bed to go and retrieve them.

Aaron Kirby and Lucy Littlejohn - for being the closest helm and crew in the fleet

Nigel James - for sailing three whole days without capsizing – defying all known precedent but sadly depriving the RNLI of further
donations for this weekend at least.

Steve Healy - for breaking his tiller extension but still getting back and out for the next race, although needing to give everyone a
wide berth as he had his Sport mode extension instead

Chris Tillyer for daring to and pulling off three port hand flyers in a row. Even the RO was reluctantly impressed.

The fleet then enjoyed the wonderful music of James Tattington who managed to successfully entertain an audience aged 14 to
at least 84 (a musician we would highly recommend) and lots of conversation and reminiscences for the rest of the evening.

Monday dawned and it was another beautifully sunny day for the final race day sponsored by Kevin Kirby Ltd. Another light wind
day – we hoped we would be as lucky as the previous two days and get enough wind to finish the final race of the
Championships. So the amazing WPNSA local knowledge was consulted and it was agreed to wait until 12 noon to see if the
unlikely sea breeze would appear. In the boat park, degree level Maths were applied to work out the different permutations if the
race was to go ahead and who needed to be
placed where to beat someone else.

Sadly, the local predictions were correct and
the breeze did not materialise. Conscious of
those travelling – it was reluctantly decided
to cancel racing and quit whilst ahead after
eight great races.

The prizegiving, sponsored by Kevin Kirby
Ltd, was made even more special as
Olympic sailors Ben Saxton and Nikki
Boniface kindly took a break from their
training schedule to present the prizes.

To the slight bemusement of Ben and Nikki,
we moved through our very personal but
highly coveted special category prizes –
including Heavyweight (Nigel James), Over
50 (Mark Aldridge), Over 60 (George Love),
Over 70 (Stuart Snell) and Youth (Hector
Bunclark). The septuagenarians also
showed their mettle with Pete Richardson
and Stuart Snell winning the Pro-Am trophy. We were delighted to award Tom Gurney, our youngest competitor the Most
Improved trophy and his fellow youth sailors Aaron Kirby and Lucy Littlejohn won the Paul Smith Most Persistent Trophy and the 2
Up Cup. And our special 40th Anniversary category of oldest boat was easily won by Dave Rowe sailing sail no. 378.

We then moved into the less important prize categories culminating in Liam Thom – 3rd place and winner of Races 3 and 4,
Jenny Ball – 2nd place and winner of races 5 and 8 and finally winner of races 1, 2, 7 and 2018 40th Anniversary National
Champion - Stuart Snell.

Finally, the Team Trophy was presented to Marconi SC who had flooded the event with 11 competitors, nearly as many
supporters and many, many purple shirts.

All that was left was to wish Ben and Nikki all the very best in their sailing endeavours, to thank Nigel and Fiona Denchfield, Henry
White, all the WPNSA staff and volunteers for running a superb event and to reluctantly head home after an amazing weekend.

Start date 1st Sept 2017

Yacht Sabre, Antonio and Bob departed Marconi SC at 8 am on the 1st September bound for Barcelona via the French canal
system. The run down to Ramsgate was uneventful, motor sailing assisted occasionally by light winds. Since Sabre also
contained Antonio’s entire collection of worldly good and possessions, space was somewhat limited on board. We became aware
that Sable had a marked list to starboard and was somewhat stern heavy, the bows being rather higher in the water than the
boats designers ever envisaged. On arrival in Ramsgate the cargo was redistributed and the problem solved although space on
board was still limited. Setting sail for Calais the following morning in sunny conditions, light winds with little cloud cover.

Crossing the first separation zone presented little difficulty, as we approached the second zone a cloud appeared. Almost round a
kilometre in diameter, flat top and bottom and entirely jet black in colour. Although we had light winds at sea level the cloud was
moving so fast it easily overtook a Polish bulk coal carrier travelling towards the Atlantic. It looked like trouble and it certainly was.
As it passed ahead of the Polish ship wisp of cloud spiralled down from the leading edge. We knew what was coming; a Tornado.
The wind hit us immediately, accompanied a few minutes later by heavy salty rain. Sabre picked up speed dramatically, water
running along the deck, the boom skimming the waves.

Fortunately we only had the main sail up at the time, we had intended to go astern of the Polish coal carrier, however the increase
in speed meant we were now rapidly closing with it. An urgent change of course followed by an interesting ten minutes or so, then
it was all over back to blue sky’s as if nothing had ever happened fortunately no damage was sustained we set a new course for
Calais and continued on our way

Calais Marina is well equipped, secure and well organised, we received no attention what so ever from the authorities regarding
customs, fuel or passports. Antonio registered with the marina office and collected our permit to enter the canals (CIVINE) 100
Euros for 31 days

Mast removal is carried out by the staff at the Chandlery situated within the facility, the travel hoist appears to be the sa me model
as the one at Burnham Marina.

The chandlery are specific in their instructions before leaving the pontoon, detach the upper shrouds completely, slacken the
lowers, free up the split pins, motor under the travel hoist. Locate the strop under the spreaders, pull the split pins, remove any
bolts. Lay the mast on top of the boat, all over in under ten minutes, pay the 60 euros job done.

A French carpenter repairing a boat in the marina provided some second hand wood to support the mast free of charge, he was
clearly impressed with Antonio, it eventually turned out he was Irish from Dublin.

The weather was good as we left Calais, entering the Canal system it soon changed we had eight days and nights of rain, day
time temperatures rarely exceeding 8C, everything was either wet or very damp, as we headed south the weather began to slowly
improve but not fast enough by any means. It soon became obvious that most canal dwellers had either already headed south,
gone home, or were sheeting up their boats for winter. As far as leisure boats were concerned we were almost on our own.

The locks on the major canals are operated by VNF staff in control towers above the locks. The larger locks have lifting gates 20
metres high, controlled by a cable and winch system, resulting in large quantities of muddy canal water descending on our heads
as we entered and left.

Thankfully these locks have floating bollards to which the centre cleat is attached, the water flow is very controlled, these are
amongst the easiest to use. They are however very muddy attempting to climb the mud encrusted ladders 16 metres to the top, in
the event of an emergency would not be a good idea you would probably never make it.

On occasions we were in locks with a 100 metre long 1000 tonne barge. that’s two 50 metre barges bolted together end to end
and bound together with hawsers winched tight as banjo strings, the locks are only just wide enough to take these barges in many
cases the Bargees don’t even moor up using forward and reverse to maintain their position the main objective is not to clout the
gates.

On one occasion we were the only boat in the lock I estimate that it took around 12000 cubic metres of water to lift Sabre the 14
metres. Just as well it had been raining for days, it has been known for the canals to run low on water during the summer months,
not a problem we encountered, quite the opposite.

The Canal de Marne which includes the Canal de I’Aisne a la Marne, the Canal lateral a la Marne, and the Canal entre
Champagne et Bourgogne de la Marne. Is not as commercially important as it once was the railway and motorway which run
alongside the canal, in many places have taken the cargo’s off the barges.

Since the Marne’s 200 kilometres long encompassing 98 locks, 12 lifting bridges, and 6 tunnels the longest being 5 km. It’s easy
to see why with few exceptions leisure craft transiting north/ south or between river systems during the summer months constitute
the majority of the traffic.

Subsequently the VNF who run the canals are heavily into head count reduction, the locks have been automated, operated by a
remote controller supplied free of charge at the first lock in the series.

Most of the lock keepers cottages are now boarded up, built in the 1880’s they require a considerable amount of work to make
them habitable. A few have been sold off and updated no doubt at considerable cost to the new owners.

It’s now clear that we had little idea as to the challenges the Marne would present. Most of the leisure craft on these canals are
large steel boats entirely self contained with all the comforts of home, a cabin roof that the crew stand on to access the bollards
which can be five to six meters above water level and 20 metre’s apart.

At 27 ft Sabre was the smallest boat we encountered, fibre glass yachts are unsuitable for life on these Canals, far to light and to
easily damaged as we found out.

The Canal de Marne locks are very violent, the sluices operated hydraulically, are either fully open or closed, the initial surge of
water throws the boat around placing a considerable strain on the cleats, lines and crew until the flow subsides as the pressures
equalise.

Large round fenders 300 to 400mm in diameter four at least are required, the sort of fenders we use in north sea marina’s are
generally as good as useless. Mooring and centre cleats with good reinforcing are essential as are strong mooring lines, anything
less will be destroyed,

An athletic crew member capable of climbing and descending five to six meter high ladders, up to 19 times a day is a great
advantage, many of the locks are only 500 metre apart. Hardly time to make a cup of tea. It’s just as well Antonio’s has plenty of
energy, some days she must have climb well over 95 metres in total and carrying the mooring ropes, and then she had to climb
down again, no job for an OAP, I lost 14 lb in 26 days as it was.

Owing to the heavy rains the water overtops the lock gates filling the lock 2 cm from the top. The fender are doing nothing, the hull
rubbing against the concrete is all that’s restraining the boat. The same applies in the down locks we had to push the boat away
from the concrete quay heading often reinforced with rusting railway track in order to deploy the fenders.

Marinas as we know them are very few, many Canal side villages claim to have a marina with washing and toilet facilities and
shops, we even took virtual tours of some villages using Antonio’s smart phone. On arrival you find four bollards on the side of
the canal. The shops, café, and bars in the villages which once existed are with few exceptions now closed and boarded up,
some with for sale signs attached for good measure

Web sites have never been updated and are out of date, at one stage we ran out of food, a retired bargee living in a lockkeepers
cottage informed us that it was 30km to the nearest shops, he was good enough to supply a loaf of bread we even had a choice
white or brown.

Larger canal side towns which can be many days motoring apart are well supplied with shops. The supermarkets where they exist
are enormous and sell just about anything you could possibly want. A combination of Home Base, Tesco’s, B&Q and Doe’s Of
Ulting as well as normal domestic items, mowing machines and agricultural equipment can be supplied from stock, no wonder the
village shops can’t compete.

The strange thing is their never seem to be many customers, generally only one checkout open and no queue I can’t understand
it!

Fuel is generally not available canal side or from marinas but has to be obtained from filling stations often some distance away.
They are open 24/7 and are fully automatic (credit cards only) Fuel cans and a trolley to transport the cans are essential, we
averaged ten litres a day.

The Balesmes Tunnel on the Champagne to Burgundy section was the longest of the six we encountered, at almost five
kilometres long with control canals either side the total length is 10 km it’s a formidable undertaking.

From the check point at Vitry-le-Francois it’s a chain of 71 up stream locks to the tunnel under the Plateau De Langres.

The traffic through the tunnel is controlled from lock No1 Heulley-Cotton on the upstream side, it’s the last lock before the control
canal.

The controller ensures that the canal retains sufficient water to function, the system holds 160,000 cubic meters pumped from the
valley below.

Once through the tunnel the Les Batailles check point controls locks 1 to eight of the 43 locks on the down side.

The lock keepers in the control locks Numbers 1 either side issue verbal instruction regarding clearance to proceed, it’s one way
traffic through the control canals and the tunnel.

They also supply fenders in the form of bulks of timber with rope loops to replace the existing fenders, should the boats beam be
considered too wide for the canal. Getting jammed in the tunnel is not advised

The tunnel’s 8 metres wide with a 1.5 metre walkway along it’s length originally used by horses to pull the barges through in the
1880s now restricted to emergency use only.

Unfortunately the lighting in all these tunnels with one exception is not all it could be, the lights in the Balesmes Tunnel are
intended to switch on and off as you progress it’s length, the first section came on and failed to switch off the rest failed to light up,
probably because Sabre had too lower profile to trigger the sensor. There is another explanation the tunnels are shut down for
maintenance during the winter months and this was the end of the season after all.

We used a torch to light up the side of the tunnel, progress was slow we took 2 hours 45 minutes to cover the distance, the
maximum time allowed in the tunnel is three hours the whole operation take’s 4 to 5 hours including the control canals, As it was
we had the place to ourselves just as well.

This was the last of the five tunnels we encountered Several of which were built by criminals from French prisons most serving life
sentences, I don’t think they had much say in the matter, they did an excellent job, as I understand it the mortality rate was
extremely high.

On reaching Maxilly-sur-Soane the end of Marne you return the remote control by posting it into a large metal container which
reads the unit automatically communicating with the control centre, once all are satisfied the lock gates open to let you out into the
Saone.

The only marinas we encountered worthy of the name were Calais and St Jean de Losne which have excellent facilities. We
arrived at one marina on the Saone just after 6 pm on a Saturday only to find the sites facilities were locked and would stay closed
until Monday along with everything else, despite the marina being full of boats and crews.

Oh and by the way that will be eight euros for the night. Antonio sorted them out on the spot, we left the following morning for St
Jean de Losne, we never did pay the eight euros.

On reaching ST Jean de Losne some 50 km south of Dijon I handed over to Simon, heading for home on the train, leaving at
10.45 am I arrived in Chelmsford at 6pm that evening not bad at all.

Elsewhere in this issue of Navigans you will find the formal notification of the AGM. It has essential information about resolutions

FLOOD GATES
The Environment Agency requires that the flood gates must be kept closed between the 1st September and the 1st May unless
the hard is in use. Please shut the gates when you come ashore unless it is obvious that another member is using the hard. If in
doubt, shut the gates. They can always be opened again.

The gap in the seawall is vital to our club but it is a privilege not a right. We must be seen to be doing the right thing by keeping
the gates shut which as well as meeting EA requirements also protects our club and our neighbours.

PARKING IN CRUISER PARK
At this busy time of boat, boat hoist and trailer movements cars must not be left unattended in the cruiser park or the cruiser
parking area of the cat park. Owners of cars in the cruiser parks must be available at all times and ready to move them at sh ort
notice.

Do not leave your car unattended in the cruiser parks even if you are ‘only nipping out to the boat for 5 minutes’. There is a very
real risk of damage to your vehicle and inconvenience to others.

OOD DUTIES
You will find a list of OOD duties towards the back of this issue of Navigans. If you are on the list, as your OOD date approaches,
you will be sent a pack of OOD guidance and an OOD access card.

If you have an OOD duty but wish to exchange the day with another club member on the list you are welcome to do so. Please let
Keith White (OOD Coordinator) know so that he sends out information to the OODs at the correct time.

COMMUNICATION WITH MEMBERS (1)
Most communications from the club are now via email whether they are invoices, messages from club officials or routine sailing
updates. It is important that the club has the correct email address for you.

Emails from Marconi Sailing Club (including the membership database – Sailing Club Manager) can have a tendency to go into
recipients SPAM box which can mean that members miss out on club information. This has caused a lot of extra work for Mike
Turner when dealing with 2018 subscriptions and fees. The problem is being addressed but, in the meantime, please check your
SPAM regularly. If you are satisfied that a message is genuinely from the club please declare it as NOT SPAM; or whatever the
equivalent is on your system.

(If your system gives you the choice of not sending MSC emails into SPAM, that’s even better.)

COMMUNICATIONS WITH MEMBERS (2)
Under the new data regulations members have the choice as to whether or not to receive routine emails from the club. Members
now need to opt in. About half of the membership have not opted in and are missing out on club information which is a pity.

Those who have not opted in probably will not have received this Navigans. If any of your fellow members complain that they
have stopped receiving club information please ask them if they have opted in.

The new data regulations give people more control over their personal data but it does mean that they have to be proactive to
ensure that they receive wanted messages.

The two items above on COMMUNICATIONS WITH MEMBERS have been written by a layman but I’m sure that members will get
the general idea.

These items have been repeated from the July Navigans because the message is important.

ECPR 2018 Report
The 2018 East Coast Piers Race weekend was another success with 86 boats registering to take on the challenge of long
distance racing.

The East Coast Piers Race is a weekend of sailing held at Marconi Sailing Club in Essex in aid of the Cirdan Sailing Trust and
Essex Air Ambulance, all money raised from the weekend goes to support these charities in what they do.

This year we were proud to also be Allen Endurance event, part of the 3 event series.

With free on site camping available from Friday through to Monday many competitors arrived on Friday to take advantage of the
glorious sunshine and to get their boats set up early.

Mighty Oak Brewery very kindly donated 7 firkins of beer (over 500 pints) of beer to the event with all beer being sold at £2 a pint
with all the money going to charity. Obviously this proved to be very popular and visitors to the bar made a fair dent in the beer
supplies on Friday night.

When Saturday morning arrived there was a light breeze coming from the East but it was building all morning. The race briefin g
took place at midday with the first race due to start at 1pm. The wind direction was perfect for sailing up and down the river so the
race officer set a course which went to Thirslet Spit mark and then back past Marconi SC to an inflatable.

The first race was more popular than the second, mainly due to a game of football which was showing in the bar.

The second race was a little more testing with slightly less wind on the race course but the approach of running average laps
helped out the slower dinghies who didn’t have to go as far as the big catamarans.

Overall it was David Annan in his Musto Skiff who took the dinghy win and Grant Piggott and Will Smith who won the catamaran
racing.

The race briefing for Sunday is always held on Saturday evening due to the early start of Sundays racing. The briefing kicked off
at 6pm with a full marquee of competitors keen to understand the 3 race courses available.

To cater for dinghies from a PY of 1030 or faster and foiling catamarans the 3 race courses are 48 miles, 27 miles and 13 miles.

The end of the briefing was rudely interrupted by a charcoal covered gentleman shouting THE BBQ IS READY!

Following the BBQ we once again had a the popular Monkies Wedding band who did a great job of entertaining the crowds while
they slowly worked their way through the Might Oak beers.

The early call on Sunday morning came at 7am to get competitors up and ready for the planned 9.30am start. Due to the long
distances of the races we ask competitors to take certain safety equipment with them and each boat is checked through the gate
in the sea wall to ensure everything is present and correct.

There was no breeze very early but it was teasing the race officer with the sponsors flags starting to move on shore. He decided
on a postponement of 45 minutes before we could get the races underway, it was tough keeping the competitors from crossing
over the line with the tide but with a bit of rib support they were dragged back and all started the ECPR as planned.

At this point the race committee knew there was 10 knots of breeze at Walton and that it was building.

The Colne Point race started 15 minutes later and was the race with the most sailors, this race is open to fast dinghies and
catamarans and the 27 miles proves more popular than the 48 mile course.

Next to start was the Bradwell Race – this was introduced a few years ago to cater for more dinghies and the PY was adjusted to
allow boats of 1030 or faster to attend. This year we were pleased to see a 29er and Contender taking part in the shorter course.

Due to the wind conditions and the time the course was taking the ECPR and Bradwell courses were shortened. The ECPR
turned at Clacton Pier and the Bradwell Race sailors didn’t do the additional dog leg back up river.

In the East Coast Piers race it was John Tuckwell and his crew John who took the line honours award. Mark Mawditt and his crew
Tiffany took line honours in the Colne Point Race. For Bradwell it was the 29er sailed by Sophie Johnson and Dylan who came
through the line first.

OVERALL WINNERS:
ECPR – Simon Northrop and Caleb Cooper sailing an F18
Colne Point Race for Cats – Rob Forrester sailing a Shadow
Colne Point Race for Dinghies – David Annan sailing a Musto Skiff

With Sail Racer supporting us with GPS tracking and with the support of Allen we were able to award some additional prizes

Anthony, a local Marconi sailor won the award for Best Display of an Allen Sticker, keep an eye on the ECPR Facebook page to

Prizes were then awarded for the fastest speeds on the courses and the fastest on corrected time.

A raffle is also held over the weekend with this years prize being a summer clothing package from Zhik worth over £500. This year

Topper NS1 at Marconi SC a Remarkable Success

The weekend of September 8th & 9th saw the first of the International Topper Class Association National Series Events for the
2018-19 season take place at Marconi SC. This was the first time a Topper National Series Event has been held at Marconi SC
and what an event it was.

The class was out in full force with 155 boats registered to take part in the event. For many this was the first real experience of big
fleet sailing at a truly tidal location this provided an extra challenge for the fleet which most seemed to handle without any great
drama.

It must be said that all at MSC where mightily impressed by the Topper Class Associations event machine, very organised and
very positive – this made for a very good event weekend. The weather also played ball with mostly sunshine a decent breeze, this
helped to make the weekend very enjoyable for the sailors who seemed to be having a very good time indeed.

The only thing more impressive than the ICTA event machine was the sailors themselves, brilliant on and off of the water. The
race officer remarked that being thanked by large numbers of the sailors as they crossed the line to return home after the days
racing made an extremely pleasant end to to two great days of sailing and was very much appreciated.

The recently finished Bridge Deck development was remarked upon as being one of the best facilities they have ever seen for
visibility of the sailing area and radio communications. The large clear hard was also seen as being one of the best the well
travelled fleet has enjoyed, if possibly a bit lumpy. The large amount of space was also enjoyed particularly as it is mostly grassed
providing a boat friendly rigging surface.

The sight of so many Toppers at Marconi was inspiring – perhaps even inspiring enough to be the start of more things Topper at
Marconi SC.

Helm of the Year 2018
The annual Helm of the Year event took place on Saturday 22nd September. The winningest helms from each fleet (based on
results in the Spring and Summer racing series) represent their fleet in a closely fought sailing regatta in Picos. The event takes
place over seven races, with competitors swapping boats each time to ensure no undue advantage/disadvantage from the boats.
The goal is to see off the competition and become Helm of the Year. Serious stuff.

Seven competitors took part – Jason Clarke (Cadets), Julie Spencer (Slow H’Cap Fleet), John Burgoyne (H’Cap fleet), Jenny Ball
(Sprint 15), Steve Thomas (Medium Cat), Will Harrison (Fast Cat), Ian Ivermee (Cruiser).

Nigel James was Race Officer, assisted by Jon Pearse and set a course off the club with a committee boat start and finish.
Jason took an early lead in Race 1, closely followed by Jenny and John. Jenny managed to get inside Jason at the end of lap
one and just about held off Jason and Jon to take the first win. Will Harrison led the start of Race 2 with Jenny, Jason and John

hard on his heels but he held his nerve and took the win. In Race 3, Jenny forgot that Pico’s don’t get the start line as quick as a

Important notice to members
The following notice was issued to members by email on 18 th December 2018, Ed.

Routine testing of our water system this week has detected some growth of Legionella bacteria within the disabled showers.

There have been no cases of Legionnaires’ Disease reported.

MSC wishes to be completely transparent with our members.

For information:

Legionnaires’ is a very rare but serious disease caused by inhalation of contaminated water

Symptoms appear within 2-10 days of exposure, with symptoms similar to pneumonia (fever, cough, shortness of breath)

Those most at risk are the elderly, people with compromised immune systems or chronic lung disease

If you have used the disabled showers and are at all concerned please consult with your GP

What are we doing to address the issue?

The disabled showers & toilets have been closed

A specialist company with expertise in removing the bacteria will decontaminate the affected systems this week

We will take further samples after the decontamination to confirm clearance of the bacteria from the whole site

We will revisit our risk assessment for the prevention of Legionella at MSC and put in place further preventative measures to
mitigate against the risk of future contamination

Thank you for your understanding.

If you have any concerns please feel free to contact Bryan Spencer either by using commodore@marconi-sc.org.uk or by phone
.

CRUISER MOORING CHANGES 2019
We are in the middle of the changes for this year – along the lines outlined at the cruiser AGM whereby we are trying to get the
bigger boats into A row and group where possible into like displacement types. This is not completely possible but this is our best
shot. Normally we would notify you all individually of changes to your positions but because of the volume of changes this would
be a lot of phone calls.

You will still receive the final version as part of your membership pack.

Please take the time to read carefully the information below – it contains information you will need for this season.

THREE YEAR CYCLE OF MOORING LIFTING AND RELAYING
In the season prior to our current system of lifting and relaying all deep water moorings, thirteen boats went adrift. This was clearly
unacceptable so the decision was taken to lift and then inspect moorings annually, before laying. We are now in the position that
breakaways are rare, mainly from chafe above the buoy. The current system involves a lot of work and is weather dependant,
which can result in late laying and retrieval. It is also very difficult to set up alternative dates to get back on track.

For several years now the mooring subcommittee have been experimenting with leaving the moorings down for longer periods.
The visitor’s mooring which had been down for fifteen years, with cathodic protection on the scope, was retrieved this year. On
inspection the main ground chain had deteriorated very little. I have inspected the mooring down to the centre at the beginning of
every season and have had to replace the scope twice. This was done easily from the barge. The brand new mooring for the Tony
B, which has a rope riser, has been down two winters and three summers. When it was retrieved at the end of this season there
was again very little wear. Chafe was evident on the rope riser but this can be guarded against. If you order a new rope riser from
EYE make sure that they fit anti chafe protection before they splice in the hard eye.

The main problem we now have is with moorings that drag. This is random and happens if the anchor doesn’t set at laying. Once
the mooring has been laid for some time and the anchors set they tend to stay there. At the moment we are lifting secure
moorings with the risk of relaying and then dragging the following season.

The mooring subcommittee have therefore decided that we should adopt a three year cycle for lifting and laying our moorings
which is a common system in commercial moorings.

For us it will mean that for 2019 season moorings in C row and the end of D row that use the barge will be laid with the aim of
leaving them in situ for three years. They will receive an inspection down to the centre from the barge at the beginning of each
season. The mooring owner will be on the barge for this and any remedial work will be carried out.

This will apply to B row moorings from 2020 season then A row from 2021 and at the end of that season C row and Deep water D
will be retrieved.

For this to work the standard of the mooring equipment will need to have minimum wear at the point of laying. All shackles will
need to be welded and ideally cathodic protection provided. To assist mooring owners the mooring inspection will take place one
week earlier than normal and we will provide a welding facility with welder in attendance. Dates for this will be in the Cruiser
Handbook as usual.

Check your mooring early now is not too soon!!! If you need new chain or shackles let Bob know as soon as possible.

There will be several logistical problems to overcome but with cooperation and tolerance this should be achievable. But at the end
of three years we will be in the position of only needing to lift and relay one row of moorings a year and the moorings left in will be
more secure.

4.Review of 2018 cruises – Robin Good

, 1st of the year was fitting out supper, a nice start to the season. 47 people turned up. An alternative caterer was used as Jenny
couldn’t do the date, resulting in the price being a bit higher. Mayday holiday cruise 3 boats to Brightlinsea, lovely warm a nd
sunny.

Late May bank holiday tides dictated off to Harwich. Only 2 Marconi boats and some visitor boats. It was a busy period for
Harwich and we couldn’t get pre-booked in anywhere without going on swinging moorings or anchoring. Subsequent drop-outs
meant we eventually booked into Lavington easily. It was very breezy but had a good sail up the Wallet. Recommend the Ship for
the walk and meal.

Mid June off to France with 5 Marconi boats heading initially to Ramsgate. Weather forecast not favourable but decision m ade to
go. 1 boat dropped out in the morning but a bumpy trip to Calais for the rest. 2 hours from Calais onto Gravelines. Nice and quiet
for families and holidays. The drop out by jow had caught us up. Weather prevented from going onto Dunkirk so took bus ride to
Dunkirk instead which was pretty eye-opening. Visited the war museum and took the train back to Gravelines. Next day trip home
from Gravelines was more pleasant. Last night at Ramsgate then home.

Begininning July Heybridge Basin Regatta, 11 boats attended. Good weather and Bar-B-Q. Co-incided with their regatta weekend
luckily. Lots going on.

Mid July East Coast 2 weeks holiday strong N’thly winds at the start meant 2 night in Lavington or Shotley. Headed to Southwold
as planned with huge electrical storm following behind us. Strong tides going into harbour but all safely arrived.15 boats in
Southwold. One night the Commodore opened the sailing club for us to enjoy their hospitality and a Bar-B-Q behind the

General report same as last year but going forward some amendment to the way we do things. Since taking over the mooring
matrix hasn’t been changed regarding the spacing between moorings and boats are getting bigger. Propose to increase the

Also been looking at 3 year cycling the moorings. At the moment we lift and relay everything every year, on retrieval this year we
have had problems with the hydraulic system and are about 10 moorings behind schedule. More sessions will have to be included
and very weather dependant. To try and reduce our work in future from next spring is to relay C row and leave in for 3 years, at
end of season leave C row and lift B then following year relay B row and leave for 3 years and then A row would follow the sa me.
So every year taking out just one row of moorings rather than all rows. When the mooring has been down for 12 months we will lift
onto the centre of the barge for the owner to come and inspect and together look if any new chain needed. We haven’t had any
mooring gear failures for several years now, the gear is getting better. We will do the inspection for C row next spring a week
early. This will formalised in some sort of report. Several areas logistically we need to address, changing boat, moving or n eeding
to retrieve/relay due to deterioration. We will pick the riser up down to the ground chain, inspect the bit of ground chain we can
see and full inspection on the risers/buoys. At this point owners may want to take strops off for the winter. Still set up 3 sessions
but instead of trying to get 20 moorings up or more, we will only be scheduled to lift about 10 on the tide so the team is under less
pressure. Any shackles would be replaced on the water, if the whole riser needed replacing we would prep it ashore and take it
out and attach it on the water. The ground anchors are the responsibility of the owners and we wouldn’t be laying any that has
any doubt on the condition. There are anchors that have been down 40 years but they do have a shelf life. Retrieval of moorin g
buoys and putting a temporary rope on the riser causes problems as they are more vulnerable to being lost and having to be
recovered by a grapple. You can’t guarantee you get in the middle and could hook into the wrong mooring. Most problems used to
be with the shackles but changing the source that problem has gone away over the last few years. Recommendations of new
chain or new rope if leaving in for 3 years. New chain definitely but rope does not deteriorate so much other than chafing. If you

2018 Commodore’s Report to the AGM
Michaela Dowley
25th November 2018

Good morning and welcome all to the 2018 Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting. This report will
comment on the main business of the Board and Management Committee over the past season.

Responsibility for the Club rests with the Board of Directors, and for the previous year has comprised
these six people:

Murray Bates - Vice Commodore looking after premises and site
Peter Clayton - Vice Commodore with responsibility for moorings and equipment
Pat Shaw - Rear Commodore for sailing
Liz Kirby - Rear Commodore for events
Sue Shenton - Treasurer
Myself, Michaela Dowley - as Commodore I have been managing director and chair

Ray Ball has yet again served as company secretary, providing invaluable support to committees and
shouldering the bulk of the administrative burden of the Club.

I can report that the Board and management committee have met regularly since the last AGM and I
would like again to extend thanks to all those who take the time to serve on the main and various sub
committees.

It has been another exceptionally busy year for us both in terms of activities, events and also in projects
and developments around the Club. My final report as Commodore will focus on those successes and set
out our plans for the coming year.

I am very pleased to report that our current membership stands at 445. This compares to around 436 in
2017 and 430 in 2016. We are now a little unsure of the accuracy of the 2016-2017 figures so in fact we
think this is an even bigger increase that it seems. At our most recent management meeting no-one round
the table could remember a time where membership levels were this high. This is a true achievement at a
time where sailing clubs all around the country are struggling to maintain their membership levels. I went
to a club conference yesterday where some clubs were discussing their minimum membership number
required to stay afloat. This increase in membership hasn’t happened by chance and is thanks to our
continual drive to move forwards within Marconi. From encouraging younger members onto our
committees to running exceptional open days and building our training centre to name a few examples.

Without stealing all the material from the sailing secretary’s report, some of our on the water highlights
include: regular sail training, the East Coast Piers Race in July, Cadet week in August, our first RYA
dinghy training courses being delivered, Topper National Series Event in September, Marconi leg of the
Harkers yard gig racing in October, the Marconi keelboat championship held at Queen Mary in October
and the massive increase in use of our club kayaks and stand up paddle boards. Everywhere we look
there have been more and more opportunities for members to get out on the water.

I would like to say a couple of specific thank yous. First to Clive Shenton, who has been Race Chairman of
the East Coast Piers Race for the past 14 years. Clive, along with the ECPR committee have worked
tirelessly over the years to keep this event running. It continues to be an internationally recognised event
with competitor numbers increasing where many similar events are being scaled down and even
cancelled. This is a testament to Clive’s commitment to the race and our charities, the Cirdan Sailing Trust

and Essex Air Ambulance whom we continue to support. Clive has been a driving force behind the fairly

aside after over a decade of involvement in running the galley. We said a big thank you to Tina at her last
event a few weeks ago. I think we can all agree that no one felt unwelcome in our galley during her
tenure.

2019
Although I am stepping down as Commodore at this AGM, I would like to take the opportunity to talk to
you about our plans for 2019, as these have been in discussion for quite some time. After a few years of
experiencing a very cramped social space in the Mamgu bar, we have taken the decision to knock through
downstairs to expand the bar area by at least the same size again. The plan is to create a multi-purpose
room for both training and social use, as usually these two activities do not take place at the same time.
On the back of a members’ survey carried out a few years ago, we have also decided to add a veranda to
the northern aspect of the clubhouse, overlooking the river. This is something that we know the
membership have been asking for and we are excited about this addition to the club’s premises. This
project is in the early stages but we plan to carry out works during 2019. We also hope to expand our fleet
of keelboats and will be looking towards grant funding and sponsorship opportunities to help finance these
purchases.

We also know that we cannot be complacent with our membership numbers and will continue to drive
forward with new initiatives that we believe will make our Club more attractive to new members. We will
also work hard to make sure we retain members. We have created a new role on the management
committee of ‘new members liaison’ as we are aware that there has been a gap in this area - it’s really
important that we keep new members engaged and integrate them into club life. Liz Kirby and the publicity
team will also be undertaking a communications review to see how we currently communicate information
to our members and what changes we need to make to ensure this is effective in the changing
environment.

Finally, I would just like to reflect on my 9-year term on the Board, the past 5 serving as Commodore.
Starting at the beginning. I was a fresh faced 23/24-year-old just back from a gap year traveling round the
world having completed a degree in Biochemistry the year before, when I took a surprise call from Simon
Elwell. All I can say is that flattery will get you everywhere. As Commodore at the time, Simon had already
managed to recruit some of my ‘millennial’ friends onto the management committee as a webmaster and
social secretary and to be honest, I felt a bit left out. Simon told me there was a vacancy for Rear
Commodore on the Board and knowing I was looking for a job, he said with great authority that it would be
an excellent addition to my CV and I was just the type of person he was looking for. I had a lot of respect
for Simon and although the world of biochemistry and helping to run a sailing club are miles apart, I did as
he suggested and joined the Board. 9 years later (thanks Simon) and the club is almost unrecognisable,
yet is still the same.

Providing stability have been people such as Murray and Peter on the Board and the likes of Simon, Clive,
Pat and Mike on the main committee, making sure we never strayed from the real ethos of our much-loved
club. As a team we have achieved a huge amount over the past 5-10 years. We are no longer a cruiser
club and dinghy club operating separately, but I think we are truly getting towards being fully integrated.

We have an RYA training centre, our own in-house sail training programme, new, modern club boats, a
vibrant social scene, kayaks, paddleboards, a rowing gig, national recognition for our new initiatives in
sailing and a growing membership. Yet we have also retained our friendly, welcoming atmosphere, which
is so important to what this club is. We also have an abundance of volunteers and thanks to Simon’s
vision a decade ago, we are seeing those ‘young members’ taking the club forward and we have
continued to do that recently, creating more new roles for younger members to fill on our main
committees. This is vital to secure the future of the club and its management.

I went to the RYA East region club conference yesterday, with 50 Clubs in attendance. I was asked to
present Marconi as a case study in two sessions - the benefits of being an RYA training centre and the
effects of a diverse committee. During this conference I was approached by a number of clubs, all within

our use of social media, how we generated interest in keelboats and how we have managed to make sure

2018 Sailing Secretary’s Report to the Agm
Hi all,

Well another year has passed and another season is over as I find myself once again in front of you to deliver my report as Sailing
Secretary although sadly this will be my last one, for a while at least, I promise nothing!

It’s been a fantastic year of sailing once again and it is now my pleasure to share with you what has been going on outside of your
own experiences.

There have been fewer changes this year but some of those changes have of course not been without controversy. We like to
make sure that everyone is still awake and as such reversed the order of starts on Sunday dinghy racing. Mostly so that we stood
a chance of being on time for the start but also it meant that there was less crossover between the fleets.

The dinghy and cat racing fleets are still well supported and the extended season has meant that we’ve all had some good racing.
The Solo fleet is still quite strong and the Sprint 15 fleet continues to grow, the medium cat fleet has less Dart 18s out racing
sadly. The Sprint 15’s haven’t let the lack of organised racing at MSC stop them sailing and have been seen sailing down river to
join in the polar series at Stone Sailing club, it’s great to see inter club collaboration.

This year’s Open Day was seamlessly carried out by Liz and seemed to be even more successful than ever. There were lots of
new sailors that came along on that day. Many new members took part in Cadet Week and have joined us regularly for our Sail
Training days. These have also seen record numbers attending this season, with the adults joining in as well; all these are good
signs for the future.

The adult learners, or Turtles as they are known, these are a rapidly expanding group of adults who are showing great
enthusiasm for learning to sail. They are so enthusiastic that there’s talk of them honing their skills during the winter months. We
have had many graduates of this programme throughout the years and it really looks like there is a bright future for them, and the
club going forward.

The Training centre side of things continues to progress. We have trained up yet more Powerboat drivers under Pat’s careful
tutelage and the dinghy courses were also a great success with many of the new members taking up these courses as
introductions to sailing. Many thanks should go to both Bob Collins, as Training centre principal and Jenny Miller, who has taken
over from Rhiannon Hitt as Chief Instructor, for running this aspect of club life.

The Cruiser sailing fleet have had a full season of trips, this year venturing across the North Sea before the borders come down!
Thankfully they made it back in time to provide their invaluable help with the ECPR as Mother Boats keeping an eye on the Cats &
Dinghies as they race to Walton pier and back. There have also been the traditional rallies around the East Coast to Brightlingsea,
to Ipswich and beyond although I believe he’s looking for more to join him on Rob’s tours …. It should be noted that Rob has
gladly accepted Pete Clayton’s offer of organising the mother boats for the piers race and will this year be bringing this back under
his role as Cruiser fleet captain.

The Cruiser Racing fleet have seen a buoyant year of racing in the BJRC championship, which has seen a good turn out from
Marconi boats with Monkey Business 2nd in the IRC championship and Blue Moon 3rd. The Autumn series was also well
supported and went to Blue Moon in a close fought battle with Monkey Business taking it by only one point in the last race. Ned
Kelly the club’s own cruiser, this year skippered by Lana, came home solidly mid fleet in 14th place of 28 starters.

The British Keelboat League or BKL for short, saw us again send a team to compete in the local qualifier in Burnham and put in a
sterling effort for a scratch team with very little experience sailing together.

As a result of the interest drawn by the BKL Peter Ward organised a Keelboat championship for the beginning of the season to
blow the cobwebs off. 12 teams headed to Queen Mary Reservoir in balmy April conditions but sadly the memo of wind didn’t
make it and instead we sat waiting for the sea breeze to kick in. It was a long wait! Thankfully it was rescheduled and instead took
place in the polar opposite conditions, good wind but pouring rain! It was really close racing and very little separated the teams at
the front, it came right down to the wire with the youthful team of Nickalls and Jacks taking it. It was great to see so many people
from different parts of the club competing against each other.

There have been a number of opens held at the club this year, with Sprint 15’s visiting in April, the Larks in May and the bi g one
the Toppers visiting in September for the first of their National series events. 148 sailors descended on us of which a couple of
MSC members also competed. It was a great event generating income and positive publicity for the club.

Of course we also had the East Coast Piers Race, another good year with great conditions for Saturday but Sunday was a little
light for the start which meant that a lot of competitors had to be towed to the start line. But thankfully it filled in towards the end to
create a great race.

Bart’s Bash sadly had to be cancelled this year, and it’s the last time I trust a long range forecast of 2 days. Pretty much as soon
as the joint decision to cancel happened the forecast improved, the 60 Mph winds disappeared and were replaced with pouring
rain. So although it wouldn’t have been a particularly pleasant race it would have been manageable, ho hum hindsight is a
wonderful thing.

Colin Wardell’s dinghy cruises are still a popular feature of the sailing calendar. They’ve been on voyages from the club to any
pub that is willing to serve them, they had to go as far afield as the West Solent this year! The quest to find the perfect pint
continues and they will again be out next weekend when the cruiser members are lifting their moorings. Hardy Souls!

STONE GIG RACE – SUNDAY 17TH FEB
Despite a worrying forecast of S.F4-6 winds, we awoke to a very still and misty morning which had cleared to blue skies and a
light southerly breeze by the time we wheeled Elettra out of the container.

We launched at Marconi and the Men’s crew rowed up against the tide to Stone to make it easy for us.

March 2019 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

We had only 3 Ladies but managed to borrow another crew from Stour Sailing
Club to complete our team. The ladies were set a very long 3 mile course , a short
leg towards Marconi, a long leg round Thirslet, and a long leg against the Ebb
back inside a mark to the finish.

I aimed for a great start but ended up nose over the line (30 second penalty),
although this did lead to an exciting first leg and a fight for water round the first
mark. Unfortunately Clare pulled her Achilles half way around the course although
didn’t tell us till after we finished (Get well soon Clare) after over 40 minutes on
the oars!

For the men’s, the course was shortened & we loaned Nigel to ‘Fly’ (as they were
suffering with Flu), and chose to start right inshore for some back – eddy help,
rowing between Scrubbing Posts and the shore, this had us right up the front of
the line although others had ‘water’ on us and we had to slot in to the fighting pack at the first mark, we kept going well and ended
up 10th , just ahead of Nigel in ‘Fly’

On the mixed – the short course stayed, and we now had only 1 lady fit to row, so
managed to borrow another from Stour. Again Elettra had a competitive start and
Larry squeezed us in to the melee to fight around the first mark, with other’s oars in
our faces and someone bumping in to our tiller, Larry said he closed his eyes as we
rounded the first mark. Elettra finished 11th

tide again!)

Fortunately there were a couple of pictures of the men’s start posted by other clubs,

properly so I’m afraid the only action shot is pretty poor. There was some Drone

fill our ladies team!

WILDLIFE AT STANSGATE – ADDERS
We share our site at Stansgate with a variety of wildlife. Indeed, it is their home whereas we only pop in from time to time.

As the weather warms up adders will be coming out of hibernation and will be on the move. They will mind their own business as
long as they are left alone.

Be aware for example when reaching under boats or when walking in long grass where they may be basking. The younger
members of your party should be warned.

WILDLIFE AT STANSGATE – RATS
For your own protection against being bitten be very careful when moving anything that could be hiding a rat’s nest. Obvious
things are upturned boats, boats themselves if hatch covers have been left off, boat covers, piles of wood, trailers and anywhere
else that might form a cosy nesting place for rodents. Warn your family, particularly younger members, who may move a boat
without thinking.

As well as the risk of being bitten the other danger when rats have been near standing water (puddles on boat covers or on the
ground for example) is Well’s Disease. Well’s Disease is caused by rats’ urine in water. (There is a lot of information about Well’s
Disease online.)

Where there is water that has a high risk of rat infestation take great care not to ingest the water or let any wounds come into
contact with it.

The most effective way to protect yourself from Weil's disease is to avoid contact with infected water. However, there are steps
you can take to lower your risk of infection.

if you have cuts do not allow them to be submerged in the water;

never swallow water unsuitable for drinking;

wash all equipment and clothing in clean water;

clothing that can survive bleaching should be disinfected or bleached to kill the bacteria;

if you have a wound always use clean fresh water to clean wounds as soon as possible

Fleet News
= 5 hile Sprint 15
SPRINT 15 TRAVELLER TROPHY OPEN MEETING @ MSC – 6TH – 7TH APRIL
22 competitors took part in the first 2019 Sprint 15 Summer TT at Marconi SC on 6th and 7th April. We were also pleased to
welcome back Nigel and Fiona Denchfield as guest Races Officers for the event.

June 2019 Navigans 10

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Saturday dawned with a decent breeze, albeit with very murky weather conditions – but very welcome after the very strong winds
experienced this winter.

With the tide running against us – we were in for a weekend of clear starts. Race 1 got underway at a good pace with half the
fleet tacking into the bay to find the slacker tide – and the other half opting to go up the lay line in stronger tide, but with more
constant wind. Paul Grattage headed inshore first and although he had to put in an extra two tacks, rounded the windward mark
first. Jenny Ball and Liam Thom tacked when they ran out of water and fortunately, this turned out to be a good line to clear the
mark. Others who stood on further in the bay found the breeze got a bit softer whilst those who had gone up the middle found
they were putting in extra tacks to clear the mark against the tide – so there was all to play for on the upwind legs, whilst the
downwind leg were more straightforward. Paul held his lead to win, with Jenny second, Liam third and David Ball in fourth in a
pattern that would repeat itself. Jon Pearse, Jim Bowie and Gordon Deuce were close behind.

Race 2 got away swiftly with a similar pattern on the upwind leg. By the second lap, the front runners were opting to stay closer to
the lay line, avoiding the softer winds right inshore and taking advantage of a slight lift off the shore about ten boat lengths from
the windward mark. At the end of Race 2 Paul took first place, with Jenny second, Liam third and David fourth – followed by Jim,
Steve Healy and Jon.

There was then a slight pause to re-lay the windward mark for Race 3, during which Geoff Tindale kept everyone entertained by
capsizing and getting his mast stuck in the mud.

Race 3 was the legendary long distance race – a figure of eight course around Osea and Northey Islands. Following a short
windward leg, the fleet turned at the mark and started the fetch up towards Maldon. The tide had started to turn so some of the
fleet headed closer to the island but experienced more fickle wind so those who had stayed clear of the lee of the island fared
better. By the end of Osea Island, Paul had created a solid lead which proved unassailable for the rest of the race. Behind him
were Liam, David, Simon Hare, Gordon in the middle with Jenny, Jason Clarke and Kevin Kirby closer to shore.

The fleet then turned and ran down the back of Northey Island - Liam and Simon rounded the far end of the island and crossed
the causeway behind Paul and followed by Jenny, David, Gordon and Steve Healy. A little further back, some fleet members got
a bit brave about which side they were going to leave the Causeway markers. Andy Perks rudders bumped the causeway – and
everyone around him laughed until theirs did the same. Keith Chidwick later complained Jenny’s briefing said they would
definitely clear the causeway – until it was pointed out to him she meant if you aimed at the bit that actually had water over it.

The breeze had filled in nicely and was now against the tide, so conditions were a bit more choppy. The fleet stood on from the
end of Northey Island and then cut across the channel to the other side of Osea Island – everyone carefully monitoring how
others were faring on their different lay lines. Jenny tacked earlier at the end of Osea island, cutting the corner and catching up
with Liam but with David, Steve and Gordon were catching up further out in the stronger tide and wind. Jenny put in another
tack back out into the channel and just did enough to get ahead of Liam who followed in close pursuit all the way to the finish line.
June 2019 Navigans 11

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

The final result was – you guessed it – Paul first, Jenny second, Liam third, David fourth with Gordon, Steve and Jim behind.
Despite the race lasting over an hour, the fleet saw some remarkably close finishes.

The fleet waved goodbye to Abbie Clarke, Geoff Tindale and Rob Wilson who sailed back to their neighbouring home club at
Stone and then headed in for a well deserved dinner with plenty of good racing to talk about and looking at the more promising
wind forecast for Sunday morning which was finally showing a bit more than 2 knots.

On Sunday, there was indeed a decent breeze, albeit another grey and murky day. The Race team started laying the course but
the wind unexpectedly died to nothing and with the typical Blackwater tide, the Race Officer decided to delay the start of the race
and move the race course further out of the main channel. This proved to be wise as the wind filled back in again but from a
slightly different direction which allowed the course to be set accordingly although a final shift at a minute to go made for an
interesting start. A group of the fleet had opted for a port hand start whilst others started on starboard and then tacked off. The
rain had caused everyone’s tell tales to stick to the sail making it tricky to find good boat speed in a light breeze against the tide.
Jenny tacked first for the mark but it became clear she was not going to make it with the tide so the rest of the fleet stood on
further. In the meantime, Steve Healy had headed straight up the middle of the river, tacked round the mark into a clear lead.
Behind him, only David cleared the mark to go into a solid second place whilst even those who had stood on had to tack back one
or more times and/or hit the mark. Paul, Liam, Jenny, Aaron Kirby, Jim, Kevin and Jon rounded in a bunch, although there were a
few penalty turns to be done on the way to mark 2. Paul, Liam and Jenny set off in pursuit of Steve and David. On the
penultimate lap, Liam and Jenny got a better breeze by standing further out. David tacked out to join them whilst Paul stood on –
which allowed Liam and Jenny to move into second and third place with David and Paul fighting out a photo finish. But a great win
for Steve. Newcomer, Abbie Clarke also fared well in the lighter breeze putting in an impressive 15th place behind fellow Stone
sailor Rob Wilson and Shanklin’s Yvonne Pike – both of whom are also relative newcomers to the Sprint 15.

The Race Officer re-set the course to take account of the new wind direction for Race 5 and again the fleet opted for a mixture of
port and starboard starts. Gordon, Jon and Jason got great starts at the pin end and with the windward mark now on the far side
of the channel, off the Osea shore, the fleet split significantly up the beat. Those who took the left hand side of the course fared
better over the tide but this was offset by coming into the mark on port and having to duck the incoming boats on starboard.
However, some of those coming in on starboard had misjudged the tide and either had to double tack or risk bumping into the
mark. Gordon took the early lead but the upwind legs became the defining elements of Race 5 with places changing each lap
and at least three different leaders during the course of the race. On the final upwind leg, a lift enabled Jenny to get inside of
Liam and Gordon and get to the mark on starboard as Paul came in on port. Jenny just about held on to take the race win with
Paul second, Gordon third, Liam fourth and Steve fifth.

The fleet headed home after a great weekend of sailing! Big thanks go to the Race Officers, Race Committee and Support boat
crews for setting up and delivering five great races in conditions that were cold, and at times, wet!

Congratulations to:

Abbie Clarke – winner of the New Comer Award – her first TT having only moved from a Topper to a Sprint 15 late last season!

Jason Clarke – Youth winner and 11th placed overall

Aaron Kirby – winner of the Chairman’s Award for driving over 6 and half hours to attend the event (and then back again)

Handicap Fleet
'LARKONI' AT MSC

A small flock of larks descended on Marconi
SC for the annual Larkoni weekend, and as
usual received a terrific welcome and
magnificent hospitality from the Club. The
catering was first class, especially the
chocolate cake; it was worth the trip just for
that.

The early arrivals on Saturday were able to
examine the effects of several force 9
squalls on the River Blackwater and were
grateful not to be racing until Sunday.

The fleet launched on Sunday into the
forecast 10-12kt wind and prepared to do
battle with wind and tide running
perpendicularly to each other. Glenn Enkel
and Julie Bachelor shot off into the lead
chased by the Denchfield pairing. The
Enkel boat pulled away for a comfortable
win, which was to be the pattern for most
races. Worthy of note was the performance
of a very old Baker built Lark in the hands of club sailors Andy Perks and Sara Townsend.

Race 2 wasn't quite a repeat run. The wind decided to do its own thing and rose to 18-22kt, creating some interesting water
conditions for the run, especially where it crossed the main channel. Simon Cox crewed by 9 year old son George got into his
stride, and took second place behind the flying Enkel boat.

Race 3 began in similar wind, and whilst Enkel sailed away to secure 1st, Dave Russell and Clare Clarke found the go button and
for most of the race were ahead of the Denchfields. The final run proved to be Dave's undoing and some good use of the tide
allowed the Denchfields by. Race 4 was sailed in fewer breezes, but that didn't matter to the Enkel/Bachelor pairing, they picked
up their 4th win of the day.

Ashore, after a splendid roast dinner, the Larkies took part in a club social featuring a 80s quiz. We were hampered though by the
lack of questions about Lark sailors in the 1980s.

The final two races took place on Monday. Race 5 saw Enkel/Batchelor take a 5th win, chased home by the Coxes.

The final race saw great excitement at the start with 4 Larks all aiming at the same patch of water at the tide biased starboard end
of the line much to the amusement of the Cox boat that was clear of the ensuing carnage. The Denchfields were the recipients of
two Larks barging in from windward whilst the third baled out. We won't say whose fault it was, but the Enkel boat was the first of
the two to begin penalty turns. This allowed the Cox boat to take an early lead which much to young George's delight they held to
the finish.

Many thanks to Marconi for hosting a fun weekend that provided very different sailing conditions to the usual.

Nick Tovey
You may have heard by now that Nick Tovey sadly passed away on 16th March 2019 aged 82. His funeral was held at St
Andrews Church, Sandon, Chelmsford on 9th April and it was so nice to see a so many past and present members of Marconi
Sailing Club attend. Thank you all very much for coming long.

He was born and brought up in Surrey, Nr Guildford but came to Essex when he became an apprentice at Marconi
Communications in the late 50’s. He lived with his new wife Daphne in Bicknacre. Their first child Fenella was born the year after
they got married, then Peter a couple of years later. They later moved to Howe Green, Sandon where they lived for over 50 years.

As a child part of his family owned a holiday house on the beach at Tankerton, Whitstable (called “Kiora”) where they all spent
many happy summer holidays and this is where he learnt to sail. On our last visit to the area he related a story of helping to shunt
steam engines in the coal yard beside Whitstable Harbour.

As part of the Marconi Athletic and Social club there was a newly formed sailing section which he joined in 1959, picking up his
new boat, an Enterprise (sail number EK 2353) also called “Kiora” on the same day as his Wife and new daughter, who was 10
days old, had been discharged from hospital. So after a few hours interval Fenella was introduced to the sailing club alongside his
new boat. Daphne and Nick enjoyed many years of racing their Enterprise both at the club and at open meetings.

Nick was also very active in the running of the club being made Sailing Secretary in 1963 and 64. This was the time when the club
moved from the Barge “Mangu” at Heybridge to the current site at Stansgate in Steeple. He alongside his fellow committee
members were responsible for the original lay out of the new club site including setting up the Race box, the mete and the di nghy
park (now the cruiser park) and for the original laying out of the moorings, the foot prints of which remain today. He went on to
become the Rear Commodore in 1965 for 3 years, then again in 1972. He was Vice Commodore in 1966, then a Vice President
from 1970 to 1992. Nick and Daphne forged many longstanding friendships though their activities at the club.

June 2019 Navigans 15

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

By this time Nick has moved from Dinghies to Cruisers. His first cruiser was a Vivacity 20 called “Persephone” which he bought as
a kit and fitted out himself, He went on to own a Westerly Jouster ( 21 ft) “Janthena” which he and his family sailed to France,
Belgium and Holland in for 3 weeks. Nick, Daphne, Fenella and Peter spent many happy summers sailing up and down the East
coast on various different boats. There was one occasion coming back from Ramgate they had to cross the Thames estuary in
fog. Nick was able to navigate with very limited electronic equipment by taking echo sounding and managed to predict precisely
when the Boat in front of them (Vic Tate’s “ Snow Goose”) was going to go aground on Black Tail Spit, on the edge of the Maplin
Sands – she did! His great seamanship ultimately influenced the whole family in their own sailing careers.

In later years Nick sailed “Northey” a classic ‘South Coast One design’ yacht with his friend Ian, and I am sure there could be
many tales to be told there also!

Outside of sailing Nick enjoyed bell ringing, eventually becoming Tower Captain at Sandon Church, where he and Daphne were
very active in the Church community.

They also had a love of dogs and was introduced to the Saluki breed by a friend of Daphne’s. They went on to show and breed a
number of dogs, attending Crufts and many Championship shows across the country. As with all things they soon became
involved in the committee and organisation of The Saluki and Gazelle Hound Club.

Throughout this time Nick was still working for Marconi’s – now Marconi Radar, working on joint projects with the Royal Navy –
which he loved. He would often go on Sea trials for the systems he was working on (mostly defence mechanisms) which at the
time was all top secret. He would regale stories of having to do helicopter crash training and being hauled across to another ship
while at sea using a harness, ropes and pulleys, suspended over the ocean!

He retired from the Marconi’s in 2002 – a rare thing these days to stay working for the same firm for his entire career and was
commended accordingly.

He continued to attend the Church, ring bells at various local churches regularly, show dogs, and took great interest in the sailing
antics of his children: Fenella Miller and Peter Tovey; and 5 grandchildren: Jennifer, Nicholas and Michael Miller, and Rebecca (
Leech) and James Tovey. He was immensely proud of every one of them and of all their respective partners who he warmly
embraced into the family, attending three of their weddings in the last few years. It gave him great joy to see the family growing.
He was always keen to know how the Sailing Club was developing and growing, and took great pleasure in watching the
Wednesday evening racing in recent years.

He lived his life to the full, making a difference to many people, in a quiet, modest and generous way, with a dry sense of humour
and with paying great attention to detail in everything he did.

He will be very much missed by all who had the privilege to know him and his legacy lives on in his extending family.

Fenella Miller
