The RYA Dinghy Level 1 Course – Start Sailing
The RYA Dinghy Level 1 sailing course is designed to be an introduction to the sport of sailing. The course covers all you need to
know to get afloat under supervision.

Marconi Sailing Club are an RYA (Royal Yachting Association) training centre and offer the RYA Level 1, Level 2, First Aid and
Powerboat courses to our members.

THE SAILING COURSE
Assumed knowledge: None

Minimum duration: 2 days

Minimum age: None (although under 14s may prefer to learn through the Youth Sailing Scheme)

Course content: How to sail in all directions, including an awareness of launching and recovering

Ability after course: Able to sail in light winds under supervision

The RYA Level One course is for beginners who have done little or no dinghy sailing before. It is the first part of the RYA training
scheme and its aim is to provide basic boat handling techniques and essential background knowledge. By the end of the course
you will be able to sail safely under supervision. It is recommended that all participants consolidate this course with the RYA Level
2 (Basic Skills) course which gives you further skill to get out sailing proficiently on your own.

WHAT WILL YOU COVER?
You will cover a variety of topics both on and off the water. This will typically include:

On Water:

Sailing in all directions

Turning the boat

Confidence in the boat

Capsize recovery

Off Water – Knowledge in:

Weather

Tides

Rules of the road

Basic navigation

June 2019 Navigans 17

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Students practice a capsize by the shore so they know what to do if the boat should turn over.

WHAT WILL I NEED?
For your RYA Dinghy Level 1 sailing course you will need to bring:

Some sailing gear to wear which should include:

Wetsuit (full length if possible)

o Buoyancy Aid (we do have some BAs at the club which you may be able to borrow)

o Warm/waterproof top if the weather is looking a little chilly. You may also want a hat and gloves

o Sun cream if the weather is looking sunny

o Shoes suitable for being in the water and grippy

Lunch. Some days our on site galley (cafe) is open. Sundays are usually always open but not every Saturday. You will
be made aware of availability when you book

If under 18, you need a parent or guardian present at the club for the duration of the course

HOW DO I BOOK?
You can find out more about the RYA Dinghy Level 1 course and book by contacting Bob at training@marconi-sc.org.uk

HOW MUCH DOES IT COST?
Courses typically cost about £110 and are available to members only.

I’M NOT A MEMBER? CAN I BOOK A COURSE?
If you’re not yet a member but are interested, you are always welcome to come a join the club or come along to our open days
where you’ll find unique offers for courses and membership on those days. Open Days are run once a year, usually in May. It’s
important to note that you can join the club all year round, not just at Open Days so do pop down to the club site to have a look
around and talk with the members.

EVENT REPORT
East Coast Piers Race weekend once again a success with 86 entries taking on the long distance racing challenge.

August/September 2019 Navigans 4

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

East Coast Piers Race (ECPR) is a
weekend of sailing held at Marconi Sailing
Club in Essex, with all funds raised from
entry and weekend activities going to
chosen charities the Cirdan Sailing Trust
and Essex Air Ambulance.

ECPR 2019 was part three of the Allen
Endurance Series. We’re pleased that so
many boats pre-entered this year, it
makes organising such a complex event
much easier.

The weekend kicked off early, with many
competitors arriving onsite Friday to claim
the best camping pitches and take full
advantage of the stunning Essex
sunshine to get boats rigged, tweaked and tuned ready for the weekend of racing. With several major competing events either
side of ECPR we were glad to see the F18’s and RS800 fleet make small but strong turnouts to the event.

DRINK MIGHTY OAK BEER, RAISE £££ FOR CHARITY
Some keen sailors also opted for equipment test sails Friday afternoon, before settling down in the newly refurbished “Mamgu”
bar for a pint (or three..) of Mighty Oak Brewery beer, who for the second year were incredibly generous in their donation of 7
firkins of beer (over 500 pints). All the funds raised from Mighty Oak’s excellent beers (at £2.50 a pint) going to charity. Of course,
any socially conscious sailor can’t help but do their bit for charity in said scenario!

SATURDAY RACING AROUND THE CANS
Saturday morning saw many competitors still flooding in through the gates early, and lots of activity in the boat park to get ready
for the afternoons racing around the cans. The Nacra 20 fleet turned up en-mass and dominated the boat park with length, width
and height, making even a Tornado look small!

Race briefing kicked off at 12:00 for the all-in Saturday races, with 43 boats competing. The breeze showed up and competitors
were treated to good conditions. Race 1 turned into an epic 1 hour 45 minute marathon multi-lapper, in front of club, much to
spectators and travelling family-member’s enjoyment.

Race 2 was a considerably shorter affair to get everyone back for the #cometothebriefing for the Sunday long distance races.
Overall Saturday winners in the Catamaran fleet and taking home the ‘Cool Cats’ trophy were Grant Piggott and Simon Farren on
their Nacra F20 Carbon. Winner of the Dinghy fleet was Andrew Stickland in a Musto Skiff.

As per the usual ECPR format, the race briefing for Sunday was held on Saturday evening due to the early race start on Sunday.
This year was a particularly bleary eyed start of 8am… The briefing kicked off at 6pm with a full marquee of competitors keen to
understand the 3 race courses available. To cater for dinghies up to 1046 PY and foiling catamarans the 3 race courses are 48
miles, 27 miles and 13 miles.

ALLEN’S GENEROSITY GOES DOWN VERY WELL
This year the race chairman, Andy Dowley, had a nice surprise to finish up the briefing on – Free beer! Race sponsors Allen,
kindly contributed a £250 donation to cover the cost of 100 pints of the Mighty Oak charity fundraising beer. Inevitably there was
the quickest exit from any race briefing, with possibly the most politest and orderly taking of free beer ever witnessed. Great job
Allen and Mighty Oak, competitors and non-competitors saluted your generosity.

Next up was the BBQ, getting our hungry sailors re-fuelled and ready for a night of live rock from, possibly the loudest band we
have ever had a Marconi, Essex based ‘Stiff InThe Morning’. To say they rocked would be an understatement, they went down a
storm, a personal favourite being their cover of ‘By the way’ by the Red Hot Chilli Peppers.

THE SUNDAY LONG DISTANCE RACES
The traditional ECPR wakeup call of ‘Sweet Caroline’ by Neil Diamond roused bleary-eyed sailors, much to the race organisers
delight many boats were ready and waiting for the 06:30am opening of the hard and scrutineering. Due to the long distances of
the races competitors have to take certain safety equipment with them and each boat is checked through the gate in the sea wall
to ensure everything was present.

The full distance East Coast Piers Race of 48NM started at 8am, with the fleet storming off, but the breeze was not going to last,
and as the 27NM Colne Point Race exited the river so did the breeze.

From that point on it was a case of finding and staying in the pressure, with mammoth holes appearing in the course. All races
played like an accordion, compressing and expanding as they reached the front and back of the gusts along the course. The
volunteers on the spotter mother boats moored along the course were treated to a slow but tight race.

30 Years on the Boards
An event like ECPR involves a large number of volunteers performing all manner of vital jobs. Many of the volunteers have given
many years of service. Here’s an inside story from two of them… Ed.

Mike and I first manned the leader boards for the East Coast Piers Race in 1989. The control area then was upstairs in the
clubhouse within a screened off area. This continued until 2001, Barbara Davies joining us in 1996. Not a lot changed in those
years, reports came back from the “gates” via volunteers from the Territorial Army with old fashioned radios for a few years then
by cadets using mobile phones. The large boards we used were revamped as they had been used by the club for many years at
the Regatta which Marconi ran every May Bank Holiday. In 2001 the double decker bus was used as the control. It was driven to
the club on the Friday evening after the school run and parked behind the sea wall at the end of the clubhouse. This gave us
much more space and freed the clubhouse for increasing numbers of visitors using the galley. In the early years food was
provided by a catering van outside the clubhouse. The three of us continued to work in the bus until 2018.

In 2018 we were able to use the new race control which proved very good, great views of the Blackwater. So to 2019 our Swan
Song! I think we have all enjoyed our years on the boards. We

have seen the race develop from one race to Walton Pier and back to adding shorter Colne races for catamarans and monohulls
and a Bradwell race. GPS tracking has been used and will in the not too distant future take over from the leader boards. There are
also many other members involved in the running of the ECPR on the day and behind the scenes; preparations are already
underway for 2020.

Next year we will be watching from the sea wall, with binoculars but no pens or panic!

Maggie Boreham

GOALS SET & ACHIEVED! – A REPORT FROM OUR BKL TEAM
The youth (U25) team for this event from stern to bow: Jack Collis, Daniel Nickalls, Jack Wardell and David Nickalls (author).

Leading up to the weekend of the BKL qualifier we were fully aware of how under-prepared we were compared to the top teams
competing. Making use of the club SB20 for a training day, we set ourselves two goals:

Firstly, enjoy the event and come away with a ‘positive’ feeling.

Secondly, come away in the top half with at least one race win. This would improve on our low finish and best result of second
place from two years ago. We knew this goal would be hard, especially finishing in the top half.

The format of the weekend was 11 teams competing in a round-robin, each sailing 12 races with 6 teams racing at a time. The
racing was held at Royal Southern Yacht Club in RS21s.

The weekend started with a glorious day, sun
shining and a gentle force 3 blowing from the
south. Champagne sailing conditions led to
burnt shoulders and arms on both Jack
Wardell and Jack Collis (known by the other
teams as ‘vest-guy’; he was the only one in
the entire fleer who dared to show his
shoulders).

The first race showed that our training had
paid off, rounding the windward mark in
second place. This was promptly shut down
by a more experienced team turning up into
our kite – red flag for us, penalty turns. We
finished in fifth, feeling positive, but knowing
that we still needed to learn a lot about
keelboat racing. The next race saw an improvement, finishing third. Our third race saw a brilliant start, winning the pin end and
sailing on for our first race win of the event – part of goal two achieved! We swapped off to watch some of the other teams
compete.

In the afternoon our first race started well, sailing clear ahead of all but one boat. The two lead boats were boat-on-boat the whole
way round the course with the Royal Southern team (eventual champions) leaving us the wrong side of a port/starboard shut door
on the final downwind. This tore a second race win from our grasp. We settled for second place and discussed how they managed
to goose-wing faster downwind!? Clearly we are improving, but aren’t quite there yet. With a knot or two less wind the rest of the
day our results didn’t improve. We managed to get one more second, losing out to the local team again! In this instance an
August/September 2019 Navigans 7

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

unfortunate umpire absence at a port/starboard incident inside the 3-boat length at the windward mark led to an ‘all-clear’ call. We
felt this was an uncharacteristic mistake from an otherwise excellent race and umpire team – tough break. Our worst result of the
day (and weekend) was a sixth (last), where we tried the ‘pro strategy’ of goose-winging to try to recover a place or two… it didn’t
work out. Again, lots to learn!

The second day was forecast for higher wind, but it did not appear! With only three races remaining we would have to push hard if
we wanted to finish in the top half. The first race of the day did not go to plan. Shifty wind led to a biased committee boat start,
one which we didn’t win. A heavy team in light air meant we struggled to regain places, only recovering one – thanks to a slick
drop at the leeward mark. We finished that race with a fourth. Our tactics clearly had to change, we switched our focus to
watching the wind, and choosing course tactics over boat-on-boat interactions.

The second to last race of the day was another committee boat bias. We won the start and by this point had worked out that we
were likely to be the second fastest boat in that fleet, the faster boat was (yet again) the locals! We hit the windward layline on
starboard on a right-shift, forcing a port/starboard incident inside the zone, turns for them this time! We then sailed on to win the
race. We watched, very impressed to see the Royal Southern team recover after their turns to finish in second, they’re a very
quick team! The last race again had a heavy starboard bias, now with less wind and a building tide pushing us back from the line.
After a poor pre-start we decided to start behind the fleet and tack off into a patch of wind on the right hand side of the course.
With the wind further dropping into shifty patterns we followed our own race, gaining on all legs – both upwind and downwind (our
previous Achilles heel). We eventually crossed the line first, an amazing way to finish the weekend, sailing from sixth to first! This
would not have been achievable at the beginning of the weekend, showing just how much we’d all improved.

Final result:

5th place, 3 race wins. Definitely fulfilled both targets.

Thank you also Peter Ward, without your involvement and support MSC would have remained unrepresented at this event!

MARCONI SC GRANT APPLICATION SUCCESSFUL
Good News!

Marconi SC have been successful in gaining a £10000 grant from Sport England towards our SB20 Keelboat Project.

The project aims to secure the long term future of this type of sailing at the club by developing a fleet of boats. This follows the
clubs commitment to this last season when an SB20 was purchased on a trial basis to gauge response. The response was
overwhelmingly positive from all who managed to get out and sail the SB20. The grant enables the purchase of three more SB20s
and the club will now be in a position to offer regular small fleet racing and one off events using these four boats.

The award of the grant was the result of extensive work by Sue Shenton and the logistics involved in sourcing suitable boats and
conveying them to the club has been taken on by Peter Ward. There is great support for this project from the board and the
committee, it is intended to add an area of sailing to the club portfolio which up to now has been absent. The single SB20 which
entered this year’s ECPR did quite well and came in second endorsing the suitability of these boats for our location.

It’s planned that the boats purchased with the aid of the grant will arrive at the club shortly before Cadet Week and its hoped that
the boats can be rigged and tested in order for them to be made available for organised sailing during camping fortnight.

Pioneer
On 31st August, 11 Marconi sailors took a day trip on the Pioneer – a 70ft Essex
Fishing Smack, the last of her kind, restored in recent years by the Pioneer
Sailing Trust in Brightlingsea.

Originally built in 1864 at Rowhedge, Pioneer was designed as a dredging
fishing vessel, working out of Brightlingsea and dredging deep sea oysters. She
was lengthened by 11ft in 1889 and a deep well was created which enabled her
to travel further for her catch which could then be kept alive on the journey home
– travelling around the British Isles and across to North Holland. She did not
get an engine until 1929 but was decommissioned in 1939 and was used as a
houseboat for just three years before she sank in the Strood Channel at Mersea
Island. Fast forward to 1998 when an operation began to dig her out of the mud
from where she was transported to Great Totham for a full refurb and rebuild and
remarkably by 2004 she was fully restored, re-rigged and sailing again.

And a very fine ship she is too.

Pioneer is now moored off East Mersea and managed from Harkers Yard in Brightlingsea. In addition to restoring Pioneer,
traditional boat building skills were rejuvenated at Harkers Yard who restore other traditional wooden boats and successfully built
and re-introduced rowing gigs – including our very own Elettra. The Pioneer now takes primarily young people out sailing to learn
the joys of being on the water and build new skills, confidence and make new friends and the boat yard continues to promote boat
building skills, including recruiting apprentices each year.

All of which was the perfect context for a group of Marconi sailors to book a day trip – Pete and Fen, Sam and Pat, Dave and
Jenny, Dave, Clare and Jason and Gordon and Jane all turned up eager and ready for a great days sailing. We met with Carol,
Lance and Brian who were going to look after us for the day and swiftly headed down to the launch to be taken out to Pioneer’ s
mooring.

It was a beautiful morning as we motored the length of Brightlingsea creek and across to East Mersea – bright and sunny but not
much wind, although the forecast promised more to come. We were deposited on board and given a tour with various
instructions – the most important of which was how to use the heads without breaking them - which of itself involved quite a work
out using the manual pump.

The next duty was to rig the mizzen, jib and staysail which involved most of us. Jenny however, disappeared below to fire up the
cooker and the kettles. Which is just as well, because the wind shifted, all the sails had to be lowered again and we motored off
the mooring – but at least we had tea and coffee.

We motored out punching a strong spring flood – several of us had binoculars and were scanning the horizon to work out where
any wind was and what direction it might fill in from. Meanwhile, Dave R, Jason and Pat got to work cooking vast quantities of
bacon rolls. Once out in clear water, the mizzen, jib and stay sail were set (again) and we put Fen on the helm.

Bacon rolls appeared and we were all very happy – although the wind was more reticent. But we thought it had appeared as we
cut through the middle of a race course of racing cruisers at the Inner Bench Head buoy which happened to be their turning mark.

So engine off and Jenny was put on the helm. And the wind basically went light and round in circles for the next two hours – or
at least, that was Jenny’s excuse. Every time the breeze looked like it had filled in, it would back 30 degrees and then fall away.
The only comfort was looking at all the other boats out on the water who were going through the same thing.

Carol, the Skipper, announced that the helm had put them in the middle of the Sargasso Sea and was officially useless as a result
– which was a bit harsh. At one point, we even got overtaken by our own tender (about the size of the Workboat) – progress was
very slow.

August/September 2019 Navigans 8

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

The Skipper and Crew decided to put out the dredge nets and Jenny was abandoned at the back of the boat as everyone else
crowded round to see the catch. Which is just as well because Jenny cannot bear the sight of fish or sea animals generally so
she was quite happy. Various star fish were cleared of mud, examined and then released back to their home territory.

The wind was bending round from the west to the east and we thought a sea breeze would come in but then it shifted back to the
west, the boat tacked without moving and it looked like the breeze had come in properly and heading straight out of the
Blackwater.

Cue lots of people suddenly interested in helming now that there was actual wind and less risk of abuse from Carol. Pete was up
first and enjoyed a steady breeze for about 5 minutes – which then promptly headed so he handed it over to Gordon. It appeared
that the East Cardinal mark which marks the Mollyette had turned into a magnet because as the wind bent and no matter whether
we bore away or got headed onto the other tack, we still seemed to be aiming at her. Fortunately, we managed to keep clear
enough not to bounce off her.

By which time we needed to turn around and head for home against the strong ebb. Jane took over the helm and headed us
back towards the Colne Bar. Jason then took the helm as we headed back past the Inner Bench Head and despite a decent
breeze, found that the spring ebb tide was really very strong. Dave Clarke then took over for a bit, followed by Clare – before
Carol resumed command as we got closer to East Mersea and needed to head towards to the mooring.

As we approached, the mizzen was stowed and the plan was to sail onto the mooring with the jib and staysail. The jib was
stowed as we approached the mooring but this proved to be a mistake as the spring ebb tide proved too strong for the staysail
alone and the Pioneer started to drift backwards. So reluctantly, the engine was switched on in order to get us to the mooring.
After an efficient pack down, it was back aboard the launch for the final journey back up Brightlingsea creek to Harkers Yard.

We all had a wonderful day’s sailing and our hosts, Carol, Lance and Brian were fantastic company. The Pioneer Trust have and
continue to achieve wonderful things – so do follow their progress and support them – all info available via their website:
http://pioneerck18.org

Jenny Ball

Nacra 15 – Story so Far…
Adam Ferneyhough’s October update on Will and Isabella (MSC Cadets) and their adventures in the Nacra 15 class following the
UK nationals and looking ahead to the worlds…

The new Nacra 15 class has been introduced competitively over the past few year as a
youth class pathway boat prior to stepping up to the full foiling Olympic Nacra 17
professional adult class boat.

Of all the British Youth Sailing Team pathway boats, the Nacra is quite an elite class. The
class is still in development and currently there are only 6 active competing boats in the
whole of the UK.

With such a small fleet, the racing is very close and competitive with lots to learn every time
they hit the water.

Recent changes in Olympic double handed racing rules and national competition guidelines
now insist that the crew and helm must be of mixed sexes. Will has been sailing the Nacra
for the past year or so, but his previous team partner has left to move into further education.
Will and Isabella had sailed and raced a few times together at the club on the 29er and
Nacra, then following some discussion decided
to team up and start competing nationally and
internationally together.

They attended their first official RYA residential coaching/training weekend together at
Calshot Activity Centre down on Southampton water, this proved quite successful for
them. Soon after they made a decision to pursue the full competitive race circuit.

Moving to the next step, they have just completed their first major competition, the
Nacra 15 UK National Championships held a few weeks ago at Weston Sailing Club
down on the South coast. For their first event, the weather was not kind to them, the
wind was blowing 20-30 knots all weekend. The Nacra being a high performance
demanding boat with 3 sails, twin trapeze and curved semi-foiling boards. This meant
that they were flat out working the boat for two full days with no time rest or lose
concentration. It’s fair to say, their fitness levels was tested to the limits. It was a very
enjoyable weekend also being part of a general catamaran open competition mixing
the starts with Shearwaters, Dart 18’s and Nacra 20 carbons to name a few.

All 6 UK boats competed and despite snapped trapeze line taking them out of 2
races, they still managed to finish in 5th place overall. The icing on the cake was due to their much younger comparable ages of
15 and 13. They won the special Junior champion trophy, giving them the official title of National Junior Champions for the coming
year.

December 2019 Navigans 5

Marconi Sailing Club www.marconi-sc.org.uk

Following the excitement of the Nationals, they put an application into RYA British Youth Sailing Team for a place in the official
National Youth Squad. We knew it was a bit of a long shot, as they hadn’t competed much together. This made us even more
surprised when they wrote back to us offering them a place. Now one of only 3 Nacra teams officially supported by the RYA
racing organisation.

Now no time to relax, this weekend they are squad training down at the National Sailing Centre in Weymouth before we travel
over to the South of France the week after to enter the Nacra 15 World championships. The event is being held at the future 2024
Olympic sailing venue in Marseille. A week long competition with 2 days of measurement followed by 5 days of racing. Around
100 Nacra 15’s will be competing from 17 different countries from across the world, it’s all very exciting.

Wish them luck….

Sailing Secretary Report – AGM 2019
Another year has passed and the Summer sailing season is over as I find myself in front of you for the first time to deliver my
report as sailing secretary. Having recently re-joined the Sailing club after a 20 year break, and taking on the Sailing secretary
role, I am yet to fully understand and know all the details and personalities of the sailing activities at Marconi Sailing Club , so my
first report maybe a bit brief but hopefully become more comprehensive as time moves on.

I apologise to any individuals who have selflessly carried out activities at the club over the last year, that I don’t mention through
this report.

I took on the role with trepidation of following in both Jenny’s and Toms footsteps, but have been greatly helped and encouraged
by Pat Shaw and the sailing Sub Committee, Thank you

It has been a good year of sailing at the club once again and hopefully my brief report will inform and reflect on some of th e
activities that have taken place during 2019.

With the permanent move to the Bridge deck race box, came changes in the starting format and procedure’s, these seem to have
settled down with minor problems being sorted out during the season.

The new position of the Race box greatly enhances the Race officers’ control of the racing by being very central, it also enhances
the safety of the competitor’s by being at a high vantage point. I have personally found that it is so much easier to manage the
racing by not being so remote for hours on end, and help is never far away when required.

The 2 major events of the Clubs Sailing calendar were again very successful and very well managed by Liz Kirby for the Open
day and Andrew Dowley for the East Coast Piers Race.

The Open day again was blessed by great weather and the very large numbers of club members organising and supporting all the
activities on and off the water. This day really does promote to the visiting public the friendliness of the club.

The East Coast Piers weekend again was very successful with large numbers of visitors and competitors returning, many very
complementary comments were received on a number of social media sites. All the races were completed, and again there were
countless volunteers from the club supporting the weekend, for which this great weekend would not be able to happen.

Cadet Week again proved to very well supported and successful event with large number of youngsters and novices taking to the
water over the week.

Monthly Sail training continues to grow year on year with 178 individual participants being recorded over the 8 sessions
throughout the year, this was well manged with 31 on the water helpers with many more assisting in the background.

The Dinghy cruising section continue with their adventures and this year they have greatly supported the Sail training days with
larger and more friendly boats to sail and learn in.

Power Boat training has continued throughout the year, which allows the club to maintain the pool of rescue boat drivers to
support the racing programme, and number of Dinghy courses have also taken place, which allows the standard of sailing and
seamanship at our club improve year on year.

The Dinghy and cat fleets are still well supported with a full racing programme being carried out apart form 2 competitions being
cancelled due to very high winds.

Midweek racing has continued to be one of the most popular series of racing throughout the year, with a good number of new and
not so experienced members taking the opportunity to use the club boats and facilities to improve their skills. Sam’s team in the
Galley provided excellent meals following the racing, which gave the participants the opportunity to discuss the finer points of the
racing rules.

The dinghy Handicap fleet has had a bit of a resurgence with an increase of Lasers taking part, so they are starting to have a
competition amongst themselves, some of the fleet are currently extending their racing season at Maylandsea

The Medium Cat has also seen a small resurgence of Dart 18’s which could potentially grow over the next couple of seasons

Sprint 15s continue to have successful racing at both home and way, and are currently racing against the growing number of 15s
at Stone in their winter series

The SB20 fleet has grown considerably over the season with the help of a grant.

Much training and practice has taken place on the boats over the year which culminated in all 5 boats taking part in their own mini
regatta towards the end of the season. Perhaps one day some of these boats might venture down to the south coast to take part
in SB20 class racing at Cowes week

A small group of cruisers have continued to successfully represent the club in the BJRC series with Blue Moon taking part in all 8
races and coming 2nd overall, McGregor III came third

On the Road this year the club members have been very successful.
